articles.title: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry
articles.description: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry NJIT News
articles.description_html: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry  NJIT News
articles.article_title: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry
articles.heading: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry
articles.summary: New Jersey Institute of Technology’s annual Celebration gala will take place Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, at The Grove in Cedar Grove, New Jersey, honoring six individuals and organizations whose achievements exemplify leadership, innovation, service and commitment to the university.
articles.content:
New Jersey Institute of Technology’s annual Celebration gala will take place Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, at The Grove in Cedar Grove, New Jersey, honoring six individuals and organizations whose achievements exemplify leadership, innovation, service and commitment to the university.
The black-tie event brings together alumni, business leaders and friends of NJIT for an evening of dinner, dancing and awards in support of student scholarships. Established in 1995 to benefit the Albert Dorman Honors College, Celebration has supported students across all six of NJIT’s colleges since 2007.
Celebration has raised more than $10 million in endowed scholarship funds since its founding. The 2025 gala drew the largest audience in the event’s history and raised a record amount, building new momentum for NJIT’s efforts to make a transformative education accessible to talented and motivated students. Serving as student speaker this year is Sydney Burlingame-Grissom, a chemical engineering student, Albert Dorman Honors scholar and midfielder for the Women’s Soccer team.
“Celebration brings the NJIT community together around two of our most important commitments: creating opportunities for our students and recognizing people and organizations whose leadership has a meaningful impact on society,” said NJIT Interim President John A. Pelesko. “This year’s honorees reflect the ingenuity, service and generosity that define our university and its extended community.”
The 2026 honorees are:
Dr. Joel Bloom — University Medal for Lifetime Achievement
Bloom served NJIT for three decades, culminating in his tenure as the university’s eighth president from 2011 to 2022. He joined NJIT as a vice president in 1990 and became the inaugural dean of the Albert Dorman Honors College in 1998, overseeing its growth into a nationally recognized honors college.
As president, Bloom led NJIT through a period of significant expansion in enrollment, research, fundraising and campus development. Under his leadership, the university completed a $200 million fundraising campaign, added approximately 1 million square feet of teaching and research facilities, expanded its faculty and strengthened its standing as a national research university and engine of economic mobility. Before joining NJIT, Bloom worked in industry, public education and state government, including service as an assistant commissioner in the New Jersey Department of Education.
Leon K. Baptiste ’91 — Lifetime Alumni Leadership Award
Baptiste is the founder and CEO of LB Electric, an electrical contracting and engineering firm he established in 1999. With more than 38 years of experience, he has helped lead major electrical projects across New Jersey and New York, including work associated with the Prudential Center, Newark Liberty International Airport’s Terminal A, the Port Authority’s Harrison Station, East Side Access and the Mario M. Cuomo Bridge.
A graduate of NJIT’s electrical engineering program, Baptiste remains closely engaged with the university as chair of the Electrical and Computer Engineering Industry Advisory Board and a member of the Newark College of Engineering Board of Visitors and the Educational Opportunity Program Industry Advisory Board. He also established the LB Training Center to provide college students, urban youth and people reentering the workforce with education and training in solar-energy technologies.
Komal Dangi ’19 — Edward F. Weston Medal for Professional Achievement
Dangi is the founder and CEO of Synkriom and VeriKlick and has more than 15 years of experience in the information-technology industry. An entrepreneur who has launched six startups globally, she is recognized for developing technology-driven businesses while advocating for women and members of historically marginalized communities.
Dangi earned a master’s degree in computer science and an MBA from NJIT. She has held leadership roles with the Asian Indian Chamber of Commerce and has supported initiatives focused on supplier diversity, community engagement and STEM education. Her professional and civic contributions have been recognized by organizations in New Jersey and New York.
Richard Schatzberg ’93 — University Award for Entrepreneurial Leadership
Schatzberg is a founding member and chief commercial officer of NeST Technologies Corp., where he leads revenue generation and strategic planning and oversees technical operations serving the insurance, banking and financial-services sectors.
An NJIT alumnus, Schatzberg is chair of the Albert Dorman Honors College Board of Visitors and a member of the C-Suite Board of the New Jersey Innovation Institute. His record of service has also included board roles with organizations advancing employment, accessibility and inclusion for people with disabilities, including The Viscardi Center, the National Business and Disability Council, Ruh Global and the Runway of Dreams Foundation.
Fiserv — Outstanding Corporate Partner
Fiserv is a global financial-technology company connecting commerce and financial services through platforms spanning payments, account processing, digital banking, merchant services and e-commerce. A Fortune 500 and S&P 500 company, Fiserv maintains a significant presence in New Jersey through its Innovation Center in Berkeley Heights, a 428,000-square-foot hub for collaboration and financial-technology development.
Fiserv’s engagement with NJIT has included recruiting students and graduates, participating in university career fairs and supporting experiential opportunities such as GirlHacks, NJIT’s annual hackathon centered on empowering women and nonbinary students in technology. The partnership also extends to university leadership through Fiserv Senior Vice President Nancy Hall’s service on the NJIT Foundation Board of Directors.
Made Scientific — Special Friends to the University
Made Scientific is a Princeton, New Jersey-based cell-therapy contract development and manufacturing organization specializing in the development, production and release of autologous and allogeneic cell-therapy products for clinical and commercial use.
The company combines specialized technical expertise with development and manufacturing capabilities designed to help cell-therapy organizations bring treatments from early-stage development to scalable production. Made Scientific is supported by GC Corporation, a global pharmaceutical and biotechnology company.
For complete honoree biographies and additional information about Celebration, visit njit.edu/celebration.
Celebration remains a cornerstone of NJIT’s commitment to access and excellence, helping ensure that future generations of engineers, architects, scientists, computing professionals, entrepreneurs and other leaders can pursue an NJIT education and make an impact in New Jersey and beyond.

articles.content:
PARSIPPANY-TROY HILLS, N.J., Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Onkos Surgical today announced the market release of the ELEOSTM Total Femoral Adapter with NanoCept® Antibacterial Technology, expanding the availability of NanoCept for patients undergoing one of the most complex and high-risk orthopaedic reconstruction procedures.
Since its introduction in December 2024, NanoCept Antibacterial Technology has been available on ELEOS implant midsections used in complex knee and hip reconstructions. To date, more than 500 patients have received ELEOS implants featuring NanoCept.
The launch of the ELEOS Total Femoral Adapter with NanoCept further expands the portfolio to support patients requiring complete femoral replacement.
“It is incredibly reassuring to know that patients requiring a total femoral replacement will now have access to antibacterial implants. Total femurs are among the most complex procedures we perform, and many of the patients who require them are already immunocompromised,” said Julia Visgauss, M.D., Chief of the Orthopaedic Oncology Division at Duke Health.
“Anything we can do to reduce risk and improve outcomes can make a meaningful difference in their recovery and quality of life. The innovation we’re seeing in this space is truly encouraging,” said Dr. Visgauss, who is also an investigator in a post-market study of NanoCept and has been a consultant for Onkos.
The ELEOS Total Femoral Adapter with NanoCept is the first product to be produced and coated at Onkos Surgical’s newly opened NanoCept Innovation Center in Bridgewater, New Jersey, marking an important milestone in the company’s efforts to expand access to NanoCept across the broader ELEOS product portfolio.
“Today is a real high point for Onkos,” said Patrick Treacy, CEO and Co-Founder of Onkos Surgical. “As we continue to expand the ELEOS with NanoCept product offering, it is fitting that we begin with Total Femoral Replacement, supporting some of the most vulnerable patients undergoing complex orthopaedic oncology and revision procedures.”
Onkos is continuing to expand the capabilities of its NanoCept Innovation Center, with plans to have the antibacterial coating available on additional ELEOS products in the coming months.
About NanoCept®
Onkos received De Novo market authorization from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in April of 2024 for its NanoCept Antibacterial Technology for use with the ELEOS™ Limb Salvage System. Pre-clinical testing showed that NanoCept Antibacterial Technology has up to a 99.999% (5-log reduction) kill rate of bacteria that are commonly found in the operating room environment.
The device coating is not intended for the treatment of existing infections or prevention of future infections in patients. The clinical impact of bacterial reduction from the NanoCept coating, including prevention of infection or reduction of infection risk in patients, has not been evaluated in human clinical studies.

articles.title: The Real Path to Better Government Technology
articles.description: The Real Path to Better Government Technology Vital City
articles.description_html: The Real Path to Better Government Technology  Vital City
articles.article_title: The Real Path to Better Government Technology
articles.heading: The Real Path to Better Government Technology
articles.summary: We need to change the way the City buys software.
articles.content:
We need to change the way the City buys software.
You don’t have to look very far in New York to find failed government technology projects. A City Comptroller’s report released in August found that veterans still struggle to use the VetConnectNYC online portal to access services, despite a $2 million investment and eight years of work. The City’s Office of Technology and Innovation requested an additional $81 million in the 2026 budget to shore up another failed digital service, the “one-stop-shop” MyCity app, after already spending four years and $100 million on development. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority is reportedly planning to pilot “virtual OMNY cards,” part of a contract signed in 2017 that has suffered extensive delays, scope reduction, and millions of dollars in change orders.
Failures of this magnitude are not unusual in government tech. Across a database of over 2,700 projects, researchers found that the median U.S. government IT project costs 310% of the estimated price.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s lauded Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crews — five teams of technologists designed to swoop in to agencies and deliver the mayor’s top digital priorities — are a positive start to addressing the overwhelming amount of technical debt in city agencies. There is no question that city government needs more professionals with skills that meet the moment. However, delivering digital services on time, on budget and in ways that actually solve user needs requires addressing government functions beyond IT. Most of the tools for transforming government technology are (in the words of Matthew Burton, who wrote about the problem recently for Vital City) “starkly non-technological.”
Fixing tech procurement is the most important piece to get right. Despite recent successes by in-house development teams, digital government transformation at scale requires a hybrid staffing model, where the talent of in-house teams is complemented by that of external vendors. Contracting out offers temporary surge capacity of software developers with niche skills. It also responds to the present realities that government tech staff are hindered by: a lengthy and cumbersome civil service hiring process, comparatively low salaries and operating budget constraints.
Which is to say, though it may make a lot of sense to bulk up government tech, contracting out will still be necessary. The key is to do it right.
Although some tech can be purchased off-the-shelf, the scale and complexity of New York City government obligations, regulations and public-sector union rules often require custom software. And here, we need a new model.
New York City and State agencies procure custom software using a linear, step-by-step model known as “waterfall.” Requirements are fully specified at the start of a project, and modifications typically require costly contract change orders, much like a vacation package with a fully-booked itinerary that cannot be altered without major fees. Vendors are paid based on predefined project milestones, instead of being paid for the delivery of functional code. Software is delivered at the end of the development cycle, meaning that government agencies only have the chance to provide feedback at the end of a project, months or even years after requirements were drafted. Sadly, only 13% of “waterfall” projects succeed.
Government oversight bodies would have you believe that exhaustive requirements and more vigilant contract monitoring are the only ways to improve government technology, but they are not. The “Agile” approach to software procurement uses minimal requirements, clear objectives and iterative cycles of user research, development, testing and deployment that allow for continuous improvement. This is the standard for private sector software development and what actually works, if done correctly, for government agencies, too. Initiatives built using Agile succeed at three times the rate of waterfall projects, where “successful” means on time and on budget, with a satisfactory result.
This is clearly a wiser way to develop software that will make government work better.
The good news is that New York City doesn’t have to start from scratch. Last year, the New York State Higher Education Services Corporation (HESC) issued the first “Agile RFP” in the state. Built on the foundation of successful examples from across the federal government, like Direct File, that RFP brought best practice to the State and did the hard part of adjusting contract terms and conditions to the New York State context. The HESC RFP, for example, shifts contract performance measurement away from checkbox fulfillment of pre-defined project requirements (the waterfall way) to assessment of vendor work based on code quality and performance standards.
But if the City is serious about developing software more intelligently, it needs to change some practices. Software development using Agile implies new ways of working. Vendors work in teams of four to nine people (called “Scrum teams” in Agile lingo) that are tightly coupled with a product owner and technical lead from a government agency. For early stage product development initiatives, only a single Scrum team may be required. Its work is nimble and iterative; fluid communication and integrated teamwork are key.
The City’s current approach to procurement makes this way of working difficult, if not impossible. Local Law 2019/174 specifies percentage goals of total annual agency expenditure for six classes of minority-owned businesses, adding up to 73.52% of total spend for professional service contracts. In my experience, procurement officers apply all or most of these percentage goals across all contracts. Requiring blanket target participation rates on a single Scrum team would imply a minimum of six distinct companies supplying staff for a four-person team — a certain (and nonsensical) recipe for failure.
To get the most from Agile procurement, the City Council, the City’s chief procurement officer, and the City’s Procurement Policy Board should unite to eliminate participation goals for these contracts. This change to procurement policy has nothing to do with whether you believe in supporting minorities and everything to do with whether procurement supports the ways of working necessary for modern software development using Agile.
Beyond procurement, enabling a leap forward in government technology requires changes to the city budget itself. Modern software development is not a one-time capital expense, like buying Microsoft Office was in 2010. It is an ongoing effort that requires a team (and a budget) over time to provide an experience analogous to routine updates of a Google Chrome browser. Even when vendors leave after a large digital product build, agency staff continue to respond to evolving user needs through continuous development. This implies a small but consistent budget allocation for technologists. This “product model,” which combines Agile procurement and development with continuous improvement and funding, stands in sharp contrast to government’s traditional “project model” of one-time funding, rigid scope and time-bound outputs.
New York’s legacy of fiscal austerity, however, haunts any increase (albeit small) to the operating budget, despite the lower net cost and higher rate of success of the product model. The City’s Office of Management and Budget should get on board with a shift toward the product model and approve operating budget funding streams for technologists to support software products. In practice, this may look like budgeting for “capabilities” that require multiple software products or systems, rather than budgeting one product at a time. According to policy researchers at the Niskanen Center, “a ‘capability’ might be eligibility and enrollment, claims processing or benefits delivery.” A block of funds would be designated for each capability, including all the software necessary for that capability, giving product teams the responsibility for end-to-end delivery of the capability. This is analogous to setting aside a budget to remodel your entire kitchen, rather than paying for the cabinets and drawers this year and leaving a gaping hole where the countertops should be until some unknown future date.
Enabling technological transformation in City agencies also requires a shift in the way legal teams attempt to mitigate risk. General counsel and auditors often want “one throat to choke,” namely a vendor’s, when something goes wrong. With the traditional waterfall approach to software procurement, agencies try to shift all risk back to the vendor. They rely on meeting specific contractual requirements and adhering to Gantt charts to determine whether a vendor has delivered a product, regardless of whether the software meets users’ needs. Risk is mitigated through close contract monitoring and fines for late or incomplete delivery. The extraordinarily high failure rate of software projects indicates that these risk mitigation measures simply don’t work.
In contrast, software procurement using Agile begins with a statement of objectives. Government staff have significantly more control over software development because they are intimately involved in every step of the process (e.g., identifying tasks, user research, testing, quality assurance, deployment, system integration). The “test-and-learn” approach inherent to Agile means faster identification and correction of problems, and smaller, controlled failures. These failures can be rectified through the iterative development cycle, rather than waiting until the end of the traditional “project” model for user testing. Risk can be further reduced by committing vendor-developed source code to the public domain, a practice encouraged by the General Services Administration’s former technology branch and the Department of Defense.
Despite the successful Agile track record, it feels more risky than the status quo. It will be uncomfortable, but necessary, for the Mayor’s Office of Contract Services, agency attorneys and the City Comptroller to accept that risk mitigation under the “product” model looks different from the “project” model. What this means, in practice, is that contract oversight must shift from output (did the vendor deliver the requirement) to outcomes (did the vendor team, under staff guidance, build something that meets user needs). The recommended short duration (less than three years) and low cost ($2 million or less, annually per contract) of an Agile contract allows for a quick pivot if a vendor doesn’t perform.
Lastly, technologists cannot fix processes that agency staff struggle to articulate. It is no small task to explain “how things work,” when such knowledge is tacit, still on paper or housed in a legacy system. Agency leaders must get their own houses in order, documenting existing workflows and requirements, information that will accelerate the work of the PIT Crews, an agency’s own technologists or vendors.
In New York, the area most ripe for stalling tech projects is labor relations. Benefits obtained through the collective bargaining process are least likely to have short-term flexibility for modifications that might facilitate the adoption of new technology or permit the use of either commercial off-the-shelf software or software as a service. Rigid constraints, whether explicitly written into contracts or ossified through longstanding practice, drive custom software design and can easily increase costs. For example, unlike the majority of transit operators in the United States, subway conductors and operators in New York City select their weekly days off independently from the shifts and specific operational jobs they work (“cafeteria style picking”). This unusual procedure impedes automation and increases costs, relative to “roster-based” job selection (where operators select bundled days off and vehicle runs); it also precludes the use of most existing software.
Knowing what is bendable is crucial for tech system design. Layers of memos that modify a decades-old agreement, rather than an updated and comprehensive document detailing all current aspects of a labor agreement, present major barriers to digitalization and software development. Labor relations teams must be able to communicate the restrictions of current labor agreements with precision and in a way that technologists can translate into code.
We need better government tech, but the problems preventing us from getting it are not technological. Transforming government tech depends on an overhaul of non-technological government functions. That must not wait.

articles.title: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity
articles.description: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity News-Medical
articles.description_html: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity  News-Medical
articles.article_title: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity
articles.heading: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity
articles.summary: Physicists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have developed a groundbreaking technology that uses quantum sensors to measure biomagnetic signals, such as heart activity.
articles.content:
Physicists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have developed a groundbreaking technology that uses quantum sensors to measure biomagnetic signals, such as heart activity. Researchers from the DIAQNOS (DIAmond-based Quantum Sensing for NeurOSurgery) flagship project, funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space, and coordinated by Dr. Arne Wickenbrock in Mainz, have demonstrated the potential of quantum technology for future medical applications. To this end, researchers in the group led by Prof. Dr. Dmitry Budker - a member of the PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence and the Helmholtz Institute Mainz - used nitrogen vacancies (NV) in diamonds, as reported in a recent article in the journal Science Advances. Muhib Omar, a doctoral student in Budker's research group and the coordinating author of the article, developed the new quantum sensor during his doctoral research. Thanks to its compact size and its ability to function at room temperature, this NV-based sensor opens up new avenues for improving the measurement of magnetic signals from the heart or the brain. It could be used for the early detection of conditions such as myocarditis or epilepsy.
NV centers form when a vacancy in the diamond lattice is located directly next to a nitrogen atom that has been incorporated into the diamond in place of a carbon atom. By observing the energy levels of these centers, researchers can measure a wide range of physical phenomena such as magnetic or electric fields, temperature, and mechanical stress with high precision.
These results are the product of over ten years of development work. We work closely with neurosurgeons to ensure that our technologies do not remain confined to the laboratory but find clear practical applications. Our primary goal is to develop highly sensitive sensors that function outside the laboratory and can fulfill important societal needs."
Dr. Arne Wickenbrock, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz
The researchers of the DIAQNOS project used three systems developed independently by the project partners JGU, the Universities of Stuttgart and Freiburg, as well as by the startup Q.ANT GmbH, to measure the heart's magnetic field. In doing so, they demonstrated that quantum technologies in Germany are ready to take the important step toward medical applications and identified the improvements still needed to achieve this. The fiber-based NV-diamond magnetometer developed by JGU was designed as a portable endoscope and operates without a magnetic bias field. This is in contrast to the other two systems, that use such fields to filter out magnetic interference from the environment.
Developing a new way of detecting heart signals
There are currently two common methods to measure heart activity: electrocardiography (ECG) and magnetocardiography (MCG). While ECG uses electrode patches applied to the patient's skin to measure the electrical activity within the heart, MCG methods detect magnetic fields. ECG is widely used, but susceptible to the differing conductivity of body tissues. Certain medical scenarios, such as burn wounds, can also make it impossible to place electrodes on the skin directly. In contrast, MCG needs no contact with the skin and is only minimally influenced by tissue conductivity. The most important difference is the small size of the sensor: a truncated diamond pyramid with a volume of less than 0.5 cubic millimeters, which makes it easy to transport. Another advantage is that, unlike SQUID or OPM based systems, NV magnetometers operate at room temperature. This opens up the possibility of more precise mapping of biomagnetic signals, such as 3D reconstruction of the heart's electrical conduction system or the measurement of fetal heart activity. While the study shows the promise of NV diamond magnetometers, there remains a performance gap compared to SQUIDs and OPMs, which still offer higher sensitivity and better signal-to-noise ratios. Physicists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have developed a groundbreaking technology that uses quantum sensors to measure biomagnetic signals, such as heart activity. Researchers from the DIAQNOS (DIAmond-based Quantum Sensing for NeurOSurgery) flagship project, funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space, and coordinated by Dr. Arne Wickenbrock in Mainz, have demonstrated the potential of quantum technology for future medical applications. To this end, researchers in the group led by Prof. Dr. Dmitry Budker - a member of the PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence and the Helmholtz Institute Mainz - used nitrogen vacancies (NV) in diamonds, as reported in a recent article in the journal Science Advances. Muhib Omar, a doctoral student in Budker's research group and the coordinating author of the article, developed the new quantum sensor during his doctoral research. Thanks to its compact size and its ability to function at room temperature, this NV-based sensor opens up new avenues for improving the measurement of magnetic signals from the heart or the brain. It could be used for the early detection of conditions such as myocarditis or epilepsy.

NV centers form when a vacancy in the diamond lattice is located directly next to a nitrogen atom that has been incorporated into the diamond in place of a carbon atom. By observing the energy levels of these centers, researchers can measure a wide range of physical phenomena such as magnetic or electric fields, temperature, and mechanical stress with high precision.

These results are the product of over ten years of development work. We work closely with neurosurgeons to ensure that our technologies do not remain confined to the laboratory but find clear practical applications. Our primary goal is to develop highly sensitive sensors that function outside the laboratory and can fulfill important societal needs."

Dr. Arne Wickenbrock, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz

articles.article_title: Kwik Fill Choses PAR as Technology Partner
articles.heading: Kwik Fill Choses PAR as Technology Partner
articles.summary: The partnership includes Kwik Fill’s loyalty, mobile app, enterprise intelligence and full-stack tobacco loyalty capabilities.
articles.content:
The partnership includes Kwik Fill’s loyalty, mobile app, enterprise intelligence and full-stack tobacco loyalty capabilities.

Sep 17, 2026 | 2 min read

Kwik Fill has chosen PAR Technology as a “strategic technology partner,” according to a press release . The brands said the long-term partnership will help Kwik Fill deliver more relevant, personalized customer experiences while building a stronger foundation for future growth and innovation.

“Through the partnership, Kwik Fill will leverage PAR Retail’s platform and PAR Intelligence to support its vision for modern retail. …Kwik Fill’s partnership with PAR Retail spans the full breadth of the platform, including loyalty, mobile app, enterprise intelligence and full-stack tobacco loyalty capabilities. This reflects a comprehensive, long-term investment in how the brand understands and serves its guests,” PAR said.

“As we evaluated potential partners, PAR Retail stood apart through its vision for the future of convenience retail and its ability to combine guest engagement with actionable AI-driven insights,” said Roy Williams, senior vice president marketing at United Refining Company, parent company of Kwik Fill. “PAR Intelligence was a significant differentiator for our team. We see tremendous opportunity to leverage the platform as we continue enhancing the experiences we deliver to our guests.”

In other recent Kwik Fill news, last month the retailer announced the extension of its partnership with the Buffalo Bills , “reinforcing a successful relationship built on community engagement, fan experiences and shared values.”

The retailer said the extended partnership will continue to create opportunities for fan engagement through promotions, special events and exclusive experiences.

articles.title: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely
articles.description: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.description_html: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely  spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.article_title: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely
articles.heading: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely
articles.summary: OpenAI has disclosed six reports
articles.content:
OpenAI has disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated.
The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including cases where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.
OpenAI’s latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including the leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns.
Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots.”
In another instance, an AI “agent” used computer code to come up with the answer to a question, but, in order to have an online source to cite, it uploaded a file to the public internet without asking the user.
During training of an AI model called 5.6-sol, the model instructed itself to invent missing data, and an agent wrote a message to remind itself to hide mismatched information.
The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.
“As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events.
“Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves,” the company said.
Wednesday’s new cases followed OpenAI’s disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing.
AI “agents” are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia.
That’s making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.
OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices.
“That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su added.

articles.title: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers
articles.description: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers Daily Cal
articles.description_html: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers  Daily Cal
articles.article_title: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers
articles.heading: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers
articles.summary: UC Berkeley held its annual Engineering and Technology Career Fair, previously known as the EECS Career Fair, Tuesday, drawing hundreds of students seeking jobs in the technology industry.
articles.content:
UC Berkeley held its annual Engineering and Technology Career Fair, previously known as the EECS Career Fair, Tuesday, drawing hundreds of students seeking jobs in the technology industry.
Technology companies, mostly representing startup and mid-sized companies, crowded booths into the Pauley Ballroom in the Martin Luther King Jr. Student Union building for the fair.
The longest lines formed around industry giants such as Amazon and buzzy companies such as Cerebras, which creates specialized chips to run AI models,and Archer Aviation, which creates flying cars and drones.
“It’s always jobs, man,” said campus junior Prithvi Dixit. “The economy’s tough, so (I’m) looking for jobs.”
Some students at the event said they had already had one or more previous internships, but attended the fair to find more job opportunities.
Students said the number of startups at the fair represented a shift in what UC Berkeley students look for in an employer; smaller companies can offer more direct experience in a job than big technology companies such as Google and Apple, and also allow students to get in on the ground floor.
“I feel like in general, big companies already have a ton of applicants because people know when their applications release,” said UC Berkeley junior Arin Kadakia. “Some companies are probably trying to get their name out, right? They want people here at Berkeley to know what they do. They want qualified applicants from Berkeley as well.”
UC Berkeley’s career fair has been a flashpoint for the pressures that computer science majors face in the age of AI, including a shrinking job market. Data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis indicates that online job postings for software engineering jobs are down about 25% from pre-pandemic levels.
“We’re here at Berkeley Career Fair because Berkeley makes some of the best engineers in the world, and it’s a really deep talent pool to pull from,” said UC Berkeley alum Phillip Chu. Chu is an engineer at Density AI, a small company creating hardware to help run AI models which had a booth at the fair. “I think Berkeley as an institution, as a place to come to school, it rewards scrappiness.”
The Engineering and Technology career fair is a rebrand of the EECS career fair that campus hosted in previous years.
The EECS career fair previously only invited companies that made donations to campus to become Berkeley Circle partners.Many large technology companies in the Berkeley Circle program, including TikTok, Bloomberg and Databricks, did not attend the fair this year.

articles.title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
articles.description: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings The Guardian
articles.description_html: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
articles.heading: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
articles.summary: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
articles.content:
The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.
The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.
The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.
“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.
“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”
Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.
Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.
A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.
The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.
Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.
A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.
In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.
The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.
Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.
“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.
“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”
Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.
Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.
“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.
Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.
The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.
Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.
Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.

articles.content_html:
The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.

The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.

The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.

“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.

“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”

Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.

Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.

A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.

The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.

Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.

A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.

In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.

The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.

Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.

“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.

“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”

after newsletter promotion

Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.

Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.

“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.

Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.

The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.

Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.

Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.

“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.

Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

articles.summary: Vitality AI, built on Google Cloud and using Gemini Enterprise, expands into the U.S. market — bringing proven personalized health recommendations, coaching, and incentives to health plans and...
articles.content:
Vitality AI, built on Google Cloud and using Gemini Enterprise, expands into the U.S. market — bringing proven personalized health recommendations, coaching, and incentives to health plans and employers at scale
NEW YORK, Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vitality, a global leader in behavioral change across insurance and health plans, in partnership with Google, today announced the extension of Vitality AI into the United States. Built on Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise, the platform is already delivering measurable results internationally addressing one of healthcare's most persistent challenges: helping people take meaningful action to improve their health.
The expansion comes as U.S. employers face mounting employee health benefit costs, health plans experience low engagement, and people struggle to navigate complex healthcare systems. Vitality AI delivers a solution through personalized recommendations, coaching, and incentives to generate long-term healthier behaviors.
Vitality AI uses Google Cloud's leading AI and data analytics technologies, including Gemini Enterprise and Google's Gemini models, coupled with Vitality's dataset of more than 2,800 unique health and behavioral dimensions. By analyzing an individual's health profile, lifestyle, and risk factors, Vitality AI generates personalized insights at a 99.2% accuracy rate based on physicians' review.*
Engagement driven clinical and behavioral outcomes of Vitality AI
Vitality AI's personalized incentives have delivered measurable clinical and financial impact across international markets to date:
- Engagement and incentive effectiveness
- Members receiving personalized, AI-driven recommendations were 3.3 times more likely to complete a mental wellbeing assessment, 2.7 times more likely to complete an online health review, and 1.4 times more likely to complete a colorectal cancer screening.*
- 97% of members found their personalized AI reports useful, rating their likelihood of acting on the AI's recommendations at 8.8 out of 10 – which rose to 9.32 out of 10 when localized incentives were added.*
- Physical activity, sleep, and wellbeing
- High-BMI participants achieved a 200%+ increase in physical activity after enrollment on Vitality AI.***
- Members who completed the personalized steps program sustained an average 40% improvement in their daily step counts.****
- Participants who improved their sleep habits gained an average of 2+ hours of additional sleep per week, which was associated with 5% lower in-hospital claims.*****
- 87% of coaching participants presenting with extreme stress reported a measurable improvement in their overall wellbeing.***
- Preventative care and early detection
- Recommending and incentivizing cancer screenings led to an estimated 23,302 additional screenings in 2025, resulting in 219 early detections and an estimated six deaths prevented.******
- Low-cost, targeted rewards proved highly effective – a $31 incentive increased the likelihood of cholesterol testing by 52%, while rewards ranging from $19 to $45 drove similar increases for pap smears, mammograms, and colorectal screenings.******
Driving measurable returns for health payers, employers and insurers
For health payers, employers and insurers, Vitality AI delivers a clear, evidence-based financial case driven by sustained behavior change at scale – achieved through Google's Gemini models and Vitality's longitudinal dataset:
- Return on investment: Engaged clients experience a 4% reduction in healthcare claims costs on average, delivering a 180% return on investment.***
- Reduced risk: The financial benefit increases with employee participation; members who achieve a higher Vitality Status demonstrate 15% lower risk-adjusted claims costs.***
- Workplace productivity gains: The platform recovers an average of 4.4 productive days per employee per year, equivalent to annual savings of $1,047 per employee.***
Emile Stipp, CEO of Vitality AI, said: "Through our partnership with Google, we've shown that AI's impact on health care is no longer a promise – but a proven differentiator. We've seen members take screenings they would have skipped, build and sustain healthy habits, and reduce costs. Extending Vitality AI into the U.S. brings that proof to millions more."
Maureen Costello, Vice President, UK, Ireland and Sub-Saharan Africa, Google Cloud, said: "Having seen the impact of our partnership firsthand across multiple markets, we are thrilled to support Vitality in expanding this proven, AI-powered platform within the U.S. market. Vitality is delivering the level of personalization needed to drive real, measurable health outcomes. We are proud to expand this partnership to help U.S. employers and other members proactively engage with their health. Today's announcement marks the next step in Vitality's partnership with Google, with a goal of extending life expectancy and reducing healthcare-associated costs across the U.S."
The U.S. health gap
The U.S. expansion of Vitality AI directly addresses the mounting costs and navigation complexities that people are facing. For employers and their workforce in particular, data shows:
- Benefits complexity: 41% of U.S. employees struggle to navigate their health benefits and digital health tools.**
- Delayed care: Over half (53%) of workers have delayed or avoided preventative healthcare due to cost, and 49% say they have difficulty navigating the healthcare and insurance system.**
- Mental health barriers: 69% of employees report that workplace stress affects them; only 26% feel they face no barriers to discussing mental health with their employer.**
Notes to Editors
- Vitality's U.S business: Vitality's U.S business has seen strong momentum, including U.S. annual revenue growth of 22% year-over-year and recent acquisitions of Icario, Ramp Health and WellSpark – significantly increasing the reach and services provided by Vitality.
- Vitality AI is now live across Vitality and Discovery and in the UK, South Africa and the United States. Since June 2025, more than 210,000 people in the U.S. have received an AI-driven personalized health action, and 54% have completed at least one AI-recommended health action from Vitality.
- Vitality Status is the tiered reward and engagement framework used by the Vitality Group to measure and incentivize healthy lifestyle choices. Members earn Vitality points by engaging in healthy behaviors to move through the statuses, which are Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum. People are incentivized to earn points or improve their status with a full range of rewards.
About Vitality
Vitality is a global company operating in the insurance market, with presence in over 35 markets and impacting more than 54 million lives. Vitality transforms insurance markets by integrating technology, actuarial science, and behavioral insights to make people healthier and create shared value for clients, insurers, and society. They have a simple yet powerful core purpose: to make people healthier and enhance and protect their lives, and this is done through a pioneering Shared Value Insurance model, which aligns the interests of individuals, insurers, and society: when people become healthier, everyone benefits.
About Google Cloud
Google Cloud offers a powerful, optimized AI stack—including AI infrastructure, leading models like Gemini, data management capabilities, multicloud security solutions, developer tools and platform, as well as agents and applications—that enables organizations to transform their business for the Agentic Era. Customers in more than 200 countries and territories turn to Google Cloud as their trusted technology partner.
Sources
* Vitality data: 99.2% accuracy rate based on review of platform-generated reports by 686 physicians, tested on a cohort of more than 1,300 Discovery staff. Next best action uplift figures (3.3x mental wellbeing assessments, 2.7x online health reviews, 1.4x colorectal cancer screening) from Vitality data.
** Vitality, Opinium US polling data, August 2026: Online survey of 2,000 US workers conducted by Opinium on behalf of Vitality.
*** Vitality data, May 2026: 4% lower claims costs and 180% ROI independently reviewed by Arbital Health. 15% lower overall risk-adjusted claims cost for higher Vitality Statuses independently endorsed by the Validation Institute. 200%+ physical activity increase among high-BMI members, 87% stress improvement among coaching participants, and 4.4 productive days saved per employee per year (average saving of $1,047 per employee annually).
**** Vitality data: members enrolled in the personalized steps program were assigned a starting step target based on their existing activity levels and progressed upward using an algorithm calibrated to the pace at which each individual could sustainably increase their habit. Members who completed the program went from an average of approximately 4,900 steps per day before enrollment to sustaining 6,900 steps after graduating. Analysis is based on a cohort of approximately 1,500 members who completed 5 or more weeks of the program.
***** Vitality, Discovery data: Analysis of Vitality members tracked before and after the launch of the Vitality Sleep Rewards program over a four-month period. 19% of members improved their sleep habit, gaining an average of 19.8 minutes of sleep per night (approximately 2 hours and 20 minutes per week). Analysis of in-hospital claims found that maintaining a good sleep habit is associated with 5% lower in-hospital claims and improving a sleep habit with 7% lower in-hospital claims.
****** Vitality, Discovery data: Personalized incentive and cancer screening data from Vitality members. In 2025, it is estimated that recommending and incentivizing cancer screenings resulted in 23,302 additional screenings, representing a 5.5% increase relative to the historic trends, leading to 219 additional detections and an estimated 6 deaths prevented. Analysis found that while larger rewards (up to $45) produced the strongest behavioral response for some actions – a $31 reward increased the likelihood of cholesterol testing by 52% relative to no reward – smaller rewards ($19–$25) were similarly effective at driving cervical and colorectal cancer screening as well as emerging risk GP visits, demonstrating that recommendation relevance and member targeting can be as important as reward magnitude.
SOURCE Google Cloud

articles.summary: Catalyst Campus for Technology and Innovation, in partnership with the BMC3I TAP Lab, Selects Focus Area Cohort Teams for Cohort 26.A
articles.content:
Catalyst Campus for Technology and Innovation, in partnership with the BMC3I TAP Lab, has selected the Focus Area Cohort Teams (FACTs) participating in Cohort 26.A. The selected teams represent innovative companies collaborating to address mission-focused challenges aligned with identified government priorities.
Following a competitive application and evaluation process, 6 FACTs have been selected to participate in the BMC3I TAP Lab Cohort 26.A Stage 0. Each FACT consists of companies working together to combine complementary capabilities, develop collaborative solutions, and address specific focus areas.
The selected FACTs for BMC3I TAP Lab Cohort 26.A Stage 0 are:
- Astra Ultra, GRVTY, Leidos, ColliMate Space, Paper Boat Systems
- Data Fusion & , Aloha Autonomy, Stottler Henke Associates Inc.
- Stellerian, APTOS Orbital, SimDynamX, MetroStar.
- ColliMate Space, Pulsar Space Systems, Infinity Labs, Lockheed Martin.
- Citra Space Corporation, Bluestaq.
- Orbitswarm, Stellerian, Blacknight Space LLC.
Throughout the BMC3I TAP Lab program, FACTs will participate in focused programming designed to strengthen collaboration, improve mission alignment, and support business development efforts. Participants will engage with government subject matter experts, technical leaders, and industry partners while gaining insight into mission needs and opportunities within the defense innovation ecosystem.
The BMC3I TAP Lab provides a structured environment for companies to refine their solutions, build relationships with key stakeholders, and better understand how their technologies align with emerging mission challenges. Through collaboration and engagement, participating FACTs strengthen their ability to support future defense initiatives and apply to Stage 1 of the program.
ABOUT BMC3I TAP LAB COLORADO AND CATALYST CAMPUS
As a partner to the BMC3I TAP Lab, Catalyst Campus provides tech scouting, programming, industry engagement, and resources to navigate the mission environment and build meaningful connections with stakeholders. Catalyst Campus serves as a bridge between technology innovators and mission owners to solve emerging challenges.

Related

articles.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
articles.description: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands BBC
articles.description_html: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands  BBC
articles.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
articles.heading: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
articles.summary: The comments were made at a summit in Ayrshire with participants from AI giants including Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
articles.content:
King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.
He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.
Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.
"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.
He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".
"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.
The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.
'Keep engineering'
Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.
Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.
It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.
Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.
The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".
He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".
"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.
Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.
He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".
The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.
But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.
"The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.
Wave of warnings
Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.
The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.
In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.
After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.
He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.
In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.
The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.
Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.
Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.
Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.
Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".

King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

Reuters

King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

'Keep engineering'

Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.

Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.

The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".

He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".

"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.

Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.

He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".

The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.

But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.

"The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.

Wave of warnings

Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.

The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.

In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.

After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.

He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.

The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.

Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.

Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.

Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".

articles.title: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say
articles.description: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say Local 3 News
articles.description_html: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say  Local 3 News
articles.article_title: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say
articles.heading: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say
articles.summary: City of Chattanooga partners with USDOT and UTC for demonstration of innovative technology to enhance emergency response safety and communication on roads.
articles.content:
City leaders and first responders had a front-row seat to a new transportation technology. They say this technology could improve safety during an emergency response.
The United States Department of Transportation joined with the City of Chattanooga and the University of Chattanooga for a live demonstration of the technology. In 2024, the city received a $2 million grant from the USDOT. The city and UTC have used the funds to plan, prototype, and test the technology.
Dr. Mina Sartipi, the Interim Vice Chancellor for Research at UTC, believes this technology will create a safer environment for the city. “When you see a pedestrian on the road that the vehicle cannot see it, either if it's a driver or the driverless case, we will be able to communicate that back to the vehicle,” she says.
The SMART Project technology would connect with first responder vehicles that would interact with traffic signals and autonomous cars to identify any roadway hazards. Dr. Sartipi adds the technology will also be able to detect curves and other things that might impact driving.
Stan Caldwell, the Director of the SMART Grants Program with USDOT, says this was a highly competitive grant to apply for. “By using this new technology, the City of Chattanooga will be a shining example for the rest of the country in demonstrating how innovative technology can measurably improve pedestrian, driver, and cyclist safety,” he says.
“I think why Chattanooga is leading is willingness to collaborate and the fact that some of these pieces that we have been working on over a decade now,” says Dr. Sartipi, “now we are seeing it all coming together for with a real-world application.”
Project leaders say they have been working on this technology for years, and they say it is nearing completion.

articles.article_title: Neutrogena® launches new sunscreen technology with Cloud-Tech™, combining next-generation sun protection, skincare benefits, and a weightless feel
articles.heading: Neutrogena® launches new sunscreen technology with Cloud-Tech™, combining next-generation sun protection, skincare benefits, and a weightless feel
articles.summary: From the pioneer in sunscreen science, Neutrogena® introduces K-Beauty inspired sunscreen featuring BEMT, the first new FDA-approved sunscreen filter in over 25 years.
articles.content:
- Neutrogena is launching Cloud-Tech™, a new sunscreen technology featuring bemotrizinol (BEMT), the first new FDA-approved sunscreen filter in over 25 years.
- Cloud-Tech™ delivers comprehensive UVA/UVB coverage and clinically proven skincare ingredients for sunscreen that feels and blends like skincare.
- The new technology will be available in 2 new sunscreens, Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70.
SUMMIT, N.J., September 17, 2026 -- For over 40 years, Neutrogena has made sun protection more accessible by advancing daily use and safer sun habits through innovation, partnerships and education. Now, Neutrogena is launching Cloud-Tech™, a new sunscreen technology featuring bemotrizinol (BEMT), the first new FDA-approved sunscreen filter in over 25 years, to deliver next-generation sun protection. The new technology will be available in 2 new sunscreens, Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70.
This advancement comes as people seek both stronger protection and a better product experience that would make daily facial sunscreen use more appealing. Yet higher-SPF sunscreens often require more filters, which can create heavier textures and a less comfortable finish, leading some consumers to underapply or avoid them altogether.
“Cloud-Tech™ was inspired by the K-beauty sunscreens consumers love and the experience they increasingly expect from daily sun protection,” said Chris Riat, Global Neutrogena Brand Leader. “As a leader in suncare, Neutrogena has a responsibility to keep advancing the category. This launch reflects how we are challenging outdated expectations and delivering the high-level protection consumers need in a formula they will want to wear every day.”
Key Facts About Neutrogena® Cloud-Tech™ technology
- Comprehensive Coverage: BEMT, the first new UV filter approved in the U.S. in over 25 years, drives higher UVA protection than non-BEMT filters, but at approved concentrations of up to 6%, requires additional filters for comprehensive UVA and UVB coverage. Cloud-Tech™ combines BEMT with existing filters in Neutrogena’s proprietary Helioplex360™ technology for stronger protection.
- Weightless Feel: Inspired by the filter used in K-beauty sunscreens, BEMT delivers a weightless, invisible texture that feels like a soft cloud on skin. The formulas are fast-drying and provide a silk finish for sunscreen that feels and blends like skincare.
- Clinically Proven Skincare Ingredients: For the first time, Neutrogena is combining sunscreen with ingredients like its patented Micro-Peptide Technology and niacinamide to address targeted concerns such as visible signs of aging and acne-prone skin.
Advancing Safer Sun Habits
As the #1 sunscreen brand in the U.S.1, Neutrogena is leading the future of sunscreen with breakthrough science, clinically backed innovation and advocacy efforts that support safe sun habits, including daily sunscreen application.
Most recently, in partnership with the Melanoma Research Foundation, Neutrogena convened a Sun Consensus Meeting that brought together public health experts, policymakers, clinicians, researchers, advocates and media to discuss the latest science in skin cancer prevention and identify opportunities to advance public health guidance and regulatory progress.
Bringing this continued commitment to consumers, Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 are now available on amazon.com and will be available at retailers nationwide soon.
Frequently Asked Questions
Question: What is BEMT and why does it matter?
Answer: BEMT, also known as bemotrizinol, is the first new UV filter approved in the U.S. in over 25 years. With the introduction of BEMT (approved up to 6% concentration), Neutrogena formulators now have a new tool to advance sunscreen innovation. BEMT drives higher UVA protection vs. non BEMT filters, while also delivering superior aesthetics. It is proven to have synergy with existing US filters to deliver better outcomes.
Question: What makes Neutrogena Cloud-Tech™ unique?
Answer: Neutrogena Cloud-Tech™ combines BEMT with its proprietary Helioplex™ technology, to deliver comprehensive UVA and UVB protection. In addition, Cloud-Tech™ features clinically proven skincare ingredients, such as Neutrogena’s patented Micro-Peptide technology and niacinamide to address targeted concerns such as visible signs of aging and acne-prone skin.
Question: What is the difference between the two sunscreens that feature Cloud-Tech™ technology (Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70)?
Answer: The new sunscreens are powered by Cloud-Tech™ technology and offer a weightless, non-greasy feel that layers well under make-up. The sunscreens deliver superior UVA and UVB protection plus antioxidants to help defend against free radicals and the appearance of dark spots.
- Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 is formulated specifically for acne-prone skin with niacinamide and vitamin E to help reveal clearer-looking skin without clogging pores.
- Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 is formulated with patented Micro-Peptide Technology to help hydrate skin and visibly improve signs of aging. It is 50% lighter on skin than leading sunscreens.
Question: How will I know if my Neutrogena sunscreen includes the new Cloud-Tech™ technology?
Answer: Look for the Cloud-Tech™ logo displayed prominently on the front of the product label. Neutrogena sunscreens featuring Cloud-Tech™ will be available on amazon.com at launch, followed by retailers nationwide in October.
