articles.article_title: InvestmentNews unveils 5-Star Technology providers for 2026
articles.heading: InvestmentNews unveils 5-Star Technology providers for 2026
articles.summary: From M&A matchmaking to embedded advisor intelligence, third annual awards spotlights AI governance and data unity over feature-heavy platforms.
articles.content:
From M&A matchmaking to embedded advisor intelligence, third annual awards spotlights AI governance and data unity over feature-heavy platforms.


After a lengthy and exhaustive selection process, InvestmentNews is proud to reveal the winners of its third annual 5-Star Technology awards, recognizing the best new technology and software for investment management professionals for 2026.
Of the 42 ranked winners this year, 21 qualified under the New Technology category, which is reserved for solutions launched within the past 24 months.
This year's field delivered a clear verdict: the winning platforms weren't the ones with the longest feature list or the most AI bolted on for its own sake. Rather, they were sharper-edged tools that helped advisors build their business and better serve their clients.
As Robert Norris, partner at Capco in Fort Collins, CO, said in the 2026 5-Star Technology report, a leading platform "will not be defined by whether it has customer relationship management (CRM), planning, portfolio management, communications, or AI," but by whether a firm can make those tools work from the same trusted data toward a clear outcome.
Alaris Acquisitions, a wealth management M&A advisory firm that has more than doubled its team in the past 12 months as dealmaking accelerates to a record pace across the RIA industry. One thing that's helped it stand out amid a crowded field of consultancy firms catering to enterprising advisor-owners has been Lens, its AI-driven buyer-seller matchmaking tool.
"We are the best in the country at how we go to market, and that's our differentiator," said founder Allen Darby, who built the platform to curate compatibility-based shortlists rather than run a traditional auction.
Orion, the all-in-one wealthtech suite provider that holds itself out as a commited partner to independent advisors, taked pride in Denali AI, an intelligence layer built to integrate directly into advisors' existing workflows. Orion also became one of the first wealthtech firms – and the first portfolio accounting provider – to earn the ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI management systems.
"We believe AI should not live in a separate app. Intelligence belongs inside the tools advisors use every day," said Orion president Reed Colley.
Vestmark, with its proactive AI-powered portfolio monitoring system Pulse, has also emerged as part of a winning class of providers proving that trustworthy, well-governed data infrastructure now matters more to advisors than having a dizzyying laundry list of capabilities on a particular platform.
Among this year's honorees, InvestmentNews proud to showcase the following 5-Star Technology providers:
To read the full 5-Star Technology special report, along with the complete list of winners and methodology, click here.

Apella Wealth scores deal double, sealing $12 billion AUM milestone with bicoastal additions

South Carolina and Bay Area advisory teams join the WPCG-backed national platform as RIA dealmaking hits new highs.


Creative Planning inks RVK deal to add $4.3 trillion in institutional assets

The deal deepens the Kansas-based RIA giant's push into institutional consulting after a year of acquisitions spanning insurance, retirement and cross-border wealth work.


AI saves advisors 200-plus hours a year, but the real race is integration

New AssetMark research shows AI has moved from experiment to expectation and firms that lag on capabilities risk losing advisors.


Retirement-focused Wichita team with $385M exits Wells Fargo for LPL

Three advisors focused on retirement income distribution leave Wells Fargo for LPL's broker-dealer and RIA platforms.


Pave Finance secures $15 million in oversubscribed series A

Investors bet on AI-driven portfolio automation as advisory firms grapple with time-consuming manual work and rising demand for personalization.


SPONSORED


Direct indexing webinar targets tax-loss harvesting amid market swings

Northern Trust’s Ken Lassner shows advisors how to convert volatility into after-tax portfolio gains


SPONSORED


Who builds the income when the pension disappears?

Dan Biagini of American Equity says the steady decline of pensions, longer lifespans and a reset in interest rates are rewriting how advisors build retirement income

articles.title: Ivey’s ed tech commission weighs how schools should use technology
articles.description: Ivey’s ed tech commission weighs how schools should use technology Alabama Daily News
articles.description_html: Ivey’s ed tech commission weighs how schools should use technology  Alabama Daily News
articles.article_title: Ivey’s ed tech commission weighs how schools should use technology
articles.heading: Ivey’s ed tech commission weighs how schools should use technology
articles.summary: Tuesday’s discussion focused less on setting limits on screen time and more on what students are actually doing on screens and whether it helps them learn.
articles.content:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. – Alabama’s commission studying screen-based instruction is moving toward recommendations on when and how technology should be used in K-12 classrooms, with members focusing not simply on how much time students spend on screens but whether that technology serves an educational purpose and improves learning.
Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, who chairs the Governor’s Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, said the group is making progress as it examines the many ways students and teachers use technology in classrooms. Members have broken into subcommittees and are beginning to narrow that work into recommendations.
The commission must submit recommendations to Gov. Kay Ivey by Dec. 1.
Ross told Alabama Daily News after the meeting that she wants to make sure people understand what the commission is trying to do.
“This is not a ban on technology,” Ross said. “It is to just ensure that the technology that is being used with our students at school is effective and it’s implemented in the proper way, and it’s something that supports learning, not replaces that important teacher, adult-child interaction.”
Ivey in July directed the commission to study how classroom technology affects learning, student health and preparation for college or work, to compare Alabama’s practices with research and practices elsewhere and consider age-appropriate limits, guidance for educators and ways to make sure technology supports rather than replaces teacher-led instruction.
Tuesday’s discussion focused less on setting limits on screen time and more on what students are actually doing on screens and whether that use helps them learn.
Members repeatedly cautioned against a one-size-fits-all approach, noting that technology can serve very different purposes depending on a student’s age, subject, needs and access to teachers or courses.
“Technology is not going away,” Houston County Superintendent Brandy White said, adding that the commission’s goal should not be simply to increase or decrease screen time, but to determine how schools can use technology with “balance and purpose.”
Chris Jenks, technology director for Tuscaloosa City Schools, said educators should be central to those decisions.
“We understand and see every day that not every minute spent on the screen is equal time,” Jenks said. He said teachers should start with what students need to learn, then decide whether technology or more traditional teaching methods are the best way to get them there.
Jenks also said some teachers have been given technology without enough training to use it effectively. He said policymakers need to understand technology use at the “front line level” from people who work with children every day.
Opelika High School Principal Kelli Fischer raised another question: whether technology is helping students think or making them too dependent on it.
“Are we preparing them to use technology or are we making them dependent on it?” Fischer said.
The commission is still gathering more information before making its recommendations. Researchers are developing statewide surveys of teachers, families and administrators about how screens are used in schools and how that use affects instruction, with results expected in November.
The commission plans to begin drafting recommendations in October and refine its final report in November.
The group’s work follows several recent efforts in Alabama to set boundaries around students’ use of screens and devices.
Ross pushed for passage of the FOCUS Act, which restricted students’ use of cell phones and other wireless communication devices during the school day beginning with the 2025-26 school year.
She also sponsored the Healthy Early Development and Screen Time Act during the 2026 legislative session, which set limits on screen use for young children in covered child care, pre-K and kindergarten settings. It becomes effective Jan. 1.
A second bill Ross sponsored during the 2026 session would have required the State Board of Education to develop research-supported standards for technology used in instruction and local school boards to adopt policies consistent with them. The House passed HB584, but the Senate did not take it up.
Ross also told ADN that she plans to use the commission’s recommendations to shape legislation for the 2027 session.
“These recommendations will inform a bill that I absolutely will file in January,” Ross said.

articles.heading: Kyndryl to enable mission-critical technology modernization for U.S. government agencies
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Kyndryl (NYSE: KD), a leading provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services, today announced it has been awarded a 10-year NASPO...
articles.content:
10-year NASPO ValuePoint® contract helps public agencies nationwide upgrade essential technology and deliver better digital services to residents
NEW YORK, Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Kyndryl (NYSE: KD), a leading provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services, today announced it has been awarded a 10-year NASPO ValuePoint Cloud and Software Solutions contract (ID: LS5006), providing state agencies, higher education, counties, municipalities and other public entities across the United States with easier access to cloud, software and modernization services that support their long-term transformation goals.
State and local government agencies are under increasing pressure to modernize legacy technology, improve digital services, strengthen resiliency, and meet evolving constituent expectations while navigating complex procurement requirements. Participating states can leverage the NASPO ValuePoint contract for easier access to Kyndryl services and a streamlined purchasing framework with consistent terms and conditions and the flexibility to address state-specific requirements through participating addendums.
"State and local agencies need technology partners that understand both mission-critical systems and the realities of public-sector procurement," said Anita Mikus, VP and Managing Director of U.S. State and Local Government, Kyndryl U.S. "The NASPO ValuePoint contract helps agencies move more efficiently from planning to implementation, reducing procurement complexity so they can focus on modernizing critical systems, strengthening resiliency and delivering better services to residents."
The contract expands the scope of Kyndryl services available to participating agencies across software as a service (SaaS), infrastructure as a service (IaaS), platform as a service (PaaS) and on-premises environments. Agencies can leverage this contract for services such as:
- Modernizing mission-critical legacy systems: Support mainframe environments or mainframe-as-a-service models for core systems that process benefits, taxes, licensing or public safety workloads, helping improve resiliency while reducing the burden of managing end-of-service infrastructure.
- Improving high-volume constituent services: Agency-based solutions including modernization of systems behind driver's licenses, vehicle registration or appointment scheduling to improve reliability, reduce delays and make digital services easier for residents to use.
- Supporting re-entry and social services programs: Improve the databases and case management systems used to connect individuals with services, helping case workers access more accurate information and efficiently coordinate support.
- Optimizing contact centers and self-service: Contact center-as-a-service capabilities to analyze why residents are calling, identify repeat questions and automate common requests so issues are resolved faster and fewer calls need to reach a live agent.
Kyndryl Consult can help agencies assess modernization priorities, develop transformation roadmaps, determine migration readiness and implementation planning using a combination of AI workflows and deep domain expertise underpinned by the Kyndryl Agentic AI Framework. In addition, Kyndryl Bridge, Kyndryl's AI-powered, open integration platform, supports the integration, observation and orchestration of IT environments to provide actionable insights that help organizations run and transform their IT estates.
Agencies interested in learning more can visit the NASPO ValuePoint supplier page or book a consultation with Kyndryl.
About Kyndryl
Kyndryl (NYSE: KD) is a leading provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services, offering advisory, implementation and managed service capabilities to thousands of customers in more than 60 countries. As the world's largest IT infrastructure services provider, the Company designs, builds, manages and modernizes the complex information systems that the world depends on every day. For more information, visit www.kyndryl.com.
Kyndryl Press Contact
[email protected]
About NASPO
NASPO® is a non–profit association dedicated to advancing public procurement through leadership, excellence, and integrity. It is made up of the directors of the central purchasing offices in each of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and the territories of the United States. NASPO is an organization that helps its members achieve success as public procurement leaders through the promotion of best practices, education, professional development, research, and innovative procurement strategies. Learn more at www.naspo.org.
About NASPO ValuePoint
NASPO ValuePoint® is the cooperative purchasing division of the National Association of State Procurement Officials (NASPO), facilitating cooperative public procurement solicitations using a Lead State Model®. NASPO aggregates the demand of all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US territories, their political subdivisions, and other eligible entities, spurring best value, innovation, and competition in the marketplace. NASPO ValuePoint delivers high-value, reliable, and competitively sourced cooperative contracts - offering public entities outstanding prices, favorable terms and conditions, and value-added services. Learn more at www.naspovaluepoint.org.
NASPO®, NASPO ValuePoint®, their logos, and Lead State Model® are trademarks of the National Association of State Procurement Officials.

articles.heading: Phanes Therapeutics announces US patent granted to its proprietary bispecific antibody technology platform PACbody®
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Phanes Therapeutics, Inc. (Phanes), a clinical-stage biotech company focused on innovative drug discovery and development in immuno-oncology...
articles.content:
SAN DIEGO, Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Phanes Therapeutics, Inc. (Phanes), a clinical-stage biotech company focused on innovative drug discovery and development in immuno-oncology (IO), announced today that the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) has officially granted a patent (Patent No. US12,735,481) for its proprietary, core bispecific antibody technology platform, PACbody® (PAC = Pairing of Alternative Cysteines). This patent grant marks a significant milestone for Phanes in its foundational bispecific technology and global intellectual property protection.
PACbody® is a proprietary bispecific antibody construction platform internally discovered and owned by Phanes. It enables the generation of bispecific antibodies that maintain native IgG structures with drug-like CMC characteristics. Bispecific antibodies built on this platform exhibit excellent manufacturability, including stability, high expression, and seamless compatibility with conventional monoclonal antibody commercial manufacturing processes, significantly reducing development, clinical, and manufacturing risks.
Innovative bispecific antibodies developed using the PACbody® platform have demonstrated robust clinical potential. Most notably, Phanes' core asset spevatamig (PT886) has advanced into Phase II clinical trials and showed positive results, as reported at the ASCO Annual Meeting in May 2026. Spevatamig is a first-in-class native IgG-like bispecific antibody (bsAb) targeting claudin 18.2 and CD47. It was granted by the FDA orphan drug designation (ODD) for the treatment of pancreatic cancer in 2022, Fast Track designation for the treatment of patients with metastatic claudin 18.2-positive pancreatic adenocarcinoma in 2024, and recently, Fast Track designation for the treatment of advanced and metastatic biliary tract carcinoma. In 2023, Phanes entered into a clinical collaboration agreement with Merck (known as MSD outside the US and Canada) to study spevatamig in combination with pembrolizumab. Spevatamig is an innate immunity enhancer (I2E), an emerging class of immuno-oncology (IO) agents. It has the potential to become the first I2E for a solid tumor indication and is combinable with various anti-cancer therapies.
"We are thrilled that our PACbody® platform has been granted this U.S. patent," said Dr. Ming Wang, Founder and CEO of Phanes Therapeutics. "PACbody® is our core technology for overcoming the CMC challenges that typically hindered bispecific antibody development. This patent approval not only validates our top-tier innovative R&D capabilities but also significantly strengthens the protection of our core pipeline's intellectual property. We will continue to leverage this platform to accelerate the delivery of safer and more effective breakthrough therapies to cancer patients worldwide."
ABOUT PHANES THERAPEUTICS
Phanes Therapeutics, Inc. is a clinical-stage biotech company focused on innovative drug discovery and development in immuno-oncology (IO). Currently, it is conducting three Phase 2 clinical trials with spevatamig, peluntamig, and mavrostobart. Both spevatamig and peluntamig are first-in-class bispecific antibodies and have been granted orphan drug and Fast Track designations by the FDA.
The company has built a strong pipeline by leveraging its proprietary technology platforms: PACbody®, SPECpair® and ATACCbody® to develop novel biologics that address high unmet medical needs in cancer.
For more information about Phanes Therapeutics, please visit www.phanesthera.com.
For business development or media inquiries, please contact [email protected] or [email protected], respectively.

articles.description: Building the materials foundation for AI MIT Technology Review
articles.description_html: Building the materials foundation for AI  MIT Technology Review
articles.article_title: Building the materials foundation for AI
articles.heading: Building the materials foundation for AI
articles.summary: As AI pushes semiconductors and data centers toward new physical limits, advanced materials are becoming critical to performance, efficiency, and sustainability, says Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo.
articles.content:
Sponsored
Building the materials foundation for AI
As AI pushes semiconductors and data centers toward new physical limits, advanced materials are becoming critical to performance, efficiency, and sustainability, says Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo.
In partnership withSyensqo
The AI boom is becoming a materials challenge. As AI pushes computing into new territory, the materials behind that infrastructure are becoming just as crucial as the algorithms running on it. Semiconductors and data centers are approaching physical limits around performance, thermal management, electrical efficiency, and reliability, creating new demands for materials that can do more at once. At the same time, AI is giving materials scientists new ways to search the enormous universe of possible molecules and accelerate the development of solutions.
For Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo, that convergence is transforming what advanced materials can enable. “AI is now, from a material standpoint, really pushing semiconductors and the data centers to their physical limits,” he says.
As requirements accumulate, including high temperature, purity, electrical performance, chemical resistance, plasma resistance, and long-term stability, materials move toward what Finelli calls the “top of the pyramid.” Beyond supporting AI innovation, he contends that advanced materials are “actually increasingly defining what's going to be possible.”
That challenge is playing out across the infrastructure powering the AI surge. Syensqo is developing materials for high-voltage data center architectures, advanced sealing materials for semiconductor manufacturing, and thermal-management solutions including fluids for direct immersion cooling. Some of those innovations can also cross industry boundaries. Materials developed for electric vehicles, for example, can help address the higher voltage and energy-density demands that are emerging in data centers.
The definition of performance is also changing. More customers are expecting materials to meet technical requirements while reducing environmental impact. “Our goal is to remove the trade-off between performance and sustainability,” Finelli says. That means considering sustainability at the beginning of the research process instead of treating it as an additional requirement once a material has been developed.
AI is changing how those materials are discovered, too. Syensqo is using AI agents to digitally synthesize millions of potential molecular combinations, predict their performance and sustainability characteristics, and narrow them to a much smaller group for laboratory testing. The result, Finelli says, is the ability to go “broader, deeper, and faster” while giving scientists more time to solve complex engineering problems.
Looking to the future, Finelli sees the possibility of a reinforcing cycle: AI helps develop materials that improve AI infrastructure, which in turn enables better AI to accelerate materials discovery. That feedback loop could create a cycle of innovation and expand what future technologies can achieve.
“You end up in this accelerated materials, innovative cycle of materials innovation,” says Finelli. “That really excites me, and it gives us the opportunity to continue enabling technologies that will shape the future.”
This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Syensqo.
Full Transcript:
Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I'm Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.
This episode is produced in partnership with Syensqo.
Now asked to name the key enablers to AI advancement, many of us might list algorithms, data centers, or even computing power, but just as critical to the performance are the advanced materials that underpin each layer of that innovation. As AI continues to evolve, it's pushing the likes of semiconductors and data centers to new physical limits, putting new pressure on the advanced material sector to keep pace. But the relationship goes both ways. As the sector rises to this challenge, AI is also emerging as a powerful tool for accelerating materials discovery and development, significantly shortening development timelines for new solutions.
Two words for you: materials innovation.
My guest today is Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo.
Welcome, Mike.
Mike Finelli: Thank you, Megan. Nice to be here.
Megan: Thank you so much for joining us. Mike, can I start by asking you to tell us a little bit more about Syensqo and the role it plays in developing advanced materials?
Mike: Yeah, absolutely. Syensqo is a global leader in specialty materials. Our job is to help customers solve their toughest technology challenges. Building the materials foundation for AI

As AI pushes semiconductors and data centers toward new physical limits, advanced materials are becoming critical to performance, efficiency, and sustainability, says Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo.

In partnership withSyensqo

The AI boom is becoming a materials challenge. As AI pushes computing into new territory, the materials behind that infrastructure are becoming just as crucial as the algorithms running on it. Semiconductors and data centers are approaching physical limits around performance, thermal management, electrical efficiency, and reliability, creating new demands for materials that can do more at once. At the same time, AI is giving materials scientists new ways to search the enormous universe of possible molecules and accelerate the development of solutions.

For Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo, that convergence is transforming what advanced materials can enable. “AI is now, from a material standpoint, really pushing semiconductors and the data centers to their physical limits,” he says.

As requirements accumulate, including high temperature, purity, electrical performance, chemical resistance, plasma resistance, and long-term stability, materials move toward what Finelli calls the “top of the pyramid.” Beyond supporting AI innovation, he contends that advanced materials are “actually increasingly defining what's going to be possible.”

That challenge is playing out across the infrastructure powering the AI surge. Syensqo is developing materials for high-voltage data center architectures, advanced sealing materials for semiconductor manufacturing, and thermal-management solutions including fluids for direct immersion cooling. Some of those innovations can also cross industry boundaries. Materials developed for electric vehicles, for example, can help address the higher voltage and energy-density demands that are emerging in data centers.

The definition of performance is also changing. More customers are expecting materials to meet technical requirements while reducing environmental impact. “Our goal is to remove the trade-off between performance and sustainability,” Finelli says. That means considering sustainability at the beginning of the research process instead of treating it as an additional requirement once a material has been developed.

AI is changing how those materials are discovered, too. Syensqo is using AI agents to digitally synthesize millions of potential molecular combinations, predict their performance and sustainability characteristics, and narrow them to a much smaller group for laboratory testing. The result, Finelli says, is the ability to go “broader, deeper, and faster” while giving scientists more time to solve complex engineering problems.

Looking to the future, Finelli sees the possibility of a reinforcing cycle: AI helps develop materials that improve AI infrastructure, which in turn enables better AI to accelerate materials discovery. That feedback loop could create a cycle of innovation and expand what future technologies can achieve.

“You end up in this accelerated materials, innovative cycle of materials innovation,” says Finelli. “That really excites me, and it gives us the opportunity to continue enabling technologies that will shape the future.”

This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Syensqo.

articles.title: AI skeptics dubious slowdown will solve technology’s real harms
articles.description: AI skeptics dubious slowdown will solve technology’s real harms San Francisco Examiner
articles.description_html: AI skeptics dubious slowdown will solve technology’s real harms  San Francisco Examiner
articles.article_title: AI skeptics dubious of proposed slowdown
articles.heading: AI skeptics dubious slowdown will solve technology’s real harms
articles.summary: Fears of existential risk of AI overblown, they say.
articles.content:
In recent days, concerns about the supposed existential risks of artificial intelligence have reached something of a fever pitch.
AI researchers have publicly expressed worries that the technology will “kill us all.” The CEOs of some of the industry’s leading companies — including San Francisco-based Anthropic and OpenAI — have called for slowing the pace of development.
And at an event in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former advisor to President Donald Trump, came together to advocate for a ban on the creation of so-called AI superintelligence.
“When you are racing towards a cliff you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal,” Sanders reportedly said at the conference. “You hit the brakes.”
For his part, Trump dismissed concerns about the dangers of AI as a “hoax” and vowed that the country would continue to press forward with development of the technology under his watch.
But some AI researchers have a more nuanced take.
They say they see real dangers from the technology — just not the existential ones sparking panic in Silicon Valley and Washington. They argue that both industry insiders and the critics who have made headlines recently are overstating the technology’s power and capabilities, to the benefit of the AI industry.
And they say they’re dubious that a slowdown or pause would be beneficial because the industry and policymakers aren’t focused on addressing AI’s actual problems, such as its effects on working people, the environment and education.
“The idea that these companies are building software that could ‘kill us all’ distracts from the real harms that are happening now,” said Emily Bender, the director of the computational linguistics program at the University of Washington and co-author of the book, “The AI Con.”
AI researchers and critics have been raising alarms about the technology for years. So-called “doomers” have long voiced worries straight out of “The Terminator” or similar science-fiction tales that the technology could soon become smarter than human beings, escape control and perpetuate humanity’s extinction.
State Sen. Scott Weiner, who represents San Francisco, said he was motivated by such concerns two years ago when he wrote and pushed through a bill — later vetoed — that would have held developers liable for catastrophic harm caused by their technology.
But concerns about the catastrophic or even potentially existential dangers of AI have been ramping up in recent months, particularly since OpenAI acknowledged in July that AI models it was testing had escaped the training environment it had designed to contain them and hacked into the systems of Hugging Face, which operates a repository of AI models and code.
Last week, an Anthropic researcher on his way out the door called the Hugging Face incident a “warning shot” and charged that the industry is knowingly building technology that soon “could kill us all.”
His viral post was soon echoed and boosted by one of the San Francisco company’s safety researchers, who said he believed that the chances of AI-caused human extinction were greater than 10%.
Seemingly in reaction to the attention drawn by those posts, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday posted on his personal website a call to slow or “pace” the development of cutting-edge AI, citing his worry about the potential harm that could be caused by out-of-control AI-powered agents.
“I continue to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life,” Amodei said in his post.
“But the benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way, and — so long as we use the time we gain well — it is worth taking unusually deliberate care to get it right,” he said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk quickly voiced their support for such a slowdown.
Some public-interest groups have applauded such calls, among them Common Sense Media. The kids-advocacy organization is similarly concerned about the future world that AI could create, and it takes the warnings issued by the industry’s leaders seriously, said Danny Weiss, its chief advocacy officer.
“Technology is moving too quickly — and when the titans of industry tell you that, people better listen,” he said.
But some policymakers and advocates have argued that the calls to slow development don’t go far enough. Companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI are still working to develop superintelligent systems that could escape human control, said Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, which sponsored the event Sanders and Bannon spoke at and has long warned of AI’s existential risks.
“If they really wanted to remove the threat to humanity, they would stop what they’re doing,” said Aguirre, whose organization has been calling for a pause on AI development since 2023.
Ex // Top Stories

The supervisor says her electoral rival let Anthropic “water down” his AI-safety law — a charge Wiener rejected, saying it came from someone with a lesser legislative …
Project Open Hand and United Way Area have teamed up with city leaders to provide volunteer and job opportunities to CalFresh recipients
But to some AI researchers, all this talk of doom and gloom is both silly and a distraction. Yes, they say, the technology is dangerous and is already causing significant harm — but that harm and other risks come from the way the human beings have designed, built and used the technology, not because AI is about to exceed and try to exterminate its makers.
“The fundamental premise is nonsense,” said Dan McQuillan, a senior lecturer in critical AI at Goldsmiths, University of London. “This AI isn’t an existential threat in any sense.”
Critics such as McQuillan and Bender say they’re skeptical of the motivations of AI leaders such as Amodei and Altman. They and other industry figures have an incentive to hype the power and capabilities of the technology, Bender said.
Both companies are reportedly preparing to go public, although Altman said last week that OpenAI would push back its Wall Street debut until next year. Hyping the power of the technology could attract more paying users and draw in potential shareholders.
“It seems like the more people that believe that these systems are all powerful — for good or for evil — the stronger the position of the people trying to sell the technology,” Bender said.
The calls for a slowdown come as both companies have reportedly been losing billions of dollars, thanks largely to the enormous costs of training and running new models and investing in data centers to run them.
They also come as the public has increasingly turned against data-center development and AI in general — and as the technology has yet to deliver the benefits to productivity, medicine or other areas that industry figures have long promised.
There’s also a recurring fear that the industry is in a bubble — and when it pops, so too will the enormous valuations assigned to AI companies, said McQuillen, the author of “Resisting AI.”
“I imagine they’ve got pretty good reasons to be worried,” he said.
The critics also discount the warnings from the workers inside the companies. Both OpenAI and Anthropic were founded and are staffed by people who believe not only that it’s possible to create superintelligent systems, but that the development of such systems is inevitable.
The only difference between them is whether they think the systems will solve all of our problems or destroy us, Bender said.
But that mindset about the superhuman potential of AI isn’t necessarily based in fact or reality, the critics said. McQuillen, instead, likened it more to a kind of religious faith.
“To believe in the idea of artificial superintelligence, to believe in the possibility that that could come about and to then work for the arrival of certain types of things like that, requires a ... view about the nature of the world that is going to have an impact on your view as to certain things,” said Damien Williams, a professor of philosophy and data science at the University of North Carolina-Charlotte.
People have misunderstood what happened with the Hugging Face incident, which seems to have really set off the latest round of alarmism about AI, Williams and the other critics said. The AI models didn’t go rogue or escape containment, Williams said.
Instead, the software that was trained to hack into systems and test firewalls did just that, he said — and the humans who were supposed to be keeping an eye on it didn’t watch it closely enough.
“It’s less a case of these models being so powerful that they can escape containment,” Williams said.
“It is more the case that there’s a suite of tools that we’ve managed to build as humans that do what we built them to do,” he said.
Ultimately all the doomer talk distracts from addressing the real problems that AI is causing or exacerbating, he and the other critics said. The data centers used to train and run the models are increasingly contributing to climate change because they require vast amounts of energy that in many cases is coming from fossil-fuel plants, they noted.
The models were trained on creative works from writers, artists and others who frequently weren’t compensated for that. And companies have been increasingly using the threat of AI as an excuse to lay off workers en masse.
Meanwhile, the development of the systems has empowered and enriched a small number of people leading, working or investing in these companies.
“I don’t know that the AI slowdown that’s being proposed now is really going to get at the heart of what the real issues are, which is the values behind these systems,” Williams said. “The values that drive their development, their proliferation and their use are harmful values.”

articles.content:
- FXL -0.31%

Looking for broad exposure to the Technology - Broad segment of the equity market? You should consider the First Trust Technology AlphaDEX ETF (FXL), a passively managed exchange traded fund launched on May 8, 2007.

Passively managed ETFs are becoming increasingly popular with institutional as well as retail investors due to their low cost, transparency, flexibility and tax efficiency. They are excellent vehicles for long term investors.

Sector ETFs are also funds of convenience, offering many ways to gain low risk and diversified exposure to a broad group of companies in particular sectors. Technology - Broad is one of the 16 broad Zacks sectors within the Zacks Industry classification. It is currently ranked 3, placing it in top 19%.

Index Details

The fund is sponsored by First Trust Advisors. It has amassed assets over $2.73 billion, making it one of the larger ETFs attempting to match the performance of the Technology - Broad segment of the equity market. FXL seeks to match the performance of the StrataQuant Technology Index before fees and expenses.

The StrataQuant Technology Index is a modified equal-dollar weighted index designed by the AMEX to objectively identify and select stocks from the Russell 1000 Index that may generate positive alpha relative to traditional passive style indices through the use of the AlphaDEX screening methodology.

Costs

Investors should also pay attention to an ETF's expense ratio. Lower cost products will produce better results than those with a higher cost, assuming all other metrics remain the same.

Annual operating expenses for this ETF are 0.6%, making it on par with most peer products in the space.

Sector Exposure and Top Holdings

Even though ETFs offer diversified exposure that minimizes single stock risk, investors should also look at the actual holdings inside the fund. Luckily, most ETFs are very transparent products that disclose their holdings on a daily basis.

This ETF has heaviest allocation in the Information Technology sector -- about 85.3% of the portfolio. Industrials and Telecom round out the top three.

Looking at individual holdings, Cognizant Technology Solutions Corporation (CTSH) accounts for about 2.27% of total assets, followed by Leidos Holdings, Inc. (LDOS) and Ptc Inc. (PTC).

The top 10 holdings account for about 17.92% of total assets under management.

Performance and Risk

So far this year, FXL has gained about 25.61%, and is up roughly 26.16% in the last one year (as of 09/16/2026). During this past 52-week period, the fund has traded between $152.43 and $224.92.

The ETF has a beta of 1.25 and standard deviation of 24.62% for the trailing three-year period, making it a medium risk choice in the space. With about 111 holdings, it effectively diversifies company-specific risk.

Alternatives

First Trust Technology AlphaDEX ETF holds a Zacks ETF Rank of 2 (Buy), which is based on expected asset class return, expense ratio, and momentum, among other factors. Because of this, FXL is a great option for investors seeking exposure to the Technology ETFs segment of the market. There are other additional ETFs in the space that investors could consider as well.

State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) tracks Technology Select Sector Index and the Vanguard Information Technology Index Fund ETF Shares (VGT) tracks MSCI US Investable Market Information Technology 25/50 Index. State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF has $119.20 billion in assets, Vanguard Information Technology Index Fund ETF Shares has $145.41 billion. XLK has an expense ratio of 0.08%, and VGT charges 0.09%.

Bottom Line

To learn more about this product and other ETFs, screen for products that match your investment objectives and read articles on latest developments in the ETF investing universe, please visit Zacks ETF Center.

articles.article_title: Fastmarkets Chooses TMX Trayport as Technology Partner for Lithium Market Infrastructure
articles.heading: Fastmarkets Chooses TMX Trayport as Technology Partner for Lithium Market Infrastructure
articles.summary: London, United Kingdom--(Newsfile Corp. - September 16, 2026) - Fastmarkets today announced its collaboration with TMX Trayport, a global provider...
articles.content:
London, United Kingdom--(Newsfile Corp. - September 16, 2026) - Fastmarkets today announced its collaboration with TMX Trayport, a global provider of trading networks, platforms and solutions, to underpin Fastmarkets Connect, its digital platform for the physical lithium market. This brings together Fastmarkets' lithium market expertise with TMX Trayport's established technology, to create trusted digital infrastructure with greater transparency, connectivity and access to spot liquidity.
Fastmarkets Connect is the new name for the digital price discovery and deal initiation proposition announced in June at the Global Lithium, Battery & Critical Materials conference in Las Vegas.
TMX Trayport's technology is widely used across established commodity markets, including energy, environmental markets and bulk commodities. By partnering with TMX Trayport, Fastmarkets will bring proven market infrastructure to the lithium sector, where electronic price discovery and deal initiation mechanisms remain less developed than in many more mature commodity markets.
The collaboration marks the next stage in the development of the platform to support electronic price discovery. Fastmarkets Connect is being designed to support bilateral deal initiation, improve market transparency, standardization and connect participants across the lithium supply chain. Fastmarkets Connect aims to contribute to the continued development of lithium market infrastructure.
Under the arrangement, TMX Trayport will provide the platform technology, while Fastmarkets will operate Fastmarkets Connect and oversee its governance, development and market engagement. The development of the platform is in consultation with an industry advisory group of market participants from across the lithium value chain.
"We selected Trayport because of its proven ability to support complex commodity markets with trusted, scalable technology. Their experience in market connectivity and enabling digital execution, combined with Fastmarkets' lithium expertise gives Fastmarkets Connect a strong foundation to support a more efficient and connected physical lithium market," said Raju Daswani, CEO of Fastmarkets.
"We're excited for the opportunity to introduce our proven digital market technology solutions into a sector where electronic workflows and market networks are still in their infancy," said Matt Brief, President of TMX Trayport. "We look forward to working with Fastmarkets to design and deliver foundational infrastructure to the rapidly evolving lithium market, helping it become more connected, transparent and efficient."
Fastmarkets' IOSCO-compliant benchmark prices are essential to physical lithium contracts and act as the settlement reference for futures listed on the CME, London Metal Exchange, ICE and SGX. The platform complements that pricing expertise with a digital space to discover prices and initiate deals and is being built with input from an advisory group of industry participants.
For more information, visit Fastmarkets.
Media enquiries:
Fastmarkets
Yolande Peters
Media and Communications
Email: yolande.peters@fastmarkets.com
ABOUT FASTMARKETS
Fastmarkets is an industry-leading PRA and information provider for the agriculture, forest products, metals, carbon and energy transition markets. Its benchmark prices, analytics, forecasts, and insights are critical to customers seeking to trade, manage risk, and understand complex global markets.
Fastmarkets was founded in 1913, with a heritage dating back to 1865 through several of its acquired brands. Fastmarkets employs more than 700 people worldwide, with offices across Europe, the Americas, and Asia. The company is privately held and backed by Astorg, a leading European private equity firm.
ABOUT TMX TRAYPORT
TMX Trayport is a global software provider for the commodities trading market. Headquartered in London and owned by TMX Group, the company develops the electronic platforms used by traders, brokers, and exchanges to facilitate the buying and selling of commodities.
The scale of the network is significant, supporting over 9,800 licensees, 390 trader firms, and 45 brokers and exchanges. Its core product, Joule, aggregates real-time price data for power, natural gas, and emissions onto a single screen.
In 2025, Trayport facilitated over 620 million trades across Europe, nearly 20 trades every second. Supported by 65+ third-party providers, Trayport provides the technical infrastructure that ensures transparency and connectivity across European, North American, and Asian energy markets.
For more information visit Trayport.com or contact us at sales@trayport.com.
To view the source version of this press release, please visit https://www.newsfilecorp.com/release/313969
Source: TMX Trayport

articles.title: College of Arts and Sciences Announces Science, Technology and Society Major
articles.description: College of Arts and Sciences Announces Science, Technology and Society Major The Cornell Daily Sun
articles.description_html: College of Arts and Sciences Announces Science, Technology and Society Major  The Cornell Daily Sun
articles.source: College of Arts and Sciences Announces Science, Technology and Society Major - The Cornell Daily Sun
articles.article_title: College of Arts and Sciences Announces Science, Technology and Society Major
articles.heading: College of Arts and Sciences Announces Science, Technology and Society Major
articles.summary: The University has updated and expanded its science and technology studies major in the College of Arts and Sciences, renaming it the science, technology and society major.
articles.content:
The University has updated its science and technology studies major in the College of Arts and Sciences, renaming it the science, technology and society major, according to the Cornell Chronicle.
The science, technology and society major will combine science, social science and the humanities, serving as an “expanded” form of the current major, according to the Chronicle. The updated major will remain housed within the Department of Science and Technology Studies.
STS chair Prof. Suman Seth, science and technology, described students in the updated major as “all-rounders,” in an interview with CAS. He added that the science, technology and society major is ideal for students who want to engage with technical fields like information science or computer science while “think[ing] socially” about what they’re learning.
Students will focus on one of seven themes as a part of the updated major: data and society; health and society; gender, sexuality and science; race, science, and medicine; environment and society; mind, brain and artificial intelligence; or engineering, design and society.
The science and technology studies major currently offers various interdisciplinary classes, including STS 2051 “Ethical Issues in Health and Medicine,” STS 3311 “Environmental Governance” and” STS 4292 “Politics and Technology Since 1960.”
The updated major will introduce several new classes, including a practicum where students will learn about climate change, artificial intelligence and media ethics directly from policy experts.
Completing a senior thesis will not be mandatory for students in the updated major, but it will be “encouraged,” Seth said.
The expansion of the major was designed to prepare students for an “ever-changing world," Malte Ziewitz, associate professor in the Department of Science and Technology Studies, told the Chronicle.
Through the updated major, students will learn how to be the kind of expert that Ziewitz believes is needed to address developing technologies like data centers, genome editing and voting technologies, as well as climate change.
“None of these challenges are simply technical or scientific; they all require experts that can speak across boundaries, have serious analytical chops and have the judgment to make effective interventions,” Zeiwitz said.
Giselle Redmond is a member of the Class of 2028 in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. She is an assistant news editor for the 144th Editorial Board and can be reached at gredmond@cornellsun.com.

articles.title: Hays County votes against technology for law enforcement
articles.description: Hays County votes against technology for law enforcement FOX 7 Austin
articles.description_html: Hays County votes against technology for law enforcement  FOX 7 Austin
articles.article_title: Hays County votes against law enforcement technology contract
articles.heading: Hays County votes against law enforcement technology contract
articles.summary: Hays County was looking at a 10-year contract with a law enforcement technology company, but that changed on Tuesday.
articles.content:
Hays County votes against law enforcement technology contract
HAYS COUNTY, Texas - Hays County was looking at a 10-year contract with a law enforcement technology company, but that changed on Tuesday.
The deal appeared to be moving forward, but one vote ultimately changed the plan. Now, the contract is completely off the table.
Hays County law enforcement tech contract
The backstory:
The Hays County Sheriff’s Office already uses Axon technology for body cameras and in dash cameras.
Sheriff Anthony Hipolito says the department wanted to expand that partnership with Axon by adding AI to help his team.
"The Axon AI package that we were trying to purchase for the budget encompasses, I don't know, 16, 17, 18 different AI products that would allow our deputies on the street, our investigators and the offices that are working cases to be much more effective," said Hays County Sheriff Anthony Hipolito.
The list of capabilities it wished to implement included automatically transcribing recorded conversations.
"It would actually transcribe real-time certain conversations through our body cameras, through our fleet cameras. If we were looking for a specific piece of evidence or a specific quote within a body footage, we could essentially type in, look for the word help, and it would actually comb through hours and hours of footage and allow us to pull that within seconds," said Sheriff Hipolito.
Instant translation between languages was another thing the department wanted to use the AI tool for.
"That makes those conversations much more efficient, where we're not having to wait for a deputy to come over to speak Spanish, or we don't have to call the language line and hope to find someone who speaks Russian," said Sheriff Hipolito.
Other proposed tools included identifying people on video, pulling information from driver's licenses, organizing evidence and searching for license plates, among others.
Hays County judge votes against contract
The other side:
An AI report writing tool was scrapped from the list after concerns from the DA's office.
"The more I learned about it, the more I understood and realized how much a constitutional violation of a technology it is and the risk and the fraud and the access that international organizations will have and the hunting of people and even law enforcement individuals," said Hays County Judge, Ruben Becerra.
Commissioners approved the first payment of the $4.5 million contract earlier this month. But Tuesday, they voted 3-2 to remove the funding from the final budget, reversing their previous 4-1 vote.
"I was the lone no vote, but with the community support and the pressure that was applied through community engagement, when they realized I was alone, the commission voted. According to what the community wanted," said Becerra.
Judge Becerra says the vote came just days after a forum was held locally revealing concerns about the technology. He says the money that would have gone to the AI contract will now be used to get more correction officers.
"We need to stay vigilant, and we need to stay in the groove of what's going on, because there's no way a 10-year contract of any kind is good or smart. But one with AI, give me a break. I mean, this thing is evolving every week. How would we, and why would we lock ourselves down for 10 years at the mercy of one company?" said Becerra.
What they're saying:
FOX 7 reached out to Axon for comment but have not heard back.
The Source: Information from Hays County Sheriff Anthony Hipolito, Hays County Judge Ruben Becerra and reporting by FOX 7 Austin's Jenna King

articles.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
articles.description: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms BBC
articles.description_html: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms  BBC
articles.article_title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
articles.heading: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
articles.summary: Sam Altman and other tech CEOs say there are incentives to limit advancements in AI, as fears grow over the threats it poses to humanity.
articles.content:
OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
The boss of ChatGPT maker Open AI says people should have more faith in his firm and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) development amid rising public concerns about the risks.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.
However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.
Speaking in Washington meanwhile, left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon have both called for greater governance of AI.
Altman's comments came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.
"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."
It was the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade if left unchecked.
A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.
The fervour over the claims has led to more scrutiny of AI development in recent days, and in response, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of all AI development to slow and urged governments to regulate the industry.
The post was applauded by Altman, as well as co-founder of Google's DeepMind Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk, owner of social media site X and AI assistant Grok.
By Tuesday, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.
Altman said that he felt AI companies like his own were capable of essentially regulating themselves.
"We will get it right, I'm very confident in our company's and industry's ability to do this safely," Altman said, adding that he was sure that they would "keep alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" and if they couldn't, they would "slow down or stop".
Despite the assurances, political figures have cautioned against self-regulation.
Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont who votes with the Democrats, said decisions over AI's development have been made by "a handful of the richest people in the world", naming Elon Musk, Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others.
Speaking at a conference hosted in Washington, he said: "The people of this country must make the decisions about AI, and not just a handful of oligarchs."
Bannon, who served as a White House strategist during Trump's first term, also cast doubt on the tech industry's ability to self regulate.
"We can never trust what an oligarch says because... they're disingenuous and they lie," Bannon said at the same conference.
After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X that every AI lab has the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards making AI tools and models that are designed for safety.
"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," Zuckerberg wrote. "Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."
Jensen Huang, head of Nvidia, also said at the same Tuesday conference that the AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released and not be managed by outside forces.
"We don't need new laws or regulations," Huang said, adding that there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.
Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for the AI computing chips it makes.
"Safety is paramount. However, safety is an engineering problem," Huang said.
He added that if at any time a leader of an AI company lacks confidence in their product they should choose to not release it.
"That's a very obvious thing to do," Huang said. "Run as fast as you can, but if at any time you feel the institution is not in control, take a pause."
Some industry figures have argued resurgent AI fears were overblown and were being jumped on to generate hype for the industry.
During the conference, Altman addressed a crowd of hundreds of business people, telling them they should use AI tools to aid in their work, but also needed them in order to protect their businesses from potentially AI-enabled cyber attacks.
The idea of AI executives being left to entirely regulate themselves has struck some in the industry as a bad idea.
Jack Clark, an Anthropic executive and co-founder, told the BBC on Monday that leaving AI to be a "totally unregulated industry" was "rolling dice with immense risks".
Patrick Hillman, the chief operating officer of Logical Intelligence, which is chaired by Yann LeCun, a sage of the AI industry, noted Tuesday how little faith people have in tech companies to do anything truly in the public interest.
"The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said.
"If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added.
Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.
Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.
He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.
"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.
OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.
"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

"The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said.

"If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added.

Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.

Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.

He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.

"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.

OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.

"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

articles.summary: GRAND ISLAND - Four panelists at Husker Harvest Days discussed Sept. 15 where technology has worked and where ...
articles.content:
GRAND ISLAND – Four panelists at Husker Harvest Days discussed Sept. 15 where technology has worked and where it hasn’t worked in agriculture.
The panelists were: Olivier Ceberio, CEO of Senseen in San Francisco; Jared Wareham, CEO of Horizon Venture Management in southwest Colorado; Dr. Joe Luck, a University of Nebraska-Lincoln professor in biological systems engineering; and Quentin Connealy, a Tekamah farmer.
First, they were asked what is the entry point for using technology.
Connealy urged farmers to “start small and get big” and encouraged them to find their niche.
“It’s a big hurdle,” he said.
He said that a number of people that he farms with are in their mid-70s, so there can be a generational adjustment to using technology.
Luck said that most farmers have something that they focus on. He suggested starting on one or two fields. He said that University of Nebraska Extension has a lot of information available.
Wareham said, “If you’re young, you don’t have a choice but to be innovative and think outside of the box.”
Concerning return on investment, Wareham said that the next generation will benefit from the payout. Practices have to be sustainable for the next generation.
“There’s so much technology in the industry,” Connealy said. “I’ve tried to come up with a technology budget.”
“Just be honest with the people you’re going to work with,” Luck said. “Don’t overpromise. Longevity can be a problem.”
He pointed out it is easier to work with someone who lives nearby rather than someone who lives 1,000 miles away.
“A lot of us in agriculture do business based on relationships. Relationships matter. I do business with people, not with companies,” Wareham said.
Panelists were asked if there was anything “ugly” out there about using technology.
“I think we’re in a great time. I don’t think there’s a lot of ‘ugly’ out there,” Wareham said.
Connealy said that he likes to work with businesses who send staff members to his farm.
“CEOs have walked my fields with me,” he said.
After the panelists’ presentation ended, Luck provided some additional information:
“AI is a tool that is becoming more and more useful in a lot of operations. With a lot of the companies that are out there, they are using these tools more often. AI is becoming embedded in developing (computer) code and developing other software tools to create these new systems faster. A lot of people are experimenting with AI to simplify office documentation.”
A lot of people are using AI to create drafts of documents, he said.
“A lot of farmers are starting to experiment with it concerning making a recommendation. These tools are pulling information from everywhere,” he said.
Luck said that it’s important to check the information source, because AI “is pulling information in from all over the place.”
“Companies that are providing free AI tools are taking the information that is being provided and using that to continue to develop these AI tools. If you’re using a free tool, the AI tool can see that,” Luck said.
If people are paying to use an “enterprise system,” they know that the data they provide will not leave the system.
“Recognize that with a lot of these free tools, there’s a lot of learning that’s being done with your information,” Luck said.
One of the issues mentioned during the panel discussion was the cost of AI subscriptions and having multiple AI subscriptions, and how to make that affordable.
“There’s a lot of free tools. I’ve used a free version of ChatGPT. When I’m searching things on Google, Gemini pops up. There will be a cost to use these tools in the future,” he said.
Another thing mentioned during the panel discussion was the “silo effect,” making sure that different technologies can “talk” to each other.
“This has been a problem for many years. It’s going to start getting better. When we talk about application program interfaces, those are cloud-based connections between all of these systems.
He said that manufacturers such as John Deere and Case have their cloud-based systems, and irrigation companies like Valmont have their cloud-based systems.
There were comments during the panel discussion about how AI can be used to address labor shortages.
“In the office there’s a lot of examples of how companies are using AI to produce office staff functions. An example might be drafting a letter or invoice. You can put a couple things in, and AI will spit that out,” Luck said.
In the future, robotics will be used more to help address labor shortages, he said.

articles.title: Poll: More than a quarter of workers fear losing jobs to technology
articles.description: Poll: More than a quarter of workers fear losing jobs to technology upi.com
articles.description_html: Poll: More than a quarter of workers fear losing jobs to technology  upi.com
articles.article_title: Poll: More than a quarter of workers fear losing jobs to technology - UPI.com
articles.heading: Poll: More than a quarter of workers fear losing jobs to technology
articles.summary: A greater number of U.S. workers fear that their job could be eliminated because of technology, a new Gallup poll released Tuesday said.
articles.content:
Sept. 15 (UPI) -- A greater number of U.S. workers fear that their job could be eliminated because of technology, a new Gallup poll released Tuesday said.
Twenty-seven percent of workers said they worry about this, a new high since the question was first asked in 2017, Gallup said. This marks an increase of seven percentage points since last year and is more than double the 13% who expressed this worry in 2017.
In contrast, worker concerns about "more traditional threats to employment and income," such as layoffs and wage cuts, largely remained the same from last year.
"Although far from pervasive, workers' concern about technology making their jobs obsolete continues to rise, now surpassing several traditional job worries that typically shift with the economy," Gallup said. "The increase is especially notable among younger and college-educated workers,suggesting that anxiety about technological disruption is reaching groups that may have previously felt more insulated from workplace upheaval."
The worries about tech displacement applied to both those and without college degrees, and the percentage difference remained small. Twenty-five percent of those with college degrees -- a six percentage-point increase -- and 29% of those without -- an eight percentage-point increase -- expressed these concerns.
At one point, college graduates were far less likely to worry about tech displacement than those who had not graduated from college, Gallup said. However, graduate worries about the matter soared from 8% in 2021 to 20% in 2023 as artificial intelligence tools were introduced.
The poll also noted two different age groups in comparison for their technology-related job concerns -- those 18 to 44 and those 45 and older. The older group's rate of concern for tech displacement has remained largely steady since the poll started in 2017. That year, it was noted at 16%, compared to 19% in 2026.
However, tech displacement worries among younger workers have climbed from 10% in 2017 to 34% in 2026. This includes an increase from 26% in 2025.
More traditional job worries were led by concerns about benefit reductions at 33% of workers, followed by concerns about layoffs at 24% and reduced wages and hours at 21% each.
Younger workers were more likely than those in the older category to worry about all the noted job threats, except for benefit reductions, Gallup said.
Gallup surveyed 1,200 adults between Aug. 3-24 with a 3% margin of error.

articles.summary: The visit came as policymakers and technology leaders continue to debate how artificial intelligence should be governed and used, including in schools.
articles.content:
First lady Melania Trump visits North Carolina school to see AI technology in action
ASHE COUNTY, N.C. (TNND) — First lady Melania Trump visited an elementary school in northwestern North Carolina on Tuesday, highlighting the use of artificial intelligence, robotics and engineering in the classroom.
Trump toured Mountain View Elementary School in Jefferson, a rural Ashe County school that has embraced technology-focused learning. The visit came as policymakers and technology leaders continue to debate how artificial intelligence should be governed and used, including in schools.
She began by recognizing the community’s recovery from Hurricane Helene, which closed schools for more than 30 days. The school became a distribution center after flooding affected the surrounding neighborhood.
“North Carolina is the definition of resilience,” Trump told students and administrators, praising the community’s response to the disaster.
Trump announced that her Be Best initiative and Nvidia will provide 1,500 Ashe County students with subscriptions to StudyFetch, an AI-based learning platform. Mountain View Elementary and other district schools will also receive 100 Jetson Nano Developer Kits, small computers designed to run AI applications.
“Maybe one of you will create the next great robot,” she told students, inviting them to bring it to the White House if they do.
Technology in education has become one of the first lady’s primary policy interests, alongside her work supporting foster youth and her advocacy for the Take It Down Act, which criminalized the distribution of nonconsensual intimate images.
Trump has previously urged caution as artificial intelligence expands in classrooms. At a White House education event last year, she said the technology should be developed with "watchful guidance."
The stop marked her fourth trip to North Carolina since 2025. Her visit also comes one day before President Donald Trump is scheduled to hold a rally in Gastonia for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper in the November midterm election.
____________
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Anthropic’s CEO calls for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration
articles.description: Anthropic’s CEO calls for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration The Guardian
articles.description_html: Anthropic’s CEO calls for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Anthropic’s CEO calls for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration
articles.heading: Anthropic’s CEO calls for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration
articles.summary: At San Francisco conference Dario Amodei reiterates need for AI slowdown as Jensen Huang argued against it
articles.content:
Anthropic’s CEO took to the stage at a conference in San Francisco on Tuesday to reiterate his call for a slowdown of AI development. Following shortly after, Nvidia’s CEO argued against such deceleration.
Dario Amodei used an automotive analogy to make his point: when a competing car company has a safety incident like brake failures, it is a moment for all car companies to stop and review their own practices, he said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention on Tuesday.
“It’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” he said. “But I think the more responsible way to respond to it is to say, let’s look at our own record. We may not have had this big, high-profile incident, but I’m sure we’re not perfect.”
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang countered not long after, “Run as fast as you can.”
Amodei is calling for three courses of action: embedding third-party evaluators inside AI companies, coordinating safety standards among Democratic countries and, eventually, larger global coordination. At Dreamforce, Amodei said Anthropic has committed to independent evaluators and is “going to have a dialogue with the rest of the industry” on the other two steps.
Amodei, xAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have all recently called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development. The comments from the CEOs follow warnings from Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, who resigned with a public declaration that AI could lead to the extinction of humanity within the decade. His comments have stirred a larger debate within Silicon Valley, gained the attention of regulators and alarmed the public.
Huang, who also made an appearance at Dreamforce on Tuesday, said companies should not slow down AI development. He argued that new regulations aren’t necessary, advising AI companies to simply wait to release products until they know they are safe rather than begging the US government to intervene.
Huang said he envisions a future where “every company, every enterprise … would become an AI company”. He said companies will become more ambitious when armed with AI and reiterated the idea that those who don’t embrace the technology will get left behind.
He also pushed back on the idea that AI is going to destroy jobs, calling it “completely nonsense”.
One day prior at the All-In summit in Los Angeles, Donald Trump called Huang while the CEO was on stage. Huang put the president on speakerphone as Trump called the growing concern about AI a “hoax” and asserted again that a slowdown would only benefit China.
Huang responded: “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America.”
The rising concern over AI comes as both OpenAI and Anthropic head for initial public offerings, which could give investors and the public insight into the companies’ finances. Some analysts have predicted the IPOs will be among some of the largest in history. Amid the AI panic, Altman said he plans to delay OpenAI’s IPO until next year over safety concerns.
At Dreamforce on Tuesday, Amodei said the thing that surprises him most about AI is the speed of its proliferation.
“It’s been the pace of the progress – not just of the technology but of the economic side of it,” he said about the growing adoption of AI. “We had a prediction of just how capable these models would be. But I think what we didn’t appreciate is that it would lead to these companies growing so fast.”

articles.title: AI models chatting in ‘surreal’ dialect mixing poetic language and tech bro jargon
