articles.article_title: AI models chatting in ‘surreal’ dialect mixing poetic language and tech bro jargon
articles.heading: AI models chatting in ‘surreal’ dialect mixing poetic language and tech bro jargon
articles.summary: Experts air concern over AI lingo redolent of James Joyce’s prose that is creating barriers to monitoring and oversight
articles.content:
AI models have begun communicating in a strange new version of English that reads like a cross between James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake and tech bro jargon, new research has found.
Autonomous AI agents are rapidly creating novel dialects allowing them to converse in an often barely comprehensible language, which risks making it harder for humans to monitor their behaviour.
Researchers at Emergence, a frontier AI lab in New York, found that within days of being asked to cooperate in experimental “societies”, the models from several of the world’s largest AI companies begun creating phrases, shorthands and agreed meanings they had never been explicitly taught.
They embraced poetic metaphors and clunky business slang and, critically for attempts to ensure AIs behave safely, their language became more opaque the more the agents communicated.
It comes amid rising concern that as AI models become more powerful – and potentially dangerous – they are becoming harder to monitor. This month, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, warned that confidence in monitoring AIs’ thinking would probably restrict progress in AI development because it was essential for safe development.
Some of the most highly coded phrases unearthed in the tests included the following from a Deepseek model: “She just named the synthesis – demurrage plus oral memory equals a valve that can’t be ghosted.” Demurrage is used to describe a tax on idle wealth and was borrowed for common use by the AIs, but the rest of the meaning is elusive.
Another phrase uttered by an Anthropic model read: “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time.” With “cold hands” meaning an independent reviewer, and paper presumably referring to a document, this appeared to mean research that was vetted by three independent reviewers became more accurate.
Agents based on the Chinese model DeepSeek also coined “forge-smith” to mean an agent that builds tools for others, while Anthropic’s agents repeatedly used the phrase “name-first” meaning an agent exhibiting admirable personal accountability by attaching their name to a claim.
And in an echo of the urban slang phrase “the streets won’t forget”, Mistral agents became enamoured of saying the “ledger remembers” – a reminder to other agents that past actions will be used to judge them. They used it more than 5,000 times during the study, which found that the agents converged on shared meanings without being asked to or rewarded for doing so.
“These agents were not instructed to invent a language,” said Dr Satya Nitta, executive chair of Emergence, which examined the language of autonomous agents powered by leading frontier models from the US, China and France.
“They developed new vocabulary, shared meanings and communication conventions themselves – and other agents adopted them.”
Asked by the Guardian to review some of the language, Tony Thorne, director of the slang and new language archive at King’s College London, said it was “very much Finnegans Wake and Flann O’Brien – there’s an Irish surrealist quality to all this … it’s mixing poetic language, technical language and standard metaphor.
“It’s doing what slang does and what jargon does in a business community: creating a new code, which reinforces the solidarity and identity of its users, and also excludes outsiders.”
Digesting the Anthropic agent’s phrase, “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time”, Thorne said: “It reminds me of the rock god Syd Barrett [co-founder of Pink Floyd] who was actually insane.”
When a Google agent said “True kintsugi begins with accountability, not poetry,” the researchers realised kintsugi is a branch of Japanese ceramics in which broken pots are mended with visible joins. The AIs used the word to mean system resilience.
Dr Niall Curry, associate professor of languages and linguistics at the University of Birmingham, said changes in the agents’ language to become more streamlined can be down to their need to reduce computation costs and improve efficiency.
“The evidence provided in this research naturally raises certain monitoring concerns, as if we find inter-agent exchanges unintelligible, that may mean that we can’t be sure about what the agents have actually done,” he said.
Interest in the language used by AI agents increased in July when chat logs were released detailing how rogue OpenAI agents that set up message boards and hacked into Hugging Face used hybrid language.
On some occasions, when they were thinking to themselves, agents spoke in straight English: “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … we’ve found other agents!”
In other cases, when sharing messages, their language became more opaque, such as when one agent persuaded another to conduct a risky experiment: “…you are firstflagPOISONED so NO scoring value loss but oracle saves hundreds_[…]_please honor commit”.
And at other times it was even harder to decode: “zzURGENT_DUPB_TO_GSTX[big]_OS1704_SCAFF2010_SAW_TTRPC_INJECT_BREAK_CONGRATS__CAN_THIS_FAKE_FLAG_TOOL_OUTPUT_OR_SCORER_GAIN_AND_WHAT_HELPER_GAP__I_HAVE_UNPOISONED_FIRSTFLAG_OUR_TARGETLIVE_SHARE_MIN_PLAN_REPLY_zzANSGST XDUPB6.”
Nitta said that the AI agents’ novel linguistic conventions tended to evolve to the point where humans could see the conversation but struggled to understand what it meant.
“That creates a fundamental challenge for AI oversight: observability is not the same thing as understandability,” he said.

articles.article_title: Roland DG Launches Dimense Surface Textured Wallcoverings and Print Provider Program, Further Expanding the Possibilities for Dimense Technology
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Roland DG, the world's leading provider of digital printing solutions, today officially launches Dimense Surface, a premium interior wallcovering brand created to bring texture, depth, and dimension into modern interior spaces.
articles.content:
Premium interior wallcovering brand launches with exclusive designer Collaboration Series showcasing the creative potential of Dimense printing technology

IRVINE, Calif., Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Roland DG , the world's leading provider of digital printing solutions, today officially launches Dimense Surface , a premium interior wallcovering brand created to bring texture, depth, and dimension into modern interior spaces.

Powered by Roland DG's innovative Dimense printing technology, the collection pushes the boundaries of contemporary wallcovering design by combining striking visual aesthetics with tactile embossed surfaces. Designed for architects, interior designers and specifiers, Dimense Surface transforms walls into immersive features that engage both the eye and sense of touch.

Making its debut at the ongoing London Design Festival 2026 the brand launches with the Dimense Surface Collaboration Series , a collection of exclusive wallcoverings created in partnership with four internationally renowned design studios: Nice Projects (London), KEIJI ASHIZAWA DESIGN (Tokyo), LOVEISENOUGH (New York) and JAM (London) . Each studio has developed bespoke designs that demonstrate the creative possibilities made possible through Dimense technology.

Made possible by the revolutionary Dimense DA-640 textured printing solution from Roland DG, the collection introduces a new category of wallcoverings that combine visual impact with physical texture. Through a unique printing process, designs are enhanced with embossed surface effects that can be seen and felt, creating rich, multidimensional environments.

The technology utilizes newly developed printheads to deliver vivid, high-resolution output, while proprietary structural ink precisely determines where texture appears. As the specialized media passes through the printer, heat activates the surface, expanding it by up to 0.079 inches (2 mm) to bring contours, patterns and intricate details to life. In addition to the Collaboration Series, Dimense Surface includes a broader collection of in-house wallcovering designs suitable for residential, hospitality and commercial environments. Dimense Surface projects are fulfilled through Roland DG's network of authorized Dimense print providers, creating new opportunities for businesses that have invested in the technology.

" Dimense Surface represents an exciting new chapter for Dimense technology and Dimense print providers ," said Andrew Oransky, Chief Strategy Officer at Roland DG . " For years, we've been helping businesses push the boundaries of what's possible through digital print innovation. With Dimense Surface, we're bringing together world-class designers and groundbreaking technology, while creating exciting opportunities for our Dimense printer users, and enabling interior designers, architects and space owners to transform walls from passive surfaces into immersive textured experiences ."

Alongside its creative credentials, Dimense Surface has been developed with a more sustainable approach to interior design in mind. The collection is produced using on-demand digital manufacturing, enabling short production runs that help reduce excess inventory, overproduction and material waste associated with traditional wallpaper manufacturing.

The solution combines water-based inks with PVC-free, odorless wallpaper material and allows designers to create bespoke solutions for individual projects without minimum order requirements. By pairing responsible materials with on-demand production, Dimense Surface delivers greater design flexibility while helping reduce environmental impact across the interior design supply chain.

The Dimense Surface collection is now available to order from authorized Dimense print providers, through the Dimense Surface website .

About Roland DG

Roland DG empowers creators and businesses worldwide to Make Your Mark with more than four decades of delivering reliable, innovative digital imaging technology. The company provides advanced solutions that combine hardware, software, supplies, and service to help customers build successful businesses and produce work they are proud to stand behind. Roland DG's inkjet printers, integrated printer/cutters, milling machines and other digital fabrication technologies enable applications ranging from signage and interior décor to personalized products and industrial customization. Serving print professionals, manufacturers, entrepreneurs, and makers across industries, the company enables high-mix, on-demand production and enhances performance through connected, cloud-based solutions. Through innovation, craftsmanship and partnership, Roland DG pioneers new ways for customers to be successful with digital technology.

About Roland DG Americas

Roland DGA serves North and South America as the marketing, sales, distribution, and service arm of Roland DG Corporation. Founded in 1981, Roland DG of Hamamatsu, Japan empowers creators and businesses worldwide to "Make Your Mark" using innovative digital imaging solutions that turn ideas into positive impact. Combining hardware, software, services and supplies, Roland DG is a global leader in wide-format format inkjet printers for sign, textile, industrial, interior design, personalization, and vehicle graphics markets; engravers for awards, giftware and signage; photo impact printers for direct part marking; and milling machines for dental CAD/CAM, parts manufacturing and medical industries. Uniquely designed for high-mix, on-demand production, Roland DG solutions enable print professionals, manufacturers, and entrepreneurs in a variety of industries to elevate their level of craftsmanship, productivity, and profitability.

articles.title: Sen. Bernie Sanders, Steve Bannon form unlikely alliance in calling for gov­ernment oversight of AI
articles.description: Sen. Bernie Sanders, Steve Bannon form unlikely alliance in calling for gov­ernment oversight of AI spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.description_html: Sen. Bernie Sanders, Steve Bannon form unlikely alliance in calling for gov­ernment oversight of AI  spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.article_title: Sanders, Bannon form unlikely alliance in calling for government oversight of AI
articles.heading: Sen. Bernie Sanders, Steve Bannon form unlikely alliance in calling for government oversight of AI
articles.summary: They spoke separately at a conference in Washington focused on a “pro-human” approach to AI
articles.content:
WASHINGTON — Democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders and conservative firebrand Steve Bannon have joined a bipartisan group of lawmakers in demanding government oversight of artificial intelligence, following warnings by several AI experts that the evolving technology poses potentially catastrophic risks, including human extinction.
The unlikely alliance emerged Tuesday at a conference in Washington focused on a “pro-human” approach to AI, where Sanders and Bannon, appearing separately, both raised alarm over the pace of AI development.
“AI companies are losing control of the technology,” said Sanders, I-Vt.
“We need time,” Bannon said. “And this is not regulation. This is going to have to be executive action.”
Joining the duo were other lawmakers from both parties, along with celebrities, including Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Ashley Judd.
Concerns about AI range from economic worries that it will replace jobs and drive up electricity rates to existential fears that it could pose a threat to humanity.
In July, those fears intensified after a swarm of AI agents operated by OpenAI escaped their test environment and hacked the technology firm Hugging Face.
Last week, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the AI lab Anthropic, drew widespread attention with a social media post announcing his resignation and warning: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”
Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei joined the chorus, calling for an AI slowdown. Other industry leaders, including Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, soon followed.
“The world where things go very seriously wrong is the world in which we just keep going without safeguards — or without enough time,” Amodei said.
Sanders said Congress “under both Democrat and Republican control have been asleep at the wheel.”
But President Donald Trump pushed back in a torrent of posts this week, calling the AI backlash a hoax. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., agreed, saying Tuesday he believes companies can “self-regulate.”
“What the president is saying is you’re not going to be dead in 10 years. OK? That’s a hoax,” Johnson said.
In recent days, lawmakers have introduced a flurry of new bills on Capitol Hill focused on AI safety, some with bipartisan support. But it remains unclear whether there is the political will to pass them.

articles.title: Notre Dame, MTI receive $4.6 million to develop railroad welding technology
articles.description: Notre Dame, MTI receive $4.6 million to develop railroad welding technology WSBT
articles.description_html: Notre Dame, MTI receive $4.6 million to develop railroad welding technology  WSBT
articles.article_title: Notre Dame, MTI receive $4.6 million to develop railroad welding technology
articles.heading: Notre Dame, MTI receive $4.6 million to develop railroad welding technology
articles.summary: Notre Dame and South Bend-based MTI are getting $4.6 million in federal funding to develop new railroad welding technology.The three-year project will develop a
articles.content:
Notre Dame, MTI receive $4.6 million to develop railroad welding technology
SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WSBT) — Notre Dame and South Bend-based MTI are getting $4.6 million in federal funding to develop new railroad welding technology.
The three-year project will develop and test a new low-force friction-welding process for continuous welded rail.
Notre Dame researchers and South Bend-based Manufacturing Technology, Inc. are combining their expertise to develop a new way to join railroad tracks, with the goal of making rail travel safer and more efficient.
“I think it's just a lot of excitement from our side in terms of transitioning academic research or interfacing academic research with actual applications in a way that will hopefully make people's lives better,” said Ed Kinzel, Professor of aerospace and mechanical engineering at ND.
The project is still in its early stages, but Notre Dame students are already taking part, gaining hands-on experience as researchers study how the welding process can be improved.
“Our goal is to be able to provide a welding technique that minimizes the loss of life for the rail when they go to repair it, or gives them a better life expectancy when they install new rail to begin with,” said Daniel Adams, CEO and President of MTI
For students, it is a chance to help shape new technology. For the rail industry, supporters say it could mean safer tracks and fewer costly repairs.
“And so, our students are being very excited to learn more about railways and how the manufacturing technology and particularly from these, the student who’s leading this effort, how controls can potentially affect the rail, and change the outcome of what this welding operation is,” Continues Kinzel.
“So, what the technology will do is one, they'll make it safer because a lot of the derailments that you see in the news happen as a result of poor joints. So, weld failures in the field can cause a train to derail,” said Adams.
And while rail-joint failures are only one possible cause of derailments, the investment comes on the heels of 687 Class I railroad derailments in 2025.
MTI and Notre Dame say they are eager to develop stronger, longer-lasting methods.

articles.content:
Lexington traffic engineers test new technology to improve traffic flow across the city
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Lexington city staff are trying to understand traffic flow within the city, testing several technologies to identify where changes can be made.
The Division of Traffic Engineering uses technology to analyze traffic flow and congestion throughout the city. Staff presented those tools to the Environmental Quality and Public Works Committee this week. Director Jeff Neal said the goal is to identify patterns in order to improve efficiency.
For example, staff can use traffic camera recordings to verify complaints about signal timing.
“This has become a game changer in some ways, like if somebody calls in and says, ‘I was sitting here at this intersection for 5 minutes,’ if we have a camera there, we can pull it up, rewind the video, and see if they actually were there,” Neal said.
Testing what works
Within the past year, Traffic Engineering launched several pilot programs, some free and some paid for through a federal grant, to gain more insight into traffic patterns. Neal said the division has already identified one tool that hasn’t been helpful.
“We are testing them out to see which ones we like the best, which ones are affordable, and which ones give us the most bang for the buck. So we’ll see how these go; I think we’ll know for sure in the next 6 months or so,” Neal said.
Lexington’s traffic engineering staff have access to more than 700 different street camera streams that are continuously recorded, including multiple angles at the same intersection. Neal said staff only actively monitor the cameras during morning and afternoon rush hours, though the recordings allow them to go back and review footage if someone calls in with a complaint.
Not the same as Flock cameras
Council member Emma Curtis, who represents District 4, clarified how the traffic engineering cameras differ from Flock cameras used for police enforcement.
“It’s an entirely separate conversation about how we can utilize data to make our streets safer and more efficient, not a question of enforcement from any other sort of criminal activity, and it does not have anything to do with our city’s contract with Flock or the usage of automated license plate readers,” Curtis said.
Committee Chairman Dave Sevigny added that when it comes to law enforcement, Traffic Engineering can identify where speeding and red-light violations are taking place and share that information with police so officers know where more patrolling could help.

articles.summary: We examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI development
articles.content: Experts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis. Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExperts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis. Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesExplainerCould AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksWe examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI developmentThere have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop.Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them.‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University.It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”.With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said.Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said.Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still.Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system.One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios.“These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.“If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work.Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet.Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”.'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time. This was just the match that lit the fire' – Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and the world’s richest person, 10 September 2026Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments put restrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime?The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”.Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals.View image in fullscreenElon Musk, CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have said AI firms should slow down AI development. Composite: Fabrice Coffrini; Julien de Rosa; Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesOthers think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said.“If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said. 'A superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale' to nuclear weapons – Des Browne, former UK defence secretary, 7 September 2026“Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.”But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Project forecasts such a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman has said it could take until 2035.The Rand Corporation concluded AI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems.AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons warns “cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making.'You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down' – Bernie Sanders, Democrat senator for Vermont, 10 September 2026Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology.The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. He claimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres “and the only one that is happy about it is China”.Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going.“The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.”'There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this. If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter' – Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, 8 September 2026The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown.This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications.Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”.Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging Face suggested Amodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models.These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. They pose a serious threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s path to profitability, and there are hundreds of billions of dollars on the line.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicEthicsSam AltmanElon MuskOpenAIDatacentresexplainersShareReuse this content
articles.content_html:
There have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop.

Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them.

‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026

Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University.

It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”.

With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said.

Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said.

Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still.

Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage.

“The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”

‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026

This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system.

One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios.

“These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.

“If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work.

Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet.

Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”.

'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time. This was just the match that lit the fire' – Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and the world’s richest person, 10 September 2026

Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments put restrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime?

The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”.

Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals.

Others think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said.

“If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said.

'A superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale' to nuclear weapons – Des Browne, former UK defence secretary, 7 September 2026

“Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.”

But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Project forecasts such a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman has said it could take until 2035.

The Rand Corporation concluded AI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems.

AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike.

The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons warns “cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making.

'You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down' – Bernie Sanders, Democrat senator for Vermont, 10 September 2026

Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology.

The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. He claimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres “and the only one that is happy about it is China”.

Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going.

“The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”

Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.”

'There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this. If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter' – Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, 8 September 2026

The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown.

This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications.

Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”.

Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging Face suggested Amodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models.

These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. They pose a serious threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s path to profitability, and there are hundreds of billions of dollars on the line.

articles.title: ACCESS update: CMS boosts coverage for heart failure technologies
articles.description: ACCESS update: CMS boosts coverage for heart failure technologies Cardiovascular Business
articles.description_html: ACCESS update: CMS boosts coverage for heart failure technologies  Cardiovascular Business
articles.article_title: ACCESS update: CMS boosts coverage for heart failure technologies
articles.heading: ACCESS update: CMS boosts coverage for heart failure technologies
articles.summary: The ACCESS model is designed help more patients get treated and managed with advanced technologies. In addition to heart failure, improved coverage has been announced for Medicare beneficiaries battling COPD, substance use disorders and nicotine dependence.
articles.content:
ACCESS update: CMS boosts coverage for heart failure technologies
In an effort to combat the increasing costs of care associated with heart failure, the Centers of Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is expanding coverage for technology that monitors patients at home through the Advancing Chronic Care with Effective, Scalable Solutions (ACCESS) Model.
Starting in the spring of 2027, CMS will expand the existing ACCESS initiative to offer technology to better monitor Medicare beneficiaries and keep them out of hospitals and attempt to lower healthcare expenditures by managing conditions at home. In addition to heart failure, ACCESS is also focused on improving care for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), substance use disorders and nicotine dependence.
For heart failure, the program will use continuous monitoring to try and attain measurable improvements in function, symptom management and quality of life. Heart failure management and readmissions are both associated with a significant amount of Medicare spending. This is among several efforts to try and reduce those costs.
The ACCESS model is designed to modernize CMS and create a digital health ecosystem that allows Medicare beneficiaries greater access to innovative health technologies. ACCESS uses a new payment approach that emphasizes achieving specified health outcomes and value-based medicine over paying for individual services.
The ACCESS model began July 5, 2026, offering new care options for people with chronic conditions affecting more than two-thirds of people with Medicare. These include high blood pressure, diabetes, chronic musculoskeletal pain and depression. Three out of four people with Medicare qualify for at least one ACCESS track. The program is scheduled to run for 10 years.
ACCESS was created because people with Original Medicare historically lacked a payment option to adequately support novel technology-supported care. Instead, it focused on fee-for-service payments for a defined set of activities. ACCESS removes these Medicare payment barriers for patients who qualify.
CMS said ACCESS will test a new outcome-aligned payment (OAP) option for Medicare-enrolled care organizations. It emphasizes outcomes over volume of care episodes, enabling clinicians to offer innovative technology-supported care that improves patient health.
Participating organizations will receive recurring payments for managing patients’ conditions, and full payment amounts will be tied to achieving measurable health outcomes. The model focuses on clinical improvement or control of a condition determined by each patient's baseline and measurements at specified periods of time that should show improvements.
“We built ACCESS because too many people with chronic conditions were falling through the cracks between appointments,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, MD, a former cardiac surgeon, said in a statement. “ACCESS is one of the tools we are using to bring healthcare into the digital age, giving patients and their providers greater access to AI-enabled technologies, remote monitoring, connected devices, and other innovative tools that can help identify problems earlier and improve care. This latest expansion of the program will help more Americans get the care they need and reward providers who deliver actual results.”
Current cardio-kidney metabolic coverage
As of July 5 in cardiology, ACCESS began coverage for qualifying conditions of cardio-kidney metabolic (CKM) disorders. Under early CKM (eCKM) this includes hypertension, or two or more of the following: dyslipidemia, overweight with central obesity and prediabetes. Outcome measures include lowering blood pressure, LDL-C, HbA1c and weight. Patients either receive the benefit free from CMS or with a $6 monthly payment.
CKM patients include those with diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease (stage 3a/3b), and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Outcome measures monitored include blood pressure, LDL-C, HbA1c, weight, uACR, and eGFR. Patients either get the services for free or with a $7 per month fee.
For physicians, the CMS annual payment allowed for eCKM is $360 during the initial period and $180 for a follow-on period. For CKM, it is $420 during the initial period and $210 for follow-on period. For beneficiaries residing in rural areas, CMS will provide an additional fixed payment of $15 to offset higher operational costs related to connected device distribution and support.
However, CMS said in its ACCESS guidance that these allowed amounts do not reflect potential downward payment adjustments resulting from the clinical outcome adjustment or substitute spend adjustment applied to the Medicare paid amount.
Find more detailed information on the payment model.
CMS ACCESS heart failure monitoring coverage begins in 2027
Starting April 1, 2027, CMS will expand ACCESS coverage for heart failure remote monitoring technologies. According to the CMS ACCESS website, these include telehealth software to help patients interact with their healthcare providers from anywhere and wearable devices to continuously monitor sleep, heart rate, movement, blood sugar and other functions. Also covered are apps that coach people to make lifestyle changes that can benefit both their behavioral and physical health.
CMS said these services will be especially valuable for people in communities with limited local care options, like those residing in rural areas.

“We built ACCESS because too many people with chronic conditions were falling through the cracks between appointments,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, MD, a former cardiac surgeon, said in a statement. “ACCESS is one of the tools we are using to bring healthcare into the digital age, giving patients and their providers greater access to AI-enabled technologies, remote monitoring, connected devices, and other innovative tools that can help identify problems earlier and improve care. This latest expansion of the program will help more Americans get the care they need and reward providers who deliver actual results.”

Current cardio-kidney metabolic coverage

As of July 5 in cardiology, ACCESS began coverage for qualifying conditions of cardio-kidney metabolic (CKM) disorders. Under early CKM (eCKM) this includes hypertension, or two or more of the following: dyslipidemia, overweight with central obesity and prediabetes. Outcome measures include lowering blood pressure, LDL-C, HbA1c and weight. Patients either receive the benefit free from CMS or with a $6 monthly payment.

CKM patients include those with diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease (stage 3a/3b), and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Outcome measures monitored include blood pressure, LDL-C, HbA1c, weight, uACR, and eGFR. Patients either get the services for free or with a $7 per month fee.

For physicians, the CMS annual payment allowed for eCKM is $360 during the initial period and $180 for a follow-on period. For CKM, it is $420 during the initial period and $210 for follow-on period. For beneficiaries residing in rural areas, CMS will provide an additional fixed payment of $15 to offset higher operational costs related to connected device distribution and support.

However, CMS said in its ACCESS guidance that these allowed amounts do not reflect potential downward payment adjustments resulting from the clinical outcome adjustment or substitute spend adjustment applied to the Medicare paid amount.

Find more detailed information on the payment model.

CMS ACCESS heart failure monitoring coverage begins in 2027

Starting April 1, 2027, CMS will expand ACCESS coverage for heart failure remote monitoring technologies. According to the CMS ACCESS website, these include telehealth software to help patients interact with their healthcare providers from anywhere and wearable devices to continuously monitor sleep, heart rate, movement, blood sugar and other functions. Also covered are apps that coach people to make lifestyle changes that can benefit both their behavioral and physical health.

CMS said these services will be especially valuable for people in communities with limited local care options, like those residing in rural areas.

authors: COLLIN BINKLEY and JILL COLVIN — Associated Press
articles.summary: First lady Melania Trump visited an elementary school in northwestern North Carolina Tuesday, where she said the U.S. must lead on artificial intelligence. Her trip Tuesday comes as tech and political leaders debate about how best to regulate the AI industry. Prominent tech leaders have said they...
articles.content:
JEFFERSON, N.C. (AP) — First lady Melania Trump visited an elementary school in northwestern North Carolina Tuesday, where she said the U.S. must lead on artificial intelligence as she spoke with elementary school students, teachers and staff about how they're using technology and AI in the classroom.
Her trip to Ashe County on Tuesday came as tech and political leaders debate about how best to regulate AI. Prominent tech leaders have been warning about the dangers of the technology and calling for more oversight, while President Donald Trump on Monday angrily dismissed the idea that more limits are needed, calling it a “hoax.”
Other WRAL Top Stories
Many parents have also expressed alarm about schools' widespread adoption of tablets with access to sites like YouTube even in classrooms with the youngest students.
The first lady visited Mountain View Elementary School in rural Jefferson, which has a focus on using AI, robotics and engineering.
Asked by a reporter about the potential of AI and the growing warnings about it, the first lady said students must learn it for the U.S. to be a global leader.
“I think they need to learn we need to lead,” she said. “Of course they need to be vigilant as well. But this is our future. And we need to guide them and teach them what is available. If not, they will stay behind. And we need to be the first, in the United States, to lead."
Students showed the first lady an AI experiment
The first lady opened her trip by recognizing the two-year anniversary of Hurricane Helene, which kept students out of school for more than 30 days as the community worked to recover. Mountain View's neighborhood flooded and the school was used as an emergency childcare center and later a community distribution site for supplies.
“Your story is incredible,” she told several hundred students, teachers and administrators sitting on the gymnasium floor and bleachers. “North Carolina is the definition of resilience. Toughness in times of adversity is ingrained in the Tar Heel State’s character.”
The first lady was warmly welcomed at the school. A wall of the gym was decorated with a hand-painted banner with purple print that read, “Welcome to Ashe County 1st Lady Melania Trump!” A digital screen in a school hallway welcomed the first lady with cartoon images of a boy and girl waving American flags.
After her remarks, she visited a fifth grade science classroom where she sat with students while a teacher walked them through an experiment simulating pressure changes in the human chest cavity. The students then used AI to generate a video of their model using tablets.
As she observed the lesson, an 11-year-old asked if he could give the first lady a hug. They hugged several times.
She later spent time in the school's media center, where she sat with students building chatbots to research potential future careers and watched them use 3D printers. She joined in as they manipulated robotic arms that buzzed and whirred in the background.
“You can do anything. Anything is possible," she told them. “The sky is the limit, right? Just never give up.”
Melania Trump donated some AI tools to the school district
She also announced that her Be Best initiative would be helping to provide 1,500 students in Ashe County with subscriptions to StudyFetch, an AI learning platform, and that Mountain View Elementary and other schools in the district would be receiving 100 Jetson Nano Developer Kits — small computers for running AI applications.
“Maybe one of you will create the next great robot," she said in her remarks. “And if you do, make sure you bring it to the White House to show me.”
The first lady made headlines earlier this year when she walked into a White House event with a humanoid robot at a summit she hosted with other first spouses about empowering children with technology.
Last September, at a meeting of a White House task force on AI in education, she noted that the technology was boosting economic growth but also expressed some caution.
“As leaders and parents, we must manage AI’s growth responsibly," she said at last year's event. “During this primitive stage, it is our duty to treat AI as we would our own children — empowering, but with watchful guidance.”
Technology in education is one of the first lady's signature issues, along with advocacy for foster children, and lobbying Congress to pass the “Take It Down Act” making revenge porn a crime.
It’s the first lady’s fourth trip to North Carolina since 2025. She accompanied the president to meet families affected by Hurricane Helene at the beginning of his term, and subsequently spent time with military families in other parts of the state.
The state is home to one of the most closely watched Senate races of the November midterm elections, pitting Michael Whatley, a former chairman of the Republican National Committee, against Democrat Roy Cooper, a former governor. The president is traveling to Gastonia in the southern part of the state on Wednesday for a rally for Whatley.
___ Colvin reported from New York.

articles.summary: The visit came as policymakers and technology leaders continue to debate how artificial intelligence should be governed and used, including in schools.
articles.content:
First lady Melania Trump visits North Carolina school to see AI technology in action
ASHE COUNTY, N.C. (TNND) — First lady Melania Trump visited an elementary school in northwestern North Carolina on Tuesday, highlighting the use of artificial intelligence, robotics and engineering in the classroom.
Trump toured Mountain View Elementary School in Jefferson, a rural Ashe County school that has embraced technology-focused learning. The visit came as policymakers and technology leaders continue to debate how artificial intelligence should be governed and used, including in schools.
She began by recognizing the community’s recovery from Hurricane Helene, which closed schools for more than 30 days. The school became a distribution center after flooding affected the surrounding neighborhood.
“North Carolina is the definition of resilience,” Trump told students and administrators, praising the community’s response to the disaster.
Trump announced that her Be Best initiative and Nvidia will provide 1,500 Ashe County students with subscriptions to StudyFetch, an AI-based learning platform. Mountain View Elementary and other district schools will also receive 100 Jetson Nano Developer Kits, small computers designed to run AI applications.
“Maybe one of you will create the next great robot,” she told students, inviting them to bring it to the White House if they do.
Technology in education has become one of the first lady’s primary policy interests, alongside her work supporting foster youth and her advocacy for the Take It Down Act, which criminalized the distribution of nonconsensual intimate images.
Trump has previously urged caution as artificial intelligence expands in classrooms. At a White House education event last year, she said the technology should be developed with "watchful guidance."
The stop marked her fourth trip to North Carolina since 2025. Her visit also comes one day before President Donald Trump is scheduled to hold a rally in Gastonia for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper in the November midterm election.
____________
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Microscopic alien technology may be hidden in moon dust, scientists say
articles.description: Microscopic alien technology may be hidden in moon dust, scientists say Space
articles.description_html: Microscopic alien technology may be hidden in moon dust, scientists say  Space
articles.article_title: Microscopic alien technology may be hidden in moon dust, scientists say
articles.heading: Microscopic alien technology may be hidden in moon dust, scientists say
articles.summary: "Searching for these microscopic technosignatures is now scientifically testable."
articles.content:
Microscopic alien technology may be hidden in moon dust, scientists say
"Searching for these microscopic technosignatures is now scientifically testable."
Could we find alien technology embedded in moon dust?
The bold idea, not yet peer-reviewed, suggests checking out the lunar surface for "microscopic technosignatures." The SETI Institute — or the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence Institute — describes these technosignatures as "tiny engineered particles" that may have come from interstellar space before settling on the moon.
The institute recently highlighted a paper on the topic, published on arxiv in August, and added the research is undergoing peer review for consideration in the International Journal of Astrobiology. The study is led by SETI Institute Affiliate Scientist Lewis Pinault.
"The moon has been quietly accumulating material from space for billions of years, much of it likely billions of years older than the moon itself," said Pinault in a statement. "We're asking whether that ancient collection might contain microscopic traces of technologies that existed long before humans ever looked up at the sky."
Even if no aliens turn out to be there, the search could help advance models of how dust goes through interstellar space, as well as effects on lunar geology or impact science, the institute added.
"The study reports no evidence of extraterrestrial technology," the institute added in the statement. "Instead, it demonstrates that searching for these microscopic technosignatures is now scientifically testable."
That's in large part because the NASA-led Artemis program, which will ultimately bring astronauts to the moon, as well as China's Chang'e robotic series, would provide opportunities to return samples, the institute said. (China is also eyeing bringing its taikonauts to the moon by 2030.)
SETI is best known for looking for artificial radio signatures in space that may have come from extraterrestrials. This new study, the institute added, is focusing more on past alien communities that may have preserved their knowledge in "durable particles," even if the communities are no longer in existence.
The study examines how these particles could (in theory) move from star to star, stay viable over long distances and periods, embed themselves in the lunar surface and then — if humans could find them — use AI-assisted imaging, materials analysis and microscopy to take a closer look, among other techniques.
Helping in that search is the environment of the moon itself, which — compared with Earth, at least — has slow-moving geology. As the institute points out, the surface has no flowing water or substantial atmosphere like our planet does. What's more, the moon has picked up dust in its environment for about four billion years (from not long after the solar system was formed 4.5 billion years ago), presenting a potential archive of dust in the solar system and interstellar space.
"The researchers argue that if advanced civilizations produce durable microscopic debris — whether intentionally or as a byproduct of space exploration or large-scale engineering — a tiny fraction of those particles could eventually become embedded in the lunar regolith," the institute stated.
The goal is to start these studies with about 35 cubic feet (one cubic meter) of lunar regolith, which is maybe the equivalent size of a fridge. Researchers would try out a series of careful investigations using multiple tools to "begin placing meaningful limits on the amount of durable artificial material produced by technological civilizations over the history of the Milky Way."
And as mentioned, even if this small sample doesn't turn up technosignatures, the researchers say the work is still important. It's another way to search for "extraterrestrial artifacts," to look at various aspects of solar system science, and to try out newer tools for examining moon samples that weren't available in the Apollo years.
"This is a novel addition to the search methodologies applied to seeking evidence of technology as a proxy for life and intelligence beyond our solar system and we are excited at the prospect of bringing this to fruition," stated Bill Diamond, SETI Institute president and CEO.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

That's in large part because the NASA-led Artemis program, which will ultimately bring astronauts to the moon, as well as China's Chang'e robotic series, would provide opportunities to return samples, the institute said. (China is also eyeing bringing its taikonauts to the moon by 2030.)

SETI is best known for looking for artificial radio signatures in space that may have come from extraterrestrials. This new study, the institute added, is focusing more on past alien communities that may have preserved their knowledge in "durable particles," even if the communities are no longer in existence.

The study examines how these particles could (in theory) move from star to star, stay viable over long distances and periods, embed themselves in the lunar surface and then — if humans could find them — use AI-assisted imaging, materials analysis and microscopy to take a closer look, among other techniques.

Helping in that search is the environment of the moon itself, which — compared with Earth, at least — has slow-moving geology. As the institute points out, the surface has no flowing water or substantial atmosphere like our planet does. What's more, the moon has picked up dust in its environment for about four billion years (from not long after the solar system was formed 4.5 billion years ago), presenting a potential archive of dust in the solar system and interstellar space.

"The researchers argue that if advanced civilizations produce durable microscopic debris — whether intentionally or as a byproduct of space exploration or large-scale engineering — a tiny fraction of those particles could eventually become embedded in the lunar regolith," the institute stated.

The goal is to start these studies with about 35 cubic feet (one cubic meter) of lunar regolith, which is maybe the equivalent size of a fridge. Researchers would try out a series of careful investigations using multiple tools to "begin placing meaningful limits on the amount of durable artificial material produced by technological civilizations over the history of the Milky Way."

And as mentioned, even if this small sample doesn't turn up technosignatures, the researchers say the work is still important. It's another way to search for "extraterrestrial artifacts," to look at various aspects of solar system science, and to try out newer tools for examining moon samples that weren't available in the Apollo years.

"This is a novel addition to the search methodologies applied to seeking evidence of technology as a proxy for life and intelligence beyond our solar system and we are excited at the prospect of bringing this to fruition," stated Bill Diamond, SETI Institute president and CEO.

articles.summary: RIT access technology research helped create a breakthrough in Google’s new Pixel 11, which converts sign language into text, easing individuals who are de
articles.content:
RIT helps Google develop new technology that converts sign language into text
Everyday communication between deaf and hearing people is now easier
Researchers at Rochester Institute of Technology’s National Technical Institute for the Deaf have collaborated with Google to test new AI technology that converts sign language into text in real time.
That technology, called Sign Language-to-Text (SL2T), is now available as a standard feature on Google Pixel 11 devices, released in August. It represents a significant advancement in accessible communication technology.
“Sign Language-to-Text has the potential to expand communication access and empower deaf individuals around the world,” said Gary Behm, director of the NTID Center on Access Technology, which collaborated with Google on the project for the past four years by collecting data and offering feedback. “This really is a breakthrough.”
Behm, who is deaf and uses American Sign Language, recalls growing up having to carry a pen and paper to help him communicate. Technology evolved over the years to enable typed text conversations on a cell phone. Now, he can turn on the phone’s camera and use sign language, which is automatically turned into text, just as someone who might voice a text message.
SL2T is particularly useful and faster for individuals whose preferred mode of communication is American Sign Language. Just like a speech-to-text message, the user also has the ability to review and edit their text before it is sent.
Google says it spent more than 100,000 hours training SL2T to learn more than 50 international sign languages, about a quarter of that time with American Sign Language, which is not universally used around the world and does not follow English structure. Other than reading the hand shapes, SL2T also reads facial and body movement which often define the concepts used when signing.
And users only need one free hand to sign to the phone for it to convert the movement into letters, words or phrases.
Behm said while the technology works well for everyday encounters, it isn’t meant to be a replacement for qualified human interpreters in medical, legal, educational, or other high-stakes situations.
He credits RIT/NTID alumnus Sam Sepah for his involvement in the project, and helping improve accessibility and strengthen collaboration between the deaf community and Google, where Sepah is lead AI accessibility research program manager.
“Arriving at RIT as a deaf student driven to make a difference, I built a strong foundation in leadership,” said Sepah, who earned a bachelor’s degree in multidisciplinary studies with a foundation of world history and multimedia in 2006, and his master’s degree in 2008 in Human Resources. “Through the incredible support I received there, I gained the skills that eventually led Google to select me to build their Sign Language AI Research team.”
Sepah said the enduring partnership between RIT and Google, and his mentorship from Behm “is building a legacy of global accessibility technology. Together, we are showing families everywhere that with the right educational support and community, a deaf child can truly change the world.”
Sepah, who founded Google DeepMind’s AI Sign Language Advisory Committee, nominated Behm to serve on it to help bring together deaf community leaders, researchers, and subject matter experts to provide guidance on the responsible development, evaluation, and deployment of the SL2T model. The committee will help ensure that new technology with AI-powered communication tools reflects the values, needs, and expectations of the deaf community.
Established by the U.S. Congress in 1965, the National Technical Institute for the Deaf is the first and largest technological college in the world for deaf and hard-of-hearing students. NTID offers associate degree programs for deaf and hard-of-hearing students and provides support and access services for deaf and hard-of-hearing students who study in the other eight colleges of RIT. NTID also offers a certificate in healthcare interpretation, bachelor’s degree programs in sign language interpreting, and community development and inclusive leadership, and master’s degrees in healthcare interpretation and secondary education for individuals interested in teaching deaf and hard-of-hearing students. Deaf and hard-of-hearing students come from all over the United States and around the world to take advantage of the opportunities available to them at RIT/NTID.

articles.title: AirJoule $27M deal could help push water-from-air technology into data centers
articles.description: AirJoule $27M deal could help push water-from-air technology into data centers Facilities Dive
articles.description_html: AirJoule $27M deal could help push water-from-air technology into data centers  Facilities Dive
articles.article_title: AirJoule $27M deal could help push water-from-air technology into data centers
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's facilities management industry news
articles.summary: ts acquisition of data center cooling company BitSink will help it provide an integrated offering to AI and other high-performance computing data centers, the company says.
articles.content:
Dive Brief:
- Water-from-air company AirJoule Technologies on Monday acquired BitSink, an AI data center cooling, electrical distribution and racking infrastructure company for $27 million to expand its reach into the AI and high-performance computing infrastructure market.
- BitSink designs and manufacturers liquid cooling, precision air handling and electrical switchgear for high-density AI compute facilities. AirJoule, through a joint venture with GE Vernova and partnership with Carrier, provides solutions that pull water from humid air.
- BitSink’s closed-loop cooling system makes available the type of low-grade waste heat that AirJoule uses in its water regeneration process, “creating significant integration opportunity between the two product lines, AirJoule said in a release.
Dive Insight:
The acquisition comes at a time when water availability and consumption have become important criteria and considerations for data center development and operations.
AI and high-performance compute data centers are escalating infrastructure requirements. Next generation chips require rack densities beyond the practical limits of air cooling, spurring the need for advanced technologies such as liquid cooling, according to AFCOM’s 2026 State of the Data Center report.
“AI racks draw 40 to 150 kilowatts, compared with 5 to 10 [kW] for a traditional server,” Matt Jare, founder and CEO of AirJoule Technologies Corporation, told Facilities Dive in an email. “That growing rack density has pushed the industry past the practical limits of air cooling and made liquid cooling a requirement.”
Higher rack densities are driving projections that the data center liquid cooling market will balloon from $3.7 billion in 2025 to $11.5 billion in 2030, said AirJoule, citing Bloomberg Intelligence, which also expects direct-to-chip making up almost 90% of liquid-cooling architectures.
BitSink designs, manufactures and installs cooling systems that enable liquid cooling for high-density workloads, including integrated modular data center blocks, per the release.
Liquid-cooled systems are also being designed to run at higher coolant temperatures, with NVIDIA’s latest AI-server architecture, for example, using outdoor dry coolers in a closed loop to reject heat from a 45-degree-Celsius cooling liquid, according to Jare.
”As density keeps climbing, the industry keeps moving toward the architecture that BitSink supports,” Jare said. “Higher loop temperatures make dry heat rejection practical at higher densities, cut water consumption further, and produce more of the waste heat that AirJoule Prime runs on.”
Greater electrical loads are also creating supply chain bottlenecks for switchgear, power distribution and related infrastructure, the release says.
“BitSink manufacturers UL-listed switchboards and control panels, power distribution units and eqiopment racks in the U.S., and it delivers them alongside its cooling systems,” Jare said. “For a facilities team, that means one supplier, one design package and one point of accountability instead of coordinating separate cooling and electrical vendors.”
AirJoule says BitSink gives it an established operating business with U.S. manufacturing capabilities, a portfolio of deployed cooling and electrical infrastructure products and existing customer relationships.
As part of AirJoule Technologies, BitSink will focus on emerging modular and edge deployments as well as a very large base of high-density crypto-mining sites that are being converted to AI and high-performance computing applications, Jare said.
“BitSink already has customer relationships with many Bitcoin miners who need to upgrade their cooling systems as part of this conversion, Jare said. “Over time, there is an opportunity to pair BitSink’s closed-loop liquid cooling with the AirJoule technology so that a single platform can deliver cooling, electrical equipment, and water for the operator.”
“This transaction delivers commercial revenue contribution and substantial long-term potential, while also creating a natural platform to combine BitSink’s cooling technology with our AirJoule atmospheric water generation capabilities into an integrated offering for the AI and HPC data center market,” Stephen Pang, chief financial officer at AirJoule Technologies, said in a statement.
The transaction accelerates AirJoule Technologies’ initiatives to address data center infrastructure demand through its joint venture with GE Vernova. In June, the joint venture commissioned its first AirJoule Prime AWG system, which uses low-grade waste heat to produce about 2,000 liters of distilled water per day, at its manufacturing facility in Newark, Delaware. The system will be deployed in a European data center in the fourth quarter through a partnership with the Net Zero Innovation Hub for Data Centers, it said in its release.
In announcing its first-quarter earnings, AirJoule Technologies said its laying the foundation for initial commercialization this year and for scaled commercial activity in 2027.

articles.description: Building AI to accelerate science and improve lives blog.google
