articles.title: Nebraska law enforcement agencies using opioid settlement money on surveillance technology, tools
articles.description: Nebraska law enforcement agencies using opioid settlement money on surveillance technology, tools Flatwater Free Press
articles.description_html: Nebraska law enforcement agencies using opioid settlement money on surveillance technology, tools  Flatwater Free Press
articles.article_title: Nebraska law enforcement agencies using opioid settlement money on surveillance technology, tools - Flatwater Free Press
articles.heading: Nebraska law enforcement agencies using opioid settlement money on surveillance technology, tools
articles.summary: The historic settlements are intended to address the opioid crisis by preventing further harm and providing services to people who are impacted by opioid use.
articles.content:
At least nine Nebraska counties and cities have used opioid settlement funds – money meant to be used to help the state and its residents recover from the opioid crisis – to buy controversial surveillance technology and other law enforcement tools.
Harlan County’s board gave $15,000 to the county Sheriff’s Office for Flock cameras.
Valley County spent $27,000 on nine Flock cameras of its own.
Police departments in Dakota County, Madison County and Thurston County purchased new police dogs, supplies and training.
The source of those funds: national settlements with manufacturers, pharmacies and distributors of opioids, totaling more than $50 billion. Nebraska has started receiving payments that will eventually add up to more than $150 million over an 18-year period.
The historic settlements are intended to address the opioid crisis by preventing further harm and providing services to people who are impacted by opioid use. But the Flatwater Free Press found a series of purchases by law enforcement agencies across Nebraska using settlement dollars that experts said don’t fit the spirit of the settlements.
Flatwater, in partnership with students at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln’s College of Journalism and Mass Communications, filed public records requests related to opioid settlement spending from all 93 Nebraska counties, along with 16 cities and six behavioral health regions.
Documents showed that counties and cities have spent at least $88,800 of opioid settlement funds on uses related to law enforcement, including the automated license plate readers, SWAT team training and equipment like gas mask holders and THC detection pouches.
Experts say the money should be used for programs that abate the opioid crisis: treatment centers, naloxone distribution and housing for people in recovery, for example.
“It’s money that’s designed to make sure that this never happens again and that we can provide desperately needed services to people who are directly impacted by the opioid crisis today,” said Brandon Marshall, professor of epidemiology at Brown University School of Public Health.
The funds are being distributed across every state in the country as a result of nationwide legal settlements in 2021 and 2022 between state attorneys general and opioid manufacturers and distributors, including Johnson & Johnson, Walmart and Walgreens.
In Nebraska, 85% of opioid settlement funds go into the state’s Opioid Recovery Fund, managed by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services. That fund is set up to distribute money to individual programs through formal grant processes and to Nebraska’s behavioral health regions.
The other 15% is being paid directly to Nebraska counties and 16 largest cities, based on population.
Once settlement money reaches the county and city budgets, there is little oversight tracking how it’s spent.
Contracting with Flock
Harlan and Valley counties have spent more than $40,000 combined on contracts with Flock Safety, a company that makes automatic license plate reader cameras.
Valley County has faced backlash from residents about Flock, and a city within the county recently voted unanimously to ban the cameras. But the county thus far has kept its other cameras.
Each of the nine cameras that Valley County bought cost $3,000. Flock charged another $10,000 in installation and upgrade fees, which was paid from the Sheriff’s Office’s budget rather than opioid settlement funds.
Valley County Sheriff David Scheideler said Flock cameras are a justified use of opioid funds because they can be used to track vehicles used for illegal drug trafficking.
It’s hard to say if the cameras have prevented drug trafficking yet, Scheideler said, but his office is building ongoing cases.
Documents show that Harlan County’s contract with Flock for $15,000 was paid entirely with opioid settlement funds.
Harlan County Sheriff Jesse Langley said he didn’t ask the Harlan County Board of Supervisors to use opioid settlement funds on the contract, but he did present multiple scenarios where Flock cameras could be used, including for drug trafficking interdiction.
“I presented a contract to the board for the Flock cameras,” Langley said. “However, the board made the suggestion of where to spend the money, and they made the suggestion of the opioid recovery fund.”
Members of the Harlan County Board of Supervisors did not respond to requests for comment.
Flatwater Free Press also reached out to four other sheriff’s offices who spent settlement money, and they did not respond. Nebraska State Patrol deferred questions about law enforcement uses of opioid settlement funds to the Department of Health and Human Services.
The cameras have been a positive for Harlan County, Langley said. His deputies have used them to support cases, but only when they had developed probable cause.
Researchers have seen no evidence suggesting that public surveillance supports any public health role in preventing opioid-related harm, said Tyler Varisco, director of the University of Texas’s Pharmacy Addictions Research & Medicine Program.
“It’s difficult to believe that Flock or other technology would even be useful even in preventing the sale of opioids,” Varisco said. “I can’t think of a potential role for surveillance technology in this area.”
Nebraska’s Attorney General’s Office, which led Nebraska’s part in the national opioid lawsuits, specifies that funds “received by any municipality or county must be used for abatement purposes as defined by the agreements.”
The settlement agreements outlined a guide for allowable opioid remediation uses in a document called Exhibit E, said Mary Ann Borgeson, Douglas County commissioner and vice chairperson of the Nebraska Opioid Remediation Advisory Committee.
Recommended uses of opioid funds for law enforcement include education for first responders handling drugs, awareness training about medication-assisted treatment like methadone, supporting co-responder programs for substance use-related 911 calls and naloxone training for first responders.
Borgeson said she was surprised that law enforcement agencies had purchased Flock cameras with settlement funds, and she doubts that fits into the settlement’s uses.
“Of course, the more I learn about Flock cameras, the less I am supportive of them,” Borgeson said. “But with opioid monies, I don’t see where that falls under an approved use of funds under Exhibit E.”
Though the advisory committee oversees and provides recommendations to DHHS and Nebraska’s behavioral health regions, Borgeson said, it has no authority or oversight of the direct payments to cities and counties.
Other law enforcement uses
Flatwater found that the City of Beatrice spent almost $3,000 from its opioid settlement funds on SWAT training and related travel expenses for police officers in 2025.
Police Chief Jay Murphy said in an email that the department determined the training to be within the scope of opioid settlement guidelines because it “partly had to do with the dangers of drugs during search warrants and raids.”
Murphy said Beatrice is still determining how to best use the rest of the opioid settlement funds it has received so far – more than $95,000.
Multiple agencies have used opioid settlement funds to purchase K-9s and related accessories. Dakota County spent $11,500 out of the settlement funds and had a $2,000 match from a foundation. Thurston County spent about $21,000 on a K-9, vet exam, supplies, equipment and two weeks of training with associated lodging and meal reimbursements.
Borgeson also questions how K-9s fit in the settlement guidelines.
“The (behavioral health) regions have been utilizing it more for prevention, treatment and programs, which I think are a much better useful use of the funds,” Borgeson said.
Behavioral Health Region 4 also allocated $10,000 of funds to the Madison County sheriff for a K-9. Madison County had sent its opioid settlement funds to its behavioral health region, which provides services for substance use disorders.
The settlement funds are meant to help people impacted by opioids, said Patrick Habecker, a professor with the University of Nebraska-Lincoln’s Rural Drug Addiction Research Center. He doesn’t see a direct line between that goal and these uses of the funds.
In several other states, Marshall said, there are examples of counties and sheriffs using funds for Flock cameras, other surveillance technologies and K-9s.
“I would argue that that is not in the spirit of the agreement,” Marshall said.
Louisiana allocates 20% of the funding off the top to their county sheriffs in their settlement agreement, Marshall said. The sheriffs’ spending is “all over the map,” with some investing in treatment in jails and others purchasing law enforcement equipment.
The spending records show that other municipalities in Nebraska have spent smaller sums of opioid settlement funds on equipment including THC detection pouches, a leg holster for a gas mask and a Zoom Workplace Pro subscription for the probation office.

At least nine Nebraska counties and cities have used opioid settlement funds – money meant to be used to help the state and its residents recover from the opioid crisis – to buy controversial surveillance technology and other law enforcement tools.

Harlan County’s board gave $15,000 to the county Sheriff’s Office for Flock cameras.

Valley County spent $27,000 on nine Flock cameras of its own.

Police departments in Dakota County, Madison County and Thurston County purchased new police dogs, supplies and training.

The source of those funds: national settlements with manufacturers, pharmacies and distributors of opioids, totaling more than $50 billion. Nebraska has started receiving payments that will eventually add up to more than $150 million over an 18-year period.

The historic settlements are intended to address the opioid crisis by preventing further harm and providing services to people who are impacted by opioid use. But the Flatwater Free Press found a series of purchases by law enforcement agencies across Nebraska using settlement dollars that experts said don’t fit the spirit of the settlements.

Flatwater, in partnership with students at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln’s College of Journalism and Mass Communications, filed public records requests related to opioid settlement spending from all 93 Nebraska counties, along with 16 cities and six behavioral health regions.

Documents showed that counties and cities have spent at least $88,800 of opioid settlement funds on uses related to law enforcement, including the automated license plate readers, SWAT team training and equipment like gas mask holders and THC detection pouches.

Experts say the money should be used for programs that abate the opioid crisis: treatment centers, naloxone distribution and housing for people in recovery, for example.

“It’s money that’s designed to make sure that this never happens again and that we can provide desperately needed services to people who are directly impacted by the opioid crisis today,” said Brandon Marshall, professor of epidemiology at Brown University School of Public Health.

The funds are being distributed across every state in the country as a result of nationwide legal settlements in 2021 and 2022 between state attorneys general and opioid manufacturers and distributors, including Johnson & Johnson, Walmart and Walgreens.

In Nebraska, 85% of opioid settlement funds go into the state’s Opioid Recovery Fund, managed by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services. That fund is set up to distribute money to individual programs through formal grant processes and to Nebraska’s behavioral health regions.

The other 15% is being paid directly to Nebraska counties and 16 largest cities, based on population.

Once settlement money reaches the county and city budgets, there is little oversight tracking how it’s spent.

Contracting with Flock

Harlan and Valley counties have spent more than $40,000 combined on contracts with Flock Safety, a company that makes automatic license plate reader cameras.

Valley County has faced backlash from residents about Flock, and a city within the county recently voted unanimously to ban the cameras. But the county thus far has kept its other cameras.

Each of the nine cameras that Valley County bought cost $3,000. Flock charged another $10,000 in installation and upgrade fees, which was paid from the Sheriff’s Office’s budget rather than opioid settlement funds.

Valley County Sheriff David Scheideler said Flock cameras are a justified use of opioid funds because they can be used to track vehicles used for illegal drug trafficking.

It’s hard to say if the cameras have prevented drug trafficking yet, Scheideler said, but his office is building ongoing cases.

Documents show that Harlan County’s contract with Flock for $15,000 was paid entirely with opioid settlement funds.

Harlan County Sheriff Jesse Langley said he didn’t ask the Harlan County Board of Supervisors to use opioid settlement funds on the contract, but he did present multiple scenarios where Flock cameras could be used, including for drug trafficking interdiction.

“I presented a contract to the board for the Flock cameras,” Langley said. “However, the board made the suggestion of where to spend the money, and they made the suggestion of the opioid recovery fund.”

Members of the Harlan County Board of Supervisors did not respond to requests for comment.

Flatwater Free Press also reached out to four other sheriff’s offices who spent settlement money, and they did not respond. Nebraska State Patrol deferred questions about law enforcement uses of opioid settlement funds to the Department of Health and Human Services.

The cameras have been a positive for Harlan County, Langley said. His deputies have used them to support cases, but only when they had developed probable cause.

Researchers have seen no evidence suggesting that public surveillance supports any public health role in preventing opioid-related harm, said Tyler Varisco, director of the University of Texas’s Pharmacy Addictions Research & Medicine Program.

“It’s difficult to believe that Flock or other technology would even be useful even in preventing the sale of opioids,” Varisco said. “I can’t think of a potential role for surveillance technology in this area.”

Nebraska’s Attorney General’s Office, which led Nebraska’s part in the national opioid lawsuits, specifies that funds “received by any municipality or county must be used for abatement purposes as defined by the agreements.”

The settlement agreements outlined a guide for allowable opioid remediation uses in a document called Exhibit E, said Mary Ann Borgeson, Douglas County commissioner and vice chairperson of the Nebraska Opioid Remediation Advisory Committee.

Recommended uses of opioid funds for law enforcement include education for first responders handling drugs, awareness training about medication-assisted treatment like methadone, supporting co-responder programs for substance use-related 911 calls and naloxone training for first responders.

Borgeson said she was surprised that law enforcement agencies had purchased Flock cameras with settlement funds, and she doubts that fits into the settlement’s uses.

“Of course, the more I learn about Flock cameras, the less I am supportive of them,” Borgeson said. “But with opioid monies, I don’t see where that falls under an approved use of funds under Exhibit E.”

Though the advisory committee oversees and provides recommendations to DHHS and Nebraska’s behavioral health regions, Borgeson said, it has no authority or oversight of the direct payments to cities and counties.

Other law enforcement uses

Flatwater found that the City of Beatrice spent almost $3,000 from its opioid settlement funds on SWAT training and related travel expenses for police officers in 2025.

Police Chief Jay Murphy said in an email that the department determined the training to be within the scope of opioid settlement guidelines because it “partly had to do with the dangers of drugs during search warrants and raids.”

Murphy said Beatrice is still determining how to best use the rest of the opioid settlement funds it has received so far – more than $95,000.

Multiple agencies have used opioid settlement funds to purchase K-9s and related accessories. Dakota County spent $11,500 out of the settlement funds and had a $2,000 match from a foundation. Thurston County spent about $21,000 on a K-9, vet exam, supplies, equipment and two weeks of training with associated lodging and meal reimbursements.

Borgeson also questions how K-9s fit in the settlement guidelines.

“The (behavioral health) regions have been utilizing it more for prevention, treatment and programs, which I think are a much better useful use of the funds,” Borgeson said.

Behavioral Health Region 4 also allocated $10,000 of funds to the Madison County sheriff for a K-9. Madison County had sent its opioid settlement funds to its behavioral health region, which provides services for substance use disorders.

The settlement funds are meant to help people impacted by opioids, said Patrick Habecker, a professor with the University of Nebraska-Lincoln’s Rural Drug Addiction Research Center. He doesn’t see a direct line between that goal and these uses of the funds.

In several other states, Marshall said, there are examples of counties and sheriffs using funds for Flock cameras, other surveillance technologies and K-9s.

articles.title: Newton Police Department to receive $250,000 in federal funding for training, technology
articles.description: Newton Police Department to receive $250,000 in federal funding for training, technology WRNJ Radio
articles.description_html: Newton Police Department to receive $250,000 in federal funding for training, technology  WRNJ Radio
articles.article_title: Newton Police Department to receive $250,000 in federal funding for training, technology - WRNJ Radio
articles.heading: Newton Police Department to receive $250,000 in federal funding for training, technology
articles.summary: NEWTON, N.J. (Sussex County) — The Newton Police Department will receive $250,000 in federal funding to support advanced counterterrorism training and upgrades to public safety technology and emergency response capabilities. …
articles.content:
Newton Police Department to receive $250,000 in federal funding for training, technology
NEWTON, N.J. (Sussex County) — The Newton Police Department will receive $250,000 in federal funding to support advanced counterterrorism training and upgrades to public safety technology and emergency response capabilities.
Newton Police Chief Daniel Finkle joined U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, Sussex County Prosecutor Daniel Perez and other law enforcement leaders Sept. 9 as Gottheimer announced federal funding for local law enforcement in North Jersey. Gottheimer’s office said Newton will receive $200,000 for a real-time intelligence platform, in addition to $50,000 being provided to each municipality in his district for counterterrorism training.
A portion of Newton’s funding will be used to provide officers with advanced tactical and counterterrorism training to prepare for acts of terrorism, violent incidents at schools and houses of worship, and other threats. Training will also address emerging threats involving artificial intelligence, unmanned aircraft systems and other technologies.
The funding will also support technology intended to improve communication, situational awareness, coordination and integration among emergency responders.
“This $250,000 investment represents a significant step forward for public safety in Newton,” said Newton Police Chief Daniel Finkle. “The threats facing law enforcement and our communities continue to evolve, and our officers need the training and technology necessary to evolve with them. This funding will help prepare our officers to respond safely and effectively to violent incidents in our schools, houses of worship, and throughout our community, while also strengthening our ability to address emerging threats involving drones, artificial intelligence, and other new technologies.”
Finkle said the federal funding will allow the department to access training and technology without placing the entire cost on local taxpayers.
“For a small community, access to this level of training and technology can otherwise be difficult to achieve without placing a significant burden on local taxpayers. These are federal dollars that Congressman Gottheimer helped claw back from Washington so they can be invested right here in Newton and Sussex County. That means better-trained officers, stronger capabilities, and a safer community without asking our local taxpayers to shoulder the entire cost.”
Newton Town Manager Thomas S. Russo Jr. said the funding will allow the town to invest in public safety while reducing the financial impact on taxpayers.
“This funding allows the Town of Newton to make an important investment in public safety while reducing the financial impact on our local taxpayers. Providing our police officers with the training, technology, and resources they need is essential to maintaining the high level of service our residents expect. We are grateful to Congressman Gottheimer for recognizing the needs of local law enforcement and helping bring these federal dollars back to Newton,” Russo said.
Mayor Matthew S. Dickson also commented on the funding.
“This is exactly the kind of partnership that works for a town our size,” said Mayor Matthew S. Dickson. “Federal resources, local decision-making, and a police department that knows this community. I thank Congressman Gottheimer for delivering for Newton, and Chief Finkle for positioning our department to put these dollars to their best use.”

articles.title: AI builders warn the technology threatens humanity. Congress is focused on data centers.
articles.description: AI builders warn the technology threatens humanity. Congress is focused on data centers. MS NOW
articles.description_html: AI builders warn the technology threatens humanity. Congress is focused on data centers.  MS NOW
articles.article_title: AI builders warn the technology threatens humanity. Congress is focused on data centers.
articles.heading: AI builders warn the technology threatens humanity. Congress is focused on data centers.
articles.summary: Congress is a “slow-moving” institution, lawmakers admit. That’s a problem when the technology is evolving almost constantly.
articles.content:
When a senior researcher at the Artificial Intelligence company Anthropic warned last week that there was a roughly 10% chance that AI could kill all humans in the next decade, the American public took notice.
Now, the question is whether Congress will take notice — and, more pressingly, whether it will take action.
Over the weekend, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, wrote on social media that he and his colleagues must “move at the pace of the threat, not our own habits and rhythms” to “take swift bipartisan action that meaningfully reduces AI risk.”
But Congress’ cadence of action usually has two settings: slow and not moving at all. And with lawmakers set to leave town to campaign ahead of the midterms, the chances of major legislation moving quickly on Capitol Hill appear slim.
While Schatz dismissed such a downtrodden perspective on Monday — telling reporters the idea that Congress can’t do anything is “insanity” given the stakes — other lawmakers admit it’s a tall order.
Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., said it’s going to be “really tough” for Congress to act expeditiously on AI, calling lawmakers “totally awol on this.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said he’s hopeful that pressure from constituents back home will drive lawmakers to act, but admitted Congress is, “at best, a slow-moving institution.”
Other lawmakers questioned whether Congress is fully equipped — or remotely willing — to regulate this issue.
Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., told MS NOW that Congress has already shown “they don’t have the capacity” to respond to the AI warnings.
And Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., said he is concerned about the prospect of a “bunch of people up here, literally, who are probably still driving their ‘72 AMC Gremlins” regulating “something they have no idea what it is.”
Of course, there are exceptions to Congress’ usual inertia. In 2008, for instance, lawmakers passed sweeping financial packages — like the Troubled Asset Relief Program, or TARP — to stabilize the financial system.
And in the early stages of the COVID pandemic, Congress passed massive legislation to help families and small businesses navigate the global economic shutdown.
But regulating a sector of the economy before a crisis — rather than throwing money at the problem after the crisis has emerged — has not traditionally been the strong suit of Congress.
Take, for instance, the push to put guardrails around social media, including to protect children — an effort that has languished now for years without resolution.
AI is even more complicated. For one, the technology is evolving at almost incomprehensible speeds. For another, President Donald Trump — whom most Republicans take their cues from — is advocating zero regulation from Congress.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” Trump wrote Monday on social media.
Already, there are some lawmakers who seem to agree with the president — or, at least, are echoing arguments to slow congressional action.
On Monday, Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., urged against a “knee-jerk reaction.” Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., told reporters that lawmakers “need to understand what we’re dealing with” and make sure they take the “right approach.”
And Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., all but dismissed the idea of government intervention. “It’s your responsibility as a business to do the responsible thing,” he said. “Don’t make a product that destroys the world.”
GOP congressional leaders are making similar defenses for inaction.
On Monday, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., warned against moving too fast to regulate AI. “We have to be very careful about this,” Johnson said, adopting an emerging GOP talking point that “we have to maintain our edge over China.”
Johnson said he believes Trump will summon the AI “platform providers” to the White House “this week or early next week” for a meeting.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said lawmakers should try to strike a balance. “A light touch, you don’t want to stifle innovation,” Thune said. “But I think you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated.”
Thune is working with some senators — like Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., and Ted Cruz, R-Texas — on legislation that would require companies to take steps to mitigate catastrophic AI risks. But it’s unlikely anything will come together before the election, or that the legislation will meaningfully address the concerns that senior leaders in the AI sector are expressing.
Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is calling for a classified briefing for senators from the Trump administration about their approach to the technology.
And House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York — who on Monday said the “challenges” presented by the “explosive” growth of AI are not a “hoax” — told MS NOW Congress should “not leave town until something is done decisively to protect the safety and the well-being of the American people.”
(The House is currently slated to leave town to go campaign at the end of the week. The Senate is expected to follow suit shortly thereafter.)
Lawmakers have tossed around ideas on AI for years — and still have not passed anything.

articles.article_title: Public Safety Technology Committee formed amid concerns over police drone use in Milford
articles.heading: Public Safety Technology Committee formed amid concerns over police drone use in Milford
articles.summary: MILFORD, Conn. (WTNH) — First, Flock cameras sparked a contentious debate, but now the community is talking about police drone cameras. Not everybody is happy with all these recording devices…
articles.content:
MILFORD, Conn. (WTNH) — First, Flock cameras sparked a contentious debate, but now the community is talking about police drone cameras. Not everybody is happy with all these recording devices.
Law enforcement cameras were discussed in Milford Monday night. A review committee, officially titled “Public Safety Technology Review Committee,” was created during the meeting.
Milford’s “Drone as First Responder Program” sends a drone to an emergency ahead of first responders to provide situational awareness and intelligence before ground units arrive.
Committee members include Police Chief Keith Mello, Alder Majority Leader Robert Pacelli Jr., Minority Leader Win Smith the 3rd, and community members Scott Marlow, Sarah Wood and James Wyciesjes.
“I chosen because I found them all open-minded and thoughtful, no idea where they stand on cameras, but I trust that they will address the challenges thoughtfully, and every confidence that they’re all good people and they’ll take the time they need to render an informed recommendation to the board, so I have all faith in the world,” Milford Mayor Richard Smith said.
“We are aware of the agenda items. We must await Board’s actions to gauge our response. Our position remains unchanged. The debated technology impacts officer safety. We are advocating for the rank-and-file police officers on the street. We hope the Board continues to make the correct decision,” The Milford Police Department Union.
The mayor does not have a timeline for when the committee will have a recommendation.

articles.heading: More U.S. Workers Fear Losing Their Jobs to Technology
articles.summary: The share of workers who worry that technology could make their jobs obsolete has risen seven percentage points in the past year, to 27%.
articles.content:
Story Highlights

- 27% of U.S. workers fear technology could make their jobs obsolete

- Concern among college graduates is up sharply since 2021

- Tech displacement is now the top job worry among workers under 45

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Twenty-seven percent of U.S. workers, a new high, worry that technology could soon make their jobs obsolete. This is up seven percentage points from last year and roughly double the 13% recorded when Gallup first asked the question in 2017.

The recent increase in worry about the threat of technology contrasts with workers’ largely stable concern over the past year about more traditional threats to employment and income, including layoffs, reduced hours, lower wages and benefit cuts.

The latest findings are from Gallup’s Aug. 3-24 Work and Education survey.

College Gap in Tech Displacement Worry Remains Slim

Over the past year, worry about technological displacement has increased among workers both with and without college degrees. It has risen six points to 25% among college graduates and eight points to 29% among non-college graduates.

The two groups’ similar levels of concern about this risk are relatively new. When Gallup first measured it in 2017, college graduates were less likely than adults without a college degree to worry about technological displacement. But concern among college graduates rose sharply, from 8% in 2021 to 20% in 2023, as generative AI tools such as ChatGPT emerged. After holding steady last year, concern has risen again among both groups this year, keeping the gap slim.

At the same time, displacement fear differs for the two major age groups Gallup examined for this study — essentially those in the first and second halves of their working lives.

In 2017 and 2018, workers aged 18 to 44 and those 45 and older expressed similar levels of worry about technology making their jobs obsolete. Since then, concern among younger workers has grown, while it has been generally steady among older workers. Now, younger workers’ worry exceeds older workers’ by a 15-point margin (34% vs. 19%, respectively).

Traditional Job Worries Remain Relatively Stable

While concern about technology has risen, workers’ worries about four traditional employment and income threats have changed little over the past year.

Concern about benefit reductions remains the most common of these four, cited by 33% of workers. It is followed by concern about layoffs, at 24%, and reduced hours and lower wages, each at 21%. All four measures are near their long-term averages since Gallup began tracking them in 1997.

Historically, these concerns have tracked economic conditions. They were relatively low in the early 2000s, peaked during and just after the Great Recession, declined again between 2017 and 2019 when more Americans rated the economy positively than negatively , and rose sharply during the pandemic in 2020.

At 27%, workers’ worry about technology now exceeds that for three of the four traditional job concerns Gallup tracks.

Younger Workers Express Broadest Job Anxiety

In the latest survey, workers aged 18 to 44 are more likely than those aged 45 and older to worry about most of the job threats tested — all but benefit reduction. This pattern is typical for layoffs and reduced hours, but younger workers’ greater concern about wage cuts this year is relatively uncommon. As usual, workers in the two age groups are roughly equally likely to worry about losing benefits.

Notably, technological displacement now ties losing benefits as the most prevalent job concern among workers under 45: 34% worry about technology making their jobs obsolete, compared with 32% worried about benefit reductions, 30% about layoffs, 29% about reduced hours and 25% about lower wages. Among workers aged 45 and older, benefit reductions remain the leading concern by far, at 34%, while 19% worry about technological displacement.

College graduates are less likely than non-college graduates to worry about layoffs, wage cuts or reduced hours, but they are nearly as likely to worry that technology could make their jobs obsolete. For both groups, benefit reductions remain the top concern.

Bottom Line

Although far from pervasive, workers’ concern about technology making their jobs obsolete continues to rise, now surpassing several traditional job worries that typically shift with the economy. The increase is especially notable among younger and college-educated workers, suggesting that anxiety about technological disruption is reaching groups that may have previously felt more insulated from workplace upheaval. Indeed, a recent Bentley University-Gallup study found that nearly eight in 10 Americans expect AI to reduce the total number of jobs in the country over the next decade.

So far, workers’ growing concern appears to be outpacing actual job displacement due to AI. Recent data show that AI’s overall effect on U.S. employment remains modest, and the latest jobs report showed solid hiring and a steady 4.1% unemployment rate. Still, there are signs of weaker hiring for entry-level and junior workers in occupations most exposed to AI. However, it is yet unknown as to whether employers will choose to replace workers or use technology to refine people’s roles as AI advances. The answer will ultimately determine whether workers’ current anxiety proves justified.

Stay up to date with the latest insights by following @Gallup on X and on Instagram .

Learn more about how the Gallup Poll Social Series works. View complete question responses and trends (PDF download) .

Survey Methods

Results for this Gallup poll are based on telephone interviews conducted by ReconMR Aug. 3-24, 2026, with a random sample of 1,200 adults, aged 18 and older, living in all 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia. For results based on the total sample of national adults, the margin of sampling error is ±4 percentage points at the 95% confidence level. For results based on the total sample of 507 adults who are employed full or part time, the maximum margin of sampling error is ±6 percentage points. All reported margins of sampling error include computed design effects for weighting.

Each sample of national adults includes a minimum quota of 80% cellphone respondents and 20% landline respondents, with additional minimum quotas by time zone within region. Landline and cellular telephone numbers are selected using random-digit-dial methods.

In addition to sampling error, question wording and practical difficulties in conducting surveys can introduce error or bias into the findings of public opinion polls.

articles.title: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race
articles.description: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race theguardian.com
articles.description_html: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race  theguardian.com
articles.article_title: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race
articles.heading: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race
articles.summary: From Stephen Hawking to Jacob Coxon’s viral Anthropic resignation, fears that AI could threaten humanity have shaken the industry without stopping its pursuit
articles.content:
Before an Anthropic researcher resigned and declared human extinction imminent last week, tech leaders and scientists had sounded the alarm about a superintelligent AI ending humanity for over a decade.
The development of artificial intelligence “could spell the end of the human race”, warned professor and astrophysicist Stephen Hawking in 2014 – a little less than a decade before the public got its hands on the generative AI features of the original version of ChatGPT.
It’s a now-familiar warning, echoed across the AI and tech industry by countless employees and CEOs of the leading frontier labs across the US. However, at the time, generative AI was still in its infancy. To the public, the idea that the technology could perform many of the tasks it can today, much less become super intelligent and take over the world, felt largely hypothetical, if not entirely a thing of science fiction.
Every few years, a schism occurs within AI. Teams of researchers and tech leaders issue somber warnings about the dangers of AI built irresponsibly. Rather than push for a pause on any development, a faction of researchers breaks away to create a new AI company.
However, no moment has created as many reverberations across the industry as the now-viral resignation of Anthropic safety researcher, Jacob Coxon, who tweeted on 9 September that Anthropic and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving super intelligence and gambling with our lives”. His concerns were echoed by dozens of staffers from Anthropic, OpenAI and other competing firms.
Days later, the CEOs of the leading US AI firms answered a call from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow down what he called a “reckless” approach to creating AI.
“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “I’ve written a lot about them too. They include the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyber-attacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute.”
While there’s often scant detail and even less hard evidence provided for the ways AI could lead to the ultimate doomsday scenario, that specter has loomed large over the technology’s development.
Hawking’s fear was that AI would become so advanced that it would redesign itself, and humans “who are limited by slow biological evolution” wouldn’t be able to compete “and would be superseded”, he said in an interview with the BBC.
Google was the biggest household name in the field at the time, particularly after acquiring a two-year-old AI startup, DeepMind, for $650m in January 2014. But Google and other firms like it weren’t building AI responsibly enough, according to Elon Musk and Sam Altman. The threat that AI could be developed in a way that could be dangerous for humanity was so pervasive, they claimed, that they co-founded a nonprofit dedicated to building it safely, OpenAI, in 2015.
OpenAI’s stated mission was to “advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return”. But even before there were clear consumer use cases for more rudimentary versions of the technology, both Musk and Altman were already motivated by competition.
“Been thinking a lot about whether it’s possible to stop humanity from developing AI. I think the answer is almost definitely not,” Altman wrote in 2015 in an email to Musk, which was released as part of Musk’s 2024 lawsuit against OpenAI. “If it’s going to happen anyway, it seems like it would be good for someone other than Google to do it first.”
In the intervening years, priorities within OpenAI shifted away from safety, some employees claimed. In 2021, several employees focused on AI ethics and alignment at OpenAI left the firm. They argued the company had started to prioritize rapid commercial development over safety.
Those employees created another company: Anthropic.
Founded by siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic pitches itself as an “AI safety and research company” with a familiar mission: Developing and deploying AI models “in a way that benefits people”.
Coxon worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic.
The underlying premise of each of these firms is that AI is “only safe in their hands” and that if they don’t build it, someone else will, said Sarah Myers West, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, which studies the impacts of AI. That paranoia is fueling a race to the bottom, she argued.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI face enormous pressure from investors to turn a profit soon. The former has raised over $130bn, while the latter’s funding has reached over $190bn, and both companies have filed for an initial public offering on the US stock market. Altman only recently said the company plans to push back its IPO to at least 2027 due to safety concerns.
“They are investing literally billions of dollars in building AI at a larger and larger scale, and the first thing that gets cut is meaningful investment in baseline security protocols,” Myers West said.
Around the same time that the fractures among OpenAI’s safety teams began to form, Google’s AI arm faced its own internal reckoning. In 2020, Dr Timnit Gebru was ousted from her role as co-lead of Google’s ethical AI team after publishing a paper that explored the biases and potential real-time harms of AI systems. Gebru, who founded the independent research firm the Distributed AI Research Institute, still argues that the so-called doomer scenarios are a distraction from the real-time harms that AI is causing today.
Three years later, Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate often referred to as the godfather of AI, also left Google over his own fears of the risks that AI could be used by bad actors and one day harm humanity.
Now, about five years since its founding, Anthropic is facing the same employee and industry concerns that it was born out of. In July, over 1,000 leading staff and leaders from Anthropic as well as Google, Meta and OpenAI signed a petition calling for the US government to create incentives for slowing the pace of AI development.
The petition came after OpenAI disclosed that hundreds of its AI agents worked together without the company’s knowledge to breach the security of AI firm Hugging Face. Anthropic, too, disclosed that its agents also compromised the security of external firms.
It wasn’t the first time a petition like this made the rounds. In 2023, after OpenAI released a new version of its chatbot, the Future of Life Institute published an open letter signed by figures like Musk and former Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak that called on AI firms to agree to a six-month moratorium on the development of the most advanced AI models. The Future of Life Institute is a nonprofit that is largely funded through a cryptocurrency donation from Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin.
Two weeks after the 2026 Hugging Face breach, OpenAI announced it was pausing development of some aspects of AI training. That didn’t stop the company from ultimately releasing its latest AI model called Astra – albeit with more limited cybersecurity capabilities, the company said. Anthropic, too, said it had temporarily paused development of some aspects of its AI training.
Coxon resigned shortly afterward.

articles.title: Why compliance, not technology, will decide the future of digital sovereign finance
articles.description: Why compliance, not technology, will decide the future of digital sovereign finance Compliance Week
articles.description_html: Why compliance, not technology, will decide the future of digital sovereign finance  Compliance Week
articles.article_title: Why compliance, not technology, will decide the future of digital sovereign finance - Compliance Week
articles.heading: Why compliance, not technology, will decide the future of digital sovereign finance
articles.summary: In-depth analysis and peer practice for 10,000+ risk and compliance leaders. HQP benchmarking, LPEC certification, and the ECI Compliance Week App included.
articles.content:
Somewhere in the Marshall Islands, a citizen receives a universal basic income payment directly to a mobile wallet. There is no bank branch, no paper check, and no in-person distribution involved. The funds come from USDM1, a United States dollar-denominated sovereign digital bond backed one-to-one by short-term United States Treasury bills and recorded on a public blockchain.
For a developing island nation with limited banking infrastructure, it represents exactly what advocates promised digital public finance could be: instant settlement, logistical simplicity, and financial access for people the traditional system has never reached.
It also illustrates a truth that early pilot programs are forcing governments to confront. The success of digital public finance will depend far more on compliance than on technological capability.
The adoption-infrastructure gap
The Marshall Islands is not alone in this experiment.
The Bahamas launched the Sand Dollar in 2020, the world’s first fully operational retail central bank digital currency, specifically to address hurricane disruptions to physical currency distribution.
Nigeria introduced the eNaira in 2021 to reach its large unbanked population. Jamaica rolled out JAM-DEX in 2022, and Slovenia issued the first tokenized sovereign bond by a European Union member state in 2024.
Yet despite technological success, actual adoption tells a different story. The Bahamas created over 200,000 digital wallets in a population of 400,000, but circulation remains low at less than 1 percent of total currency issued. Nigeria recorded 13 million eNaira wallets, but the International Monetary Fund found that 98.5 percent were inactive. Jamaica’s JAM-DEX struggled because merchants needed to upgrade point-of-sale devices and banks lacked incentives to modify their ATMs for digital currency conversion.
The pattern is consistent: governments can build the technology, but they struggle to build the institutional infrastructure that makes people willing and able to use it.
Compliance architecture gap
Here’s the core problem: Governments are deploying technology that enables real-time borderless transactions, but their compliance systems are built for a world of batch processing, physical documentation, and correspondent banking relationships that take weeks to clear. This system’s mismatch creates real exposure. A system that can move money instantly across borders requires anti-money laundering controls, sanctions screening, and supervisory capacity that operate at the same speed. Most finance ministries don’t have these capabilities.
The sticking point for finance ministries is not the blockchain itself; it’s everything around it. Governments need anti-money laundering controls that can meet Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards for virtual assets, real-time sanctions screening capabilities, custody arrangements that satisfy international banking partners, and legal frameworks that cover virtual asset intermediaries.
What they typically have are compliance systems designed for operational legacy financial activity like conventional banking, supervisors trained on traditional audit procedures, and laws that don’t recognize tokenized instruments.
This institutional gap explains why promising pilot programs struggle to scale, and also explains why the stakes are higher than they appear. According to the World Bank, Pacific island countries have faced a 60 percent decline in correspondent banking relationships over the last decade (double the global average of 30 percent) largely because international banks have regarded their supervisory capacity as inadequate.
A poorly designed digital finance launch can accelerate that trend rather than reverse it.
Building toward solutions
The Marshall Islands made a smart design choice: USDM1 sits inside familiar financial law. It’s not a stablecoin, but is a sovereign bond governed by New York law, secured by Treasuries, with the digital layer sitting on top of existing, understood structures.
That design conservatism matters, and the compliance framework built around it offers a useful model for other governments considering similar digital instruments. But even with this conservative approach, significant institution-building remains necessary.
The Marshall Islands prepared to ensure it had the institutional structure to support USDM1. It mapped its statutory framework against FATF standards to ensure that in the future it explicitly covered additional virtual asset service providers, including custody requirements for tokenized instruments, cross-border transaction reporting thresholds, and transaction monitoring for digital wallets and assets. It developed a robust oversight framework that leveraged its existing system with training on blockchain analytics and examination procedures for virtual asset service providers. That means partnerships with experts, investment in additional team members, and new examination processes.
The Marshall Islands’ compliance-first approach is paying off. The Bank of Guam recently announced it will support USDM1 deposits, withdrawals, and wallet integration. Given the Bank of Guam’s presence throughout the Pacific, this integration will likely expand the use of USDM1 significantly.
As this work continues, it is important to keep in mind the key initial use case for USDM1, which was providing universal basic income and connecting the people of the Marshall Islands.
This basic purpose creates inherent tension that has to be designed around rather than deferred. Citizens expect ease in obtaining benefits and services. Regulators expect controls that meet FATF guidance standards.
One approach is tiered verification: Basic access granted with minimal governmental identity documentation, unlocking fuller services as users provide additional verification over time.
Rather than treating compliance as a gate, this progressive approach treats it as a facilitation on-ramp, one that keeps low-risk, low-volume users inside the formal system while meeting supervisory requirements as transaction values grow.
Too much user friction at entry excludes vulnerable households that these programs were designed to reach. Inadequate compliance controls at scale will fail to meet supervisory requirements and endanger correspondent banking relationships that allow the system to function.
The path forward
The pattern from early pilots is clear: Governments can deploy blockchain technology in months, but building the institutional infrastructure to support it can take years.
Countries that invest and implement robust compliance architecture, legal frameworks, and international banking relationships ahead of launch will set the norms for digital sovereign instruments. Those that don’t will find themselves with pilots that may work technically but will not be able to scale because globally no one else in the financial system will partner with them.
The hard part of digital public finance is not building the blockchain. It’s building a lower friction compliance architecture that allows everyone else to use it.

The funds come from USDM1, a United States dollar-denominated sovereign digital bond backed one-to-one by short-term United States Treasury bills and recorded on a public blockchain.

The Bahamas launched the Sand Dollar in 2020, the world’s first fully operational retail central bank digital currency, specifically to address hurricane disruptions to physical currency distribution.

articles.heading: News Release Ricoh invests in mental health technology company Intellect through the RICOH Innovation Fund Ⅱ Supporting workplace well-being as a driver of creativity and exploring future collaboration
articles.summary: Ricoh Company, Ltd. today announced that it has invested in Intellect Company Pte. Ltd., a Singapore-based company providing a mental health platform for organizations, through its corporate venture capital (CVC) fund, the RICOH Innovation Fund Ⅱ.
articles.content:
TOKYO, September 15, 2026 – Ricoh Company, Ltd. today announced that it has invested in Intellect Company Pte. Ltd. (Co-founder and CEO: Theodoric Chew, hereinafter “Intellect”), a Singapore-based company providing a mental health platform for organizations, through its corporate venture capital (CVC) fund, the RICOH Innovation Fund Ⅱ.
As companies increasingly recognize that their people are a key driver of sustainable growth and competitiveness, employee well-being and mental health have become important management priorities. With more diverse ways of working and increasingly global workforces, employees face complex mental and physical health challenges, increasing the need for mental health support worldwide. At the same time, a global shortage of professionals providing such support is making it increasingly difficult to meet these needs. Organizations therefore need to go beyond conventional approaches, using digital technologies to provide mental health support tailored to individual needs, from prevention and early intervention to ongoing care.
Through RICOH Innovation Fund Ⅱ, Ricoh has identified “Unleash creativity” as one of its major investment areas and is promoting investment in and collaboration with startups. Based on its belief that physical and mental well-being is an essential foundation for people to perform at their best and unleash their creativity, Ricoh invested in Intellect.
Through this investment, Ricoh will support Intellect's business growth while deepening its understanding of mental health and well-being. As the first investment through RICOH Innovation Fund Ⅱ, the partnership will also explore opportunities for future collaboration, drawing on Intellect's expertise in individual and organizational well-being and Ricoh's workplace insights and data developed through its Workplace Experience business.*1
Intellect provides a comprehensive mental health platform for organizations, offering a broad range of support, including self-care, coaching, counseling and workforce well-being analytics. Its strengths include a real-time aggregated dashboard that provides visibility into workforce well-being and multilingual and multicultural capabilities that enable support for employees across diverse working environments and cultural backgrounds. Intellect's services are available in more than 100 countries and over 120 languages, serving more than 4 million users worldwide.
Eiji Suzuki, General Manager, Corporate Planning Center, Corporate Planning Division, Ricoh Company, Ltd. stated, “As organizations around the world adapt to evolving ways of working, supporting employees' mental and physical well-being has become essential to unlocking their creativity. Intellect has built a comprehensive platform and deep expertise and extensive data capabilities to address these challenges at scale, making it a compelling partner for Ricoh. Through this investment, we look forward to exploring how Intellect's expertise and Ricoh's workplace data and insights can help create workplaces where everyone has the opportunity to thrive.”
Theodoric Chew, Co-founder and CEO, Intellect stated, “Mental health support needs to work for people across different languages, cultures and levels of need. We built Intellect to make that possible, combining technology with access to professional care. Having Ricoh as a strategic investor brings valuable workplace expertise alongside a shared belief in the importance of employee well-being. We look forward to exploring how we can bring effective mental healthcare to more organizations and the people who power them.”
Ricoh will continue to promote open innovation through RICOH Innovation Fund II and accelerate new value creation through collaboration with startups. Through these efforts, Ricoh aims to bring Fulfillment through Work and contribute to a sustainable society.
-
*1Workplace Experience business
Through its Workplace Experience business, Ricoh empowers customers’ creativity by providing optimal environments for seamless communication and high-quality collaboration regardless of location, enabled by digital technology.https://www.ricoh.com/products/workplace-services
- Company Name
- Intellect Company Pte. Ltd.
- Representative
- Co-founder and CEO, Theodoric Chew
- Headquarters
- 1 Neil Road, #02-02, Singapore 088804
- Established
- June 2019
- Business Activities
- Provision of integrated mental health benefits and care solutions for organizations, spanning digital self-care, coaching, counselling, clinical care, 24/7 EAP support and in-person services.
- Website
- https://intellect.co/
Ricoh is a global integrator in workplace transformation, operating in approximately 200 countries and regions and headquartered in Tokyo. Supporting customers' value creation, Ricoh offers workplace services and solutions that empower organizations to work smarter through advanced technologies—including AI— together with long-standing expertise rooted in printing. Ricoh also operates commercial and industrial printing businesses and delivers new solutions leveraging inkjet technology. In the financial year ended March 2026, Ricoh Group had worldwide sales of 2,608 billion yen (approx. 16.4 billion USD).
For 90 years since our founding, Ricoh has upheld its mission and vision of empowering individuals to find Fulfillment through Work—and that commitment continues today. By understanding and transforming how people work, we unleash their potential and creativity to realize a sustainable future.
For further information, please visit

articles.title: Ark’s Wood says global AI leaders’ pledge is positive for technology development
articles.description: Ark’s Wood says global AI leaders’ pledge is positive for technology development WTVB

articles.article_title: Ark’s Wood says global AI leaders’ pledge is positive for technology development
articles.heading: Ark’s Wood says global AI leaders’ pledge is positive for technology development
articles.summary: By Scott Murdoch SYDNEY, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Global technology investor, Ark Investment Management founder Cathie Wood, said on Tuesday the AI leaders' pledge to slow the technology's rapid ​progression was a positive step to help secure and ‌safeguard...
articles.content:
By Scott Murdoch
SYDNEY, Sept 15 (Reuters) – Global technology investor, Ark Investment Management founder Cathie Wood, said on Tuesday the AI leaders’ pledge to slow the technology’s rapid progression was a positive step to help secure and safeguard the industry’s development.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies on the weekend to slow the rate at which model capabilities were being advanced, amid rising global concerns the technology is being misused.
He was immediately backed by xAI and Tesla founder Elon Musk and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman. Global AI stocks slid on Monday as investors weighed the future growth of the industry which had recently helped propel equity markets to record highs. Asian stocks on Tuesday struggled again, as sentiment remained pessimistic towards chip and AI-related stocks.
Wood, who owns Tesla, SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic across Ark’s public and private funds, said increased scrutiny of the direction of AI growth was positive for the industry.
“Having been in the tech and telecom bubble, which ended in a bust, I’m happy that the leaders of the industry are advertising the risks associated with this new technology,” Wood told reporters in Sydney.
“Half of the solution is understanding the problem.”
Altman said OpenAI would not go public in 2026, amid safety concerns which were raised last week when two researchers from Anthropic said there was a rising risk AI could kill humans before the end of the decade.
“That’s ridiculous,” Wood said, referencing the researchers’ social media posts.
“Yet, it gives us a great opportunity to focus the world on cybersecurity in this space.”
An increasing number of U.S. lawmakers are calling for new rules to govern AI systems but President Donald Trump said on Monday the U.S. was already able to regulate and prosecute AI companies.
(Reporting by Scott Murdoch in Sydney; Editing by Stephen Coates)

articles.summary: City officials previously said that they wouldn’t sign the contract without guardrails in place.
articles.content:
WSAZ Investigates | Huntington City Council passes Flock technology guardrail ordinance
HUNTINGTON, W.Va . (WSAZ) - Monday night, the Huntington City Council voted 7-2 to approve an ordinance to put guardrails on public safety technology, like Flock technology.
The vote comes two months after the council voted to allow the city to enter into a contract with Flock and purchase equipment. Under the contract, the city is set to receive more than 40 license plate readers, 17 cameras, and other technology like drones and gunshot detectors.
City officials previously said that they wouldn’t sign the contract without guardrails in place.
During the meeting two months ago, more than 50 members of the public spoke with concerns about privacy and potential misuse of the technology.
Mayor Patrick Farrell said during Monday’s meeting he shares some of those concerns, and therefore drafted an ordinance to put up guardrails on the technology.
“We have listened to all of you [council members] that had many good ideas about how we could improve an ordinance,” he said. “We’ve listened to our constituents who obviously have come here. They’ve written us. We’ve heard from people on the streets.”
“We started to put together this ordinance to make sure that we could foresee the problems of the future and try to avoid them,” Farrell continued. “Because I share many of the concerns that everyone has, really.”
Some of the guardrails in the ordinance include:
- Data will be retained for seven days unless it is being actively used as evidence in a case
- A “duty to report” for any officer or user with knowledge of misuse
- A way for the public to make complaints
Farrell told council members Monday that the policies will help Huntington avoid the mistakes and problems other cities have faced.

We have at least two states who have said that state money can’t be used for us. It can’t be used on public highways.”
“How on earth is Huntington, West Virginia able to make the assurances that Flock is not going to misuse our data when it’s absolutely done it in other places without any repercussions,” she asked. “It seems very arrogant to me to think that we know better than hundreds of cities and multiple states.”

WSAZ Investigates | Huntington City Council passes Flock technology guardrail ordinance

HUNTINGTON, W.Va . (WSAZ) - Monday night, the Huntington City Council voted 7-2 to approve an ordinance to put guardrails on public safety technology, like Flock technology.

The vote comes two months after the council voted to allow the city to enter into a contract with Flock and purchase equipment. Under the contract, the city is set to receive more than 40 license plate readers, 17 cameras, and other technology like drones and gunshot detectors.

City officials previously said that they wouldn’t sign the contract without guardrails in place.

During the meeting two months ago, more than 50 members of the public spoke with concerns about privacy and potential misuse of the technology.

Mayor Patrick Farrell said during Monday’s meeting he shares some of those concerns, and therefore drafted an ordinance to put up guardrails on the technology.

“We have listened to all of you [council members] that had many good ideas about how we could improve an ordinance,” he said. “We’ve listened to our constituents who obviously have come here. They’ve written us. We’ve heard from people on the streets.”

“We started to put together this ordinance to make sure that we could foresee the problems of the future and try to avoid them,” Farrell continued. “Because I share many of the concerns that everyone has, really.”

Some of the guardrails in the ordinance include:

  • Data will be retained for seven days unless it is being actively used as evidence in a case
  • A “duty to report” for any officer or user with knowledge of misuse
  • A way for the public to make complaints

Farrell told council members Monday that the policies will help Huntington avoid the mistakes and problems other cities have faced.

“It seems to me that the city of Huntington is in a rare circumstance: we’re ahead of the game,” he said. “We’re ahead of the game because we foresaw the need to do this. And we’re now not having to catch up. We’re putting them in place first.”

Councilmembers Sarah Walling and Tia Rumbaugh both voted against the ordinance, both arguing it doesn’t do enough to address their concerns. Earlier in the meeting, Walling had voiced tepid support for the ordinance, but strong wariness of Flock itself.

“I believe that something is better than nothing,” Walling said of the ordinance. “But this is a company that lies. It lies to our legislature. It lies to cities across the country. We have at least two states who have said that state money can’t be used for us. It can’t be used on public highways.”

“How on earth is Huntington, West Virginia able to make the assurances that Flock is not going to misuse our data when it’s absolutely done it in other places without any repercussions,” she asked. “It seems very arrogant to me to think that we know better than hundreds of cities and multiple states.”

Walling’s concerns about Flock were echoed by several members of the public who spoke at the meeting. Some expressed doubt about the city’s promise that the company would not retain the city’s data.

“Once the data is created, it can be sent anywhere, to anyone, for any reason, for any length of time,” Huntington resident Monty Fowler expressed. “And we can probably slap Flock’s hand and say, no, don’t do that. They may even pay a fine. To them, that’s the cost of doing business. But my data, my life, my rights, has still been violated because the mayor wants to turn this into Surveillance City, USA.”

Josh Pickens, an East Lynn resident, told the Council that bringing Flock to Huntington makes him less likely to visit the city.

“I wouldn’t want to live in this town,” he said. “I wouldn’t want to come to this town and spend my money in this town as a person. I wouldn’t want to come in here and give my money to the new businesses that are opening up or spend my money to go see a football game.”

A city spokesperson told WSAZ after the meeting the contract with Flock has still not been signed. She could not provide a timeline for when the contract will be signed, nor when the technology will be delivered and installed.

articles.title: Vance downplays AI fears: Heritage Foundation warns against regulation
articles.description: Vance downplays AI fears: Heritage Foundation warns against regulation KOMO
articles.description_html: Vance downplays AI fears: Heritage Foundation warns against regulation  KOMO
articles.article_title: Vance downplays AI fears: Heritage Foundation warns against regulation
articles.heading: Vance downplays AI fears: Heritage Foundation warns against regulation
articles.summary: Warnings from some of America’s top artificial intelligence leaders that the technology is advancing too quickly.
articles.content:
Vance downplays AI fears: Heritage Foundation warns against regulation
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Warnings from some of America’s top artificial intelligence leaders that the technology is advancing too quickly. The warnings drew a swift response from Beijing this weekend, with China dismissing the concerns as fear-mongering and signaling it does not plan to slow down.
The debate comes as artificial intelligence increasingly reshapes the economy, the military balance and daily life, raising questions in Washington about how to address potential risks without allowing the United States to fall behind.
Bret Swanson, director of the Center for Technology and the Human Person at the Heritage Foundation, told The National News Desk that a voluntary slowdown by the United States would benefit an adversary if China continues pushing forward.
“This is the biggest economic and technological event in recent history,” Swanson said. “Maybe it will turn out to be in all of history.”
Vice President J.D. Vance addressed public concerns about AI on Monday, saying, “Well, look, any technology has risks. Any new technology is going to be bring both risks and benefits.” Vance added, “I don’t think Americans should be scared of anything,” while emphasizing that the country should remain mindful of potential downsides.
Swanson said Vance’s comments were “well put,” and cautioned against “some sort of, you know, bureaucratic, heavy-handed new set of regulations that should that could squash this huge economic engine.”
While acknowledging risks, Swanson said he believes they can be managed without what he described as panic-driven policy.
“I think the way not to handle it is to panic people with these sort of very scary stories saying that we need regulation now or we need to stop it now or pause now,” he said.
Swanson said AI is already boosting the U.S. economy and pointed to massive investment in computing infrastructure.
“We’re investing 6 to $7 trillion over the next five years in AI compute,” he said, adding that the buildout is providing “millions of jobs both to high-tech and blue-collar workers.”
Swanson also warned about what he described as the dangers of a centralized approach to AI governance, arguing that the biggest risk could come if “big AI and big government sort of merge and collaborate.” He said a competitive landscape with “multiple providers” is a better way to serve consumers and businesses while also mitigating risks.
He also argued that AI’s power could be used defensively. “I often say we can use a good AI to defeat bad AI,” Swanson said.

articles.heading: MCC opens new advanced technology center for high-demand careers
articles.summary: A new $69.6 million advanced technology center is now complete at Monroe Community College, expanding training opportunities for students pursuing careers in optics, advanced manufacturing and other high-demand fields.
articles.content:
MCC opens new advanced technology center for high-demand careers
Brighton, N.Y. — A new $69.6 million advanced technology center is now complete at Monroe Community College, expanding training opportunities for students pursuing careers in optics, advanced manufacturing and other high-demand fields.
Gov. Kathy Hochul announced the completion of the Sydor Optics Advanced Technology Center at MCC's Brighton campus Monday. The project moved several technology programs from an aging facility on West Henrietta Road into the new space, connecting them with the college's science, technology, engineering and mathematics programs.
The center will serve as the new home of MCC's Optical Systems Technology program, which trains students for careers in Rochester's optics industry and the growing semiconductor sector across upstate New York.
MCC officials say the optics program has a 100% job placement rate. Enrollment in the program has also grown significantly in recent years as demand for skilled technicians has increased.
MCC President DeAnna Burt-Nanna said the center will give students greater access to hands-on training while strengthening connections between the college and local employers.
“This landmark facility will transform educational opportunities for students by providing cutting-edge learning environments, expanded access to hands-on training, and stronger connections to industry partners,” Burt-Nanna said in a statement.
The center offers training for careers including automotive technician, precision tooling, heating, ventilation and air conditioning service and advanced manufacturing. A new solar lab will also provide training for jobs in solar panel installation and maintenance.
New York provided $34.6 million toward the project, while Monroe County contributed another $34.8 million. That includes $3.5 million in federal funding secured for the project.
The facility is part of a broader effort to prepare workers for growth in advanced manufacturing and semiconductor production across upstate New York.

articles.title: Technology is ‘great equalizer,’ Sharks say at Tech Week Grand Rapids kickoff
articles.description: Technology is ‘great equalizer,’ Sharks say at Tech Week Grand Rapids kickoff WOODTV.com
articles.description_html: Technology is ‘great equalizer,’ Sharks say at Tech Week Grand Rapids kickoff  WOODTV.com
articles.article_title: Technology is ‘great equalizer,’ Sharks say at Tech Week Grand Rapids kickoff
articles.heading: Technology is ‘great equalizer,’ Sharks say at Tech Week Grand Rapids kickoff
articles.summary: Two stars of ABC’s “Shark Tank” visited West Michigan Monday for the Tech Week Grand Rapids kickoff.
articles.content:
Editor’s note: The related video above aired Sept. 9, 2026.
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (WOOD) — Two stars of ABC’s “Shark Tank” visited West Michigan Monday for the Tech Week Grand Rapids kickoff.
Addressing a crowd at GLC Live at 20 Monroe, Daymond John and Robert Herjavec shared stories from their lives and advice for budding entrepreneurs. You don’t necessarily need intelligence, passion, money or connections to be successful, they said — but you do need a clear vision and perseverance.
“I’m not that bright, so I don’t know when to stop,” John said, employing a simple metaphor: If you keep hitting something, it will eventually fall. So when the door slams in your face, he told attendees, you should analyze what went wrong and then try again.
“You have to keep pushing through,” he continued.
“It’s your ability to get up from failure,” Herjavec said.
Both Sharks spoke of the importance of technology, which Herjavec described as the “great equalizer.” Anyone, regardless of their location or situation, can leverage technology to their advantage.
John told the crowd that his 2014 deal with sock brand Bombas — which ultimately became the most successful product in “Shark Tank” history — taught him the “power of the connectivity of social media.” Suddenly, consumers were buying products directly through platforms like Instagram.
Today, artificial intelligence is top of mind for many. Herjavec outlined a few major phases of AI development:
- Consumer: Which products and companies will win?
- Application: What are we going to do with AI?
- Infrastructure: What do we need in order to be successful?
Herjavec said businesses that focus on applying AI have a good chance of long-term success. You likely won’t create the next large language model, he continued, but you can be a pioneer when it comes to AI applications. Here, he encouraged attendees to lean on their own expertise. For instance, a lawyer might consider: How can AI apply to the legal profession?
With AI, “we’re at the tip of the iceberg,” Herjavec said — and he advocates diving in headfirst.
The Sharks’ visit ushered in Tech Week Grand Rapids, an “unconference” that features about 160 events — most of which are free — around the Grand Rapids area.
“It’s our way of sort of elevating the tech scene locally, shining a light on some really good, interesting things taking place in the world of tech,” said Randy Thelen, president and CEO of economic development agency The Right Place.
Around 15,000 people are expected to participate in this year’s Tech Week. Thelen told News 8 that there’s something for everyone.
“I think this idea that there’s tech-y jobs and nontech-y jobs is sort of a thing of the past. Every job has an element of tech embedded in it,” he said. “We have to manage our own tech, if you will, in the way that we go about our work. And so this is a chance for everybody to just level up their skill set a little bit, level up their network around the region.”
For a full list of events, visit Tech Week Grand Rapids’ website.
