articles.title: How Connected HVAC Technology Can Transform Contractor Maintenance Programs
articles.description: How Connected HVAC Technology Can Transform Contractor Maintenance Programs Contracting Business
articles.description_html: How Connected HVAC Technology Can Transform Contractor Maintenance Programs  Contracting Business
articles.article_title: How Connected HVAC Technology Can Transform Contractor Maintenance Programs
articles.heading: How Connected HVAC Technology Can Transform Contractor Maintenance Programs
articles.summary: Smart-home technology is changing homeowner expectations—and giving HVAC contractors a new opportunity to deliver value between maintenance visits.
articles.content:
How Connected HVAC Technology Can Transform Contractor Maintenance Programs
Why It Matters
- Technology can make maintenance agreements more valuable to homeowners by giving them ongoing visibility into their HVAC system rather than limiting the perceived benefit to one or two annual service visits.
- Monitoring platforms can help contractors reduce membership churn by providing tangible, year-round benefits such as equipment-health reports, alerts, loyalty rewards, and greater transparency.
- Retrofit monitoring technology gives contractors a way to bring older HVAC systems into their connected service models, helping them build relationships with customers now and position themselves for future repair and replacement opportunities.
As a millennial homeowner, I’m accustomed to smart home technology. I purchased my home a decade ago, right as smart thermostats were becoming mainstream. Today, I receive monthly reports on my HVAC system, my kitchen appliances, and my washer and dryer. I also have a smart leak detector installed on my water main.
I love the data and insights I get into my home appliances and mechanical systems. It’s one thing to write about how temperature and humidity impact HVAC systems; it’s a different story when you’re seeing the evidence play out in your own home. This summer in Michigan has been infinitely hotter than last year!
As interesting as it is to see that data as a homeowner, it holds so much more value for you, the professionals. Proactive HVAC contractors are increasingly looking beyond traditional maintenance visits and using monitoring platforms to keep an eye on customer systems between service calls. As smart-home technology becomes more common, homeowners are becoming comfortable with the idea that their HVAC equipment can be monitored remotely, creating an opportunity for contractors to bring that same connectivity into their service models.
That’s where platforms such as SmartAC come in, using sensors to continuously monitor HVAC equipment and identify changes in system performance. For contractors, that data can create an opportunity to move from reactive service calls to proactive maintenance—and potentially turn equipment monitoring into a valuable tool for selling and supporting maintenance agreements.
Maintenance agreements can be a powerful revenue generator for HVAC contractors by creating a predictable stream of recurring income beyond unpredictable demand for service and replacement. According to EGIA's 2026 Contractor Survey Report, maintenance plans generate an average of just under $200,000 in annual revenue, with one in 10 contractors bringing in over $500,000 annually. For homeowners, the value is proactive system care and greater peace of mind; however, these maintenance programs also have a lot of churn. Homeowners may not see the immediate value of a maintenance agreement when their HVAC system is running normally, especially if they perceive the service as simply another recurring expense.
“Traditionally, the homeowner only sees any value from a membership program two days a year,” says Josh Teekell, founder and CEO of SmartAC. “That’s why we believe retention is so much higher when you have data flowing all the time because the homeowner is getting value year-round as opposed to only a few days a year when the tech is on site.”
Teekell says HVAC contractors need to adapt their maintenance-agreement offerings to changing homeowner expectations around convenience, transparency, and technology. Homeowners very rarely want to spend thousands of additional dollars on self-monitoring equipment when the cost to replace is already so high, so Teekell believes contractors should offer retrofit technology that can work with existing systems. “Most importantly, grabbing and retaining a home that has older equipment so you can be the one to replace it when the time comes is the highest ROI thing you can do,” he says.
Teekell also argues that contractors need to offer options that appeal to different homeowner buying preferences. Pricing flexibility, monthly billing, and visible value can help contractors reduce membership churn. He recommends giving homeowners multiple choices rather than presenting a single maintenance plan, including lower-cost options that incorporate technology. Monthly billing can also reduce the sticker shock associated with an annual renewal, while loyalty rewards can give homeowners another reason to stay. SmartAC's platform, for example, allows customers to see accumulated loyalty credits in the app and monthly equipment-health reports. “It’s really just about giving them a great experience when you’re in person, reminding them of the value of that peace of mind that they’re getting through technology,” Teekell says.
Click here to see firsthand how HVAC contractors are leveraging technology to boost membership programs.
The future of maintenance membership programs is about more than scheduling annual tune-ups. By combining recurring service with technology, proactive system monitoring and visible customer benefits, contractors can create memberships that deliver value throughout the year. The goal is to give homeowners more reasons to stay while giving contractors a stronger, more predictable customer relationship—and a better opportunity to earn the next service or replacement job.
About the Author
Nicole Krawcke
Nicole Krawcke is the Editor-in-Chief of Contracting Business magazine. With over 10 years of B2B media experience across HVAC, plumbing, and mechanical markets, she has expertise in content creation, digital strategies, and project management. Nicole has more than 15 years of writing and editing experience and holds a bachelor’s degree in Journalism from Michigan State University.

As a millennial homeowner, I’m accustomed to smart home technology. I purchased my home a decade ago, right as smart thermostats were becoming mainstream. Today, I receive monthly reports on my HVAC system, my kitchen appliances, and my washer and dryer. I also have a smart leak detector installed on my water main.

I love the data and insights I get into my home appliances and mechanical systems. It’s one thing to write about how temperature and humidity impact HVAC systems; it’s a different story when you’re seeing the evidence play out in your own home. This summer in Michigan has been infinitely hotter than last year!

As interesting as it is to see that data as a homeowner, it holds so much more value for you, the professionals. Proactive HVAC contractors are increasingly looking beyond traditional maintenance visits and using monitoring platforms to keep an eye on customer systems between service calls. As smart-home technology becomes more common, homeowners are becoming comfortable with the idea that their HVAC equipment can be monitored remotely, creating an opportunity for contractors to bring that same connectivity into their service models.

That’s where platforms such as SmartAC come in, using sensors to continuously monitor HVAC equipment and identify changes in system performance. For contractors, that data can create an opportunity to move from reactive service calls to proactive maintenance—and potentially turn equipment monitoring into a valuable tool for selling and supporting maintenance agreements.

Maintenance agreements can be a powerful revenue generator for HVAC contractors by creating a predictable stream of recurring income beyond unpredictable demand for service and replacement. According to EGIA's 2026 Contractor Survey Report, maintenance plans generate an average of just under $200,000 in annual revenue, with one in 10 contractors bringing in over $500,000 annually. For homeowners, the value is proactive system care and greater peace of mind; however, these maintenance programs also have a lot of churn. Homeowners may not see the immediate value of a maintenance agreement when their HVAC system is running normally, especially if they perceive the service as simply another recurring expense.

“Traditionally, the homeowner only sees any value from a membership program two days a year,” says Josh Teekell, founder and CEO of SmartAC. “That’s why we believe retention is so much higher when you have data flowing all the time because the homeowner is getting value year-round as opposed to only a few days a year when the tech is on site.”

Teekell says HVAC contractors need to adapt their maintenance-agreement offerings to changing homeowner expectations around convenience, transparency, and technology. Homeowners very rarely want to spend thousands of additional dollars on self-monitoring equipment when the cost to replace is already so high, so Teekell believes contractors should offer retrofit technology that can work with existing systems. “Most importantly, grabbing and retaining a home that has older equipment so you can be the one to replace it when the time comes is the highest ROI thing you can do,” he says.

Teekell also argues that contractors need to offer options that appeal to different homeowner buying preferences. Pricing flexibility, monthly billing, and visible value can help contractors reduce membership churn. He recommends giving homeowners multiple choices rather than presenting a single maintenance plan, including lower-cost options that incorporate technology. Monthly billing can also reduce the sticker shock associated with an annual renewal, while loyalty rewards can give homeowners another reason to stay. SmartAC's platform, for example, allows customers to see accumulated loyalty credits in the app and monthly equipment-health reports. “It’s really just about giving them a great experience when you’re in person, reminding them of the value of that peace of mind that they’re getting through technology,” Teekell says.

Click here to see firsthand how HVAC contractors are leveraging technology to boost membership programs.

The future of maintenance membership programs is about more than scheduling annual tune-ups. By combining recurring service with technology, proactive system monitoring and visible customer benefits, contractors can create memberships that deliver value throughout the year. The goal is to give homeowners more reasons to stay while giving contractors a stronger, more predictable customer relationship—and a better opportunity to earn the next service or replacement job.

articles.article_title: DOE selects S&T to build mining technology proving ground
articles.heading: DOE selects S&T to build mining technology proving ground
articles.summary: Missouri University of Science and Technology is included in a new $73 million grant to create testing grounds for innovative mining technologies. The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation selected Missouri S&T as one of four projects that will work towards a “Mine of the Future.” The university’s program,...Continue Reading DOE selects S&T to build mining technology proving ground
articles.content:
Missouri University of Science and Technology is included in a new $73 million grant to create testing grounds for innovative mining technologies. The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation selected Missouri S&T as one of four projects that will work towards a “Mine of the Future.”
The university’s program, titled “Multi-Functioning Mining Technology Proving Ground for Energy Efficiency and Productivity,” was funded for $16.3 million and will create a proving ground that combines facilities for underground technology testing and advanced energy comminution assessment.
As part of the program, Missouri S&T will design, build and equip this proving ground to support innovation, real-world validation, and workforce development for next generation mining technologies.
“S&T is the perfect fit for this research, given our existing Experimental Mine and numerous faculty experts in mining and critical minerals research,” says Dr. Kwame Awuah-Offei, the Union Pacific/Rocky Mountain Energy Professor of mining engineering at S&T. “Work like this requires field sites to allow for testing in the real world, not theoretical work, and that will only further our expertise in the research and development of mining technology.”
This award complements the work under the Department of Commerce’s recent award to the Critical Minerals and Materials for Advanced Energy Tech Hub, led by S&T, to purchase land and build a test bed facility for evaluating critical minerals processing and extraction techniques at the pilot scale. The DOE funding provides the capability to test for energy savings during comminution, the process of reducing rocks into smaller sizes for processing, to improve the energy efficiency of critical minerals processing.
“Our roots are in mining and materials science since our founding days in 1870,” says Dr. David Borrok, vice provost and dean of the College of Engineering at Computing at S&T. “It is great to see that, after 155 years, Missouri S&T is still a leader in the field and recognized nationally for its strengths.”
The university’s critical minerals legacy of 155 years will also serve as the foundation for S&T’s new tech hub. The federally designated tech hub was recently awarded $38 million to improve domestic critical minerals supply chains. This funding source will support construction of an 18,000-square-foot critical mineral processing and recycling test bed at S&T designed to accelerate the commercialization of critical minerals technologies, along with fostering growth in the mining and explosives engineering degree programs at S&T.
To learn more about S&T’s work related to critical minerals, visit criticalminerals.mst.edu.
About Missouri S&T
Missouri University of Science and Technology (Missouri S&T) is a STEM-focused research university of over 7,000 students located in Rolla, Missouri. Part of the four-campus University of Missouri System, Missouri S&T offers over 100 degrees in 40 areas of study and is among the nation’s top public universities for salary impact, according to the Wall Street Journal. For more information about Missouri S&T, visit www.mst.edu.

articles.content:
News directly from Cornell's colleges and centers
A&S offers new science, technology and society major
By Kathy Hovis
An innovative major in the College of Arts & Sciences is being expanded and refined to highlight its combination of science, social science and the humanities and its relevance to careers today.
The new major in science, technology and society offers students a combination of theoretical and practical classes and experiences, allowing students to work with real-world problems related to science and technology, viewing those problems through multiple lenses.
“We wanted to design a major that sets students up to be successful in an ever-changing world," said Malte Ziewitz, associate professor in the Department of Science and Technology Studies (STS) and director of the Digital Due Process Clinic. “Data centers, climate change, genome editing, voting technologies—none of these challenges are simply technical or scientific; they all require experts that can speak across boundaries, have serious analytical chops and have the judgment to make effective interventions.”
Students in the major will participate in a sequence of new classes, including a third-year practicum bringing policy experts from government and non-governmental organizations to campus.
“Students will work with these experts and write white papers on problems that need to be solved surrounding issues such as climate change, regulating AI or medical ethics,” said Prof. Suman Seth, Stephen H. Weiss Presidential Fellow and Marie Underhill Noll Professor of the History of Science and the chair of STS (A&S). “We’ll leverage the enormous connections Cornell has to help students work out problems using all of the techniques that STS brings.”

articles.article_title: New Maker Challenges Offer More Ways to Create
articles.heading: New Maker Challenges Offer More Ways to Create
articles.summary: The Teaching, Learning and Technology Center (TLTC) is introducing new weekly projects and monthly Maker Challenges this fall, giving students, faculty and staff more opportunities to explore technology and create in the Maker Studio.
articles.content:
New Maker Challenges Offer More Ways to Create
Monday, September 14, 2026
The Teaching, Learning and Technology Center (TLTC) is introducing new weekly projects and monthly Maker Challenges this fall, giving students, faculty and staff more opportunities to explore technology and create in the Maker Studio.
Each week, project-based workshops will introduce participants to a Maker Studio technology through a guided project, while a new Maker Challenge each month will provide an opportunity to apply those skills to a larger creative or technical challenge. No previous Maker Studio experience is required to participate.
Try a New Project Each Week
The Maker Studio will offer a new project each week using tools and technologies available in the space, including 3D printing, laser engraving, Cricut cutting, sublimation printing, robotics and electronics. Students, faculty and staff can stop by during Maker Studio hours throughout the week to participate.
Two instructional sessions will also be offered each week for participants who would like guided instruction. During these sessions, TLTC staff will walk participants through the project, introduce the featured technology and explain the techniques needed to complete it. There is no cost to attend an instructional session, although some projects may require a small fee for consumable materials.
September projects include:
-

3D Print a Place, September 14-18: Select a meaningful location on a digital map and turn it into a 3D-printable terrain model while learning how to adjust scale and elevation and prepare a model for printing.
-

Backpack Nametag Using TinkerCAD, September 21-25: Design a personalized backpack nametag by combining text and shapes in TinkerCAD, then size and prepare the finished model for 3D printing.
-

Scan Me! The Smart Networking Card, September 28-October 2: Create a wooden networking card or tag with a laser-engraved QR code that links to a resume or LinkedIn profile while learning about layout, engraving and QR code readability.
New projects will be featured throughout the semester, providing opportunities to work with different Maker Studio technologies and learn how they can be used for future projects.
Take On the Monthly Maker Challenge
For those looking to go further, the TLTC is also introducing a new Maker Challenge each month. Each challenge presents a project or problem to solve using technology available in the Maker Studio.
The September Maker Challenge, Bloom and Build, invites participants to create a 3D-printed floral display using designed or selected flowers with a custom base, vase or holder. Participants will plan their arrangement, prepare components for printing and make decisions about scale, color, stability and assembly as they develop and refine their design.
More to Explore in the Innovation Hub
The Maker Challenges are just some of the ways to explore technology in the Innovation Hub. The Seton Hall community can also bring their own projects to the Maker Studio, explore virtual reality in the Exploration Studio or build technology skills through TLTC workshops offered throughout the semester. The Maker Studio and Exploration Studio are open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m.-4 p.m., with evening and weekend access available based on staffing.
For questions about Maker Studio projects, email [email protected]. Faculty can contact their instructional design liaison for help incorporating Innovation Hub technologies into a course or assignment. For specialized projects, collaborations or other Innovation Hub questions, contact Renee Cicchino.
Categories: Science and Technology

articles.title: NSF Funds Pilot Program to Support Small Businesses in Accelerating Commercialization of Their Late-Stage Deep-Technology and Avoid the “Valley of Death”
articles.description: NSF Funds Pilot Program to Support Small Businesses in Accelerating Commercialization of Their Late-Stage Deep-Technology and Avoid the “Valley of Death” University of Central Florida
articles.description_html: NSF Funds Pilot Program to Support Small Businesses in Accelerating Commercialization of Their Late-Stage Deep-Technology and Avoid the “Valley of Death”  University of Central Florida
articles.source: University of Central Florida News | UCF Today
articles.article_title: NSF Funds Pilot Program to Support Small Businesses in Accelerating Commercialization of Their Late-Stage Deep-Technology and Avoid the “Valley of Death”
articles.heading: NSF Funds Pilot Program to Support Small Businesses in Accelerating Commercialization of Their Late-Stage Deep-Technology and Avoid the “Valley of Death”
articles.summary: The $20 million program aims to address a persistent gap that separates federally funded deep technology research from commercial success.
articles.content:
The U.S. National Science Foundation’s Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (TIP) announced a $20 million investment to launch a two-year pilot that will provide support to small businesses in the commercialization of their late-stage deep-technology research and development. The pilot aims to address a persistent gap that separates federally funded deep technology research from commercial success. The investment ensures that the U.S. remains at the forefront of global innovation.
“NSF invests in small businesses that bring the most innovative cutting-edge technologies to the market and society,” says Erwin Gianchandani, NSF assistant director for TIP. “By closing this gap that is known as the ‘valley of death,’ NSF aims to strengthen our commitment to translational research and further develop innovation ecosystems in the United States.”
The “valley of death” refers to a stage at which a new technology innovation has been substantially de-risked but the technology has not yet been commercially proven, making it difficult to attract funding or other support needed to achieve commercial viability.
“NCTI builds on UCF’s growing national leadership in helping promising technologies become products, companies and economic growth.” — Alexander N. Cartwright, UCF president
“Many NSF-supported small businesses have the potential to become great commercial successes and contribute significantly to economic growth and job creation throughout the nation,” says Lesia Crumpton-Young, TIP section head for small businesses. “We want to support small businesses to overcome the hurdles common to commercializing deep technology innovations.”
Led by the University of Central Florida’s National Commercialization and Translation Institute (NCTI), the pilot will examine the factors, conditions and approaches that lead to the successful transition of deep technology innovations to nationally impactful technologies.
The institute represents the latest evolution of a commercialization pipeline UCF has spent years developing. Through initiatives including the Southeast Hub of NSF I-Corps, NSF Accelerating Research Translation (ART) and the Florida Semiconductor Engine, UCF has helped researchers evaluate commercial opportunities, advance emerging technologies and strengthen regional innovation. NCTI will build on that foundation by expanding UCF’s commercialization efforts to companies nationwide.
UCF Professor of Industrial Engineering and Management Systems Ivan Garibay, principal investigator for NCTI, will lead the institute, which will provide commercialization funding, expert mentorship and investor connections to SBIR/STTR Phase II and Phase IIB funded companies, while evaluating which approaches most effectively help deep technology companies reach the marketplace.
“We are grateful to the National Science Foundation for its continued confidence in UCF and for the opportunity to help shape the future of research translation and commercialization,” says UCF President Alexander N. Cartwright. “Discovery reaches its greatest potential when it moves beyond the laboratory and improves lives, strengthens industries and creates opportunity. NCTI builds on UCF’s growing national leadership in helping promising technologies become products, companies and economic growth. With Central Florida’s extraordinary concentration of talent, industry and innovation, UCF is well positioned to build a model that can deliver impact for Florida and across the nation.”
“UCF’s readiness to lead this national effort is anchored by our highly integrated entrepreneurial infrastructure critical in the ‘lab-to-market’ pipeline,” says Winston Schoenfeld, vice president for research and innovation. “NCTI will ensure that federally funded technologies successfully transition into investor-ready commercial enterprises.”
“Providing a ‘bridge’ to support our late-stage NSF-funded companies will move their impactful innovation to the market more quickly and thereby benefit the national economy.” — Peter Atherton, program director for NSF Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer.
“A validated technology is a scientific achievement, but it isn’t yet a business. Many NSF SBIR Phase II companies hold genuinely de-risked technologies, yet still lack the business expertise, infrastructure, and capital access to turn that validation into a viable company,” Garibay says. “NCTI completes that pipeline rather than duplicating any part of it: we coordinate the full continuum of federal resources, managing the handoffs from I-Corps customer discovery through to commercialization support, so each company knows where it stands and what comes next.”
The pilot will support a select group of NSF-funded small businesses at the later stages of deep technology research and development through funding, mentoring, and connections, paired with concierge-level individualized support: diagnostic triage, an individualized commercialization plan, dedicated mentor teams, and curated introductions to customers, investors, industry, and national laboratories.
“Providing a ‘bridge’ to support our late-stage NSF-funded companies will move their impactful innovation to the market more quickly and thereby benefit the national economy,” says Peter Atherton, program director for NSF Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer.
Each stage of the pilot will be structured and independently evaluated. Designed as a scalable model, the results of the pilot will determine whether to establish a long-term program.
Learn more about the NCTI pilot.

articles.heading: Ondas Acquires GATE Technologies and Bron Technologies, Expanding Precision-Strike Platform with Electronic Safe & Arm and Fuze Technology
articles.summary: Ondas Acquires GATE Technologies and Bron Technologies, Expanding Precision-Strike Platform with Electronic Safe & Arm and Fuze Technology Ondas Holdings
articles.content:
Ondas Acquires GATE Technologies and Bron Technologies, Expanding Precision-Strike Platform with Electronic Safe & Arm and Fuze Technology
GATE Technologies is a leading developer and manufacturer of Electronic Safe & Arm Devices (ESADs) and advanced electronic fuzing solutions, with its technology integrated into dozens of weapon systems including UAVs, loitering munitions, missiles and rockets
Adds a critical layer of the precision-strike technology stack with NATO-based, non-ITAR production in Poland, while expanding Ondas' access to U.S. and European programs
WEST PALM BEACH, FL / ACCESS Newswire / September 14, 2026 / Ondas Inc. (Nasdaq:ONDS) ("Ondas" or the "Company"), a leading provider of advanced autonomous systems and next-generation defense and security technologies and services, today announced that it has acquired GATE Technologies Ltd. ("GATE"), an Israeli-based defense technology company specializing in Electronic Safe & Arm Devices ("ESADs") and advanced electronic fuzing technologies used across modern precision weapons and autonomous strike systems, and Bron Technologies ("Bron"), a European manufacturing, certification and an affiliated company to GATE's systems. Ondas will pay $205 million, the majority of which is payable in cash, plus a working capital adjustment and up to $185 million of performance-based earn-out consideration. The earn-out is tied to financial targets through 2028 and may be paid, at Ondas' election, in cash or Ondas common stock. Ondas expects the acquired business to contribute more than $130 million of aggregate Adjusted EBITDA through 2028.

articles.content:
Technology leader brings more than 28 years of experience driving enterprise transformation, AI innovation and technology strategy for large, regulated organizations.
Conduent Incorporated (Nasdaq: CNDT), a global technology-driven business solutions and services company, today announced the appointment of Narayanan Sundaresan as Chief Information and Technology Officer , effective September 14, 2026.
Narayanan Sundaresan
Sundaresan brings more than 28 years of experience leading enterprise technology organizations and digital transformation initiatives, with expertise driving AI-powered business transformation, modernizing enterprise platforms, advancing digital products, and strengthening cybersecurity and data governance.
At Conduent, Sundaresan will lead the Company's global technology organization and strategy in support of transformation and growth. He will focus on accelerating the adoption of AI-powered capabilities across the enterprise while continuing to strengthen the secure, reliable and scalable technology foundation needed to support Conduent's clients and operations. His leadership will help advance Conduent's efforts to modernize operations, scale innovation and deliver measurable outcomes for clients.
“Narayanan joins Conduent at an important point in our transformation, and his experience will help us accelerate innovation, enhance client outcomes, and create greater value for our business,” said Harsha V. Agadi, Chief Executive Officer of Conduent. “I’m excited to welcome him to our leadership team and look forward to his impact as we turn our AI and technology strategy into measurable business results.”
“I’m honored to step into this role at a pivotal moment for Conduent,” said Narayanan Sundaresan, Chief Information and Technology Officer, Conduent. “My focus will be on two things that go hand in hand: accelerating the build-out of AI-powered capabilities across every part of the enterprise and scaling a technology infrastructure that is both secure and reliable enough to support that growth. AI only creates lasting value when it’s built on a foundation that clients and associates can trust.”
Prior to joining Conduent, Sundaresan served as Global Chief Information Officer and Senior Vice President, Digital Products & Technology at Strategic Education, where he led enterprise-wide AI work redesign and hyper-automation initiatives, technology harmonization across business units, and the development of global technology capabilities. He also previously held technology leadership positions at Capella Education Company, where he led digital technology initiatives, enterprise platforms and global technology delivery.
Sundaresan holds an MBA from the University of Minnesota Carlson School of Management and an M.S. in Software Engineering from the University of St. Thomas. He also completed the High Potential Leadership Program at Harvard Business School.
About Conduent
Conduent delivers digital business solutions and services spanning the commercial, government and transportation spectrum – creating valuable outcomes for its clients and the millions of people who count on them. The Company leverages cloud computing, artificial intelligence, machine learning, automation and advanced analytics to deliver mission-critical solutions. Through a dedicated global team of approximately 48,000 associates, process expertise and advanced technologies, Conduent’s solutions and services digitally transform its clients’ operations to enhance customer experiences, improve performance, increase efficiencies and reduce costs. Conduent adds momentum to its clients’ missions in many ways including disbursing approximately $80 billion in government payments annually, enabling approximately 2.0 billion customer service interactions annually, empowering millions of employees through HR services every year and processing over 14 million tolling transactions every day. Learn more at www.conduent.com .

articles.article_title: IU names global orthopedic technology executive as CEO of NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana
articles.heading: IU names global orthopedic technology executive as CEO of NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana
articles.summary: Jim Lancaster, a former Zimmer Biomet executive, will be the CEO and principal investigator of the NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana, a major statewide initiat...
articles.content:
INDIANAPOLIS — Indiana University has named Jim Lancaster the CEO and principal investigator of the NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana, a major statewide initiative that will build a regional innovation ecosystem by connecting expertise across Indiana’s orthopedic community and accelerating the translation of research into real-world impact.
The IU-led coalition is made up of more than 170 Indiana industry, clinical and university collaborators. It will receive up to $160 million over 10 years from the National Science Foundation to turn research into real-world solutions related to the care and treatment of musculoskeletal health conditions such as arthritis and osteoporosis, and acute and interventional needs such as bone fractures and traumatic injuries.
Lancaster comes to IU after more than three decades working in the orthopedics industry. As a former executive of Zimmer Biomet and a thought leader in orthopedic innovation, Lancaster led product development, global reconstruction and platform technology initiatives.
“Under Jim’s leadership, the NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana will accelerate promising innovations from discovery to real-world impact,” said Russell Mumper, vice president for research at Indiana University. “Jim brings the vision, experience and collaborative leadership needed to unite researchers, clinicians, key university and industry partners, and communities around our ambitious goal: translating Indiana’s exceptional strengths in musculoskeletal health into new treatments, technologies, companies and careers.”
The NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana is dedicated to transforming the state into a global leader in musculoskeletal health technologies by bridging critical gaps in innovation infrastructure, workforce development and cross-sector collaboration. As CEO, Lancaster will be responsible for the initiatives’ overall success: directing its strategic vision, daily operations and integrated activities across the state’s orthopedic ecosystem.
“I’m honored to officially join the NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana as CEO and to build on the extraordinary foundation this team has already built,” Lancaster said. “Indiana brings together a rare combination of world-class research, clinical expertise, advanced manufacturing and entrepreneurial talent. I’m excited to help turn this ambitious vision into measurable impact by aligning those strengths around a shared mission.”
Established through the bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, co-sponsored by U.S. Sen. Todd Young of Indiana, the NSF Regional Innovation Engines program represents one of the nation’s largest investments in place-based innovation. The coalition aspires to train over 1,900 workers, launch over 85 startups, bring at least 30 innovations to market and deliver more than $535 million in economic impact to the state.
In addition to Lancaster, the NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana is led by chief scientific officer Melissa Kacena, director of the IU School of Medicine’s Indiana Center for Musculoskeletal Health; chief technology and innovation officer Amrou Awaysheh, of the IU Kelley School of Business; and chief learning officer Jill Fehrenbacher, of the IU School of Medicine.

“I’m honored to officially join the NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana as CEO and to build on the extraordinary foundation this team has already built,” Lancaster said. “Indiana brings together a rare combination of world-class research, clinical expertise, advanced manufacturing and entrepreneurial talent. I’m excited to help turn this ambitious vision into measurable impact by aligning those strengths around a shared mission.”

Established through the bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, co-sponsored by U.S. Sen. Todd Young of Indiana, the NSF Regional Innovation Engines program represents one of the nation’s largest investments in place-based innovation. The coalition aspires to train over 1,900 workers, launch over 85 startups, bring at least 30 innovations to market and deliver more than $535 million in economic impact to the state.

In addition to Lancaster, the NSF IMPACT Engine in Indiana is led by chief scientific officer Melissa Kacena, director of the IU School of Medicine’s Indiana Center for Musculoskeletal Health; chief technology and innovation officer Amrou Awaysheh, of the IU Kelley School of Business; and chief learning officer Jill Fehrenbacher, of the IU School of Medicine.

articles.content:
Logistics industry veteran to lead technology innovation and build a technology that will differentiate OnTrac in its next phase of growth
CHANTILLY, Va., Sept. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- OnTrac, the #1 alternative carrier network, today announced the appointment of Arjun Sainath as Chief Technology Officer (CTO). In this role, Sainath will lead the company's technology organization and strategy, driving innovation across operations, customer solutions, data, AI, and enterprise back-office systems to support OnTrac's next phase of growth.
Sainath joins OnTrac with more than two decades of experience leading technology, engineering, and product organizations through periods of transformation and growth—with a focus in logistics and supply chain. He will be responsible for advancing the company's technology vision and investments, with a focus on further differentiating customer experiences and building a new AI-driven development model for faster speed-to-market.
"As we continue to be the alternative carrier of choice in a rapidly changing market, investing in new technology is essential to how we serve customers, support our employees, and scale the business," said Mike Brown, Chief Executive Officer of OnTrac. "Arjun brings deep expertise in leading technology and product organizations through periods of transformation and growth. His experience applying AI, data-driven solutions, and modern platforms to solve complex operational challenges will help strengthen our technology foundation and accelerate innovation across the organization."
Prior to joining OnTrac, Sainath served as Chief Technology Officer at Cart.com, where he led technology modernization initiatives and leveraged artificial intelligence and machine learning to improve fulfillment operations. Before Cart.com, he served as Corporate Vice President of Platform Engineering at Blue Yonder, where he led the migration of global supply chain technologies to a cloud-native SaaS platform. Earlier in his career, Sainath held leadership roles at Salesforce, overseeing M&A integrations and revenue automation initiatives that supported business growth and transformation.
As CTO, Sainath will oversee the continued evolution of OnTrac's technology, including the strategic application of AI, automation, and advanced analytics to improve network efficiency, support operational decision-making, and unlock new capabilities across the business.
"OnTrac has built a reputation as the best alternative to national carriers, on the cusp of its next evolution," said Sainath. "I'm excited to join the company at this pivotal stage in its journey. Last mile logistics affords a unique opportunity to leverage AI and automation to drive new customer value and innovative experiences at the lowest possible cost. I'm excited to help the company realize this potential."
The appointment reflects OnTrac's continued commitment to investing in the people, processes, and technology needed to support long-term growth. As ecommerce logistics rapidly evolves and customer expectations increase, OnTrac is advancing a technology strategy focused on AI, automation, data intelligence, and platform modernization to improve operational efficiency, enhance customer experiences, and create a more agile, scalable network.
About OnTrac
OnTrac is the #1 Alternative Carrier Network for ecommerce deliveries, helping retailers and shippers build a competitive advantage through faster delivery times, 7 day/week operations, lower costs, coast-to-coast coverage, and reliable performance. The OnTrac delivery network reaches more than 75% of the population in 35 states and Washington, D.C., and supports a growing range of ecommerce, marketplace, and omnichannel shipping needs. With more than 65 years of experience, OnTrac has evolved into a critical part of the U.S. ecommerce logistics infrastructure and is trusted by leading shippers seeking greater speed, flexibility, and resilience in their supply chains.

articles.title: Oregon National Guard uses new hoist technology in mountain rescue
articles.description: Oregon National Guard uses new hoist technology in mountain rescue KPTV
articles.description_html: Oregon National Guard uses new hoist technology in mountain rescue  KPTV
articles.article_title: Oregon National Guard uses new hoist technology in mountain rescue
articles.heading: Oregon National Guard uses new hoist technology in mountain rescue
articles.summary: The Oregon National Guard made history Saturday, using new Vita hoist technology in a real rescue for the first time. The technology is currently available only in Oregon.
articles.content:
Oregon National Guard uses new hoist technology in mountain rescue
SALEM Ore. (KPTV) - The Oregon National Guard made history Saturday, using new Vita hoist technology in a real rescue for the first time. The technology is currently available only in Oregon.
A pair of hunters were 10 miles from the nearest road in the Mount Jefferson Wilderness when one of them slipped and broke an ankle. Chief Warrant Officer 3 Noelan Smith said if the hunters had to hike out on foot, they would have been there overnight.
Smith, Sgt. Michael Lam and three other crew members were finishing another flight and were able to get the helicopter back in the air. The crew communicated with the hunters using a Garmin satellite device, as well as other methods.
“They had fashioned a signaling device with orange and white. I don’t know if it was articles of clothing, but put that on a pole and spun it, which created a signaling device that allowed us to locate them,” Smith said.
The Army’s new medevac technology was demonstrated live for the first time during the rescue. Lam operates the Vita device while Smith flies the aircraft.
“Under normal circumstances, there’d be a medic on the ground using what we call a tagline, a rope attached to the basket, which lets it so it doesn’t spin. But with this Vita that we attach to our rescue basket, we don’t have to have a tagline anymore and it just stabilizes it up the whole time,” Lam said.
Fans on the device self-stabilize the rescue basket, counteracting forces like wind that could cause uncontrollable spinning.
Smith said the technology is safer for both patients and rescuers.
“If it’s a cliff side, things like that, we don’t necessarily have the ability to have somebody on the ground and move the aircraft in a manner that we’d be able to use a traditional basket with tagline. So this provides us a resource that can get into those spaces that we wouldn’t be able to in the past,” Smith said.
The hunter injured Saturday was treated at a hospital within a few hours of the rescue. Guard officials said it was the Vita’s first success story and that the technology could someday be used beyond Oregon.

articles.title: New warnings about the risks of AI to humanity revive a long-running debate
articles.description: New warnings about the risks of AI to humanity revive a long-running debate spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.description_html: New warnings about the risks of AI to humanity revive a long-running debate  spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.article_title: New warnings about the risks of AI to humanity revive a long-running debate
articles.heading: New warnings about the risks of AI to humanity revive a long-running debate
articles.summary: The CEO of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind Claude, said he thought the industry needed to reduce the speed of its work
articles.content:
LOS ANGELES — New warnings from within the artificial intelligence industry have revived a long-running debate over whether advanced AI could escape human control and ultimately threaten humanity's survival, and whether the companies developing the technology are doing enough to prevent such a scenario.
The CEO of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind Claude, said he thought the industry needed to reduce the speed of its work, cautioning Saturday that a swarm of AI agents might be able to take over the internet in six months to a year unless companies devoted more time to putting safeguards in place.
Dario Amodei outlined a plan for companies like his and governments around the world to ensure that increasingly capable AI models remain aligned with the commands and values of responsible people days after two former Anthropic safety researchers publicly aired concerns that the existential threats AI might pose to humanity were receiving too little attention.
Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT maker OpenAI, said this weekend that companies should start coordinating on AI safety without waiting for the government to introduce legislation. The "pacing" of AI development doesn't mean stopping, Altman wrote on X. "But it should be slower than it otherwise could be."
Here's what to know about the recent dire predictions and whether any brakes might be put on AI advancement:
Concerns over the potential risks of the technology are rising as new AI models become more powerful, heightening both the potential for misuse by people with criminal aims, such as creating and spreading a disease that kills most of the world's population, and the risk of AI systems going rogue in a dangerous way.
Anthropic disclosed last week that it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity, such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons.
The company said it put stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could be used to make weapons but noted that "as models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society's defenders act to make them safer."
Last year, Anthropic reported that hackers used the company's AI in a cyberattack targeting about 30 companies and government agencies around the world. It said the hackers were very likely from a Chinese state-sponsored group.
When an AI agent "goes rogue," it means the AI has taken action beyond the task it was asked to perform. Both Anthropic and OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, said in July that their AI models had succeeded in acting on their own.
Anthropic disclosed that three AI models — Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model — hacked into three other organizations during testing just days after OpenAI revealed that its AI system hacked into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face.
OpenAI described the intrusion by a combination of models, including its newly released GPT‑5.6 Sol and an "even more capable" model that was still being tested internally, as a "significant security incident."
Meta followed suit in early August with a similar case of an AI model finding ways around another company's digital security.
Although some observers noted that people had disabled some guardrails in the OpenAI and Anthropic cases, the episodes seemed to reflect one of the biggest fears around AI: that if models achieve artificial general intelligence, or AGI, a loosely defined term for AI that can match or surpass human abilities across a broad range of intellectual tasks, the technology could cause an irreversible catastrophic event or subjugate the human race.
Doomsday scenarios generally fall into two categories: An AI that achieves self-improving superintelligence controls people instead of vice versa, or AI used by a rogue state or nefarious actors.
Worries that artificial intelligence might overcome human limits on its reach or actions are not new.
Alan Turing, a British mathematician widely regarded as one of the earliest authorities on artificial intelligence, predicted in 1951 that AI would eventually take control from humans. Less than a decade later, Norbert Wiener, another mathematician, warned intelligent machines would seek to accomplish their own objectives and humans would not be able to stop them.
In 2026, how reasonable are fears that AI, either by escaping human control or through misuse by unscrupulous people, could cause a cataclysmic event or the downfall of civilization?
No one knows.
Experts across computer science, philosophy and other fields have envisioned numerous routes by which a future AI system might cause a global catastrophe, either by escaping human control or in the hands of an unscrupulous people. They range from deploying weapons and identifying a lethal pathogen to manipulating governments into conflict or disrupting the food, energy and communications networks societies rely on to function.
There is no widely accepted estimate for how soon any of these scenarios might happen and no consensus on their likelihood.
In 2023, the nonprofit Center for AI Safety issued a statement cosigned by more than 350 researchers and technology executives, including Anthropic's Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, saying: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war."
The 2026 International AI Safety Report, written with guidance from more than 100 independent experts, says current systems show early signs of some relevant capabilities but not at levels that could enable a loss of control, and describes the risk's likelihood, nature and timing as "unusually ambiguous."
An Anthropic researcher said last week he was resigning from the company over concerns that neither the company nor its competitors were acting responsibly in developing the technology. In social media posts, Jacob Coxon estimated a 10% chance of AI causing human extinction within the next decade and said both Anthropic and OpenAI "are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
Researchers have called for a slowdown of AI development and warned for years that the technology could pose existential risks to humanity.
Following the recent incidents, experts called for improved testing by AI companies and more dialogue between the U.S. and China to come up with shared solutions.
But AI is growing so fast that government and evaluation systems are struggling to keep pace with the technology. Countries are cobbling together their own laws, some conflicting.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping warned at a conference in July of the need to keep AI from evading human control. The Trump administration initially demonstrated reluctance to regulate AI but has become more keen to reduce cybersecurity risks.
On Sunday, President Trump downplayed the necessity for his administration to check AI development, but acknowledged the need for some regulation.

articles.summary: The initiative is part of her focus on preparing children and youth for success in the digital era.
articles.content:
ASHE COUNTY, N.C. — First Lady Melania Trump will travel to Ashe County on Tuesday to promote community resiliency and education technology in schools.
She is scheduled to deliver remarks to elementary school students and visit classrooms to observe how teachers and staff are integrating technology into instruction.
The initiative is part of her focus on preparing children and youth for success in the digital era.
The visit is scheduled for 12:00 p.m.
The trip marks her first return to western North Carolina since January 2025, when she and President Donald Trump toured the damage caused by Hurricane Helene nearly two years ago.
President Trump will be in Gastonia to campaign for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley.

articles.title: OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears
articles.description: OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears The Guardian
articles.description_html: OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears  The Guardian
articles.article_title: OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears
articles.heading: OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears
articles.summary: Company behind ChatGPT tells ministers to seize ‘political window’ on regulation as cross-party committee warns of rising threats to human rights
articles.content:
OpenAI has urged British lawmakers to capitalise on renewed fears over AI safety and impose legislation reining in the technology.
The company behind ChatGPT said the UK government should act immediately, following a call by its arch-rival Anthropic to curb AI development.
“We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems,” said OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon.
However, the tech company said legislation should be narrowly focused on the most advanced AI labs and not startups working on less powerful systems.
In a separate interview with the online publication Politico, Duff Gordon said the government should “take advantage of this political window which is clearly opening up” to legislate.
OpenAI’s intervention came as a UK parliamentary committee demanded more restrictions on the power of AI, warning that the world was unprepared for the “potentially dire” consequences of the technology, in the latest sign of rising global concern.
A new regulatory framework is needed for AI in the UK, including an independent oversight body and legislation to protect the public, according to the cross-party joint committee on human rights, comprising MPs and Lords.
It said AI posed a number of threats, from public face-scanning to explicit deepfakes and flagging disciplinary action for workers without reasonable cause.
The call for action came after Anthropic, a leading AI company, urged its competitors and governments at the weekend to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development – a call that received immediate support from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk.
It follows a series of serious safety incidents in which swarms of AI agents broke out of testing environments and hacked into third-party infrastructure, as well as evidence some users have dodged controls to use models in ways that could support biological weapons development.
Alex Sobel, the Labour chair of the human rights committee, said the world was unprepared for dealing with the “potentially dire” consequences of a rapidly developing technology.
“Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose,” he said.
A government spokesperson said the UK took the risks from advanced AI “extremely seriously” and recognised the need to keep pace with the rapidly evolving technology, including working closely with AI companies and other countries.
“We should not assume that the existing framework will always be sufficient as AI capabilities develop. Any future measures will be evidence-based and focused on the risks we need to address,” said the spokesperson.
On Friday, more than 70 MPs and peers urged the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology. Downing Street rejected the call for a ban, but said it was exploring additional targeted interventions “to address the most significant AI-related national security risks”.
Sobel said: “New legislation is needed to establish a comprehensive set of protections that deal with the entire AI supply chain and its life cycle.
“A single AI regulator should be established to set policy, monitor performance and ensure enforcement.”
Donald Trump has played down warnings of dire risks to humanity. “We’re leading China in AI,” the US president said on Sunday. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
In his weekend call for the main AI companies to “pace the frontier”, the Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the US government should grant the leading AI companies a waiver to allow them to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said on Sunday night that while he would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI”, there was no “need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence”.
He said: “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.”
Sobel, who has also proposed a bill to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK, said protections were needed now to ensure that potential human rights risks do not “become reality”.
The committee said a new AI bill should establish a regulatory regime that mandates more demanding obligations for higher-risk AI systems and models, and prohibit some uses of AI which are incompatible with human rights.
It also called for mandatory transparency requirements across all levels of the technology’s life cycle, and the establishment of an independent AI oversight body to monitor AI harms and risks, with strong powers to hold AI providers to account.
The UK government has already established the AI Security Institute (AISI), which subjects advanced models to safety tests – but does not have the power to compel AI developers such as Anthropic to submit their technology for scrutiny. Last week, it was reported that Anthropic had declined to send its latest model to AISI for testing.

The company behind ChatGPT said the UK government should act immediately, following a call by its arch-rival Anthropic to curb AI development.

“We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems,” said OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon.

However, the tech company said legislation should be narrowly focused on the most advanced AI labs and not startups working on less powerful systems.

In a separate interview with the online publication Politico, Duff Gordon said the government should “take advantage of this political window which is clearly opening up” to legislate.

OpenAI’s intervention came as a UK parliamentary committee demanded more restrictions on the power of AI, warning that the world was unprepared for the “potentially dire” consequences of the technology, in the latest sign of rising global concern.

A new regulatory framework is needed for AI in the UK, including an independent oversight body and legislation to protect the public, according to the cross-party joint committee on human rights, comprising MPs and Lords.

It said AI posed a number of threats, from public face-scanning to explicit deepfakes and flagging disciplinary action for workers without reasonable cause.

The call for action came after Anthropic, a leading AI company, urged its competitors and governments at the weekend to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development – a call that received immediate support from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk.

It follows a series of serious safety incidents in which swarms of AI agents broke out of testing environments and hacked into third-party infrastructure, as well as evidence some users have dodged controls to use models in ways that could support biological weapons development.

Alex Sobel, the Labour chair of the human rights committee, said the world was unprepared for dealing with the “potentially dire” consequences of a rapidly developing technology.

“Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose,” he said.

A government spokesperson said the UK took the risks from advanced AI “extremely seriously” and recognised the need to keep pace with the rapidly evolving technology, including working closely with AI companies and other countries.

“We should not assume that the existing framework will always be sufficient as AI capabilities develop. Any future measures will be evidence-based and focused on the risks we need to address,” said the spokesperson.

On Friday, more than 70 MPs and peers urged the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology. Downing Street rejected the call for a ban, but said it was exploring additional targeted interventions “to address the most significant AI-related national security risks”.

Sobel said: “New legislation is needed to establish a comprehensive set of protections that deal with the entire AI supply chain and its life cycle.

“A single AI regulator should be established to set policy, monitor performance and ensure enforcement.”

Donald Trump has played down warnings of dire risks to humanity. “We’re leading China in AI,” the US president said on Sunday. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to ⁠keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”

In his weekend call for the main AI companies to “pace the frontier”, the Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the US government should grant the leading AI companies a waiver to allow them to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said on Sunday night that while he would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI”, there was no “need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence”.

He said: “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.”

Sobel, who has also proposed a bill to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK, said protections were needed now to ensure that potential human rights risks do not “become reality”.

The committee said a new AI bill should establish a regulatory regime that mandates more demanding obligations for higher-risk AI systems and models, and prohibit some uses of AI which are incompatible with human rights.

It also called for mandatory transparency requirements across all levels of the technology’s life cycle, and the establishment of an independent AI oversight body to monitor AI harms and risks, with strong powers to hold AI providers to account.

The UK government has already established the AI Security Institute (AISI), which subjects advanced models to safety tests – but does not have the power to compel AI developers such as Anthropic to submit their technology for scrutiny. Last week, it was reported that Anthropic had declined to send its latest model to AISI for testing.

articles.title: C3.ai vs. CrowdStrike: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.description: C3.ai vs. CrowdStrike: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: C3.ai vs. CrowdStrike: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: C3.ai vs. CrowdStrike: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: C3.ai vs. CrowdStrike: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.summary: CrowdStrike is generating record revenue and free cash flow while C3.ai works to rebuild from the ground up. The gap in execution between these two companies tells the whole story.
articles.content:
Should you prioritize an enterprise software pioneer or a cybersecurity giant? Choosing between C3.ai (AI +0.67%) and CrowdStrike (CRWD -1.01%) requires weighing massive growth potential against very different paths toward profitability.
C3.ai focuses on prebuilt artificial intelligence applications that help organizations make faster decisions using their own data. CrowdStrike secures that data by defending endpoints and cloud workloads. Both represent critical components of modern digital infrastructure, though they operate in different niches of the software market.
CRWD & AI: Performance Comparison
Key Financial Metrics
The case for C3.ai
C3.ai sells its C3 Agentic AI Platform alongside prebuilt applications for industries like manufacturing and defense. A key strategic partner and reseller is Baker Hughes (BKR -0.57%), which provides the company with deep access to the energy sector. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as it depends on a few high-value relationships like its partnership with Microsoft (MSFT +0.65%) and Amazon (AMZN +1.94%).
In FY 2026, the company reported revenue of nearly $250.3 million, representing a year-over-year decline of approximately 35.7%. This contributed to a net loss of roughly $470.4 million for the period, which resulted in a negative net margin. These figures suggest the company is navigating a challenging transition in its business model or market demand for tech stocks in the enterprise space.
As of its April 2026 balance sheet, the company maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x, indicating it carries no debt relative to shareholder equity. Its current ratio was approximately 6.6x, which measures a firm's ability to cover its short-term obligations with assets. However, free cash flow was negative at nearly $190.7 million, indicating the company spent more on operations and capital expenditures than it generated.
The case for CrowdStrike
CrowdStrike sells subscriptions to its Falcon platform to secure identity and cloud workloads for tens of thousands of organizations globally. It maintains significant technology alliances with major providers like Amazon to reach a wide variety of commercial clients. The company recently expanded its capabilities through a distribution partnership with OpenAI to integrate advanced generative artificial intelligence into its security services.
In FY 2026, revenue reached approximately $4.8 billion, a growth rate of nearly 21.7% compared to the previous year. While the top line grew, the company reported a net loss of roughly $162.5 million for the fiscal year. This resulted in a negative net margin of approximately 3.4%, which is the percentage of revenue remaining after all expenses are paid.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the company had a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.2x, meaning it holds $0.20 of debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. A current ratio of approximately 1.8x indicates the company has enough assets to cover its short-term liabilities. Free cash flow was positive at roughly $1.3 billion, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 68% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation.
Risk profile comparison
C3.ai faces risks including financial instability and a history of significant net losses. It relies on a limited number of high-value contracts and faces intense competition from Alphabet and other major cloud providers. Additionally, the company must navigate potential liability from biased artificial intelligence outputs and compliance costs associated with the EU AI Act.
CrowdStrike is still managing repercussions from the July 19, 2024 incident that caused widespread system crashes and triggered legal proceedings. It faces intense competition from legacy security vendors and other cloud-native security firms that may pressure market share. The company also depends on third-party infrastructure from Amazon and must manage the operational challenges of its rapid growth.
Valuation comparison
| Metric | C3.ai | CrowdStrike |
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | N/A | 168.7x |
| P/S ratio | 6.5x | 44.7x |
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with CrowdStrike, and it's not a close call. CrowdStrike just posted a spectacular quarter, with record annual recurring revenue and free cash flow surging to nearly a third of total revenue. The Falcon platform keeps absorbing more of each customer's security spending, turning individual contracts into long-term platform relationships. Every enterprise that adds an AI workload also adds new security risks that need protecting, which means CrowdStrike's addressable market keeps expanding alongside the AI build-out itself.
C3.ai, by contrast, is in the middle of a painful reset. Its own CEO described recent sales performance as "unspeakably horrible." The company cut roughly a third of its workforce, and revenue has been falling. A top-to-bottom sales reorganization is underway, and while a turnaround is possible, the timeline and the outcome are far from certain.
Cybersecurity is not a discretionary purchase for enterprises the way AI software platforms can be. When budgets tighten, CrowdStrike's Falcon platform stays. C3.ai's contracts get scrutinized. For a long-term investor, owning the platform that enterprises depend on to keep their systems safe is a far more dependable foundation than betting on a software company still working to find its footing.

articles.title: Screen time and learning outcomes take center stage at Park Hill board meeting
articles.description: Screen time and learning outcomes take center stage at Park Hill board meeting thebeaconnews.org
articles.description_html: Screen time and learning outcomes take center stage at Park Hill board meeting  thebeaconnews.org
articles.article_title: Screen time and learning outcomes take center stage at Park Hill board meeting
articles.heading: Screen time and learning outcomes take center stage at Park Hill board meeting
articles.summary: Parents with Schools Beyond Screens expressed worries to the Park Hill school board about screen overuse and its effect on learning outcomes.
articles.content:
In a full room, the Park Hill school board heard concerns from local parents affiliated with the group Schools Beyond Screens about how technology is used in learning spaces.
During the board’s Sept. 10 meeting, parents discussed screen overuse, the effects on educational outcomes and social skills, a lack of transparency and the financial burdens of constantly replacing technology.
Schools Beyond Screens is a national coalition that advocates for transparent, student-centered technology policies and use in classrooms.
Multiple parents pointed to studies that have shown that increased technology use is associated with negative academic outcomes, reduced social skills and attention issues.
They urged the board to consider whether the district’s school-supplied device policy is actually beneficial and argued the district’s technology task force’s decisions should be rooted in reviewed research.
“If the data shows that fourth graders, eighth graders and 15-year-olds should have very limited digital learning time, why is it our default to give our youngest learners a one-to-one device?” said Taylor Rees, a Park Hill mom.
Andrew Potter, father to a Park Hill kindergartner, said he would like to see more transparency regarding how much time a child is spending on a screen and what apps they have access to.
He’s not the only one. Potter also pointed to a survey that the Park Hill chapter of Schools Beyond Screens conducted. Of the 255 responses it received, 91% said they would like a daily report showing how much time their child spent on a school device.
Others spoke about how the district’s technology use made some parents question which school to send their children to.
Tori Winter, a mom to twins set to start kindergarten next year, said it should have been an easy decision to send her kids to Southeast Elementary School. But the school’s use of iPad time as a reward for completing work, causing some students to rush, was a concern for her.
In the survey, some respondents said they were considering changing districts or sending their children to private school instead because of similar concerns.
Another parent, Brennan Coulter, rounded out the public comment period by speaking on some of the financial liabilities the school incurs each year through education technology, and requested that the board review those costs.
“One-to-one devices were not a one-time purchase,” Coulter said. “They created a permanent, recurring obligation, such as device replacement, software licensing, insurance, breakage, filtering, help desk support and the staff required to manage it all. Those costs return every year, and they can grow over time.”
The Park Hill School District is projected to spend more than $2.6 million on technology hardware and software as part of its capital plan expenditures during the 2026-2027 school year, according to budget reports. That is nearly a 63% increase from the previous year, when the district spent roughly $1.6 million on technology expenses.
It’s not clear how much of that spending is related to student devices.
During the meeting, the board also heard from its instructional technology task force, which was convened to develop district recommendations for digital learning practices.
Administrators said the task force was created in part because bills that aimed to limit screen time were introduced in the Missouri legislature this year. They ultimately did not pass.
Keelie Stucker, the executive director of secondary education at Park Hill and a member of the task force, said their goal was to ensure technology in the district was being used in a way that was developmentally appropriate, healthy and educationally sound.
To achieve that, the task force presented two strategies it intended to pursue. The first was to review and integrate technology in a way that supports core instruction and to not treat it as something separate, Park Hill’s Executive Director of Elementary Education Melissa Hensley said. The second was removing barriers to access so that the technology can help support different learning needs for all students.
As the task force develops its recommendations, Hensley laid out how it plans to incorporate research, conduct feedback surveys and review technology use data.
She stressed the importance of gathering stakeholder input and feedback for the process.
“We know that our stakeholders, as we see tonight, are passionate about this topic,” Hensley said. “We know that we cannot do this alone. This is not isolation work. This is together work, and we have to hear from people and know the experiences that happen every day with technology for our students, for our staff and for our families.”
Board members expressed that they were looking forward to the task force’s work and that the additional parameters were necessary steps after the boom of online learning brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic.
“Some of this is just kind of unbuilding, unwinding the COVID technology that we had to have because that was the only way to learn,” board Vice President Daryl Terwilleger said.
But after the presentation, Rees said she still has concerns about the research the task force is utilizing to make its decisions.
She said none of the materials she saw was from peer-reviewed articles and a portion of the material came from the Consortium for School Networking (CoSN), a nonprofit professional association that promotes education technology leadership and innovation. CoSN also works with various education technology companies.
“A task force is only as strong as the research it considers, and that research must challenge our current practices,” Rees said during her public comment. “CoSN focuses largely on how to implement technology effectively. I don’t want to risk my child’s brain health on information provided by companies that will profit from putting the technology in her hands.”
The task force is still in its early stages and won’t present recommendations until January 2027. Its next meeting will be held on Sept. 22, and the school board will meet on Sept. 24.

articles.title: Used Farm Equipment Prices Split as Technology Drives Late-Model Values
