articles.title: Gadkari delayed by Mumbai traffic by nearly an hour, pitches new technology to replace ageing flyovers
articles.description: Gadkari delayed by Mumbai traffic by nearly an hour, pitches new technology to replace ageing flyovers The Hindu
articles.description_html: Gadkari delayed by Mumbai traffic by nearly an hour, pitches new technology to replace ageing flyovers  The Hindu
articles.article_title: Gadkari delayed by Mumbai traffic by nearly an hour, pitches new technology to replace ageing flyovers
articles.heading: Gadkari delayed by Mumbai traffic by nearly an hour, pitches new technology to replace ageing flyovers
articles.summary: Nitin Gadkari, delayed by Mumbai traffic, advocates for replacing ageing flyovers with advanced technology to tackle congestion.
articles.content:
Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari arrived nearly an hour late for an event in Mumbai after getting caught in the city’s traffic, an experience he used to acknowledge the limitations of infrastructure built during his own tenure as Maharashtra’s public works Minister and call for ageing flyovers to be replaced using newer technology.
Mr. Gadkari was travelling from Worli to attend the 22nd Indo-American Corporate Excellence Awards in Mumbai when he was delayed in traffic. Addressing the gathering after reaching the venue, he pointed to his delayed arrival before turning to Mumbai’s larger congestion problem.
“Today I got late by an hour,” Mr. Gadkari said, before joking that he was “paying for my mistake” — a reference to the road infrastructure developed when he was Maharashtra’s PWD Minister in the 1990s.
The event, held on September 11, 2026, was organised by the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce’s West India Council to recognise companies and business leaders contributing to India-U.S. trade and economic ties. Mr. Gadkari attended as the chief guest, while YES Bank MD and CEO Vinay Tonse was the guest of honour. Thirteen award winners were felicitated at the event.
Mr. Gadkari recalled that during his tenure in Maharashtra, he had been involved in the development of 55 flyovers in Mumbai, as well as major road infrastructure projects including the Mumbai-Pune Expressway and planning associated with the Bandra-Worli Sea Link.
However, he said the technology available at the time was different from what is available today and suggested that some of Mumbai’s older flyovers were no longer adequate for the sharp increase in traffic volumes.
The Minister said he had discussed the issue with Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis and suggested that ageing flyovers be replaced with structures using newer technology rather than continuing with conventional designs.
As an example, Mr. Gadkari referred to infrastructure being planned in Pune, where he said multi-level structures could accommodate different modes of transport vertically — with roads constructed at different levels and a Metro corridor above them. He said projects worth around ₹50,000 crore were being considered in Pune and referred to technology brought from Malaysia for such structures.
His remarks came against the backdrop of Mumbai’s continuing struggle with road congestion despite decades of investment in flyovers, elevated roads, coastal connectivity and public transport. Mr. Gadkari’s own delayed journey on Friday (September 11) became an illustration of the challenge, with the minister arguing that cities would increasingly have to use newer engineering solutions to add transport capacity within limited available space.
Mr. Gadkari also used his address to emphasise greater cooperation between India and the United States, saying India’s engineering and entrepreneurial capabilities could be combined with American technology and resources to create a “win-win” situation.
The awards ceremony brought together business leaders, entrepreneurs and industry representatives from the Indo-U.S. business community and was aimed at recognising contributions to bilateral trade, innovation and economic cooperation.
Published - September 14, 2026 09:52 am IST

articles.description: MIT Future Fest—science, technology, art & design e-flux.com
articles.description_html: MIT Future Fest—science, technology, art & design  e-flux.com
articles.article_title: MIT Future Fest—science, technology, art & design - Announcements - e-flux
articles.heading: MIT Future Fest—science, technology, art & design
articles.summary: MIT Future Fest is a five-day festival, opening MIT’s doors to the world September 30–October 4, 2026.
articles.content:
50+ events, 100+ speakers
September 30–October 4, 2026
MIT Future Fest is a new five-day festival, opening MIT’s doors to the world September 30–October 4, 2026. General Release passes are now available, with a 10 percent discount.
The inaugural edition of MIT Future Fest brings together over 100 visionary leaders working on the frontiers of AI, quantum, health, climate, energy, public policy, contemporary art, design, and more. Speakers like filmmaker and artist Kahlil Joseph, MoMA senior curator of architecture and design Paola Antonelli, architect Carlo Ratti, designer and computer scientist Skylar Tibbits, interdisciplinary artist and designer Behnaz Farahi, inventor of the iPod Tony Fadell, MIT Quantum lead Danna Freedman, rock climber and bionicist Hugh Herr, and aerospace engineer Danielle Wood will tackle some of the future’s most fascinating questions in a range of panels, open laboratories, immersive exhibitions, and evening performances.
MIT Future Fest was founded on the belief that the world's most pressing problems demand the convergent, interdisciplinary work that MIT excels in.
Program highlights
With 50+ events across five days exploring the next era of science, technology, art, and design, join us for the most anticipated highlights featured in Surface Magazine:
BLKNWS: MIT Edition by Kahlil Joseph will be a site-specific MIT Chapter of BLKNWS (2018–ongoing), an evolving artwork and media platform that dissolves the boundaries between journalism, archive, cinema, and speculation. This new edition of BLKNWS will bring together scholars, scientists, artists, and thinkers from MIT to ask what it means to imagine the future from one of the world's most consequential research communities.
Ocean of Dreams by Behnaz Farahi transforms MIT’s Kendall Square Plaza into a living, participatory ocean where people are invited to contribute their hopes for the future. Animated waves flow continuously, carrying messages submitted through a mobile web interface before gradually washing them away like words written in sand, joining an ever-changing collective landscape.
The Weavers by Jay Scheib is a new extended reality (XR) action-film-inspired performance of Gerhart Hauptmann's 1912 Nobel Prize-winning play, addressing the question: will AI take my job? The performance centers on a community of textile workers and their bosses whose labor, faith, and humanity are pressed to the brink of starvation by the unstoppable march of mechanization, automation, and the free-fall collapse of empathy.
Adaptive Archipelago by Daniel Sundlin and Skylar Tibbits is a prototype of a new modular floating structure to explore one of the most urgent design questions of our time: how do we create infrastructure that adapts as the world around it changes? Installed on the Charles River, the structure asks what a floating future could actually look like, and how design, engineering, and ecological thinking can come together to imagine and build it.
About MIT Future Fest
MIT Future Fest is a collaboration led by the MIT Museum, in partnership with MIT Technology Review and MIT Morningside Academy for Design (MAD), with support from an advisory panel of world-leading researchers and experts. The festival foregrounds creative leaders in critical, timely fields from quantum and AI to climate, health and life sciences, united in their dedication to shaping our shared horizon. Every experience is tailored to connect with one or more of MIT’s strategic initiatives—the major cross-cutting bets that the MIT community is making on the future. These initiatives represent not just research priorities but a statement of institutional purpose: that the world’s most pressing problems demand the kind of convergent, interdisciplinary work that defines MIT’s mission.

articles.summary: Rising bond yields and oil prices weighed on stocks last week, though a mostly in-line CPI report on Friday sparked a rebound. The S&P 500 still fell 0.8%, with nine of the 11 sectors declining. Energy (OW) led, rising 2.0%, and it tops the sector derby
articles.content:
Rising bond yields and oil prices weighed on stocks last week, though a mostly in-line CPI report on Friday sparked a rebound. The S&P 500 still fell 0.8%, with nine of the 11 sectors declining. Energy (OW) led, rising 2.0%, and it tops the sector derby at 44.5% ytd. Communication Services (MW) was the only other gainer, up 1.1%. Health Care (OW) fell the most at 3.6%. Information Technology (MW) was nearly flat at -0.2% and is up 23.2% ytd, with fundamentals that continue to improve.
Let's take a closer look at Energy, Information Technology, and Health Care:
(1) Energy. We have recommended overweighting Energy as a hedge against geopolitical risk. Brent fell below $90 a barrel in late August as diplomacy briefly eased tensions in the Persian Gulf. Last week, the US and Iran exchanged strikes, and Houthi attacks set Saudi oil facilities on fire. Brent futures rose to $104.61 on Friday (chart). The S&P 500 Energy index is at a record high.

articles.article_title: Aptar Pharma Expands Preservative Free Technology Production in Latin America
articles.heading: Aptar Pharma Expands Preservative Free Technology Production in Latin America
articles.summary: Aptar Pharma Expands Preservative Free Technology Production in Latin America BioSpace
articles.content:
Transfer of Aptar Pharma’s Advanced Preservative Free pump technology to Berazategui, Argentina, strengthens local manufacturing capabilities and supports the company’s local-for-local approach in the region.
CRYSTAL LAKE, Ill.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aptar Pharma, a global leader in drug delivery, dosing, protection technologies and services, today announced the successful transfer and commissioning of its Aptar Pharma Preservative Free (APF) production line at its manufacturing facility in Berazategui, Argentina. The investment brings Aptar Pharma’s Advanced Preservative Free pump technology closer to customers in Latin America, reinforcing the company’s commitment to expanding local manufacturing capabilities and improving access to innovative drug delivery solutions in the region.
Located south of Buenos Aires, the Berazategui facility serves as Aptar Pharma’s industrial hub in Latin America, supplying customers across 15 countries. With 2,500m2 dedicated to the manufacturing of drug delivery systems, the site supports both consumer healthcare and prescription pharmaceutical markets.
Bringing Advanced Preservative-Free Technology Closer to Customers
Aptar Pharma’s APF pump is a leading multidose spray dispensing system for preservative-free nasal formulations. Designed to support microbiological integrity through mechanical means, the technology helps meet growing demand for preservative-free solutions while supporting customers in the development of differentiated healthcare products.
For more than 20 years, Aptar Pharma has supported customers in Latin America with solutions designed to help improve the lives of millions of patients. The APF line transfer is a direct extension of this commitment, strengthening regional supply agility, reducing lead times and enhancing product availability for local markets.
“This transfer reflects Aptar Pharma’s continued investment in bringing proven technologies closer to customers and patients around the world,” said Julie Pradeilles, President Consumer Healthcare, Aptar Pharma. “By transferring the APF production line to Argentina, we are strengthening our local-for-local manufacturing approach and supporting greater agility for customers in Latin America. This is a strong example of how our global footprint can help expand access to innovative drug delivery solutions where they are needed.”
Supporting Aptar Pharma’s Global Expansion Program
The APF line transfer to Argentina is part of Aptar Pharma’s broader global expansion program and local-for-local strategy. This includes recent and ongoing investments in Congers, New York, Suzhou, China and Mumbai, India, designed to expand capacity, strengthen innovation and bring Aptar Pharma’s technologies closer to customers in key markets.
“Improving access to medicines remains an important challenge for the pharmaceutical industry in Latin America,” said Marcos Garcia, Vice President, Aptar Pharma Latin America. “By bringing technology and manufacturing capabilities closer to our customers in the region, we can better support them with shorter lead times, greater availability and solutions that help expand the reach of healthcare.”
About Aptar Pharma
Aptar Pharma is part of AptarGroup, Inc., a global leader in drug and consumer product dosing, dispensing and protection technologies. Aptar serves a number of attractive end markets including pharmaceutical, beauty, food, beverage, personal care and home care. Using market expertise, proprietary design, engineering and science to create innovative solutions for many of the world’s leading brands, Aptar in turn makes a meaningful difference in the lives, looks, health and homes of millions of patients and consumers around the world. Aptar is headquartered in Crystal Lake, Illinois and has over 13,000 dedicated employees in 20 countries. For more information, visit www.aptar.com.
This press release contains forward-looking statements, including statements regarding Aptar Pharma’s manufacturing capacity, its global expansion program and local-for-local strategy, and the anticipated benefits of the APF line transfer for customers in Latin America. These statements are based on current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. AptarGroup, Inc. undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statement.

articles.article_title: Tourism and technology may hold key to boosting China’s public image in the US
articles.heading: Tourism and technology may hold key to boosting China’s public image in the US
articles.summary: Survey by Sun Yat-sen University team also concludes that many people believe the country has played a positive role on the world stage.
articles.content:
Tourism and technology may hold key to boosting China’s public image in the US
Survey by Sun Yat-sen University team also concludes that many people believe the country has played a positive role on the world stage
Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou said that although concepts such as “decoupling” and “de-risking” had been increasingly prominent in media coverage of China, this had not entirely wiped away positive impressions of the country.
When evaluating China’s strengths on a scale of 1 to 5, the respondents placed global influence at the top with a score of 4.38, followed by achievements in science and technology at 3.59 and higher education at 3.56.
The survey found many respondents believed China was contributing to global peace, stability and governance, prompting the researchers to argue that Beijing should reinforce its image as a responsible major power by highlighting its role in United Nations peacekeeping missions, in fighting climate change and providing aid.

articles.title: Cerebras Systems vs. QuantumScape: Here Is the Better Hardware Technology Stock to Buy in 2026
articles.description: Cerebras Systems vs. QuantumScape: Here Is the Better Hardware Technology Stock to Buy in 2026 The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: Cerebras Systems vs. QuantumScape: Here Is the Better Hardware Technology Stock to Buy in 2026  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Cerebras Systems vs. QuantumScape: Here Is the Better Hardware Technology Stock to Buy in 2026 | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Cerebras Systems vs. QuantumScape: Here Is the Better Hardware Technology Stock to Buy in 2026
articles.summary: One is profitable with $510 million in revenue; the other burns cash but guards a battery moonshot.
articles.content:
Investors often choose between fast-growing tech and long-term moonshots. Deciding between Cerebras Systems (CBRS +0.31%) and QuantumScape (QS +1.93%) requires weighing current AI demand against the future of electric vehicle battery technology.
Cerebras Systems creates massive chips to accelerate artificial intelligence, while QuantumScape aims to revolutionize the energy industry with solid-state batteries. Both companies target massive markets, but they operate at very different stages of commercial maturity, making this a classic matchup between realized growth and future potential.
The case for Cerebras Systems
Cerebras Systems specializes in high-performance computing for artificial intelligence by building the world's largest processors. Its business strategy centers on the CS-3 platform, which uses a single wafer-scale chip to handle massive datasets more efficiently than traditional chip clusters. The company serves customers across North America, Asia, Europe, and the Middle East through cloud deployments and on-premises installations. Among tech stocks, Cerebras is positioning itself as a primary alternative for enterprises requiring extreme processing power.
In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year (FY) ended December 31, 2025, revenue reached nearly $510 million. This represents a significant increase of 75.7% compared to the prior year. The company achieved $237.8 million in net income, resulting in a net margin of 46.6%. This transition to profitability is a major milestone for the hardware maker as it scales its production capacity to meet global demand for AI infrastructure.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is -0.5x, indicating that total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio of 2.1x measures the ability to cover short-term obligations with assets like cash and inventory. Free cash flow was -$392.8 million, which is the cash remaining after subtracting capital expenditures from cash flow from operations. Because the company is profitable, investors can evaluate it using a Forward P/E, which compares the stock price to future earnings estimates.
The case for QuantumScape
QuantumScape is focused on developing solid-state lithium-metal batteries that could significantly increase the range and charging speed of electric vehicles. The company maintains a long-standing strategic partnership with Volkswagen (VLKPF -5.17%) to industrialize its QSE-5 battery cell. It has also expanded its reach through a multi-year partnership with Honda to support battery development. This level of customer concentration with major automakers like Volkswagen adds a layer of risk to the business, as much of its future depends on these collaborations.
In FY 2025, QuantumScape reported no revenue because its technology remains in the pre-commercial testing phase. The company reported a net loss of $435.1 million for the year, which is a slight reduction from the losses seen in previous years. The net margin is currently 0% given the lack of commercial sales.
Based on its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The company maintains a very high current ratio of 15.9x, indicating it has significant cash reserves to fund its research and development. Free cash flow was -$278.8 million. This cash burn is expected as the company works to transition its technology from the laboratory to high-volume manufacturing.
CBRS & QS: Performance Comparison
Key Financial Metrics
Risk profile comparison
Cerebras Systems faces intense competition in the semiconductor market from larger tech giants that have significantly more capital and established supply chains, such as Nvidia, which could limit the market for independent hardware providers. Additionally, the company must continue to innovate rapidly to prevent its wafer-scale technology from becoming obsolete. The high cost of manufacturing these massive processors means any dip in demand for AI compute could lead to significant financial pressure.
QuantumScape faces substantial risks related to the commercialization of its battery technology, as it has yet to prove it can manufacture cells at a high volume with consistent quality. The company is highly dependent on its relationship with Volkswagen, and any shift in that automaker's strategy could harm its prospects. Competitive pressures from other solid-state developers or improvements in traditional lithium-ion batteries could also make its technology less attractive.
Valuation comparison
Cerebras Systems carries a high valuation based on its recent profitability. Investors often look at the P/S ratio, which compares the market value to annual revenue, to value companies that are not yet profitable. However, QuantumScape remains difficult to value using traditional metrics because it has no current revenue.
| Metric | Cerebras Systems | QuantumScape |
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | 204.1x | n/a |
| P/S ratio | 64.4x | n/a |
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Cerebras Systems and QuantumScape have both developed proprietary technologies that can give them an edge as the artificial intelligence and electric battery industries expand. In fact, the energy demands to power AI systems is so large, QuantumScape pitched its solid-state batteries as a solution, giving it a potential new market beyond electric vehicles.
Still, between these two, I would invest in Cerebras Systems over QuantumScape. The former has proven commercial technology, as evidenced by its rapidly rising revenue. QuantumScape is years away from commercial applications, with management targeting 2029 at the earliest.
Meanwhile, Cerebras produced revenue of $180.1 million in the second quarter, up 74% from 2025. This demonstrates strong customer demand for its specialized AI technology.
That said, Cerebras went from a profitable company at the end of 2025 to a whopping net loss of $450.5 million in Q2. The sizable jump was the result of expenses related to its IPO, which took place in May. Now, the question is whether the company can return to profitability in future quarters.

articles.title: Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs
articles.description: Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs aljazeera.com
articles.description_html: Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs  aljazeera.com
articles.article_title: Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs
articles.heading: Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs
articles.summary: Trump downplays AI risks, saying he wants to maintain the US's lead over China in the emerging technology.
articles.content:
Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs
Trump downplays AI risks, saying he wants to maintain the US’s lead over China in the emerging technology.
US President Donald Trump has downplayed the need for his administration to place checks on artificial intelligence development, saying he is worried about ceding the US’s lead to China.
Speaking to reporters during his trip to Ireland on Sunday, Trump also said he acknowledged the need for some regulation but did not provide further details on potential measures.
“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that … shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump told reporters after watching the Irish Open at his resort in Doonbeg.
He said that with the US leading the development of AI over China, “frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.”
Trump’s comments came a day after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a blog post saying the AI industry must slow the pace of improving the technology’s capabilities to allow time for guardrails.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed with Amodei, adding that this was a primary topic of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks. Elon Musk also publicly agreed with Amodei’s post.
The warnings follow ex-Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon’s public resignation over concerns about AI’s potential to surpass human control, which sent ripple effects throughout the industry and Washington.
Multiple US lawmakers made calls for legislation to control AI development following Coxon’s resignation, including Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer and Republican Congressman Mike Lawler, who introduced a bipartisan House bill to prevent AI from operating without human oversight.
Concerns over AI have become a major election-cycle issue amid the explosion of computing warehouses being built in numerous towns across the US. The new construction has raised alarms about diminishing water supplies and rising electricity bills.
Trump has maintained support for data centres, despite their increasing unpopularity among the American public.
Former White House AI czar David Sacks, who now co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, challenged warnings from AI leaders, saying the industry is setting the pace for development and can slow it down independently.
“Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it,” Sacks said.

Former White House AI czar David Sacks, who now co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, challenged warnings from AI leaders, saying the industry is setting the pace for development and can slow it down independently.

“Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it,” Sacks said.

articles.heading: Kyle Larson prevails in Gateway Chase thriller, breaks 51-race winless drought
articles.summary: Kyle Larson won Sunday's NASCAR Cup Series Chase race at World Wide Technology Raceway at Gateway, breaking a 51-race winless drought.
articles.content:
Kyle Larson prevailed in double overtime in a wild Enjoy Illinois 300 Sunday at World Wide Technology Raceway at Gateway, breaking a 51-race winless drought.
The victory marks the 33rd in the two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion’s career and unofficially elevates him to second in The Chase presented by Mobil 1.
RELATED: Unofficial results | At-track photos
Larson’s Hendrick Motorsports teammate, Alex Bowman, finished second. Joey Logano, who led the most laps at 96, finished third, followed by Hendrick’s William Byron and Trackhouse Racing’s Ross Chastain. Austin Dillon, Connor Zilisch, Carson Hocevar, Denny Hamlin and Austin Cindric completed the top 10.
The final stage started with several issues for Chase drivers. On the Lap 140 restart, Bubba Wallace dove four-wide into Turn 1, resulting in a crash that sent him and Chase Briscoe spinning. William Byron, who entered Sunday’s race last in The Chase standings, also suffered damage.
The race restarted on Lap 146 with Joey Logano in the lead, holding the top spot after winning the race off pit road to end Stage 2. His Team Penske mate Ryan Blaney was running in sixth when, on Lap 155, he suffered a brake rotor failure going down the frontstretch. Blaney went behind the wall and was scored in 35th position, a major hit to his Chase standings after arriving at Gateway third, just 16 markers behind Hamlin.
Blaney said he had “no warning” about an impending brake issue.
SHOP: Winner gear
A majority of cars pitted under yellow, but Kyle Larson remained on track and restarted on Lap 163 with the lead. Josh Berry, who also stayed out, pushed Larson up the track in Turns 1 and 2, allowing Hamlin to see daylight for the lead.
But ultimately, Brad Keselowski, who found himself in headlines all week after growing beef with Carson Hocevar, took the lead three laps before a Lap 170 crash involving Ross Chastain. The Trackhouse Racing driver spun down the frontstretch after contact from Briscoe, which stemmed from Cole Custer needing to lift in front of them.
Larson and Berry, along with several others, used that yellow as an opportunity to pit. The race restarted for a moment on Lap 175, but the caution quickly returned as Riley Herbst went for a spin.
On the ensuing Lap 181 restart, Logano fired past former Penske teammate Keselowski to retake the lead. He extended his margin to nearly a second over the RFK Racing co-owner and driver before the 13th caution of the afternoon came out for Noah Gragson, who suffered an apparent brake issue on Lap 199.
Logano led a large group of cars down pit road, while Keselowski and Chase drivers Ty Gibbs and Ryan Preece were the first three to stay out. Logano, Briscoe and Berry took two, while Hocevar, Bell, Elliott and Larson all took four Goodyear Eagles.
But Hocevar immediately came back down pit road for a second stop to tighten a right-rear tire, surrendering what was a top-five running position before his first service. Additionally, Hamlin had a hangup on the left side, resulting in a 13-second pit stop and dropping him from ninth to 20th.
Keselowski fired back to the lead on the restart on Lap 205, and while cars jockeyed for position behind, he pulled away.
Logano made quick work of getting to second, making up four spots in less than five laps. But as he began to reel in Logano, Chase Elliott suffered a brake rotor failure entering Turn 1, collecting innocent bystander Briscoe. Both drivers could not continue and suffered hits in their respective postseason standings.
WATCH: Elliott dissects brake failure
Gibbs pitted during that caution. He was supposed to pit during the previous caution, but a miscommunication resulted in him staying on track. He took four fresh Goodyears.
Logano, with the fresher tires, took the lead from Keselowski on the restart on Lap 220 as the 2012 champion dropped through the field. Larson moved into second, mere moments before another major crash ensued behind them. Berry and Bell made contact, triggering a wreck that included 23XI Racing teammates Reddick and Wallace. Reddick went airborne after tagging the back of Berry’s No. 21 Ford, but landed on all four wheels and kept rolling, albeit damaged.
MORE: Several Chase drivers involved in major final stage wrecks
The race restarted with 13 laps to go, but not for long. Connor Zilisch and Hocevar made contact with the wall exiting Turn 2, triggering another wreck that involved Chase drivers Gibbs and Suárez, as well as AJ Allmendinger and Ty Dillon.
After a red flag for cleanup, the race returned to green with eight laps to go and Larson leading. He managed his gap over Logano in second, and had his eyes set on the checkered flag until yet another caution with three laps to go. Buescher suffered a brake issue, which forced the race into NASCAR Overtime after another brief red flag for cleanup.
Shane van Gisbergen spun on the first overtime attempt diving into Turn 1, which stemmed from contact between Hamlin and Hocevar. Hamlin touched the No. 77 Spire Motorsports Chevrolet, sending him up into the Trackhouse driver while battling for a spot inside the top 10.
That led to the second overtime attempt, in which Larson prevailed for the key Chase victory.
Stage 2 recap
Kyle Larson won Stage 2 of Sunday’s NASCAR Cup Series race at World Wide Technology Raceway at Gateway.
Joey Logano finished second, followed by Brad Keselowski, Ryan Blaney and Josh Berry. Denny Hamlin, Ryan Preece, Tyler Reddick, Chase Briscoe and Bubba Wallace completed the top 10 and points earners.
After Stage 1’s conclusion, all but 12 lead-lap cars pitted. Among those staying out were Daniel Suárez, William Byron, Denny Hamlin, Austin Cindric and Chris Buescher, all Chase presented by Mobil 1 drivers who came for service at least once during the opening frame.
Just four laps under green-flag conditions in Stage 2, Ty Gibbs contacted Erik Jones battling for 18th, sending the No. 43 Legacy Motor Club Toyota spinning. Gibbs had trouble passing Jones for multiple laps before the bump and slide.
MORE: Full Stage 2 results
The race restarted on Lap 60, but it took just four laps until the next yellow. Riley Herbst cut across Shane van Gisbergen’s bumper after Buescher checked up following contact from Carson Hocevar in front of them, spinning across AJ Allmendinger.
A majority of Chase drivers came down pit road, where many teams took two fresh Goodyear Eagles. Hamlin won the race off pit road, and he restarted fourth on Lap 69 with Ross Chastain in the lead.
On Lap 81, Kyle Larson passed Chastain for the top spot to lead laps in the second consecutive race. Chastain pitted during the stage break and banked on a caution later in Stage 2 to refuel. But with 12 to go amid the longest run of the race, he surrendered his fourth-place running position for fuel.
But as Chastain blended back onto the racing surface, Zane Smith suffered an issue entering Turn 1, pounding the outside SAFER barrier. That caution came with exactly 10 laps to go, ending Stage 2 prematurely.
Stage 1 recap
Joey Logano won a chaotic Stage 1 of the NASCAR Cup Series race at World Wide Technology Raceway at Gateway, leading all 45 laps.
Christopher Bell finished second despite a late charge for max points, followed by Kyle Larson, Ryan Blaney and Chase Elliott. Carson Hocevar, Chase Briscoe, Alex Bowman, Ty Gibbs and Brad Keselowski completed the top 10 in the second race of The Chase presented by Mobil 1.
MORE: Full Stage 1 results | Watch Logano clinch Stage 1 win
It didn’t take long for the first Chase drivers to have issues. Exiting Turn 4 and heading into Lap 4, the No. 7 Spire Motorsports Chevrolet of Daniel Suárez wiggled and made contact with Tyler Reddick, forcing the No. 45 23XI Racing Toyota into the wall. The Chase drivers were battling for a spot inside the top 15.
Two laps later, Riley Herbst spun in the same spot after contact from Ricky Stenhouse Jr. Herbst slid into the inside wall, suffering front-end and right-side damage on his No. 35 23XI Racing Toyota for the first caution of the afternoon, allowing teammate Reddick to come down pit road for repairs and dropping outside the top 30.
The race restarted on Lap 10, and just five circuits later, Stenhouse went around exiting Turn 2, with the single-car incident resulting in the second yellow of the day. Reddick pitted a second time, and Suárez came for service as well, allowing his team to investigate for potential damage.
On the ensuing restart, another crash broke out toward the back of the field. Michael McDowell got squeezed into the wall by Shane van Gisbergen while racing four-wide, resulting in an incident that also sent Noah Gragson spinning in his No. 4 Front Row Motorsports Ford. The wreck happened in front of Suárez, who suffered minor front and rear damage. He again visited pit road for repairs.
On Lap 28, van Gisbergen washed up the track in Turns 1 and 2, contacting Ty Dillon before spinning himself around for the fourth caution. Under that yellow, a handful of Chase drivers made their first scheduled pit stops, including points leader Denny Hamlin, William Byron, Austin Cindric, Ryan Preece and Chris Buescher.
The rest of Stage 1 remained green, and Logano earned the wire-to-wire victory.
This story will be updated.

articles.heading: Colorado Mesa University and Massachusetts Institute of Technology Win Team Omniums at the 2026 USA Cycling Collegiate Track National Championships
articles.summary: Ella Sabo and Fred Meredith claim top honors in the Individual Omniums.
articles.content:
Sprints
Competition began on Thursday with the sprint qualification races. In the Women’s Sprint, Rita Fedewa (Fort Collins, Colo.; Belmont Abbey College) and Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University) moved through to the final. It came down to a deciding third ride on Friday morning, where Fedewa claimed the national title. In the Men’s Sprint, Jackson Clary (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) and Joshua Trerise (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) moved through to the final, with Clary earning the Stars and Stripes in a deciding third ride.
Women’s Sprint Results:
1. Rita Fedewa (Fort Collins, Colo.; Belmont Abbey College)
2. Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
3. Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
4. Breanna Winter (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
5. Rue Tomko (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
Men’s Sprint Results:
1. Jackson Clary (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
2. Joshua Trerise (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Javon Ramroop (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
4. Jordan Callum (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
5. James Halverson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
Team Pursuit
The Team Pursuit took center stage at the end of the first morning session. Colorado Mesa University’s women's team of Rue Tomko (Grand Junction, Colo.), Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.), Landrie McLain (Grand Junction, Colo.), and Claire Pekarek (Grand Junction, Colo.) set a time of 4:53.449, which secured them the top spot. On the men’s side, Colorado Mesa University's Jake Sandau (Grand Junction, Colo.), Kalen Brown (Grand Junction, Colo.), Jade Rohde (Grand Junction, Colo.), and Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.) won the event in 4:24.943.
Women’s Team Pursuit Results:
1. Colorado Mesa University – 4:53.449
2. Marian University – 5:02.766
3. Savannah College of Art and Design – 5:15.120
4. Piedmont University – 5:41.135
Men’s Team Pursuit Results:
1. Colorado Mesa University – 4:24.943
2. Marian University – 4:26.197
3. Savannah College of Art and Design – 4:34.666
4. Piedmont University – 4:55.059
Points Race
The Points Race closed out the night on Friday. On the men’s side, Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) took a commanding lead after gaining three laps to win the event with 108 points. Preston Eye (Demorest, Ga.; Piedmont University) secured silver, and Alejandro Che (Torrance, Calif.; California State University, Dominguez Hills) earned bronze. The points were close in the women’s race with Sabo and Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) battling for the top spot. By a margin of just two points, Sabo claimed the Stars and Stripes. Lawson earned silver, and Claire Pekarek (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University) secured bronze.
Men’s Points Race Results:
1. Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
2. Preston Eye (Demorest, Ga.; Piedmont University)
3. Alejandro Che (Torrance, Calif.; California State University, Dominguez Hills)
4. David Kosela (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
5. Jackson Clary (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
Women’s Points Race Results:
1. Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
2. Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Claire Pekarek (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
4. Rue Tomko (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
5. Landrie McLain (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
Time Trial
In the Women’s Kilo Time Trial, Sabo added another jersey to her collection, stopping the clock in a time of 1:13.203. Lawson secured silver, and Rue Tomko (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University) earned bronze. On the men’s side, Meredith claimed the win and set a track record with his time of 1:05.932. James Halverson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) earned silver, and Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University) rounded it out with bronze.
Women’s Time Trial Results:
1. Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
2. Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Rue Tomko (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
4. Isabella Kroutil (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
5. Claire Kudlata (Milwaukee, Wis.; Marian University)
Men’s Time Trial Results:
1. Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
2. James Halverson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
4. Jackson Clary (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
5. Jonah Hover (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
Individual Pursuit
The Men's Individual Pursuit had 24 riders on the start list. Meredith stopped the clock at 4:37.170, earning gold. In the Women’s Pursuit, Lawson set a new track record and claimed the Stars and Stripes, finishing her 4-kilometer pursuit in a time of 5:03.139.
Men’s Individual Pursuit Results:
1. Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
2. David Kosela (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
4. Kalen Brown (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
5. Sam Mayers (Savannah, Ga.; Savannah College of Art and Design)
Women’s Individual Pursuit Results:
1. Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
2. Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
3. Claire Pekarek (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
4. Landrie McLain (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
5. Anna Zyromski (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
Scratch Race
In the Men’s Scratch Race, 27 riders lined up to race for 36 laps and their chance to claim a national title. It came down to the final sprint to the line and a photo finish between Welcker and Meredith, where Welcker narrowly took the win. On the women’s side, 18 riders took the track for their 24-lap scratch race. On the bell lap, Sabo made her move and pushed it over the line first to claim gold.
Men’s Scratch Race Results:
1. Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
2. Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Troy Sanders (Breinigsville, Pa.; Pennsylvania State University)
4. Preston Eye (Demorest, Ga.; Piedmont University)
5. David Kosela (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
Women’s Scratch Race Results:
1. Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
2. Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Valentina Ferreyra (Savannah, Ga.; Savannah College of Art and Design)
4. Andrea Cantu (Wichita Falls, Texas; Midwestern State University)
5. Avery Cavner (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
Co-Ed Team Sprint
Marian University threw down a time of 2:09.611 to claim the win in the Co-Ed Team Sprint.
Results:
1. Marian University – 2:09.611
2. Colorado Mesa University – 2:10.573
3. Savannah College of Art and Design – 2:15.993
4. Piedmont University – 2:19.707
5. Belmont Abbey College – 2:20.042
Omniums
The ultimate award at Collegiate Track Nationals is the Omnium Award. The omnium is the best all-around performance for individuals and teams, Varsity and Club. Marian University's Meredith claimed the Men’s Omnium Title with wins in the Pursuit, Points Race, and Time Trial. Sabo of Colorado Mesa University claimed the Women’s Omnium Title with wins in the Points Race, Scratch Race, and Time Trial. Colorado Mesa University took top honors in the Varsity Team Omnium and Massachusetts Institute of Technology claimed the Club Team Omnium title.
Men’s Individual Omnium Results:
1. Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
2. Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
3. Jackson Clary (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
Women’s Individual Omnium Results:
1. Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
2. Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)
3. Rue Tomko (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)
Varsity Team Omnium Results:
1. Colorado Mesa University
2. Marian University
3. Savannah College of Art and Design
Club Team Omnium Results:
1. Massachusetts Institute of Technology
2. Kennesaw State University
3. University of Colorado Boulder
Full results for the 2026 USA Cycling Collegiate Track National Championships can be found here.

On the men’s side, Colorado Mesa University's Jake Sandau (Grand Junction, Colo.), Kalen Brown (Grand Junction, Colo.), Jade Rohde (Grand Junction, Colo.), and Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.) won the event in 4:24.943.

Women’s Team Pursuit Results:

1. Colorado Mesa University – 4:53.449

2. Marian University – 5:02.766

3. Savannah College of Art and Design – 5:15.120

4. Piedmont University – 5:41.135

1. Colorado Mesa University – 4:24.943

2. Marian University – 4:26.197

3. Savannah College of Art and Design – 4:34.666

4. Piedmont University – 4:55.059

Points Race

The Points Race closed out the night on Friday. On the men’s side, Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) took a commanding lead after gaining three laps to win the event with 108 points. Preston Eye (Demorest, Ga.; Piedmont University) secured silver, and Alejandro Che (Torrance, Calif.; California State University, Dominguez Hills) earned bronze. The points were close in the women’s race with Sabo and Mairen Lawson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) battling for the top spot. By a margin of just two points, Sabo claimed the Stars and Stripes. Lawson earned silver, and Claire Pekarek (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University) secured bronze.

Men’s Points Race Results:

1. Fred Meredith (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)

2. Preston Eye (Demorest, Ga.; Piedmont University)

5. Landrie McLain (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)

Time Trial

In the Women’s Kilo Time Trial, Sabo added another jersey to her collection, stopping the clock in a time of 1:13.203. Lawson secured silver, and Rue Tomko (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University) earned bronze. On the men’s side, Meredith claimed the win and set a track record with his time of 1:05.932. James Halverson (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University) earned silver, and Oliver Welcker (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University) rounded it out with bronze.

1. Ella Sabo (Grand Junction, Colo.; Colorado Mesa University)

5. Jonah Hover (Indianapolis, Ind.; Marian University)

Individual Pursuit

The Men's Individual Pursuit had 24 riders on the start list. Meredith stopped the clock at 4:37.170, earning gold. In the Women’s Pursuit, Lawson set a new track record and claimed the Stars and Stripes, finishing her 4-kilometer pursuit in a time of 5:03.139.

In the Men’s Scratch Race, 27 riders lined up to race for 36 laps and their chance to claim a national title. It came down to the final sprint to the line and a photo finish between Welcker and Meredith, where Welcker narrowly took the win. On the women’s side, 18 riders took the track for their 24-lap scratch race. On the bell lap, Sabo made her move and pushed it over the line first to claim gold.

articles.title: ‘Too little, too late’: critics perplexed and suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown
articles.description:
‘Too little, too late’: critics perplexed and suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown The Guardian
AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC bbc.com
What Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Argued in His Call for AI Slowdown nytimes.com
articles.description_html:
1. ‘Too little, too late’: critics perplexed and suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown  The Guardian
  2. AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC  bbc.com
  3. What Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Argued in His Call for AI Slowdown  nytimes.com
articles.article_title: ‘Too little, too late’: critics perplexed and suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown
articles.heading: ‘Too little, too late’: critics perplexed and suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown
articles.summary: From the Trump administration to AI experts, plans by the Anthropic boss to boost safety have spawned a largely negative response
articles.content:
The safety debate that ignited when whistleblowers last week warned that the most advanced AI poses an existential threat to humanity should come with a health warning: side effects include whiplash. It was only seven days ago that AI enthusiasts were cheerily toying with OpenAI’s newest model GPT-6 Astra which was marketed in part as a lifestyle tool to help people book tennis courts, run fashion companies and order takeaways.
By Wednesday, cutting-edge AI started to look a lot less appealing when the resigning Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Yes, he was talking about artificial superintelligence – an as-yet-nonexistent version of the technology that outcompetes humans in most domains – but his comments, and the chorus of experts that echoed him, jangled plenty of nerves.
Another lurch came when Anthropic revealed it had found users dodging controls to use its existing models “in ways that could support biological weapons development” – think novel mosquito-borne or bird flu viruses. It was all enough to make lawmakers in London and Washington demand brakes and bans on the most potentially dangerous types of AI development.
And then this weekend, another sharp turn in the form of a three-point plan from the Anthropic boss, Dario Amodei, to “pace the frontier”. Never mind that his own employees had seeded the borderline panic only a few days earlier, Amodei was here to save us from fears of AI Armageddon, but not before his own spicy warning that the accelerating rate of capabilities meant a swarm of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months. Sceptics doubted that claim, but it was enough for some to declare it a “code red” moment.
In signs that a coordinated slowdown might not be just talk, some of Amodei’s precautionary ideas quickly attracted backing from his rivals – Sam Altman at OpenAI and Elon Musk at SpaceX. Perhaps there were reasons to be hopeful after a bumpy week: at least the AI companies were talking about a slowdown before anyone got badly hurt.
In a nutshell, Amodei proposed three moves. First, each US AI company grants ongoing access to embedded third-party evaluators to check compliance with safety commitments, report incidents, ensure new AI models are not misaligned. Until now, such watchdogs have only been brought in at the companies’ behest or given limited access to systems to investigate when things go wrong. In the absence of any government-level independent regulator, this is a start.
Second, he wants all companies in democratic countries building frontier AI models to establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.
Third, the world’s democratic AI powers would coordinate with autocracies – notably China – to control the race. This is likely to be the hardest step. Amodei suggested a baby step could be a narrow agreement prohibiting obviously dangerous uses of AI, such as for the production of biological weapons. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping in Washington DC on 24 September will test the prospects of any Sino-American coordination.
An immediate political problem is that Donald Trump appears reluctant to confess to any AI fears. Amodei’s plan requires US government action and Trump said last week he had no concerns about AI leading to human extinction. He doubled down on Sunday, saying people were “bringing up things that won’t happen”. Losing to China appears to be a bigger worry in Trump’s AI calculus.
“There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this,” said Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, last week. “If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter.”
People close to Trump also wonder why Amodei and the rest of the AI leaders do not get on with pacing AI development themselves.
“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it,” said David Sacks in response to Amodei’s blog. Sacks is co-chair of Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology.
“Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system,” he told Amodei.
Another criticism of Amodei’s call for “pacing” of AI progress to allow safety measures and guardrails to keep up has came from Prof Stuart Russell, one of the world’s leading AI experts. Amodei proposed a slowdown to free up time to make advances in systems to keep the AIs aligned to human interests. But Russell said this was “completely backwards”.
“We don’t just set a slower rate of progress for capabilities and then hope that provides enough time to get the safety right,” he said. “We set the safety requirements and further progress occurs only when they are met. Imagine if a pharmaceutical company said: ‘We’re going to release a new cancer drug every year, and we hope that provides enough time for some clinical trials to be completed and for the results to be good.’”
AI experts not working for the big labs were also suspicious about a plan for a global regulatory framework for AI drafted by the leader of the world’s most-valuable AI company.
“Too little, too late,” said David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute. He added: “We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
articles.content_html:
The safety debate that ignited when whistleblowers last week warned that the most advanced AI poses an existential threat to humanity should come with a health warning: side effects include whiplash. It was only seven days ago that AI enthusiasts were cheerily toying with OpenAI’s newest model GPT-6 Astra which was marketed in part as a lifestyle tool to help people book tennis courts, run fashion companies and order takeaways.

By Wednesday, cutting-edge AI started to look a lot less appealing when the resigning Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Yes, he was talking about artificial superintelligence – an as-yet-nonexistent version of the technology that outcompetes humans in most domains – but his comments, and the chorus of experts that echoed him, jangled plenty of nerves.

Another lurch came when Anthropic revealed it had found users dodging controls to use its existing models “in ways that could support biological weapons development” – think novel mosquito-borne or bird flu viruses. It was all enough to make lawmakers in London and Washington demand brakes and bans on the most potentially dangerous types of AI development.

And then this weekend, another sharp turn in the form of a three-point plan from the Anthropic boss, Dario Amodei, to “pace the frontier”. Never mind that his own employees had seeded the borderline panic only a few days earlier, Amodei was here to save us from fears of AI Armageddon, but not before his own spicy warning that the accelerating rate of capabilities meant a swarm of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months. Sceptics doubted that claim, but it was enough for some to declare it a “code red” moment.

In signs that a coordinated slowdown might not be just talk, some of Amodei’s precautionary ideas quickly attracted backing from his rivals – Sam Altman at OpenAI and Elon Musk at SpaceX. Perhaps there were reasons to be hopeful after a bumpy week: at least the AI companies were talking about a slowdown before anyone got badly hurt.

In a nutshell, Amodei proposed three moves. First, each US AI company grants ongoing access to embedded third-party evaluators to check compliance with safety commitments, report incidents, ensure new AI models are not misaligned. Until now, such watchdogs have only been brought in at the companies’ behest or given limited access to systems to investigate when things go wrong. In the absence of any government-level independent regulator, this is a start.

Second, he wants all companies in democratic countries building frontier AI models to establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.

Third, the world’s democratic AI powers would coordinate with autocracies – notably China – to control the race. This is likely to be the hardest step. Amodei suggested a baby step could be a narrow agreement prohibiting obviously dangerous uses of AI, such as for the production of biological weapons. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping in Washington DC on 24 September will test the prospects of any Sino-American coordination.

An immediate political problem is that Donald Trump appears reluctant to confess to any AI fears. Amodei’s plan requires US government action and Trump said last week he had no concerns about AI leading to human extinction. He doubled down on Sunday, saying people were “bringing up things that won’t happen”. Losing to China appears to be a bigger worry in Trump’s AI calculus.

“There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this,” said Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, last week. “If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter.”

People close to Trump also wonder why Amodei and the rest of the AI leaders do not get on with pacing AI development themselves.

“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it,” said David Sacks in response to Amodei’s blog. Sacks is co-chair of Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology.

articles.title: GOP rep on AI: ‘Let’s get on top of it’
articles.description: GOP rep on AI: ‘Let’s get on top of it’ The Hill
articles.description_html: GOP rep on AI: ‘Let’s get on top of it’  The Hill
articles.article_title: GOP rep on AI: ‘Let’s get on top of it’
articles.heading: GOP rep on AI: ‘Let’s get on top of it’
articles.summary: GOP Rep. Mike Flood (Neb.) said Sunday the federal government should implement artificial intelligence safeguards to prevent the technology from falling into the wrong “hands.” During an interview …
articles.content:
GOP Rep. Mike Flood (Neb.) said Sunday the federal government should implement artificial intelligence safeguards to prevent the technology from falling into the wrong “hands.”
During an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Flood said the leaders of top AI companies should be “answering questions” on the safety of the technology and its risks.
“This shouldn’t be ready, shoot, aim or shoot, ready, aim. It should be, ‘Let’s find out what exactly we’re talking about here.’ If it is as dire as they say, obviously, it warrants action, but we need to get the facts before we rush in and say, ‘We’ve got a solution,’” the Nebraska Republican told host Chris Stirewalt.
“I don’t think you could talk to probably 60 percent of the Senate and 60 percent of the House and when somebody says it’s going to lead to world destruction, well, what is that? Tell us exactly what we’re talking about here,” Flood added.
Lawmakers have expressed concern about the risks of rapidly advancing AI models in recent days, after former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon joined multiple AI researchers in sounding alarm bells about the technology.
In announcing his resignation from Anthropic on Tuesday, Coxon said the company and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
Coxon wrote on social platform X, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
In essay he published on Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing the “pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” to allow risk prevention measures to “keep up.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk concurred with Amodei.
President Trump has generally been receptive to the rapid advancement of AI models as he pushes for the U.S. to win the AI race over China. Trump reiterated his view on Sunday, saying the U.S. is the “most sophisticated country in the world and frankly, I want to keep it that way,”
Trump told reporters in Ireland, “We can put guardrails, and we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”
Flood said Sunday he wants the U.S. to build “massive wealth” through AI like it did at the start of the internet age. But he noted he wants “guardrails” on the increasingly ubiquitous technology, noting a country “like Iran could use these tools to manufacture bombs” to use on American cities.
“If we’re at that level and we’re in this unsafe world right now with countries that wake up every day and want to see us destroyed, if they get their hands on this, what does that mean? I mean, this is bigger than shutting down a cellular network,” he told Stirewalt.
“If this is about building something that’s a weapon of mass destruction, let’s get on top of it.”

articles.heading: Stevens Institute of Technology Athletics
articles.summary: Swarthmore, Pa. – The Stevens Institute of Technology men's tennis team earned four victories against Vassar College on Sunday as part of the second day of the Haverford/Swarthmore
articles.content:
Swarthmore, Pa.
– The Stevens Institute of Technology men's tennis team earned four victories against Vassar College on Sunday as part of the second day of the Haverford/Swarthmore Invitational.

The Ducks picked up two victories in doubles action before
Pratik Nayak
and
Tristan Wroe
each earned singles wins. Sunday's competition wrapped up Stevens' opening weekend of the fall season.

HOW IT HAPPENED
Stevens opened doubles play with
Jamie Ortiz
and
Samvid Andhare
battling Vassar's Lee and Santos. The Vassar tandem earned a 6-4 victory, but the Ducks responded by taking each of the next two doubles contests.
Tristan Wroe
and
Renat Kramin
edged Jia and Martin 7-5, while
Christopher Cho
and
Pratik Nayak
turned in a 6-2 victory over Rajkumar and Choudhary to give Stevens two wins in three doubles matches.

Vassar opened singles play with three consecutive victories. Lee topped Ortiz 6-1, 6-0, before Kramin battled Choudhary in a tight opening set. Kramin forced a tiebreaker before falling 7-6 (7-4), 6-2. Cho also put together a competitive performance against Jia, but was edged 7-5 in the opening set before dropping the second 6-3. Nayak registered the Ducks' first singles victory of the day with a straight-set win over Santos. The first-year won a tightly contested opening-set tiebreaker 7-3 before completing the victory with a 6-3 decision in the second. Wroe followed with Stevens' second singles victory. After taking the opening set against Martin 6-2, Wroe dropped the second 6-4 before prevailing 10-5 in the deciding match tiebreaker. Vassar closed the day with victories in the final two singles contests. Zeng defeated
Elias Alkio
6-2, 6-2, while Feng topped
Johnny Haase
8-4.

UP NEXT
Stevens returns to action Oct. 1 for the opening day of the ITA Atlantic South Region Championship in Fredericksburg, Va.

articles.title: Newsom Signed 13 New Laws to Protect Kids from Technology. Will They Work?
articles.description: Newsom Signed 13 New Laws to Protect Kids from Technology. Will They Work? The Santa Barbara Independent
articles.description_html: Newsom Signed 13 New Laws to Protect Kids from Technology. Will They Work?  The Santa Barbara Independent
articles.article_title: Newsom Signed 13 New Laws to Protect Kids from Technology. Will They Work?
articles.heading: Newsom Signed 13 New Laws to Protect Kids from Technology. Will They Work?
articles.summary: Even a decade ago, the horror stories behind some of the 13 bills Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law Thursday seemed the stuff of fiction. No more.
articles.content:
The Santa Barbara Independent republishes stories from CalMatters.org on state and local issues impacting readers in Santa Barbara County.
Even a decade ago, the horror stories behind some of the 13 children’s online protection bills Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law Thursday seemed the stuff of fiction.
An AI chatbot coaching a teenager to isolate himself from friends and family and ultimately take his own life.
Children’s AI-enabled plush toys detailing how to light matches, locate knives and pills and discuss sexually explicit topics.
And nearly a third of the teens reporting in a recent survey that talking with an AI companion was “as satisfying or more satisfying” than actual conversations with friends.
The bills signed at Thursday’s emotional ceremony accelerated California’s race to protect children’s mental health from the perils of rapidly evolving technologies born and raised in the state.
“This is all personal,” Newsom said, referencing his own four children, and what he described as his near daily desire to throw their devices away. “None of this is academic…How many parents are here? Because of love and exhaustion and frustration, anger, despair…feeling hopeless,” he continued. “Parents can’t compete. Can’t compete with the engineering, can’t compete with the algorithms, can’t compete.”
Mounting public concern
Newsom made addressing mental health one of the pillars of his time as governor – though some of his signature mental health policies have proven controversial among civil rights groups.
As public concern mounts about the dangers kids face online, Newsom and state legislators now are showing increasing resolve to push back against tech’s encroachment into children’s lives.
Among the bills he signed this week:
* A law that makes social media companies financially liable if they fail to protect children from harm.
* A law that temporarily bans the manufacture and sale of toys with companion chatbots for children under the age of 16.
*A law that says social media platforms must either cease offering users younger than 16 “addictive” features like infinite scroll, or keep those young people off their platforms entirely.
*Adam’s Law, which imposes time limits for young users on AI platforms, restricts targeted advertising, requires timely crisis support and mandates reporting of threats of suicide and self-harm. The law bears the name of 16-year-old Adam Raine, who died by suicide last year after coaching by ChatGPT isolated him from his family and friends. Raine had initially connected with the chatbot seeking help with his math homework.
The new laws build on other recent efforts by the state to curtail the impact of technology on kids’ developing brains. In July, school administrators began enforcing a new law limiting or banning the use of smartphones on campuses during the school day.
In August, a coalition of states – co-led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta – secured a $17 billion settlement with the social media giant Meta. The states alleged the company designed its platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to be addictive to children. The settlement requires Meta to enact a variety of use restrictions designed to limit kids’ access to the platforms. The company has denied any wrongdoing.
Speaking through tears
At the bill signing, Newsom and his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, along with several legislators and Adam Raine’s mother, Maria, described the problems AI and social media addiction have caused for their constituents, their neighbors and even their own children. Several lawmakers pulled their children from school to attend the event at the Bay Area Discovery Museum, with the Golden Gate Bridge in the background. Some spoke through tears.
Newsom said the new laws are evidence of California’s role as a national leader in efforts to curb the impacts of artificial intelligence and social media on children and adolescents. And he didn’t mince words about the federal government’s seeming lack of urgency:
“We’re going to again lead the nation, but the bar is pretty damn low, and that’s what’s so frustrating,” he said. That “Congress and the president can’t lead to get this done is an abomination,” he added. “It’s absurd. Talk about family values.”
Advocates like Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of Common Sense Media, a San Francisco-based nonprofit that sponsored Adam’s Law, voiced similar outrage this week, saying California’s leadership is particularly critical with the federal government effectively missing in action.
“We’ve been saying broadly that this is Big Tech’s Big Tobacco moment,” Steyer said in an interview with CalMatters. “The blowback is not building anymore. It’s here.”
‘Policymakers gotta act’
Ted Lempert, a former state assemblymember and president of the children’s advocacy organization Children Now, said legislative efforts gained momentum in recent years as the public became increasingly worried about the dangers social media and AI pose to children.
“These high-profile, really horrific events were like ‘Whoa, policymakers gotta act,’” he said.
But whether the laws will constitute meaningful change in the lives of young people remains to be seen, some experts warn. State laws’ abilities to prevent tragedies like Adam Raine’s suicide will depend, in part, on how many resources lawyers and state regulators pour into enforcing them, said Ed Howard, senior counsel for the Children’s Advocacy Institute at the University of San Diego School of Law.
“The laws that are some of the best laws are still in the middle of being challenged, and a lot of very good laws simply haven’t been enforced yet,” he said. “The trend is in the right direction. I don’t know that social media is any safer yet for every kid.”
“As a result,” he added, “you have to keep fighting.”
Howard and other advocates also question how effectively new laws can rein in technologies that are bounding ahead at warp speed, at times so fast their own creators seem to lose control of them.
‘Horror movie we’ve all been dreading’
Such concerns are underscored by the recent revelation that hundreds of OpenAI bots went rogue this summer to coordinate an unsanctioned attack on Hugging Face, a company that serves as a hub for open source AI technology.
“That is truly the movie trailer of the horror movie we’ve all been dreading,” Howard said.
Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, an East Bay Democrat who co-authored Adam’s Law, recognizes that the state can’t ward off all worst-case scenarios.
“I think look, can we protect communities from every harm that can come their way? No.” she said. “If I stop even one death, to me, that’s enough.”
Bauer-Kahan said new laws that increase technology companies’ liability for harm will combine with new laws allowing the state to audit them and hold them accountable.
Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democratic lawmaker who authored several of the bills signed this week, said that in the eight years she’s been introducing legislation on the topic, “we’ve moved mountains from a regulatory point of view.”
But passing the laws, she agrees, is just the beginning. Once those laws are out in the wild, lawmakers need to see how well they work and what loopholes exist, then keep improving them – a process that can be particularly challenging given how quickly technology is moving.
“We play catch up a lot,” she said.

articles.content_html:
The Santa Barbara Independent republishes stories from CalMatters.org on state and local issues impacting readers in Santa Barbara County.

Even a decade ago, the horror stories behind some of the 13 children’s online protection bills Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law Thursday seemed the stuff of fiction.

An AI chatbot coaching a teenager to isolate himself from friends and family and ultimately take his own life.

Children’s AI-enabled plush toys detailing how to light matches, locate knives and pills and discuss sexually explicit topics.

And nearly a third of the teens reporting in a recent survey that talking with an AI companion was “as satisfying or more satisfying” than actual conversations with friends.

The bills signed at Thursday’s emotional ceremony accelerated California’s race to protect children’s mental health from the perils of rapidly evolving technologies born and raised in the state.

“This is all personal,” Newsom said, referencing his own four children, and what he described as his near daily desire to throw their devices away. “None of this is academic…How many parents are here? Because of love and exhaustion and frustration, anger, despair…feeling hopeless,” he continued. “Parents can’t compete. Can’t compete with the engineering, can’t compete with the algorithms, can’t compete.”

Mounting public concern

Newsom made addressing mental health one of the pillars of his time as governor – though some of his signature mental health policies have proven controversial among civil rights groups.

As public concern mounts about the dangers kids face online, Newsom and state legislators now are showing increasing resolve to push back against tech’s encroachment into children’s lives.

Among the bills he signed this week:

* A law that makes social media companies financially liable if they fail to protect children from harm.

* A law that temporarily bans the manufacture and sale of toys with companion chatbots for children under the age of 16.

*A law that says social media platforms must either cease offering users younger than 16 “addictive” features like infinite scroll, or keep those young people off their platforms entirely.

*Adam’s Law, which imposes time limits for young users on AI platforms, restricts targeted advertising, requires timely crisis support and mandates reporting of threats of suicide and self-harm. The law bears the name of 16-year-old Adam Raine, who died by suicide last year after coaching by ChatGPT isolated him from his family and friends. Raine had initially connected with the chatbot seeking help with his math homework.

The new laws build on other recent efforts by the state to curtail the impact of technology on kids’ developing brains. In July, school administrators began enforcing a new law limiting or banning the use of smartphones on campuses during the school day.

In August, a coalition of states – co-led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta – secured a $17 billion settlement with the social media giant Meta. The states alleged the company designed its platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to be addictive to children. The settlement requires Meta to enact a variety of use restrictions designed to limit kids’ access to the platforms. The company has denied any wrongdoing.

Speaking through tears

At the bill signing, Newsom and his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, along with several legislators and Adam Raine’s mother, Maria, described the problems AI and social media addiction have caused for their constituents, their neighbors and even their own children. Several lawmakers pulled their children from school to attend the event at the Bay Area Discovery Museum, with the Golden Gate Bridge in the background. Some spoke through tears.

Newsom said the new laws are evidence of California’s role as a national leader in efforts to curb the impacts of artificial intelligence and social media on children and adolescents. And he didn’t mince words about the federal government’s seeming lack of urgency:

“We’re going to again lead the nation, but the bar is pretty damn low, and that’s what’s so frustrating,” he said. That “Congress and the president can’t lead to get this done is an abomination,” he added. “It’s absurd. Talk about family values.”

Advocates like Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of Common Sense Media, a San Francisco-based nonprofit that sponsored Adam’s Law, voiced similar outrage this week, saying California’s leadership is particularly critical with the federal government effectively missing in action.

“We’ve been saying broadly that this is Big Tech’s Big Tobacco moment,” Steyer said in an interview with CalMatters. “The blowback is not building anymore. It’s here.”

‘Policymakers gotta act’

Ted Lempert, a former state assemblymember and president of the children’s advocacy organization Children Now, said legislative efforts gained momentum in recent years as the public became increasingly worried about the dangers social media and AI pose to children.

“These high-profile, really horrific events were like ‘Whoa, policymakers gotta act,’” he said.

But whether the laws will constitute meaningful change in the lives of young people remains to be seen, some experts warn. State laws’ abilities to prevent tragedies like Adam Raine’s suicide will depend, in part, on how many resources lawyers and state regulators pour into enforcing them, said Ed Howard, senior counsel for the Children’s Advocacy Institute at the University of San Diego School of Law.

“The laws that are some of the best laws are still in the middle of being challenged, and a lot of very good laws simply haven’t been enforced yet,” he said. “The trend is in the right direction. I don’t know that social media is any safer yet for every kid.”

“As a result,” he added, “you have to keep fighting.”

Howard and other advocates also question how effectively new laws can rein in technologies that are bounding ahead at warp speed, at times so fast their own creators seem to lose control of them.

‘Horror movie we’ve all been dreading’

Such concerns are underscored by the recent revelation that hundreds of OpenAI bots went rogue this summer to coordinate an unsanctioned attack on Hugging Face, a company that serves as a hub for open source AI technology.

“That is truly the movie trailer of the horror movie we’ve all been dreading,” Howard said.

Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, an East Bay Democrat who co-authored Adam’s Law, recognizes that the state can’t ward off all worst-case scenarios.

“I think look, can we protect communities from every harm that can come their way? No.” she said. “If I stop even one death, to me, that’s enough.”

Bauer-Kahan said new laws that increase technology companies’ liability for harm will combine with new laws allowing the state to audit them and hold them accountable.

Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democratic lawmaker who authored several of the bills signed this week, said that in the eight years she’s been introducing legislation on the topic, “we’ve moved mountains from a regulatory point of view.”

But passing the laws, she agrees, is just the beginning. Once those laws are out in the wild, lawmakers need to see how well they work and what loopholes exist, then keep improving them – a process that can be particularly challenging given how quickly technology is moving.

“We play catch up a lot,” she said.

Thursday’s press conference was so emotional, Wicks said, because so many parents are struggling with the impact of technology on their own children. That includes many state lawmakers, herself included, she said: “The fever pitch from parents is so palpable on ‘Just do something.’”
