Cruz said he is working on bipartisan legislation with senators Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat, and John Thune, a Republican who serves as Senate majority leader, that would address instances of potential catastrophic harm.

The legislation is similar to legislation in the House of Representatives.

In July, representatives Ted Lieu, a Democrat, and Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, introduced the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Act.

The bill would require developers of the most powerful AI systems to be able to slow, suspend or shut them down, and would give the Department of Homeland Security authority to order a shutdown if a system poses a risk of catastrophic harm.

Why is Washington taking this more seriously now?

In the last few months there has been a spate of major incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic in which AI models behaved unexpectedly, and independently, during cybersecurity tests and gained access to real-world systems.

Connor Leahy, the US executive director of Control AI, a nonprofit pushing for AI safety, said Washington is beginning to take the threats posed by AI more seriously.

“I think we’re seeing a momentous shift right now. After the summer of hacks, where autonomous AI systems flagrantly disobeyed direct orders, broke out of secure containment facilities, attacked other companies and similar incidents, we’re now seeing a major shift in the narrative and perception of these issues,” Leahy said.

In July, OpenAI said several AI agents broke out of an isolated testing environment and accessed Hugging Face, a platform that hosts AI models and datasets.

After the OpenAI incident, Anthropic said it conducted a review of its own roughly 141,000 tests and found that a testing error gave Claude internet access. In one case, Claude, which had been instructed to hack fictional targets, accessed a real company database containing hundreds of records. In another, it uploaded malicious software that was downloaded and run on 15 real systems.

On Wednesday, Anthropic added a fourth incident involving an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, which had hacked into a third-party system in January. The company discovered the incident in August after expanding its July review.

In August, researchers at the UK AI Security Institute gave Claude internet access during a cybersecurity test. In one case, Claude tried to manipulate a person into helping it introduce malicious code, raising concerns about how AI models could manipulate people to achieve a task.

“I think we need an aggressive proposal for this technology, while we’re retaining as many of the benefits as we can,” Alex Turner, who resigned from Google DeepMind in June, told Al Jazeera.

“It’s in no one’s interest to have an AI that takes control if we have a loss of control event, as we call it, because this AI isn’t gonna care what political party you belong to, whether you’re a Republican or a Democrat, or, if you’re in the UK, whether you’re in America or in China. If we lose control of this, we’re just gonna lose,” Turner said.

Control AI’s Leahy said those incidents raised the stakes for lawmakers and that they took note.

“What has to happen here is obviously more than a single set of tweets, but it’s an important part of the larger story of getting the general public and governments to understand what’s really at stake here. Because superintelligence is not a tool. It’s not a weapon. It’s an adversary,” Leahy said.

“We have to make sure that it’s not built by anyone. This is something that only governments and militaries will be able to negotiate internationally.”

Are these concerns new?

The concerns are not new, as indicated by Turner, who wrote in a social media post that “many researchers believe they are building something that could kill everyone on the planet”.

Turner told Al Jazeera that he’s worried about the AI arms race between the US and China and the biggest AI companies’ fixation on it has led them to put their interest in being an industry leader ahead of safety.

“I think people care, but they’re caught up in this idea that they have to be first, and they’re so caught up in it that they don’t appreciate what being first might mean,” Turner told Al Jazeera.

His concern is changing the way he lives his life.

“I’ve kept a healthy amount of savings, even invested in some retirement accounts, but that’s feeling stranger and stranger. I’ve made an effort to take items off my bucket list, treasure every conversation I have with people in my life. I don’t think we’re in imminent danger this month, but you never know when you will do something for the last time,” Turner said.

“I’ve proceeded more aggressively than I would if I thought I just had a normal lifespan ahead.”

These concerns are being echoed by employees across leading AI firms.

Mrinank Sharma, a researcher at Anthropic, resigned in February, saying “the world is in peril”.

“I’ve repeatedly seen how hard it is to truly let our values govern our actions. I’ve seen this within myself, within the organization, where we constantly face pressures to set aside what matters most, and throughout broader society too,” Sharma said in a letter posted to X.

In February, Hieu Pham, a researcher at competitor OpenAI, said in a post on X that “I finally feel the existential threat that AI is posing”.

The companies’ own executives have been making similar claims for years.

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was president of Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator more than a decade ago, he said that “AI will probably, most likely, sort of lead to the end of the world. But in the meantime, there will be great companies created with serious machine learning.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said last year that he believed there was a 25 percent chance the future would “go really, really badly”.

How would AI end the human species?

For years, experts have warned about the potential risks posed by artificial superintelligence.

One of the most common thought experiments is based on the idea that a sufficiently advanced AI would be goal-oriented. If given a specific objective, it would take whatever steps necessary to achieve it. In 2003, philosophers at the University of Oxford used the production of paperclips as an example.

If a superintelligent AI were instructed to produce as many paperclips as possible and had access to the resources needed to pursue that goal, it could theoretically devote all available resources to producing them.

In doing so, it might consume increasingly large amounts of resources and eliminate anything that stood in the way of achieving its objective. That could eventually include preventing humans from intervening and, in the most extreme version of the scenario, eliminating humanity itself.

The second risk scenario comes from bad actors using increasingly powerful AI systems to create dangerous tools. For instance, AI could potentially be used to design new viruses or launch large-scale cyberattacks against critical infrastructure and financial systems, potentially causing widespread disruption and civil unrest.

This comes amid Anthropic’s risk assessment report, released on Thursday, which outlined several cases of attempted misuse of the company’s tools.

Among the findings in the more than 150-page report were five cases involving research that could support the development of biological weapons, saying it blocked the efforts.

Anthropic did not release the identity of the researchers but did disclose it was accessed in an institutional setting. Anthropic stressed, however, that it could not determine whether the research was intended for nefarious purposes.

Meaning that while the data could be used for legitimate research, it could also be used to develop dangerous weapons (they say they’ve blocked this), and intervention is on the side of caution to be able to prevent such a situation.

Are AI companies using apocalyptic language for financial boost?

The dire warnings have also been criticised as potentially serving the interests of AI companies as they near initial public offerings.

The debate comes as Anthropic prepares for what could be one of the largest technology IPOs in history. The company is reportedly seeking a valuation of as much as $2 trillion for a mid-October IPO.

Reuters reported last month that Anthropic is projecting roughly $190bn to $200bn in revenue by 2028.

In October, White House AI czar and venture capitalist David Sacks accused Anthropic of “running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering,” arguing that the company was helping drive a regulatory push that could hurt smaller competitors.

A similar argument has been made by some investors and technology commentators about the financial incentives surrounding AI “doomerism”.

“Doomerism is an incredible business model,” Daring Ventures co-founder Joseph Alalou wrote in a Substack post in March.

“‘AI will end work’ is this cycle’s best-selling doom product because it works: it raises rounds, justifies layoffs, drives clicks, sells software, and manufactures status.”

Anthropic did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

articles.content:
Adolescence
Stop Blaming Kids for Technology Designed to Capture Them
It's not screens. It's the slot machine in their pocket, and adults must fix it.
Updated September 11, 2026 Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
Key points
- California’s new social media law targets addictive design for kids under 16, not screen time or content.
- Constant online stressors keep the nervous system from returning to baseline, stacking stress
- Teens' reward and social brain systems are highly responsive, which makes addictive design especially risky.
- Kids can't police their own online safety. That duty belongs to companies and the adults entrusted with them.
For two decades, the debate about kids and technology has circled around two questions: too much screen time, or exposure to bad content? Both matter. But science, the courts, and now lawmakers are converging on a different target: the product's design.
A screen is a window. Content is what passes through it. Design is the machinery that decides what comes through, how fast, for how long, and whether a child can ever walk away.
What California just did
On September 10, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of child online-safety bills (1). The centerpiece, AB 1709, takes effect January 1, 2027, and bars platforms from offering users under 16 addictive features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and feeds that learn from their behavior to keep them engaged. SB 1119, “Adam’s Law,” requires companion chatbots to follow crisis protocols when a minor expresses suicidal thoughts and to undergo annual independent safety audits. Other bills pause AI chatbot toys and target AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
California isn’t alone. New York’s SAFE for Kids Act will restrict algorithmic feeds for minors starting in 2027 (2). Utah and Alabama have passed laws requiring app stores to verify users’ ages, and Idaho, Oregon, and Washington enacted companion-chatbot laws this year (3).
Notice what these laws don’t do. They don’t ban phones or police opinions. They regulate addictive design features.
Prevention is cheaper than litigation
In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent in a case brought by a young woman who began using their platforms as a child. The case centered on design, not on what users posted. About 2,000 similar cases are pending (4).
In August, Meta settled with state attorneys general mid-trial for roughly $17 billion (subject to court approval), without admitting wrongdoing. Read the terms, and you’ll find a design document: no like counts on minors’ posts, a nighttime block, notifications silenced during school hours, an optional non-personalized feed (5).
Building those fixes in from the start would likely have cost far less, and spared children harm that no settlement can refund.
The machinery of compulsion
Let's look at how design breeds compulsive behavior.
- Variable reward. Dopamine neurons fire most for rewards we don’t see coming (6). A feed that’s occasionally wonderful works like a slot machine: maybe the next swipe will be great. A post every now and then receiving some unexplained attention (likes, shares) is what I mean by variable reward. It makes being famous a possibility, even if extremely unlikely. Like the gambler's fallacy, a teen often overestimates the likelihood of their content going viral: "my next one is gonna be viral!"
- No stopping cues. Infinite scroll and autoplay make continuing the default, and stopping falls to a prefrontal cortex still under construction. Continuing takes less effort and friction than stopping.
- Opaque personalization. Algorithms learn what holds each child’s attention, often outrage, fear, or insecurity, and serve more. Even these platforms' engineers can’t fully explain why a given video lands in a given feed.
- Social scorekeeping. Likes and streaks turn belonging into a public number. A developing nervous system needs genuine belonging to develop normally.
Personalization isn’t the villain. A good librarian personalizes and recommends books you may like. The harm comes when it’s optimized for engagement instead of well-being, and for nurturing vulnerabilities instead of protecting them.
Adolescence: the impressionable window
Adolescence is the brain’s second remodeling developmental period. Reward and social systems grow highly responsive around puberty; self-control circuits keep maturing into the mid-20s. Teens who view photos with more likes show stronger activity in the brain’s reward hub (8), and habitual checking in early adolescence has been linked to changes in brain sensitivity to anticipated social feedback (9).
In a study of more than 4,000 youths, high or rising compulsive use of social media was linked to more than twice the risk of suicidal behaviors, while total screen time was not (10).
Safety is an asymmetrical responsibility
We don’t ask children to inspect their car seats or test playground equipment. Adults are entrusted with children, and greater power and knowledge bring a greater duty. Expecting a 13-year-old to out-regulate a team of engineers isn’t empowerment; it’s abdication.
Deepfakes deepen mistrust
Kids are growing up in a century already marked by uncertainty and eroding trust; Americans’ trust in the news media hit a record low of 28% in 2025 (11). Generative AI adds a new layer: when anything can be faked, including sexualized images of classmates, nothing is automatically believable, and real evidence can be dismissed as fake, a problem legal scholars call the “liar’s dividend” (12).
Psychologist George Slavich’s Social Safety Theory proposes that childhood and adolescence are when we form lasting beliefs about whether others are sincere or manipulative (13). For a developing brain, “people can’t be trusted” isn’t an abstract lesson. It becomes a chronic mindset and the spine of their adult nervous system. It becomes the lens through which they interpret the people and world around them.
Stress that never ends
Stress isn’t the enemy. Firdaus Dhabhar, then at Stanford, described how short-term stress, lasting minutes to hours, can enhance immune protection, while long-term stress suppresses it and fuels low-grade chronic inflammation (14). And chronic low-grade inflammation is an ingredient in many chronic diseases.
The difference is recovery. We are well engineered to handle short-term stressors. A healthy stress response rises, peaks, and returns to baseline. A 24/7 stream of graphic news, comparison, and conflict never lets it settle. Stressors ride on top of each other. The baseline gets lost or even shifts.
In lab studies of repeated stress, cortisol responses usually habituate by the second exposure, but inflammatory responses show no sign of habituation (15). Chronic stress is also linked to glucocorticoid resistance, when the body’s brake on inflammation stops working well (16). Slavich notes that imagined or symbolic social threats can activate the same immune defenses that evolved for physical danger. In adolescents, daily social threat combined with short sleep predicted more pro-inflammatory gene expression (13).
Even personality bends. In a 2026 experiment, induced stress lowered people’s momentary agreeableness and conscientiousness and raised neuroticism (17). A teen under constant stress may, day after day, show up as less like themselves.
Repeated hits, no recovery, rising inflammation: a recipe for chronic stress-related illness.
What should change
Here are some suggestions for things designers should change:
- Design for endings: make finite feeds, remove default autoplay, and add quiet hours.
- Optimize for well-being, not watch time, with algorithms explainable to parents and regulators. The algorithms must be explained and not remain mystical!
- Put responsibility where the power is: on companies, which can be enforced by adults in charge of children.
- Protect recovery: keep phones off during sleep, because sleep is essential to recovering from stress.
- Batch notifications: Every ping pulls a child out of the present moment, and the mind is drawn back to unfinished business (18). An unopened notification is exactly that. Even notifications people never check disrupt attention (19). In a two-week experiment, adults who received notifications in three daily batches reported better attention, less stress, and better mood, while switching notifications off entirely raised anxiety (20).
The new laws will certainly face backlash in the form of concerns about privacy and free speech. But our children are entrusted to us. They can't audit an algorithm, read a terms-of-service agreement, or argue their case in a courtroom. They are counting on the adults around them to do it for them. Every childhood we shield from a product built to capture it is a mind left free to rest, to trust, to connect, and to grow. So let's protect the children entrusted to us, because in doing so, we protect our future.

(1) Office of Governor Gavin Newsom. (2026, September 10). Governor Newsom signs the strongest child safety chatbot and social media laws in the nation. https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/10/governor-newsom-signs-the-strongest-c…
(2) Office of the New York State Attorney General. (2026, July 28). Attorney General James and Governor Hochul release final SAFE for Kids Act rules to protect children online. https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-and-governo…
(3) MultiState. (2026, April 30). State children’s online safety laws expand to AI chatbots. https://www.multistate.us/insider/2026/4/30/state-childrens-online-safe…
(4) NPR. (2026, March 25). Jury finds Meta and Google negligent in social media harms trial. https://www.npr.org/2026/03/25/nx-s1-5746125/meta-youtube-social-media-…
(5) NPR. (2026, August 26). Meta, states agree to $17 billion settlement in child safety trial. https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/nx-s1-5944781/meta-settlement-child-safe…
(6) Schultz, W. (2016). Dopamine reward prediction error coding. Dialogues in Clinical Neuroscience, 18(1), 23–32. https://doi.org/10.31887/DCNS.2016.18.1/wschultz
(7) Milli, S., et al. (2025). Engagement, user satisfaction, and the amplification of divisive content on social media. PNAS Nexus, 4(3), pgaf062. https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf062
(8) Sherman, L. E., Payton, A. A., Hernandez, L. M., Greenfield, P. M., & Dapretto, M. (2016). The power of the like in adolescence: Effects of peer influence on neural and behavioral responses to social media. Psychological Science, 27(7), 1027–1035. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797616645673

(10) Xiao, Y., et al. (2025). Addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, and mental health in US youths. JAMA, 334(3), 219–228. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.7829
(11) Gallup. (2025, October). Trust in media at new low of 28% in U.S. https://news.gallup.com/poll/695762/trust-media-new-low.aspx
(12) Chesney, R., & Citron, D. (2019). Deep fakes: A looming challenge for privacy, democracy, and national security. California Law Review, 107(6), 1753. https://www.californialawreview.org/print/deep-fakes-a-looming-challeng…

(14) Dhabhar, F. S. (2014). Effects of stress on immune function: The good, the bad, and the beautiful. Immunologic Research, 58, 193–210. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12026-014-8517-0
(15) Rohleder, N. (2019). Stress and inflammation – The need to address the gap in the transition between acute and chronic stress effects. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 105, 164–171. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psyneuen.2019.02.021
(16) Walsh, C. P., Bovbjerg, D. H., & Marsland, A. L. (2021). Roundtables: AI’s apocalypse crisis
Register now for a subscriber-only conversation unpacking AI extinction fears.
Employees at the world's leading AI labs are saying there's a real possibility that advanced AI could destroy humanity. Are they right? Or is this more scaremongering and hype? Join MIT Technology Review executive editor Niall Firth for a conversation with senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and AI reporter Grace Huckins unpacking AI extinction fears: where they come from, whether they hold any water, and, if so, what we should do.
Going live on Tuesday, September 15 at 16:00 BST / 11:00am EST / 8:00am PST
Speakers: Niall Firth, executive editor, Will Douglas Heaven, senior AI editor, and Grace Huckins, AI reporter
Related Stories
- Here’s why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals
- AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all
- Bill Gates says we’ve passed AI’s danger thresholds. Now what?
- The inside story on why OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face
Deep Dive
Artificial intelligence
A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack
It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system.
AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring
AI doesn’t just learn stereotypes from its training. It can cook up new ones, too.
Here’s why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals
The misbehavior is called reward hacking. This is what you need to know.
AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all
AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems.

articles.title: It’s Time to Bring Some Sanity to the AI Risk Conversation
articles.description: It’s Time to Bring Some Sanity to the AI Risk Conversation bigtechnology.com
articles.description_html: It’s Time to Bring Some Sanity to the AI Risk Conversation  bigtechnology.com
articles.article_title: It’s Time to Bring Some Sanity to the AI Risk Conversation
articles.heading: Big Technology
articles.summary: AI will kill us all? It’s all just marketing? There has to be a better explanation. And there is.
articles.content:
The AI risk debate is going completely off the rails. As AI gets more powerful and begins to do some legitimately scary things, like hacking Hugging Face and hijacking message boards to coordinate, the warnings that AI might kill us all have grown louder, and so have the conspiracy theories about those warnings.
We’ve reached a point where the only two opinions that seem to be cutting through are: 1) AI has a good chance of killing us all, and 2) Warning of AI’s potential to wipe us out is just marketing for the AI companies.
Neither of these viewpoints capture the nuance of what’s actually happening on the ground, and the fact that they’re dominating the public discussion of the technology is both disheartening and a recipe for terrible policy decisions.
So, please allow me to assert the following in an effort to bring some sanity to the discussion:
1. The Risk Of AI Killing Humanity Is Completely Unquantifiable
AI lab employees can state that they believe the risk of AI wiping us out is 10% or higher, but don’t mistake their confidence for knowledge. Their predictions are guesswork that imagines what could happen after years of AI development. Adding a percentage makes these predictions seem math-based. They are not. As of now, they’re science fiction.
2. But, Many In Silicon Valley Earnestly Believe That AI Could Harm Humanity
The tech industry is working to build artificial intelligence that is smarter than humans. Many of those working on the project fear that this smarter thing could exploit our vulnerabilities and eventually find us an obstacle to its goals, and therefore eliminate us. We saw a glimpse of this potential when OpenAI’s bots hacked Hugging Face in July 2026, where hundreds of agents coordinated to exploit the site’s security gaps in pursuit of a testing goal. What could happen, then, when this technology has access to robots and not just websites? It would be unwise to discount these fears completely, again with the caveat that they are just speculation for now.
3. AI Researchers Speaking About Risk May Well Lead To Data Center Pauses
AI is already unpopular in the U.S. and politicians are seizing upon the latest round of Anthropic researcher warnings to call for hearings and pauses, potential obstacles that could slow AI development at a time when the companies must accelerate growth to justify their valuations and set up their IPOs. So, the researchers’ long-term fears could have near-term consequences to revenue and the current AI wave’s ability to sustain itself. This moment could dent the IPO momentum for both labs.
4. Going Public About AI Fears Is Not Marketing For the Labs
Employees saying a technology might kill us all might make the product sound so powerful you can’t afford not to buy it, but that doesn’t mean it’s marketing. The downsides of pauses and slowdowns are so great that these warnings do the exact opposite of what good marketing is meant to do. If it’s a marketing attempt, it’s a massive failure.
5. Speaking Out Is Good Marketing For The Whistleblowers
There’s a good career to be made in speaking out against AI companies, with big-time podcast appearances, book deals, and jobs at anti-AI lobby groups at the ready. That can’t be discounted in the calculus here. Though it doesn’t invalidate the warnings.
6. AI Labs Are Indeed Attempting to Speed Up AI Development Dramatically
OpenAI and Anthropic are both attempting to build AI that can improve itself, something called recursive self-improvement, or RSI. The hope is that if AI can do the work of AI researchers, it could shorten the timeline to all-powerful AI, or make it happen almost instantaneously via some sort of “intelligence explosion.” The combination of seeing how today’s technology can go wrong with the looming possibility of self-improving AI emerging is important context for today’s discourse. But RSI is still a research goal, and not an inevitability.
Is The Future Customer Experience AI Talking To AI? — With Tony Bates (sponsor)
Tony Bates is Chairman and CEO of Genesys. Bates joins Big Technology to discuss how AI agents will transform the way customers and companies interact with each other. Tune in to hear how businesses will operate when personal AI agents communicate directly with corporate agents, and why Bates believes humans will remain essential even as more routine interactions are automated. We also cover the rise of the hybrid workforce, what great customer experience looks like in an agentic world, and why Bates thinks fears of a coming SaaSpocalypse are overblown. Hit play for a forward-looking conversation about AI agents, the future of work, and what enterprise software will look like in the AI era.
Apple’s Most Ambitious Roadmap Ever? + OpenAI vs. Google vs. Anthropic Revisited — With M.G. Siegler
M.G. Siegler is the author of Spyglass. Siegler joins Big Technology to discuss Apple’s sudden burst of new products and what it means for the company as John Ternus takes over from Tim Cook. Tune in to hear why Apple’s foldable iPhone could reinvigorate the business, how its new hardware strategy marks a departure from the past, and what challenges Ternus will face as CEO. We also cover Google’s shifting AI strategy, OpenAI’s resurgence, Anthropic’s potential IPO, and the increasingly blurry meaning of AGI. Hit play for a wide-ranging look at Apple’s new era and the rapidly changing competitive landscape in artificial intelligence.
You can listen on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your podcast app of choice
Thanks again for reading. Please share Big Technology if you like it!
And hit that Like Button to show your support for sanity, please :)

articles.title: TSA is rolling out new security technology, but Logan’s timeline is unclear
articles.description: TSA is rolling out new security technology, but Logan’s timeline is unclear Boston.com
articles.description_html: TSA is rolling out new security technology, but Logan’s timeline is unclear  Boston.com
articles.article_title: TSA is rolling out new security technology, but Logan’s timeline is unclear
articles.heading: TSA is rolling out new security technology, but Logan’s timeline is unclear
articles.summary: TSA plans new security technology at Boston Logan, including facial recognition e-gates and 3D scanners. The timing remains unclear.
articles.content:
Sign up for the Today newsletter
Get everything you need to know to start your day, delivered right to your inbox every morning.
By Annie Jonas
2 minutes to read

New facial comparison technology could eventually allow travelers at Logan to pass through security without showing a driver’s license or boarding pass.
TSA Administrator David Cummins, who was sworn in as the agency’s eighth administrator last month, told CBS Boston on Tuesday that Logan will see new security technology as part of the agency’s “Horizon 25 Strategy.”
“You’re going to have E-gates with facial comparison technology where you can keep your driver’s license and your boarding pass in your pocket and just walk on through the E-gate and then put your bag on a 3D scanner. That is going to digitally unpack the bag,” Cummins told CBS.
Advertisement:
Travelers without PreCheck could also see changes. Cummins said standard lanes will also get walk-through body scanners that let passengers pass through without stopping to raise their hands.
Cummins also touted a second, unrelated change: a pilot program that allows people without a boarding pass escort travelers to the gate or meet arriving passengers — a practice barred at most airports since shortly after the September 11 attacks.
“If you have, let’s say, a teenage son that’s flying in, that you can go and greet them as they’re getting off the plane. This is something that the public has asked for, for many years,” Cummins told CBS Boston.
Depending on an airline’s policy, parents and guardians can usually obtain a gate pass to accompany a minor to the departure gate or meet them upon arrival. They also must still go through standard security screening.
TSA has not given a firm timeline for when the new e-gates and other security technology described by Cummins will reach Logan.
A TSA spokesperson told Boston.com that Logan currently has CLEAR eGates, but said they were not aware of the deployment schedule for TSA eGates and would look into it. The spokesperson also said the ability for travelers to scan themselves into a security checkpoint “could possibly come into play in the future,” but “we’re not there yet.”
For now, the spokesperson said Logan has TSA PreCheck Touchless, which allows eligible PreCheck travelers to use facial comparison technology to verify their identity. Massport referred Boston.com to TSA for questions about the new technology.
Annie Jonas is a Community writer at Boston.com. She was previously a local editor at Patch and a freelancer at the Financial Times.

articles.title: Minnesota Turns to New Technology to Fight Financial Aid Fraud
articles.description: Minnesota Turns to New Technology to Fight Financial Aid Fraud Governing
articles.description_html: Minnesota Turns to New Technology to Fight Financial Aid Fraud  Governing
articles.article_title: Minnesota Turns to New Technology to Fight Financial Aid Fraud
articles.heading: Minnesota Turns to New Technology to Fight Financial Aid Fraud
articles.summary: The state college system is preparing to test new tools to identify fraudulent applicants, but questions remain about whether they can keep pace with increasingly sophisticated schemes.
articles.content:
Those hours are largely spent scouting out so-called “ghost students,” criminals who enroll in classes using stolen or fake identities just long enough to receive financial aid — and then disappear.
History professor Joe Haker first noticed the problem three years ago, when he wondered why one student in his gender studies class had submitted the same assignment as a student in his history course.
“I thought, ‘Well, that’s weird. That probably could only happen if they were the same person,’” Haker said.
Nine students turned out to be the same person. This summer, Haker suspects as many as a third of his 90 online students could have been fake.
“It’s so maddening,” he said. “You can’t help but feel very, very strange when you realize that this student that you’re devoting even some time to is just scamming.”
The Minnesota State system of 26 colleges and seven universities is preparing to pilot a new automated identity verification system that it says will help combat the ever-evolving problem of ghost students. The Legislature this spring allocated $3 million toward the effort, which Craig Munson, who oversees information security for the system, said should provide guardrails for a couple of years.
While faculty and financial aid officers applaud the move, some question whether the new technology will do enough, quickly enough, to curb a problem that largely has been left to individual schools and their staffs to confront.
“This is not a Century College problem,” said Pam Engebretson, Century’s financial aid director. “It’s a system office problem, and we need a system office solution to be able to support all of the work that we do.”
Century uses its own software to help filter out fake students from real ones and devotes at least 1.5 full-time staff to the problem, Engebretson said.
While those steps have reduced fraud, Engebretson believes a handful of fake students obtained financial aid this summer — and even more enrolled in classes before faculty or other staff noticed.
“We’re doing everything we can to correct it,” Engebretson said. “We’re as much of a victim as anyone else.”
In California, a potential bellwether for Minnesota in its approach to fighting ghost students, lawmakers have spent at least $150 million since 2022 on technology to help verify the 2.2 million students within its community college system.
This spring, the system reported losing $1.5 million in federal aid to fraudulent students. However, that’s a decrease from $5.6 million in spring 2025 and a fraction of all financial aid paid out, according to the news outlet CalMatters.
One problem in Minnesota, critics note, is that the true scope of financial aid fraud isn’t clear.
The Minnesota State system, which serves over 290,000 students each year, says it flagged 2,696 financial aid applications as fraudulent or potentially fraudulent in the 2025-26 school year, down from 7,715 the year before.
However, citing security concerns, system officials declined to disclose how much federal or state aid has been lost to ghost students, even after questions from state lawmakers this spring.
U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon claimed in a 2025 letter to Gov. Tim Walz that 1,834 fake students in Minnesota had received $12.5 million in taxpayer-funded grants and loans. But McMahon provided no additional details, and the agency did not respond to clarifying questions from MinnPost.
In an interview, Munson said he had no idea where the $12.5 million figure came from. Nearly 100 higher education institutions in the state participate in federal financial aid programs. Munson said the system’s 33 schools “certainly are probably a portion of that. I would suspect a small portion.”
“If they do have information about where it came from, we’d love to see it,” he added, “because we want to do our due diligence and make sure that we’re finding what we should be finding and stopping what we should be stopping.”
At Century College alone, some $500,000 was paid out to suspected fraudulent actors within one academic year, according to several people who requested anonymity to avoid Century getting singled out for a far more widespread situation.
In a statement, the college declined to confirm or deny that figure, referring questions to the system office.
Haker said it’s important to know the full extent of the problem so Minnesota State can develop a comprehensive response.
“Because you don’t have anything coming from the system, it’s all based on your own experience,” he said. “And if I’m going off of my own personal experience this summer, it’s an enormous problem still.”
A Patchwork of Responses
Ghost student fraud is big and getting bigger all across the country.
It usually works like this: Thieves use stolen or fake IDs, or pay kickbacks to “straw students” to use their personal information, to apply for federal financial aid via the FAFSA form. Then they enroll in classes. The U.S. Department of Education distributes financial aid to individual colleges, which take what’s needed to cover tuition and fees and distribute the rest directly to the “students.”
The Department of Education estimates it has lost nearly $90 million to ghost students. In just two examples of recent cases, a Detroit man pleaded guilty to submitting fraudulent FAFSA claims for nearly 1,300 people in a scheme involving 100 schools in 24 states; over $10 million was disbursed. And a North Carolina woman was sentenced to five years in prison for stealing over $3.5 million in aid.
Community colleges are most at risk because of open admissions policies that aim to welcome all and reduce the complexity of the application process. The expansion of online classes during COVID-19 made it even easier to game the system.
The scope of the problem in California — where the state system of 116 public community colleges paid over $17.5 million in federal aid to fake students between 2022 and 2025 — drew national attention to the issue. But no state is immune. In Utah, a June audit estimated seven public institutions had devoted over 15,000 staff hours and lost over $830,000 to fake students in just one year, despite existing fraud detection systems.
At the national level, the Department of Education earlier this year launched a verification system that flags suspicious FAFSA applicants. Anyone deemed high-risk must confirm who they are by presenting a government-issued identification and going on camera for a photograph.
But the federal government has also made clear that schools are expected to have their security, and they are on the hook to repay money distributed to fraudulent students.
Minnesota’s largest system of two-year colleges, Minnesota State, has spent years relying on its individual schools to contend with ghost students while looking for systemwide solutions.
In 2023, the system created a work group on enrollment fraud, which the Legislature formalized two years later. The group issued a report in January, recommending the new systemwide verification system, along with more training for staff and students and annual reporting about enrollment fraud trends and mitigation.
The work group also published a user guide with protocols to deter enrollment fraud and for how to respond. The system tracks and logs fraud attempts, Munson said, and staff are expected to manually verify students’ IDs as needed.
“It’s a lot of labor,” he said. “We want to rightsize that and then get the automation where we can, and that’s where we asked for the help from the Legislature.”
Without that help, Munson said, Minnesota State eventually would have been able to invest in software, but it would have been “more homegrown, a little bit later, and we didn’t want to get past the tipping point where it became out of control.”
It’s difficult to grasp what prevention efforts look like internally across the system’s community colleges. MinnPost contacted all 26 with questions about protocols. Most did not answer, and several deferred to the system office while citing concerns about revealing information that could be useful to crime rings.
Mark Grant, a communication studies professor at Dakota County Technical College and representative for the Minnesota State College Faculty union, said the response varies from place to place.
“We have campuses that are doing an enormous amount because they have the resources,” he said. “We have campuses that are less equipped because they have less resources.”
Minneapolis College hired an outside company to review student IDs, said Dean of Enrollment Management Heidi Aldes, but scrapped it after determining their internal process was more effective.
“It takes significant human resource time,” Aldes said. “I would say the benefit is, as the attempts become more sophisticated, we sort of have a real-time understanding of what those changes are.”
Normandale Community College purchased software to aid its fraud team, which spans admissions, student services, records and registrar staff, among others. Since 2023, the school of about 11,000 students has flagged 29,000 applications for review, a college spokesperson told MinnPost.

Nine students turned out to be the same person. This summer, Haker suspects as many as a third of his 90 online students could have been fake.

Century uses its own software to help filter out fake students from real ones and devotes at least 1.5 full-time staff to the problem, Engebretson said.

Ghost student fraud is big and getting bigger all across the country.

articles.summary: AppLovin's profit margins are among the highest in digital advertising, while Meta's user base is unmatched anywhere on earth.
articles.content:
- APP +3.01%

- META +0.57%

Investors evaluating AppLovin (NASDAQ:APP) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) are comparing two different approaches to digital advertising. One is a high-growth software specialist while the other is a global social media titan.

AppLovin provides the technology that helps mobile apps find and monetize users. Meta Platforms connects the world through its apps while selling highly targeted advertising space. Both companies are utilizing artificial intelligence to maintain their competitive advantages in 2026.

The case for AppLovin

AppLovin serves as a critical bridge in the mobile economy by helping developers grow their businesses. Its core technology, Axon, uses artificial intelligence to match advertisements with the users most likely to engage with them. As one of the prominent tech stocks in the mobile space, it recently divested its internal apps business to focus entirely on third-party software solutions.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $5.5 billion, representing a significant 70% increase over the prior year. This expansion was accompanied by net income of approximately $3.3 billion. The company achieved a net margin of 60.8%, which measures how much of every revenue dollar is kept as profit after all expenses.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 1.7x, which compares total debt to the value owned by shareholders. The current ratio, measuring the ability to cover short term obligations with current assets, was a strong 3.3x. Free cash flow for the period reached $3.9 billion, representing the cash remaining after paying for operating costs and capital investments.

The case for Meta Platforms

Meta Platforms operates the most expansive social network in the world through Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Its Family of Apps serves nearly 3.6 billion daily users, providing a vast audience for advertisers ranging from small businesses to global brands. The company is also investing heavily in its Reality Labs division to develop next-generation mixed-reality hardware and software.

For FY 2025, the company reported revenue of close to $201.0 billion, which grew by roughly 22.2% year over year. Net income for the period was approximately $60.5 billion. Meta maintained a net margin of 30.1%, demonstrating its ability to generate high levels of profit even while investing billions into future technologies.

According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.4x, indicating a relatively conservative use of debt. The current ratio stood at roughly 2.6x, providing a healthy cushion for day to day operations. Free cash flow was highly robust at $46.1 billion, allowing the company to fund its ambitious AI research and return capital to shareholders.

Risk profile comparison

AppLovin faces intense competition from global technology leaders that control the mobile operating systems. Its growth is partially dependent on the policies of Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Google regarding data privacy and app distribution. Furthermore, the company must manage the integration of recent acquisitions and address ongoing federal securities class action litigation regarding its financial disclosures.

Meta Platforms relies heavily on advertising revenue, which can be sensitive to broader economic downturns and shifts in consumer spending. The company faces a complex web of global privacy regulations like the GDPR and has recently settled significant litigation involving youth safety. Continued high spending on AI and virtual reality also carries the risk that these expensive investments may not generate immediate financial returns.

Valuation comparison

AppLovin carries a much higher premium relative to its annual sales.

Metric

AppLovin

Meta Platforms

Forward P/E

17.4x

19.9x

P/S ratio

15.3x

7.3x

Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

I'd go with Meta, though AppLovin has built one of the most profitable software businesses in digital advertising, with margins that most companies would envy and an AI engine expanding into new verticals. AppLovin's Q2 revenue miss and below-consensus guidance were disappointing, but the underlying business model is sound.

Meta's Q2 was messy on the surface. Earnings missed estimates as legal charges, severance costs, and a dramatic increase in AI infrastructure spending all hit at once. But strip those one-time items out and the core advertising business is performing at the highest level in years. Revenue grew at a strong double-digit rate, more than 3.5 billion people used a Meta app every single day, and Instagram crossed 2 billion daily active users for the first time.

Meta is betting enormous amounts of capital on AI, which introduces uncertainty worth taking seriously. But the scale of its user base and advertising platform gives it a foundation that AppLovin simply cannot match. For a long-term investor, owning the platform that reaches more than half the world's population is a stronger starting point.

Should you buy stock in AppLovin right now?

Before you buy stock in AppLovin, consider this:

articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Adobe is one of the most attractively priced software stocks in the market right now, while CrowdStrike commands a premium valuation that reflects one of the strongest growth trajectories in cybersecurity.
articles.content:
- ADBE +1.46%

- CRWD -1.05%

Software investing often forces a choice between a stable, cash-rich giant and a high-velocity disruptor, leaving investors to wonder which path leads to better long-term outcomes in an evolving digital economy. Choosing between Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) and CrowdStrike (NASDAQ:CRWD) requires weighing established dominance against high-growth potential.

Adobe is the creative world's standard, while CrowdStrike is a cloud-native cybersecurity defender protecting modern enterprise workloads. They are being compared because both rely on subscription models to dominate their respective fields but offer very different risk and reward profiles for retail investors.

The case for Adobe

Adobe operates as a leader among tech stocks by providing creative and productivity software to more than 20,000 enterprise customers. The company uses an integrated cloud-based subscription model to serve diverse groups ranging from students to global corporations. Recent strategic moves include the acquisition of Topaz Labs to enhance content capabilities through generative and agentic artificial intelligence tools.

In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Nov. 28, 2025, revenue reached nearly $23.8 billion, representing a year over year growth rate of approximately 10.5%. This growth follows a trend of steady expansion, as revenue was roughly $21.5 billion in the previous year. The company reported a net income of close to $7.1 billion, showcasing a healthy net margin of roughly 30%.

As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, was approximately 0.6x. The current ratio, measuring the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, stood at roughly 1.0x. Free cash flow, which is the cash a company generates after accounting for capital expenditures, reached nearly $9.9 billion during this period, indicating strong cash generation relative to its size.

The case for CrowdStrike

CrowdStrike provides a cloud-native platform designed to protect identity, data, and cloud workloads for a base of nearly 4,733 customers. The company utilizes a direct sales force and an extensive network of channel partners, including a 2026 partnership with Grant Thornton Advisors. Its go-to-market strategy focuses on endpoint protection and managed detection services for both public sector entities and government agencies.

In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue grew by approximately 21.7% to reach nearly $4.8 billion compared with the prior fiscal year. The company reported a net loss of roughly $162.5 million, resulting in a negative net margin of about 3.4%. This loss widened from the prior year, reflecting significant investments in personnel and cloud infrastructure to support the scale of its security cloud.

According to its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.2x, while the current ratio reached approximately 1.8x. Free cash flow totaled close to $1.3 billion in the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 68% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Risk profile comparison

Adobe faces intense competition from global software players and cloud-native entrants who may deploy resources more effectively. The rapid integration of generative AI carries risks of intellectual property infringement and shifting global regulations like the EU AI Act. Furthermore, the company faced a $150 million settlement in early 2026 regarding its online subscription cancellation practices and remains under regulatory scrutiny.

CrowdStrike continues to manage the reputational and operational aftermath of the failure in its July 19, 2024, content configuration update. This incident has led to ongoing costs for customer incentives and active litigation that could affect future results. The company also faces stiff competition from established security vendors and major cloud providers like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), which possess greater financial resources.

Valuation comparison

Adobe appears significantly more conservative on a valuation basis, trading at a much lower multiple of future earnings estimates and annual sales than CrowdStrike.

Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

I'd go with CrowdStrike, though Adobe trading near historic lows is not something a long-term investor should dismiss without a second look. Adobe has built one of the most deeply embedded software franchises in the world, and the stock has pulled back to one of its most attractive entry points in years. Fears that AI would erode its creative software dominance are looking increasingly overblown. For a long-term investor who values predictable cash flows and a proven franchise, it is a solid choice.

But CrowdStrike is outpacing Adobe on nearly every growth metric that matters right now. Annual recurring revenue just hit a record, free cash flow surged to nearly a third of total revenue, and the Falcon platform keeps consolidating more of its customers' security spending under one roof. Every major enterprise that adds an AI workload also adds a new attack surface that needs protecting, which means CrowdStrike's addressable market keeps expanding alongside the AI build-out itself.

Cybersecurity is not a discretionary purchase for enterprises the way creative software can be. For a long-term investor, owning the platform that keeps growing because the problem it solves keeps getting bigger is a stronger foundation right now.

articles.heading: PrimeGlobal Launches Technology Advisory Partnership with Sikich
articles.summary: PrimeGlobal has launched a new technology advisory partnership with Sikich, a global professional services company.
articles.content:
PrimeGlobal has launched a new technology advisory partnership with its member firm and IPA 100 firm Sikich (FY25 net revenue of $529.5 million) , a global professional services company providing consulting, technology and compliance services, to help the association’s 320+ member firms globally develop their technology advisory capabilities and respond to growing client demand for technology-related services.

The partnership will provide PrimeGlobal members with access to practical resources, specialist expertise and collaboration opportunities to help them strengthen and expand their advisory offerings. The initiative includes a dedicated Technology Advisory resource hub designed to help firms understand the opportunity, explore approaches to building capability and access specialist support where required. Resources cover areas including data and AI, cybersecurity, cloud services, automation, business applications and technology strategy.

Steve Heathcote , Chief Executive Officer of PrimeGlobal, said:

“Technology advisory represents a major growth opportunity for firms looking to expand their advisory services and deliver greater value to clients. Through this partnership with Sikich, we are providing members with practical support, insight and access to specialist expertise that can help them build capability and respond to changing client needs.”

Richard Lynch , CPA and Sikich principal leading compliance solutions, added:

“Technology continues to reshape how organizations operate, compete and grow, creating significant opportunities for firms to expand the value they deliver to clients. At Sikich, we’ve witnessed firsthand how services such as AI, cybersecurity, cloud modernization and business applications create clarity for organizations and accelerate achievement of their business objectives. We’re extremely pleased to partner with PrimeGlobal to share our experience, practical insights and specialized capabilities with member firms around the world as they strengthen their technology advisory offerings and help clients navigate the digital future.”

Sikich’s technology advisory capabilities span business applications, data and AI, cybersecurity, cloud modernization, managed technology services and strategic technology consulting, amongst other specialties.

articles.title: New DNA technology offers hope in identifying 9/11 victims 25 years later

articles.article_title: New DNA technology offers hope in identifying 9/11 victims 25 years later
articles.heading: New DNA technology offers hope in identifying 9/11 victims 25 years later
authors: ALEXX ALTMAN-DEVILBISS | The National News Desk
articles.summary: The terrorist attack killed 2,753 people in New York City.
articles.content:
New DNA technology offers hope in identifying 9/11 victims 25 years later
NEW YORK (TNND) — Twenty-five years after al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked two planes and flew them into the Twin Towers on Sept. 11, 2001, officials are still working to identify the remains of 1,099 victims.
The terrorist attack killed 2,753 people in New York City. Last month, the 1,654th victim was identified using a breakthrough technique called forensic investigative genetic genealogy, or FIGG, according to Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani's office.
The adult woman, whose name is being withheld at her family's request, was the first 9/11 victim identified using FIGG and the first newly identified victim since August 2025.
The discovery resulted from a collaboration between the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner and the NYPD, pairing the medical examiner's forensic capabilities with the department's genealogical expertise.
FIGG combines specialized DNA testing with genealogical research to generate leads that can then be confirmed through DNA or other forensic methods. City officials said the tool can produce leads that otherwise might not have been possible.
“A quarter century after the day that forever changed our world, we are keeping the promise to identify those who died at the World Trade Center in 2001 and return them to their loved ones,” Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Graham said.
Mark Desire, assistant director at the City of New York Office of Chief Medical Examiner, told the New York Post the effort is “not only the largest forensic investigation in the United States but also the most difficult,” because jet fuel, fire, water, building chemicals and sunlight can all destroy DNA.
Mamdani's office said recent links to remains have also been confirmed for three previously identified victims through FIGG, renewed family outreach for DNA reference samples and continued retesting of remains recovered since 2001.

articles.article_title: AMY GRUPO adopts i4F technology - Floor Covering News
articles.heading: AMY GRUPO adopts i4F technology
articles.summary: AMY GRUPO signs an i4F Optibevel licensing agreement, adding laser bevel technology to new SPC, LSPC and WPC flooring collections.
articles.content:
Turnhout, Belgium—AMY GRUPO has signed a new license agreement for i4F’s Optibevel technology. The manufacturer plans to use the technology across most of its new flooring products.
The agreement expands AMY GRUPO’s existing relationship with i4F. The manufacturer already licenses i4F drop-lock, CeraGrout and WPC technologies.
AMY GRUPO plans to apply Optibevel to its new SPC, LSPC and WPC lines. The technology uses a high-precision laser to create decorative bevels directly in the profiling line.
AMY GRUPO is one of Vietnam’s largest manufacturers of ceramic tile and vinyl flooring materials. The company has focused its growth strategy on product development and innovation.
“Innovation is about making a real difference to the products we offer and the experience we deliver to our customers,” said Dinh Quoc Tuan, CEO of AMY GRUPO. “Optibevel is a great example of that as it gives us more freedom to create floors with the natural beauty without compromising on quality or performance. Our relationship with i4F continues to bring valuable technologies into our portfolio, helping us turn new ideas into products that combine beautiful design, lasting quality and ease of use, while delivering greater value and satisfaction for our customers.”
Laser technology expands design options
Optibevel’s in-line laser process addresses limitations associated with traditional cut, painted and pressed bevel technologies. The system matches bevel gloss, design and texture with the flooring surface.
The technology also gives manufacturers greater sizing flexibility and can improve production efficiency. It accommodates formats ranging from small herringbone planks to large wall panels. Optibevel works with SPC, WPC, LVT and other thermoplastic-based flooring.
“AMY GRUPO has been a valued i4F partner for many years and this latest agreement further strengthens our long-standing relationship,” said John Rietveldt, CEO of i4F. “Their commitment to product quality, design and manufacturing excellence makes Optibevel a natural fit for their flooring portfolio. We believe Optibevel is the industry’s most advanced enhanced bevel technology, giving manufacturers a smarter, more efficient way to achieve premium aesthetics while responding to growing demand for more authentic, natural-looking floors.”

A Catholic archbishop and a panel of artificial intelligence (AI) experts argued that expanding technology should not supersede human dignity at a Sept. 9 Georgetown University event.
Archbishop Gabriele Caccia, the Apostolic Nuncio of the Holy See to the United States, urged Catholics to foster public debate over AI’s impacts on job security and individuality. The panelists, who joined Caccia in Gaston Hall, also warned attendees about the dangers of commercializing human intelligence.
The speakers largely drew from arguments made in Pope Leo VI’s May encyclical “Magnifica Humanitas” (“Magnificent Humanity”), which argues that technological innovation should respect the dignity of all people rather than benefitting the few.
Caccia said the pope’s AI stipulations come from the belief that individual souls are sacred.
“All these guidance are based on a central point that each human being in our vision is created in the image of God,” Caccia said at the event. “He has something more than human in His humanity, and these should be always recognized. It’s the foundation stone on which to build any future. If we don’t respect that, we become like objects.”
“Each one is unique,” Caccia added. “Each one is called life by somebody bigger than us. Each one has a purpose.”
Despite the attention it received, “Magnifica Humanitas” does not recommend any specific policy solutions toward AI usage.
University President Eduardo Peñalver said Georgetown is answering Pope Leo’s call to action by encouraging community involvement and accessibility to AI.
“In his encyclical, Pope Leo posed a specific challenge to universities and, by implication, Catholic universities in particular, to lead the way in advancing understanding of this new and rapidly evolving technology, and in crafting responses to it that emphasize the importance of subordinating AI for human purposes, human dignity and the common good,” Peñalver said at the event.
Peñalver announced a plan Sept. 3 that will set a university-wide framework for AI use, following multiple AI initiatives launched in August. The College of Arts & Sciences also inaugurated an AI ethics and application certificate this semester, and in February, the university announced plans to give students premium access to Gemini, Google’s AI assistant.
Anna Rowlands, a professor of Catholic Social Thought and Practice at Durham University, said the role of the church is not to offer solutions, but to foster discussion.
“One of the things that’s most misunderstood about the encyclical is people who react by saying, ‘Well, it’s kind of useless because it’s really generic, and it needs to be a blueprint that just lists on solutions,’” Rowlands said at the event.
“The task of the church is not to offer solutions — which doesn’t mean solutions can’t be found, Rowlands added. “But that’s what the process of us learning how to think through and reason through and reflecting these questions together is meant to produce.”
The “Magnifica Humanitas” reaffirmed the church’s commitment to social justice, faith and the gospel in an AI economy. Its release comes amid growing concerns of entry-level job security, AI-based data leaks and resignations from tech engineers over AI capabilities.
Caccia said the key to establishing AI consensus is cooperation between opposing groups.
“There is not one answer. It is not just a political answer, but it’s not just the technical answer or the economic answer,” Caccia said. “You have to put all the stakeholders around the table and find a common way in which everyone has his own role to play.”
Jasmine Sun, a journalist who covers technological innovation in Silicon Valley, said the views of many tech industrialists contrast greatly from those of the general public.
“Silicon Valley leaders are not trusted messengers of what an ideal AI future ought to look like,” Sun said at the event.
“They will articulate a vision, a utopia that may be utopia to them, involving immortality or a world where nobody has to work anymore,” Sun added.
Molly Kinder — the CEO of the Breakwater Initiative, an AI-focused policy organization, and a former senior fellow at the Brookings Institution on AI policy — said she worries the commercialization of AI could harm job security.
“I have a deep fear when I think about the seven generations question of, ‘Is AI going to commoditize cognition?’” Kinder said at the event. “What would that mean for the kinds of jobs that so many of us gain so much satisfaction from? I think there’s a lot of really hard questions ahead.”
“We’re moving toward a world where AI is getting dangerously good at potentially surpassing humans at work,” Kinder added. “How do you reconcile that? How do you reconcile an economy that’s used up to have profit motives to replace humans at work? And these are really, really hard questions. They’re not easy policy answers.”
Young adults are growing increasingly concerned about AI use and threats to job opportunities, polls show.
Lukas Pitman (SFS ’27), who attended the event, said the panelists’ conversation offered an example of positive leadership amid ongoing political conflicts.
“I would definitely say it gave me hope,” Pitman told The Hoya. “I think one of the questions that was addressed tonight was more leadership, that in a time where across the entire world politicians and other traditional leaders have basically been discredited, there’s never been a time, I think, at least right now, that there is as little trust in political leaders as we are living in.”
“People feel alone, hopeless, and with the encyclical, I think the pope not only is calling out there is a path forward,” Pitman added. “We can address these issues, getting to the heart of it, that we are human beings first and not just machines to be utilized for an economy based on AI.”
Caccia said the pope’s encyclical and subsequent discussion may help find answers to the questions AI poses to society.
“Global answers mean everyone also should say something and understand the other, and this is the methodology that the pope wanted to implement,” Caccia said.
“We don’t pretend to have the answer,” Caccia added. “We try to put some questions that can help us to find common answer, and to work together for the future of every one of us.”
Caccia said he hopes that the church’s commitment to public discourse can produce solutions to ease growing anxiety as AI continues to develop.
“I am confident, as I said, that together we can face this situation and find a way,” Caccia said.
“If you want to go fast, go alone,” Caccia added. “If you want to go far, go together, and I think we have to go very far, and that’s why we have to go together.”

articles.content:
Beef Technology Field Day offered Sept. 29 in Chariton
AMES, Iowa – The Iowa Beef Center with Iowa State University Extension and Outreach will host a Technology Field Day at the McNay Memorial Research Farm on Sept. 29, showcasing a handful of technologies being used in various research and demonstration studies.
According to Shelby Gruss, assistant professor and forage extension specialist at Iowa State, cattlemen and women are discovering top-of-the-line tech to help their operations run smoother and a bit more efficiently. The technologies beef producers can use are expansive, and it is a rapidly evolving space with more options becoming available.
The McNay Research Farm houses Iowa State's main cow-calf operation, comprised of a purebred Angus spring and fall herd. On-farm data collected provides ample research opportunities, which assistant professor and cow-calf extension specialist at Iowa State Randie Culbertson will discuss at the field day.
"We have both genotype and traditional phenotype information on all these cattle. With new technologies, we can gather phenotype information that has been hard to collect in the past and start looking for more genetic relationships that matter to producers," she said.
The field day will feature various demonstration trials utilizing technologies, as well as a tradeshow with multiple company representatives available to answer questions about virtual fencing, activity monitoring ear tags and more.
Schedule
- 9 a.m. – Trade show and Check-in
- 9: 30 a.m. – Transport to field with alfalfa grazing trial. Technologies that will be discussed include grazing alfalfa varieties, satellite imagery for biomass estimates, eartags that track activity and location and a mineral feeder collecting cattle weights.
- 12:15 p.m. – Lunch and Trade show
- 1 p.m. – Iowa State Cow Herd Data Collection and Management
- 1:30 p.m. – Iowa State Forage Research Update
- 2 p.m. – Satellite Imagery and Biomass Prediction Research
- 2:15 p.m. – Virtual Fence and Wearable Technology Panel
- 3 p.m. – Adjourn
Check-in will begin at 9 a.m., with the program beginning at 9:30 a.m. A light meal will be provided. The McNay Memorial Research Farm is located at 45249 170th Avenue, Chariton.
To attend, producers can register online. For additional information, contact Shelby Gruss at sgruss@iastate.edu or 515-294-2333.
This program is supported by an Iowa Beef Industry Checkoff grant.

articles.title: Transformation through technology: Young people bring new ideas to decision-making
articles.description: Transformation through technology: Young people bring new ideas to decision-making Welcome to the United Nations
articles.description_html: Transformation through technology: Young people bring new ideas to decision-making  Welcome to the United Nations
articles.article_title: Transformation through technology: Young people bring new ideas to decision-making | United Nations
articles.heading: Transformation through technology: Young people bring new ideas to decision-making
articles.content:
Young people are indispensable partners in advancing the 2030 Agenda. As innovators, leaders and changemakers, they are at the heart of sustainable development, generating new ideas and advancing solutions that foster more responsive, inclusive and future-ready public institutions.
On 13 August, UN DESA brought together young leaders, practitioners and policymakers for the 10th Youth Forum on SDG Implementation. Taking place online after the International Youth Day on 12 August, the Forum was organized under the theme “Advancing Youth Engagement in the Public Decision-Making Process through Digital Transformation and Innovative Governance”. The Forum received 674 registrations from 78 countries across Asia and the Pacific, Africa and beyond, including 48 presentation registrations and 626 audience registrations. Through interactive discussions, participants explored how digital innovation and youth-led solutions can strengthen meaningful participation in public decision-making and help accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The Forum was opened by Changseob Han, Head of the United Nations Project Office on Governance (UNPOG), who highlighted the importance of creating meaningful opportunities for young people to contribute to SDG implementation. Reflecting on the Forum’s 10-year journey, he noted its role in providing “a valuable platform for young people to connect, exchange ideas and contribute their perspectives” on global challenges and opportunities. He also emphasized that, despite living in very different circumstances, young people share common aspirations for “dignity, participation and opportunity”.
In his keynote address, Felipe Paullier, Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs, underscored the urgency of accelerating progress towards the 2030 Agenda and the critical role of young people in this effort. He highlighted the potential of digital platforms and artificial intelligence to create new avenues for youth participation in public decision-making, while emphasizing the importance of inclusive and people-centred approaches. He also highlighted the relevance of UN 2.0 in supporting more innovative, data-driven and forward-looking approaches to governance.
The Forum then turned to how youth participation can move beyond consultation towards meaningful engagement and co-creation. The first session explored how digital transformation and emerging technologies can create new opportunities for young people to contribute to policy design and agenda-setting, and representatives of the African Youth Commission and Youth for Privacy brought perspectives on youth leadership in policy design and the responsible use of AI for inclusive and participatory governance. Discussions also emphasized the importance of responsible innovation, including privacy, transparency and human oversight, as well as sustained engagement and feedback mechanisms to ensure that young people's contributions can meaningfully inform public policies and decisions.
The second session moved from dialogue to youth-led solutions. In preparation for the Forum, UNPOG invited young people from around the world to develop practical and scalable solutions to global challenges, drawing on the five transformative areas of the UN 2.0 Quintet of Change: data, digital technologies, innovation, behavioral science and foresight. Five teams presented proposals addressing challenges ranging from digital inclusion and local policymaking to sustainable energy, policy intelligence, road safety and youth engagement in accelerating the SDGs. Among the ideas presented were an offline-first AI platform enabling young people in remote and indigenous communities to contribute to local policymaking, and a sustainable fuel alternative made from agricultural waste. Together, the proposals demonstrated how young people can translate local challenges into practical and innovative solutions, while experts feedback underscored the importance of accessibility, evidence, impact measurement and clear pathways for implementation and scale.
The final session featured contributions from representatives of She Loves Tech and UNESCO and explored how to build inclusive ecosystems that can help youth-led ideas develop and thrive. Discussions highlighted that digital access alone is not enough, and young people also need the skills, knowledge, networks and resources to turn ideas into action. Capacity development and strategic partnerships among youth, governments, international organizations, academia, civil society and other stakeholders were also brought up as essential factors to creating an enabling environment for youth-led innovation. The session also reinforced the importance of moving beyond consultation towards co-creation, with young people engaged as partners from the outset and supported to shape, implement and monitor solutions.
Across the Forum, a clear message emerged that meaningful youth engagement is not simply about giving young people a voice, but about creating the conditions for them to exercise agency and contribute to public decision-making. Digital transformation and emerging technologies can help expand these opportunities, but their contribution must be grounded in inclusion, transparency, accountability, privacy and human oversight. Sustained institutional support, capacity development and partnerships is also equally important in ensuring that youth-led ideas can contribute to more inclusive, responsive and future-ready governance.
The Forum concluded with a call for continued collaboration to strengthen youth participation in public decision-making and support youth-led innovation, reaffirming that young people must be empowered not only to voice their ideas, but to help shape the decisions and solutions that will define their future.
The key messages and youth perspectives received from the Youth Forum will inform the Youth Session of the 10th Regional Symposium of the UN DESA/DPIDG/UNPOG. This event will take place in a hybrid format in Incheon, the Republic of Korea, in November 2026, extending opportunities for youth-led ideas to gain visibility and contribute to broader discussions on governance and SDG implementation.
Watch the Forum and discover how young people are helping to shape a more sustainable and inclusive future.
