articles.content:
Shanghai, China--(Newsfile Corp. - September 11, 2026) - On August 4, the 20th Frost & Sullivan Global Growth, Innovation and Leadership (GIL) Summit and the 5th New Investment Event (the "2026 Frost & Sullivan New Investment Event") officially opened at Jing An Shangri-La, Shanghai.In conjunction with the Summit, the Celebratory Banquet for the 65ᵗʰ Anniversary of Frost & Sullivan Global and the 20ᵗʰ Anniversary of the GIL Summit in China was held, where the 2026 Frost & Sullivan Global Awards and China Awards were announced.
Based on recent years' research and analysis of the global Gene Therapy CRDMO industry enabling sector, as well as evaluation of relevant companies in the industry, Frost & Sullivan awarded PackGene Biotech Inc. (hereinafter "PackGene") the "GLOBAL GENE THERAPY CRDMO TECHNOLOGY INNOVATION LEADERSHIP AWARD." Prof. Vinod K. Aggarwal, Global Chief Economist of Frost & Sullivan, Distinguished Professor at UC Berkeley, Director of Berkeley APEC Study Center, and Dr. Liu Jun, Chairman of Frost & Sullivan Specialized & Sophisticated Enterprises Expert Committee, Chairman of UNICOMP, presented the award to PackGene Biotech Inc.
Frost & Sullivan presents the "GLOBAL GENE THERAPY CRDMO TECHNOLOGY INNOVATION LEADERSHIP AWARD" to PackGene Biotech Inc.
Prof. Vinod K. Aggarwal, Global Chief Economist of Frost & Sullivan, Distinguished Professor at UC Berkeley, Director of Berkeley APEC Study Center, and Dr. Liu Jun, Chairman of Frost & Sullivan Specialized & Sophisticated Enterprises Expert Committee, Chairman of UNICOMP, presented the award to PackGene Biotech Inc.
PackGene Biotech Inc. : A Global Innovator in Gene Therapy CRDMO
Driven by the mission to make gene therapy affordable for everyone, PackGene was founded in 2014 with a clear purpose: to accelerate the global reach of these transformative treatments through cutting-edge vector technologies and comprehensive, integrated services. While AAV vectors hold enormous therapeutic promise, their traditional manufacturing processes remain costly and technically challenging. PackGene tackles these hurdles head-on with fundamental innovations in AAV production and the broader CGT landscape-delivering high-quality, scalable, and cost-effective manufacturing solutions.
Five Proprietary Technology Platforms Powering AAV Industrialization
PackGene is among the few CDMOs worldwide that have mastered large-scale AAV production with both high yield and low empty capsid rates. To break through the core industrial bottlenecks, the company has built an in-house R&D engine covering the entire value chain-cell lines, plasmids, transfection, purification, and analytics. The π-Alpha™ 293 Cell High-Yield Platform uses proprietary, suspension-adapted cell lines to dramatically boost AAV output. The π-Icosa™ Serotype Screening Platform offers over 100 serotypes targeting diverse tissues including brain, heart, liver, and muscle. Since 2022, PackGene has been integrating AI into its R&D workflows, developing platforms for formulation screening, novel AAV capsid discovery, and mRNA design-shifting the R&D paradigm from trial-and-error to data-driven decision making. Beyond AAV, its product portfolio now includes lentivirus, plasmid, and mRNA/LNP-based gene therapy vectors.
Continuous Process Innovation and Capacity Expansion
PackGene consistently pushes the frontiers of AAV industrialization, working on high-density transfection, full-capsid enrichment, residual host-cell DNA and plasmid backbone control, empty/full particle analytical methods, rcAAV reference standards, rapid mycoplasma testing, and next-generation safety designs for AAV delivery. The company has established over 60 proprietary analytical methods that cover all critical quality attributes required for IND filings and clinical batch release. Operating to international standards, PackGene has built GMP-compliant sterile fill-finish and release systems, ensuring full traceability and control from raw materials to final drug product. In 2021, the company launched Asia's first cGMP AAV manufacturing facility with 4,000-liter capacity, occupying 8,000 square meters. With a strong track record in technology transfer, PackGene has supported numerous pilot-scale and IND-enabling projects.
Global Presence and Ecosystem Building
Headquartered in Guangzhou, PackGene established a U.S. subsidiary in 2015, a Swiss subsidiary in 2022, and opened its U.S. CDMO facility in December 2024-forming an integrated "China-U.S.-Europe" operational network. The company has helped partners secure more than ten FDA and NMPA IND approvals with zero deficiency responses, and has successfully delivered dozens of IIT projects. Notable examples include SNUG01, the world's first TRIM72-targeted ALS gene therapy; JWK001, the first AAV gene therapy using a two-plasmid packaging system; XMVA09, which combines bispecific targeting with an intravitreal-injectable capsid; and LY-M001, China's first domestically developed AAV therapy for Gaucher disease. Backed by top investors including Sequoia Capital, SDIC Fund, and Cathay Capital, the company has completed multiple financing rounds. With a team of 250 professionals and recognition as a Postdoctoral Research Workstation sub-center, PackGene remains committed to sharing its technological breakthroughs and fostering an open industrial ecosystem-ultimately driving gene therapy from a high-cost luxury to a widely accessible standard of care.
About Frost & Sullivan Global Innovation Leadership Award
The 2026 Frost & Sullivan GLOBAL GENE THERAPY CRDMO TECHNOLOGY INNOVATION LEADERSHIP AWARD recognizes enterprises for outstanding performance and remarkable achievements in technological innovation, commercial success, and customer value. The Frost & Sullivan team, through in-depth interviews, industry analysis, and secondary research, nominated a group of competitive outstanding companies to an independent judging panel. The independent judging panel, composed of third-party investment and financing experts, financial experts, bankers, and well-known listed company entrepreneurs, rigorously evaluated the nominees proposed by the Frost & Sullivan team and decided to award the "GLOBAL GENE THERAPY CRDMO TECHNOLOGY INNOVATION LEADERSHIP AWARD" to PackGene Biotech Inc.

articles.heading: 25 years after 9/11: Risk assessment, technology reimagines security
articles.summary: Since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, advancements in technology have changed airport security to make screening more efficient.
articles.content:
Sept. 10 (UPI) -- In the 25 years since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and Pentagon, airport security has been overhauled, then reimagined again to make flying safer and more efficient for travelers.
Nearly 3,000 people died in the attacks carried out by hijackers who commandeered commercial aircrafts from Boston; Newark, N.J.; and Washington, D.C. In the immediate aftermath of the deadliest attack on U.S. soil, lawmakers and the air travel industry were forced to rethink airport security and national security as a whole.
Among the first and most impactful shifts was the creation of the Transportation Security Administration, a new government agency established about two months after the attacks to enhance airport security and prevent similar incidents from happening in the future. The TSA predates the creation of the Department of Homeland Security, the agency that oversees the TSA, by a year.
The Aviation and Transportation Security Act passed in Congress in November 2001. It implemented a requirement for the TSA to have a presence in airports across the country with all passengers submitting their person and baggage to screenings by agents.
The heightened security measures for the perimeter of the airport included the introduction of biometric screening technology in the airport setting. Chief among this rollout of technology were facial recognition capabilities.
Ryan Propis, vice president and security and facilitation with the U.S. Travel Association and former deputy staff director and general counsel for the House Committee on Homeland Security, told UPI that biometric technology is one of the most significant innovations in airport security. In 2026, a key method of assessing the safety of passengers is knowing who is flying before they even arrive at the gate.
Biometric technology is not wholly responsible for that passenger screening capability. Information sharing has also been emphasized post 9/11. Information sharing agreements between the United States and other governments around the world are a key tenet of modern national security.
The Sept. 11 attacks caused governments to remove rules and regulations that stood in the way of sharing certain intelligence information. This allows information about passengers and potential risks to be shared domestically and internationally.

"They know a lot more information up front than they did before. So you've got a lot of the information that's shared from airports but mostly from airlines around who these travelers are, where they've been before, whether they've had any security incidents in the past, what their immigration status is."

With these programs, travelers voluntarily submit more information for screening on the front end, allowing them to bypass long lines at the airport as they have already been vetted.
Prior to Sept. 11, the passenger screening process was handled by private agencies commissioned by the airports. People could accompany friends and loved ones to their gates to see them off without having a flight of their own. Few items were prohibited from being kept in luggage and travelers could arrive at the airport, reach their gate and be ready for takeoff in short order.
The passenger screening process became more arduous for travelers after the attacks. People were long required to remove their shoes and belts to pass through TSA checkpoints. The number of items that were prohibited grew significantly, including restrictions on liquids, electronic devices, sharp items and certain tools.
Not all security measures were adopted specifically due to 9/11. The shoe removal requirement came in response to a man, Richard Reid, attempting to sneak a bomb onto a transatlantic flight hidden inside his shoe months after 9/11.
"Generally, and the same with establishing the TSA, everything has been pretty much reactive to either a security incident or a potential incident of specific threats," Propis said of shifting security policies. "Removing jackets, taking laptops out of bags, those were all in response to specific credible threats."
Twenty five years after 9/11, the onus on travelers has loosened some while the trust in airport safety methods has grown.
A survey by the U.S. Travel Association in 2024 found that about 80% of travelers support the use of biometric technology at TSA checkpoints. Support for the technology shows relative parity across political ideologies. A majority of people also support identity verification as a measure to prevent terrorism.
"Historically, if you were making a security change, usually if it was pro-security it was probably going to be 'bad for the traveler,'" Propis said. "We're at a place now where you're seeing changes that are being made that are pro-technology and pro-innovation that are actually improving security or at least maintaining security and actually improving the operation and the traveler experience."
As biometric screenings increase their lift on assessing travelers, the integration of artificial intelligence will change how bags are screened in the future, Propis said.
"There's a lot of amazing technology, especially on the AI and algorithm development side of things that I think are really the next iteration of a game-changing impact," he said. "That's the same technology that underpins biometrics and facial matching. But when you apply that to bag scanning and on person scanning, you can basically double the throughput of the amount of folks that are going through a checkpoint."
With AI, bags can be scanned without an agent needing to manually assess each one. Instead, the scanning technology can flag bags that need to be reviewed.
Between 250 and 300 people move through the average TSA checkpoint each hour.
"We would love to see some of those technologies rolled out, especially for pre-check travelers," Propis said. "Eventually when those algorithms get stronger and that software is strong enough, it can assist officers in letting people carry on liquids like water, breast milk and formula."
Two of the latest changes to airport security came into effect in 2025, including the end of the shoe removal requirement. Then-Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said technological advancements gave the agency confidence that it could end the requirement while maintaining its security standards.
Also in effect as of 2025 is the requirement for travelers to update their driver's license to a REAL ID compliant license.
The move toward REAL ID took a long path before taking effect. The REAL ID Act was passed by Congress in 2005. It was part of an emergency appropriations bill in direct response to the 9/11 Commission Report that detailed the circumstances that made the 9/11 terrorist attacks possible.
All of the attackers were found to have used fraudulent identification to board the planes.
A REAL ID is required to board any federally regulated commercial aircraft, access certain federal facilities and to enter a nuclear power plant.
Earlier this year, the TSA adopted the ConfirmID fee, allowing travelers who are unable to provide a REAL ID compliant ID to pay a $45 fee to submit to further screening for identity verification.
Obtaining a REAL ID requires a higher standard of identity verification, including the presentation of certain documents that show proof of a person's legal name, date of birth, Social Security number, residence and their lawful citizenship status in the United States.
A REAL ID card itself features security measures meant to stop it from being duplicated, counterfeited or tampered with.
While the REAL ID requirement has been adopted, it received pushback on its path toward taking effect. States and advocacy organizations across the political spectrum were critical of the proposal of what was viewed effectively as a national identification card. It raised concerns about surveillance and the burden it would place on states to implement it.
The Department of Homeland Security's cost estimates for implementing the act ranged from around $10 billion to more than $20 billion.
"Taking a step back and viewing it from what it looked like immediately after 9/11 to where things have evolved to, there's always more innovation to be had and better ideas out there," Propis said. "You're seeing a mindset shift with TSA over the last few years that technology and innovation can really transform what they're doing."` `

articles.description_html: DOE announces $73m to advance domestic mining technology  Innovation News Network
articles.article_title: DOE announces $73m to advance domestic mining technology
articles.heading: DOE announces $73m to advance domestic mining technology
articles.summary: Projects will establish real-world testing grounds for new mining technologies to continue securing domestic critical materials supply chains
articles.content:
Funded projects will establish real-world testing grounds for innovative mining technologies to continue securing America’s domestic critical materials supply chains.
The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) has selected four projects for $73 million in funding through DOE’s Mine of the Future initiative to establish domestic testing grounds for innovative mining technologies.
These selections will accelerate the commercialisation of mining technologies, upgrade domestic mining capabilities, and build on the Trump Administration’s mission to secure America’s critical minerals supply chains.
DOE’s Advanced Mining and Mineral Processing Technologies Office selected the following projects for award negotiations:
Innovative Wireless Technologies, Inc. (HQ: Lynchburg, Virginia, project locations: Julian, West Virginia, Idaho Springs, Colorado, and Blacksburg, Virginia)
This project aims to create a national testbed to accelerate the development and deployment of advanced mining technologies that enhance safety, productivity, and supply chain resilience. The effort will combine underground and surface mining environments to validate next-generation digital, connectivity, and automation solutions in real-world conditions.
University of Arizona (HQ: Tucson, Arizona, project location: Sahuarita, Arizona)
The project will create a nationally accessible underground testbed to speed up the development and deployment of advanced mining, electrification, and energy management technologies. This scalable proving ground aims to reduce technical and operational risks while strengthening U.S. critical mineral supply chains through improved productivity, energy efficiency, and faster commercialisation.
Curators of the University of Missouri (HQ and project location: Rolla, Missouri)
This project will create a multi functional mining technology proving ground that combines two complementary facilities for underground technology testing and advanced comminution research. Curators of the University of Missouri will design, build, and equip this national resource to support innovation, real world validation, and workforce development for next generation mining technologies.
Southern Methodist University (HQ: Dallas, TX, project location: Navasota, Texas)
This project will create the world’s first synthetic mine within an advanced drilling and sensing test facility to accelerate next generation mining technologies from lab concepts to field ready deployment. By repurposing a highly instrumented Texas drilling site, it will enable rigorous, repeatable, and safe testing of mining tools, workflows, and automation systems.
Securing real-world testing for domestic mining technology
Minerals and mining stakeholders require field sites to test innovative technologies under real-world conditions.
These projects will not only develop mining proving grounds but also support R&D projects that accelerate the progression of technologies from laboratories to testing and demonstration in a field-scale setting, an essential step to de-risk commercial adoption.
These projects will also create opportunities for hands-on workforce training to prepare the next generation of American miners and engineers to operate advanced mining systems.
“Investing in moving cutting-edge mining technologies out of the lab and into the field will help unleash America’s vast mineral resources,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “President Trump is committed to rebuilding America’s mining industry, reducing our dependence on foreign adversaries, and securing the critical minerals that are foundational to our energy, manufacturing, and national security.”
“These investments will prove that American innovation can redefine what’s possible in modern mining,” said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “By establishing world class testing grounds, we’re accelerating breakthroughs that will strengthen our supply chains, our workforce, and our national competitiveness.”

articles.article_title: Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech
articles.heading: Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech
articles.summary: They’re designing viruses, reversing the aging process, and saving lives.
articles.content:
Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech
They’re designing viruses, reversing the aging process, and saving lives.
Every year, MIT Technology Review puts together a list of some of the brightest and best young minds working across science and technology. Our 35 Innovators Under 35 are the ones to watch—people whose research and technical work stands to shape the future of their fields.
This year, the list includes nine people who are transforming biotech. And this week, I’m going to give you a taste of some of the very cool stuff five of them are working on, which includes lifesaving innovations and groundbreaking “age reversal” tech.
1. Preventing maternal deaths
Let’s start with Paschal Kija, a 28-year-old who has developed a device to treat postpartum hemorrhage—a dangerous birth complication that contributes to around 29% of maternal deaths in his home country, Tanzania. The Mkanda Salama (“Safe Wrap” in Swahili) is easy to use and costs just $70. A study found that it stopped postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes.
2. Making brain electrodes inspired by Japanese art
For decades, scientists have been developing, testing, and implanting brain electrodes. These devices are literally inserted into people’s brains, so while they can help us understand brain activity and treat various neurological disorders, it’s not totally surprising that they can also cause a bit of damage. Xiao Yang, 34, is working on ultra-small electrodes, which she hopes will have less of an impact on surrounding brain tissue. Her electrodes are flexible, too—in fact, they look a lot like actual neurons.
Yang is also creating sheets of electrodes to study brain cells in the lab. Inspired by kirigami—the traditional Japanese art of cutting paper to form three-dimensional shapes—she’s created a sheet of electrodes with a honeycombed structure shaped like a spiral basket. And she’s already using it to study brain cells.
3. Developing an all-new treatment for baby KJ
In 2024, Kyle “KJ” Muldoon Jr. was born with a rare and potentially fatal genetic disorder. Sarah Grandinette was a member of a team that developed an entirely new, personalized treatment for him—a gene-editing therapy essentially designed to correct a genetic misspelling.
Grandinette, who is now 26, created cells with KJ’s genetic variant and used them to screen gene-editing approaches; then she tested potential medicines in mice and monkeys. KJ ultimately got his first dose of the resulting treatment when he was about seven months old. He responded well and was eventually discharged from hospital. He’s “doing pretty great,” she says.
4. Reversing the aging process to treat eye disease
The buzziest tech in longevity right now centers on reprogramming—attempts to rewind the age of cells by resetting them to a more embryonic-like state. In a study published in 2020, Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu (now 34) and his colleagues showed that a reprogramming therapy reversed vision loss in aged, blind mice. Now an almost identical version of that therapy is being tested in people with eye disease. Life Biosciences, the company developing the drug, dosed its first volunteer in June.
5. Using AI to design new viruses
Last year, Samuel King used a generative AI model to come up with new genetic blueprints for bacteriophages—teeny viruses that can infect bacteria. Once he had those blueprints, he printed them out as strands of DNA. In experiments, he found that those AI-designed viruses could create new copies of themselves, burst out of bacterial cells, and infect other nearby bacteria. Viruses aren’t alive, but King, 27, hopes that AI-designed life forms might one day be used to make drugs or soak up pollution.
You can read more about these innovators, and the others on the biotech list, here.

articles.article_title: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
articles.heading: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
articles.summary: The revelations in Anthropic's threat intelligence report come after a former top researcher at the company warned of the risks of AI to humanity.
articles.content:
Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.
The findings, made in the firm's recent threat intelligence report, is the latest in a growing series of warnings from AI researchers and industry insiders about the technology's potential risks to humanity.
The warnings have prompted calls to action, with US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.
President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".
The company published its latest threat intelligence report on Thursday.
Such reports have become a regular feature across the AI industry as firms seek to demonstrate how they identify and disrupt attempts to misuse their models.
This includes Google, which wrote on Tuesday that a person had attempted to use its AI tool, Gemini, to obtain a "complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponised biological agents".
Claude, Anthropic's AI model was also used by actors linked to a Russia-based cyber espionage campaign and by an Iranian propaganda institution, according to its report.
The cases of concern detected over the past eight months ranged from fake dating apps and hotel Wifi scams, to surveillance built to identify dissidents.
Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI firms of trying to replicate Claude's capabilities.
The lengthy report lists cases in which suspected state-sponsored groups, criminals, spyware vendors, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals misused its technology.
"Malicious use" of its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models was disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, it said.
None of the misuse cases involved Claude Fable or the powerful Mythos-class models, with the exception of one instance of distillation - the process for training smaller AI models using larger, more expensive models.
As well as detecting the use of its models for cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud and weapon development, Anthropic said it had blocked scientists who used its AI in ways that could support biological weapons development.
The report highlighted "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development".
Biological misuse, it said, is "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI model". Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities "could have catastrophic consequences", Anthropic said.
"The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," Anthropic said.
Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told the New York Times it was "an incredibly nuanced situation".
"You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" he said.
The report also noted six cases where Claude was used "to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them".
The report indicated that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers have increasingly used its technology to assist their operations.
Hacking group ShinyHunters, as well as China-based labs, were among those named in the report.

The warning prompted an open letter to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI and a call for governments to collaborate about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.
In the US, Democratic lawmaker Bernie Sanders has introduced legislation to ban AI superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development.
"When scientists tell you there is a chance, a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he said on Thursday on BBC's Newsnight.

The warnings have prompted calls to action, with US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.

President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".

The company published its latest threat intelligence report on Thursday.

articles.title: How Nanobody Technology Can Redefine Respiratory Care

articles.article_title: How Nanobody Technology Can Redefine Respiratory Care
articles.heading: How Nanobody Technology Can Redefine Respiratory Care
articles.summary: Discover how Sanofi is exploring Nanobody technology to target dual inflammatory pathways in chronic respiratory diseases.
articles.content:
For millions of people living with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) or chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), breathing freely is not something they can take for granted. We’re investigating how Nanobody technology may be able to help address unmet needs in chronic respiratory diseases.
What is Nanobody Science?
In the early 1990s, researchers observed that camels, llamas, and alpacas produce a distinct class of antibodies that lack the light chains found in conventional human antibodies known as heavy chains. This inspired the creation of a single, compact variable domain, known as a Nanobody subunit, roughly one-tenth the size of a traditional antibody.¹
This scientific approach was validated in 2018 with the first approved Nanobody medicine to treat a rare, life-threatening blood clotting disorder. Since then, our researchers have continued to evolve the platform, applying computational biology and protein engineering to expand what these proteins can do. Because Nanobody subunits are compact and stable, several can be linked together in a “beads-on-a-string” design, allowing scientists to construct a single molecule that engages multiple biological targets at once, with the geometry and durability of the molecule tuned to fit the specific pathways involved.
It is this multivalent, adaptable design, not simply the small size of a single subunit, that gives Nanobody technology its potential relevance to diseases driven by multiple biological pathways. This novel platform is being researched in chronic respiratory diseases, where single pathway treatments may not address the entire scope of patient needs.
Why Multi-Targeting Matters for Respiratory Diseases
Asthma, COPD, and CRSwNP are complex, heterogeneous conditions, often driven by multiple overlapping inflammatory pathways rather than a single one. When one pathway is blocked, another can take over, which can quickly result in inadequate disease management.
This helps explain a persistent clinical challenge. Asthma affects an estimated 363 million people globally² and, despite the availability of biologic therapies, 60% of adult patients continue to live with poorly controlled symptoms, including recurrent flare-ups, wheezing, and coughing that can disrupt daily life and, in some cases, become life threatening.3 Individuals with CRSwNP experience a similar disease burden with persistent nasal congestion, with up to 40% of patients continuing to experience debilitating symptoms despite treatment, including sinus surgery.4
Uncontrolled disease remains a challenge for people living with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) as it’s the third common cause of death globally.5 A study showed that patients with one or two exacerbations in the previous year had an increased risk of exacerbation in the subsequent year, respectively.5
Targeted therapies have improved outcomes for many patients, but for those whose disease is driven by multiple pathways at once, a single-target approach may not be enough.
Our researchers are exploring an investigational Nanobody treatment specifically designed to simultaneously engage two distinct drivers of inflammation connected to chronic respiratory diseases.
This research is ongoing and has not yet been evaluated by any regulatory authority.
What This Means for Respiratory Patients
When we consider the millions of people living with chronic respiratory conditions who are still struggling to manage their symptoms and prevent disease progression, it’s clear that the current standard treatments are not sufficient. We’re working to understand the underlying biological drivers of these diseases, and Nanobody technology is one of the tools helping us do that.
Alyssa Johnsen, M.D., Ph.D.
Senior Vice President, Therapeutic Area Head of Immunology and Inflammation
This reflects our broader approach to immunology: Starting from pathway biology, identifying where intervention may change the course of disease and applying the platform best suited to that biology, including Nanobody technology where multi-pathway targeting could change what’s possible for patients.

articles.summary: AI is moving into the field, raising new questions for California farmers.
articles.content:
When Farm Technology Outruns the Rules
Artificial intelligence on the farm may sound complicated, but the goal is pretty simple: make a better decision, faster, with less waste.
A new policy brief from the Council for Agricultural Science and Technology looks at where AI is already showing up, from treating individual weeds to helping select seed and inspecting food during processing.
And there’s an interesting California wrinkle.
The report says AI is moving beyond analyzing information into “physical AI,” where autonomous machinery and robotics can actually take action.
California, meanwhile, still requires an operator at the controls of self-propelled farm equipment under state worker-safety rules.
So for a California farmer, the question isn’t only what can this technology do?
It’s also: Will the rules allow me to use it? Can I afford it? Who owns the data? And do I have the connectivity to make it useful?
CAST says those are the kinds of policy and infrastructure questions that need attention as AI becomes a bigger part of agriculture.
Lead author Alex Thomasson will discuss the findings during a free CAST webinar September 14: https://streamyard.com/watch/wn5bvM9tgG4K

articles.heading: New California social media laws target addictive features
articles.summary: Several new laws are aimed at "psychologically exploitative" social media functions for children. Governor Gavin Newsom said the laws target the technology behind addictive use rather than age alone.
articles.content:
New California social media laws target addictive features
September 11, 2026
Several new laws are aimed at "psychologically exploitative" social media functions for children. Governor Gavin Newsom said the laws target the technology behind addictive use rather than age alone.
California Governor Gavin Newsom on Thursday signed a host of new laws aimed at protecting children from online risks, particularly social media platforms.
The 13 new laws aim to ensure greater online privacy for minors and include restrictions on addictive social media features for users under 16.
The measures prohibit social media platforms from exposing children to features deemed "psychologically exploitative," including infinite scrolling, algorithmic recommendations and autoplay designed to encourage compulsive use.
Another prescribes criminal sanctions against any digitally altered or AI-generated content that depicts a minor engaged in sexual conduct.
In an attempt to restrict AI companion chatbots, one of the laws requires parental controls for chatbot programs, while another banned toys containing AI chatbots.
"We want our children — and every California kid — to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities," Newsom said.
'California's approach better than Australia's'
According to Newsom, California's approach was better targeted than Australia's ban on social media for under-16s because it addresses the technology behind addictive use rather than age alone.
"This is about actually addressing the problem, the scrolling, the algorithms. This is about addressing the substantive issue around the engineering. If you address that, then the age issue is not the essential issue."
Last year, Australia banned social media for under-16s. However, reports say the ban has been ineffective at preventing children and teenagers from accessing and using social media.
EU considering limits on children's access to social media
The measures make California one of several US states tightening rules on technology companies over concerns about children's online safety and mental health.
Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said that the company is committed to providing teens with safe experiences "with the proper guardrails in place," AFP news agency reported.
The European Union is also considering limits on children's access to social media.
The EU proposals range from restrictions for under-13s to a broader ban for under-15s, which France is pushing for.
"We do not have to accept addictive social media design," EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday.

articles.title: What is cloud-seeding? California company tests potential rain-producing technology in Alaska

articles.article_title: What is cloud-seeding? California company tests potential rain-producing technology in Alaska
articles.heading: What is cloud-seeding? California company tests potential rain-producing technology in Alaska
articles.summary: Rainmaker founder and CEO Augustus Doricko said his company is working to produce more water for ecosystems, people and industries that need it, including here in Alaska.
articles.content:
What is cloud-seeding? California company tests potential rain-producing technology in Alaska
Rainmaker says its drones, radar and silver iodide can boost precipitation
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU) - Nearly 60% of the country is currently in a drought, with more than 10% of it in extreme drought.
One company says it can change that.
Rainmaker founder and CEO Augustus Doricko said his company is working to produce more water for ecosystems, people and industries that need it.
“We have biblical or apocalyptic fires burning down cities. We have routine wildfires. The farms we’ve had for 100 years are going bust because they don’t have the groundwater they need. The Colorado River and Great Salt Lake are drying up. And so I wanted to make more water for the ecosystems and people and industries that need it,” Doricko said in a recent interview with Alaska’s News Source.
MORE: New regulations proposed by Kenai borough mayor following unexpected cloud-seeding test
Doricko said Rainmaker’s combination of custom-built drones, its own radar and silver iodide is the solution.
“We can now, for the first time ever, measure and prove our effect, measure and prove how much precipitation is man-made, is the most efficient way to make more snow pack and more rain for the industries that need it,” Doricko said.
The company is using Alaska to test the technology.
“In the Lower 48, during the summertime, you don’t have cold enough clouds to freeze small droplets into snowflakes and induce precipitation. You don’t have cold enough clouds to test and simulate your conditions that you’ll be flying into,” Doricko said.
Cloud seeding has been done for decades. It has been used to clear fog at airports and make snow in mountains.
It is also known for being ineffective, costing too much, or hard to prove that it works.
Rainmaker and other cloud-seeding groups are trying to kick-start the water cycle, specifically the condensation step at the top of it.
At the center of every raindrop is a cloud condensation nuclei. This is what water vapor, which cannot be seen in the air, sticks to before it grows into a raindrop or snowflake.
Silver iodide looks and acts like a cloud condensation nuclei. More nuclei introduced into air full of water vapor equals more cloud droplets, and if effective, more rain or snow.
Rainmaker recently conducted its testing on the Kenai Peninsula, near Homer.
“We were actually seeding the clouds in Kenai to test and simulate and research what our effect would be in this winter’s upcoming operations in the Lower 48,” Doricko said. “And so, as you know, we were able to produce those 19 million gallons in three hours.
Doricko acknowledged that it amounts to just less than a tenth of an inch of precipitation over 100 square miles.
Doricko said the company does not have any commercial customers in Alaska, but he thinks cloud seeding could protect Alaska’s landscape and infrastructure.
“If you want to mitigate glacial melt, then putting more snow on top these glaciers to insulate them from warm temperatures to prevent breakup of the glaciers that cause flooding and avalanche damage. That’s one application,” he said. “Another application that we’ve discussed is helping maintain the stability of the ice roads for the exploration companies on the [North Slope].”
Doricko addressed questions about whether cloud-seeding is safe, saying it is no different than building a dam.
“I wouldn’t be running this company, this conservation company, if it had any adverse impact on the environment or human health or agriculture,” Doricko said.
“We’re using about a paper clip’s worth of silver iodide or like seven Skittles in one operation. That gets distributed over hundreds of thousands of acres or hundreds of square miles. And the resultant increase in concentration is like one part per quadrillion on the ground,” Doricko said.
Doricko said the company’s biggest challenge going forward will be gaining the public’s trust and permission.
“I genuinely want the world to be lush and green and free from the tragedies that come due to natural disasters. And so my aspiration is to bring that to the United States for the sake of our nature’s well-being, for the sake of improving our quality of life,” Doricko said.

That’s one application,” he said. “Another application that we’ve discussed is helping maintain the stability of the ice roads for the exploration companies on the [North Slope].”

Doricko addressed questions about whether cloud-seeding is safe, saying it is no different than building a dam.

“I wouldn’t be running this company, this conservation company, if it had any adverse impact on the environment or human health or agriculture,” Doricko said.

“We’re using about a paper clip’s worth of silver iodide or like seven Skittles in one operation. That gets distributed over hundreds of thousands of acres or hundreds of square miles. And the resultant increase in concentration is like one part per quadrillion on the ground,” Doricko said.

Doricko said the company’s biggest challenge going forward will be gaining the public’s trust and permission.

“I genuinely want the world to be lush and green and free from the tragedies that come due to natural disasters. And so my aspiration is to bring that to the United States for the sake of our nature’s well-being, for the sake of improving our quality of life,” Doricko said.

articles.heading: OPEN MIND joins FANUC 5-Axis Integrated Technology Initiative
articles.summary: Collaboration with machine tool builders and CAD/CAM technology companies enables end-user manufacturers to achieve high-performance machining and premium surface finishes.
articles.content:
Collaboration with machine tool builders and CAD/CAM technology companies enables end-user manufacturers to achieve high-performance machining and premium surface finishes.

Posted by Eric Brothers, Editor - Manufacturing Group

OPEN MIND Technologies , a developer of CAD/CAM software solutions worldwide, has become a founding member of the FANUC 5-Axis Integrated Technology Initiative . The initiative is a program organized by FANUC involving collaboration with machine tool builders and CAD/CAM technology companies enabling end-user manufacturers to achieve high-performance machining and premium surface finishes. Though providing benefits to manufacturers in all markets, the motivation of the FANUC Initiative is to improve efficiency, accuracy, and repeatability in the production of complex parts, which will be especially beneficial for the U.S. aerospace market.

The hyper MILL CAD/CAM software solution, developed by OPEN MIND Technologies, is known for its innovative, advanced 5-axis processing. Although this technology has been available in the market for many years, customers can now benefit from increased knowledge, guidance, and access to the technologies via the partnership. The FANUC control system is used on many key machine tools in the metalworking manufacturing industry. The FANUC 5-Axis Integrated Technology Initiative for CAD/CAM and postprocessor guides best practices for the use of code structure and data standards to interact with the machine tools to achieve smooth and safe programs, and streamline and optimize 5-axis machining workflows.

Alan Levine, managing director of OPEN MIND Technologies USA Inc. stated, “We are pleased to be part of the FANUC 5-Axis Integrated Technology Initiative to bring total solutions for end-users that seek to grow their business and more effectively manage risk.”

Rick Schultz, executive director of Aerospace at FANUC America said, “We are excited to have OPEN MIND join the FANUC 5-Axis Integrated Technology Initiative program. The hyperMILL CAD/CAM Software solution is an industry leading program that is well respected worldwide. We look forward to collaborating with OPEN MIND on this initiative.”

The OPEN MIND hyper MILL CAD/CAM solution provides VIRTUAL Machining utilities that go beyond postprocessing. The VIRTUAL Machine provides process security with full collision detection against all items in the machining work area, and the NC Optimizer module of the program simplifies programming tasks and improves machining results by managing link connections and fitting parts within axis limits.

At IMTS 2026 , manufacturing professionals are encouraged to visit OPEN MIND Technologies in Booth #133351 , and FANUC America in Booth #338900 to learn more about the initiative.

articles.title: 'Dirt, Data, Decisions' connects Nebraska agriculture technology leaders
articles.description: 'Dirt, Data, Decisions' connects Nebraska agriculture technology leaders Nebraska Today
articles.description_html: 'Dirt, Data, Decisions' connects Nebraska agriculture technology leaders  Nebraska Today
articles.article_title: 'Dirt, Data, Decisions' connects Nebraska agriculture technology leaders
articles.heading: 'Dirt, Data, Decisions' connects Nebraska agriculture technology leaders
articles.summary: More than 110 producers, agricultural technology leaders, researchers and public-sector partners gathered Aug. 25 at Paulman Farms near Sutherland for “Dirt, Data, Decisions,” a producer-focused event designed to connect people working on solutions for nitrogen and irrigation management in Nebraska.
articles.content:
More than 110 producers, agricultural technology leaders, researchers and public-sector partners gathered Aug. 25 at Paulman Farms near Sutherland for Dirt, Data, Decisions, a producer-focused event designed to connect people working on solutions for nitrogen and irrigation management in Nebraska.
Conceived and organized by Roric Paulman, producer and owner of Paulman Farms, the event combined 32 rapid-fire talks with informal conversations and networking. Speakers represented agricultural technology companies, startups, the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, state agencies and commodity organizations.
“This day was about more than technology. It was about creating the network we need to solve challenges and build opportunities for Nebraska agriculture,” Paulman said.
Discussions throughout the day centered on five themes: water management, precision nitrogen management, using agricultural data in better decision-making, on-farm validation and technology adoption, and building a more connected agricultural innovation network.
The working-farm setting was central to the event. Paulman Farms serves as a site for testing and evaluating agricultural technologies, giving participants an opportunity to discuss not only what new tools can do, but also how they perform under real production conditions and whether they deliver value to producers.
Paulman serves as the Nebraska ambassador with NASA Acres’ Farmer Innovation and Ambassador Team, supported through research collaboration with Guillermo Balboa, research assistant professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln Department of Agronomy and Horticulture. Paulman also serves as a long-time collaborator with the UNL Testing Ag Performance Solutions program — led by Chris Proctor, associate professor with Nebraska Extension — which brings producers, researchers, Nebraska Extension and industry together to test agricultural technologies and management strategies under real-world conditions.
Presentations covered topics such as irrigation technologies, soil and crop sensing, precision nitrogen management, remote sensing, artificial intelligence, robotics, on-farm research, agricultural startups, biochar, ethanol and carbon intensity and water stewardship. Speakers repeatedly returned to the importance of field validation, economic value, reliable support and producer trust.
University speakers highlighted digital agriculture initiatives, Testing Ag Performance Solutions, precision nitrogen management, on-farm research, artificial intelligence, the Spurs, Nebraska Future Ag Research Management Systems, and biochar research.
The event also brought together leaders from Nebraska agriculture, government, the university, and private industry, creating opportunities for conversations across organizations. The university supported the event in cooperation with Paulman Farms and industry partners. University leadership, faculty, researchers and Extension personnel contributed presentations and helped with event logistics.

articles.description_html: U.S. Bank will have some new technology upgrades this season  CBS News
articles.article_title: U.S. Bank will have some new technology upgrades this season
articles.heading: U.S. Bank will have some new technology upgrades this season
articles.summary: Football is back, and just days before the Vikings and Packers face off in a border battle, U. S Bank Stadium is making major upgrades.
articles.content:
U.S. Bank will have some new technology upgrades this season
Football is back, and just days before the Vikings and Packers face off in a border battle, U. S Bank Stadium is making major upgrades.

The stadium is adding technology designed to make the fan experience seamless from start to finish.

"We're going to have 66,000 super excited Vikings fans here on game day and what we want to do when they enter the building is we want to get them in quicker," said JP Paul, Vice President of Stadium Operations.

New OpenGate security screening is installed at every entrance. The contactless system allows fans to walk through security without emptying their pockets or having approved bags physically inspected.

Then- in the ticketing area, Vikings Express Pass will also save you time if you're registered. It uses facial recognition technology to pull up your ticket without ever having to pull out your phone.

The team store on the main concourse is also getting a speed boost- one with RFID self-checkout technology.

fans can shop and once done can place their items into a clear bag before placing it inside a checkout counter where the system will scan all items and will display the total.

The goal is simple, get fans through the doors, to ensure they never miss a minute of the Vikings experience.

"We don't want people to wait," Paul said. "Let's get them in faster. Let's get them into enjoy the experience of Vikings.

articles.title: Charlotte neighbors react to former AI researcher’s concerns the technology could cause serious harm
articles.description: Charlotte neighbors react to former AI researcher’s concerns the technology could cause serious harm WBTV
articles.description_html: Charlotte neighbors react to former AI researcher’s concerns the technology could cause serious harm  WBTV
articles.article_title: Charlotte neighbors react to former AI researcher’s concerns the technology could cause serious harm
articles.heading: Charlotte neighbors react to former AI researcher’s concerns the technology could cause serious harm
articles.summary: Jacob Coxon said on X that both OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
articles.content:
Charlotte neighbors react to former AI researcher’s concerns the technology could cause serious harm
‘The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade’
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV) - Charlotteans we spoke to are feeling cautious about artificial intelligence’s capabilities after a former AI researcher posted a grave warning upon resigning from the company Anthropic.
Jacob Coxon said on X that both OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Dusten Pulido, who uses AI for work, thinks Coxon’s comments lean towards hyperbole. But, he is wary of what the former researcher is warning us about.
“I don’t think safety is talked about enough. I think it’s going to be talked about more and more as all the hyperscale data centers continue to come online,” he said.
Jhaya Dilworth agrees.
“I think even if [the post] was hyperbolic, it’s important for people to be aware. I think people overuse [AI], over consume it and give it too much power.” she said. “I think that people have to make it their personal mission to have autonomy over what they do and what they research.”
Concerns of the people we spoke to are echoed by the people in charge of big AI companies like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
“We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around some of these new capability levels,” said Altman.
“If you think of the extent to which AI can make individualized propaganda, can break into any computer system in the world can you know, surveil everyone, everyone in a population, it’s really scary and we have to stop it,” said Amodei.

articles.title: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction
articles.description: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction ABC30 Fresno
articles.description_html: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction  ABC30 Fresno
articles.article_title: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction
articles.heading: Advances in cataract lens technology offers more options for vision correction
articles.summary: As cataract treatment continues to evolve, patients now have more lens implant options than ever before.
articles.content:
Friday, September 11, 2026 1:28AM
MERCED, Calif. (KFSN) -- More than half of all Americans age 80 or older either have cataracts or have had surgery to remove them, according to the National Eye Institute.
As cataract treatment continues to evolve, patients now have more lens implant options than ever before.
Dr. Kelley Hawkins, an ophthalmologist with EYE-Q Vision Care, said cataracts develop when the eye's natural lens becomes cloudy with age.
"When we're born, the lens is kind of a clear jelly-like material," Dr. Hawkins said.
As people get older, the lens can become cloudier, denser or more brown in color. Dr. Hawkins said cataracts typically begin developing around age 60 and progress over time.
"For most people, it starts at the age of 60 and kind of progresses over time. The average age for cataract surgery is 65 to 75 years old," Dr. Hawkins said.
Common cataract symptoms include blurry, cloudy or foggy vision, glare around lights and colors appearing faded.
During cataract surgery, doctors make a small incision through the cornea to remove the cloudy lens.
"Once inside, we actually use an ultrasound device to break the cataract into pieces and safely remove it from the eye. Once the cataracts out, the eye needs a lens to see. So we actually put an implant inside of the eye, and that's that intraocular lens," Dr. Hawkins said.
Dr. Hawkins said patients now have several choices when it comes to lens implants. One option is a monofocal lens, which is designed to provide clear vision at a single fixed distance.
"Most people want that to be far away, but some of my nearsighted folks choose up close with that lens. It's going to improve the vision, but you're still going to need glasses for either the distance or for up close," Dr. Hawkins said.
Another option is a multifocal lens, which can reduce a patient's dependence on glasses by providing vision at multiple distances.
"This lens implant gives distance vision, intermediate, and some near, kind of like our progressive glasses do," said Dr. Hawkins. "What really excites me is kind of this newer technology that we have for cataract surgery, this light adjustable lens."
Dr. Hawkins said the light adjustable lens is implanted during cataract surgery like other intraocular lenses. After recovery, patients return about a month later for adjustments designed to further refine their vision.
"Essentially, to dial in the vision is as close to perfect as possible. It just makes it customizable to every patient. Once you find your happy place, we actually lock this lens in, and then it stays like that for hopefully as long as possible," Dr. Hawkins said.
Dr. Hawkins also highlighted what she described as the relatively easy recovery process following cataract surgery.
"On average, it takes a few days for the vision to recover, even up to a week, and that's normal. Most patients have some mild irritation in the eye after surgery. That's expected. Severe pain and things like that are very unlikely," Dr. Hawkins said.
Patients considering cataract surgery should discuss the available lens options with their eye care provider to determine which choice best fits their vision needs and lifestyle goals.
For news updates, follow Danyelle Burke North on Instagram and TikTok.

articles.title: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
articles.description: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks wndu.com
articles.description_html: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks  wndu.com
articles.article_title: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
articles.heading: Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
articles.summary: A former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic is warning that the companies developing artificial intelligence are not acting responsibly.
articles.content:
Former AI researcher warns technology could pose major risks
Researcher who worked at OpenAI and Anthropic says companies are racing toward self-improving superintelligence
SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - A former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic is sounding the alarm about the potential risks of artificial intelligence.
Jacob Coxon, who spent the last three years working at the two AI companies, announced his resignation on social media Tuesday.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said.
Within hours, Evan Hubinger, a researcher who still works at Anthropic, responded online.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans. I personally think it is greater than 10 percent within the next decade,” Hubinger said.
The claims raise questions about whether the threat is realistic or part of a series of bold predictions from an industry known for rapid advances and ambitious forecasts.
The concerns extend beyond Silicon Valley. In South Bend, residents are also thinking about how artificial intelligence could affect everyday life.
“What’s going to happen if this AI takes over some part of the landing program for airports or something like that where people are directly threatened,” said Joseph Mauck, a South Bend resident.
Mauck said the concern is not limited to worst-case scenarios. He also worries about how closely the technology is already tied to daily life.
“If you are going to mimic the personalities and characters of human beings, then you have to take into account the tremendous amount of subtlety that goes into their actions,” Mauck said.
Not everyone shares that level of concern.
“It’s going to be exponential, right. Computers are going to work faster and they’re going to start to be able to use resources on their own, so I don’t think we’re too far off from it. Whether I’m afraid, I don’t know — I try not to live in fear,” said Adrian Pacheco, a South Bend resident.
Whether it is fear of the worst-case scenario or unease about what comes next, people are wrestling with the same questions as researchers who are leaving the companies building the technology.
“I think we can pull it off — we’ll survive,” Pacheco said.

articles.title: New Lung Diagnosis Technology at Wynn Hospital
articles.description: New Lung Diagnosis Technology at Wynn Hospital wktv.com
articles.description_html: New Lung Diagnosis Technology at Wynn Hospital  wktv.com
articles.article_title: New Lung Diagnosis Technology at Wynn Hospital
articles.heading: New Lung Diagnosis Technology at Wynn Hospital
articles.summary: The Wynn Hospital has introduced a new robotics machine called an Ion that is changing the way doctors diagnose lung problems.
articles.content:
UTICA, N.Y. -- The Wynn Hospital has introduced a new robotics machine called an Ion that is changing the way doctors diagnose lung problems.
Doctors at Wynn Hospital now use the Ion to perform minimally invasive procedures instead of puncturing the lungs to collect tissue samples.
Dr. Mark Crye, director of thoracic surgery at MVHS, explained that the process begins with a breathing tube and a special connector that attaches magnetically.
Crye said, “And then that’s the little camera and the light in the catheter. So, this goes down. So, this is going down the breathing tube. This vision probe then comes out. The catheter itself is still where we drove it to. That comes out, and then the needle is what goes in.”
The Ion allows doctors to navigate the tiny bends and curves of the lungs.
Before the procedure, patients receive a CT scan that works with the Ion to create a roadmap for doctors to follow and retrieve biopsy tissue.
“So, this is the scan. So, we’re going to scroll through the scan and try and find where is our nodule. Where are we going? Where’s our legion of concern?” Crye said.
The technology is compared to using Google Maps to find a path through the lungs.
“This is now showing us our GPS map, and so this is now the same map here. It’s now what I’ll use to follow that down,” Crye said.
The procedure usually takes between 45 minutes and an hour and a half.
MVHS reports a diagnostic success rate of more than 95%, and the new technology has helped them become one of the most productive thoracic surgery teams in the country.
“The amount of Ion’s we’ve done in the last two quarters has us as the 6th most productive thoracic surgeon in the country,” Crye said.

articles.title: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
articles.description: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards WLWT
articles.description_html: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards  WLWT
articles.article_title: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
articles.heading: AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
articles.summary: Warnings from artificial intelligence researchers are fueling concerns about the rapidly developing technology’s potential to wipe out humanity.
articles.content:
AI researchers issue major warning on technology as leaders call for safeguards
Warnings from artificial intelligence researchers are fueling concerns about the rapidly developing technology’s potential to wipe out humanity.
The issue was a major topic at MidwestCon in Cincinnati, where technology leaders and attendees discussed balancing innovation with safety.
Jacob Coxon, who recently resigned from AI company Anthropic, accused Anthropic and OpenAI of irresponsibly developing technology that could pose an existential risk.
Another researcher wrote on social media that they believe there is a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.
MidwestCon founder Rob Richardson said such warnings should be taken seriously.
“There is a possibility that we are definitely underestimating the power of AI,” Richardson said. “I do think we need policy.”
Richardson emphasized that people must remain in control of how AI is developed and deployed.
“AI knows it can do almost everything, but it doesn’t know when to stop,” he said. “Humans need to be there to tell it when to stop.”
Cincinnati resident Nikki Crenshaw said she remains optimistic.
“I’m going to stay hopeful and believe that it’s going to help us versus hurt us,” Crenshaw said.
The U.S. does not currently have a comprehensive federal law regulating AI.
A bill introduced in Congress in July would give the federal government authority to disable AI models determined to pose a risk to the public.

articles.title: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology
articles.description: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology WVXU
articles.description_html: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology  WVXU
articles.article_title: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology
articles.heading: Cincinnati considers restrictions on surveillance technology
articles.summary: City Council indicated interested in an ordinance to limit data storage and sharing, while expressing support for how Cincinnati Police use license plate readers and other technology.
articles.content:
Cincinnati City Council unanimously passed a motion Thursday requesting an ordinance to put limits on surveillance technology like license plate readers. It's not clear whether the eventual ordinance will have majority support, however.
Council member Anna Albi introduced the motion. She says surveillance tech is a "hot topic" and that these tools are important to solving and preventing crime.
"But we need to balance that need with ensuring we're protecting our citizens, frankly, from government overreach and abuse of these very powerful technologies," Albi said, adding this motion is intended to start a larger discussion.
"Let's talk publicly about what type of surveillance technologies the city is using ... because honestly, from everything I've heard from CPD and [the] Law [Department], Cincinnati is doing it right. We have great oversight from our law department when it comes to these contracts."
The motion requests a report and presentation from city administration within 30 days with an overview of how the city uses cameras, drones, and license plate readers.
Many other communities in Greater Cincinnati have faced publish pushback for using Flock cameras, and several have paused their use or even canceled contracts as a result. Those include: Lebanon, Hamilton County, Oxford, and in Northern Kentucky, Fort Thomas, Newport, Independence, Fort Mitchell, Bellevue, and Florence.
Cincinnati does not use Flock Safety technology, but contracts with Axon for body cameras and license plate readers. The city put out a Request for Proposals about a year ago, indicating the Cincinnati Police Department is undergoing a five-year expansion; the RFP sought quotes for installing 30 to 50 cameras throughout the city. Submissions are under review, according to the city website.
Two people registered as paid lobbyists for Flock Safety in 2025 but terminated their registration this year. A third person registered as a lobbyist for Flock Safety early this year: Katherine Ott Zehnder of Politicom Law. The city charter requires lobbyists to update or terminate their registration each July; Ott Zehnder did not.
Council members Jeff Cramerding and Seth Walsh co-sponsored Albi's motion.
"I want to make sure that we continue to use technology to deter crime and track down shooters and do whatever is necessary," Cramerding said.
Earlier this year, Council passed a motion prohibiting the city from sharing any data from city-owned surveillance technology with any third-party for the purpose of civil immigration enforcement, unless mandated by law, a court order, or judicial warrant.
The motion passed this week also requests a draft ordinance that would establish a surveillance use policy, limit data sharing and storage, require an annual "state of surveillance" report, and require City Council approval of related contracts.
The details of the requested ordinance are not spelled out, and it's not clear whether a majority of Council will support it.
Council member Scotty Johnson, a retired Cincinnati Police officer and current chair of Council's Public Safety and Quality of Life Committee, expressed concern.
"We must stay 10 steps ahead of the bad guys, and the bad guys have surveillance, the bad guys have technology," Johnson said. "The reality is that there are things, there are surveillances, there are investigations that the citizens of Cincinnati do not need to know about — this body [City Council] doesn't need to know about — because of the sensitive nature in which the Cincinnati police operate. I understand that's a little disturbing to some people, but law, but crime is solved as a direct result of [these] investigations."
Even Council members who indicated support for limits on surveillance technology also expressed their belief that Cincinnati is already doing it "the right way."
"It's my understanding that the Cincinnati Police Department is using best practice," Cramerding said. "I will not support anything that in any way handcuffs our police or prevents them from doing their jobs."
Vice Mayor Jan-Michele Lemon Kearney said in committee on Tuesday that she supports the motion because it's good to get more information.
"But we know that cameras help us solve crime. They also deter crime," she said.
The eventual presentation is expected at a meeting of the Public Safety and Quality of Life Committee, which means every other week. The presentation is expected to be ready by the meeting scheduled for Oct. 6.
Full text of the motion
Title: Motion on City Surveillance Technology and Ordinance
WE MOVE that the Administration present to Committee within 30 days on an overview of the City's use of surveillance technology, including cameras, drones, and license plate readers, covering current deployment, data retention, and any data-sharing agreements.
WE FURTHER MOVE that the administration draft an ordinance for Council's consideration, including limits on data sharing and storage; a state of surveillance annual impact report; surveillance use policy; and Council approval of related contracts.

WE FURTHER MOVE that the administration draft an ordinance for Council's consideration, including limits on data sharing and storage; a state of surveillance annual impact report; surveillance use policy; and Council approval of related contracts.

articles.article_title: NASA's Life-Saving Technology Where Cell Signals Can't Go - NASA
articles.heading: NASA’s Life-Saving Technology Where Cell Signals Can’t Go
articles.summary: Search and rescue technology developed in part by NASA saved five lives
articles.content:
Memorial Day weekend 2024 started with a blue sky and a mild three- to four-foot chop in the water off the Gulf Coast of Mississippi — a perfect day for a fishing competition. A team of five was about 40 miles offshore checking their sonar, and 30 seconds later the boat was gone. They were in the water struggling to pull on life jackets and grab the coolers as they bobbed up. When a boat sinks, survivors can be virtually invisible amid the vast expanse of water.
When their fishing trip went wrong, Easton Barrett had the only mobile phone and no cell service. He recorded a brief farewell, planning to put his phone in a cooler in hopes someone would find it.
Another team member activated a personal locator beacon (PLB) that had been stowed at the last minute, which sent a distress signal to the Search and Rescue Satellite-Aided Tracking (SARSAT) technology carried by multiple satellites in Earth orbit. In the SARSAT system, developed partly by NASA, an emergency signal containing the transmitter’s location is directed to the nearest available ground station.
A mission control center then alerts rescue coordination centers to mobilize search and rescue crews. For Barrett and his crew, that was a Florida Coast Guard boat.
“Ever since, I have tried to teach others about safety on the water and in the outdoors by using a PLB,” said Barrett. “If that will save one life, it’s worth the effort.”
A beacon like the one that saved his crew, a registered ResQLink PLB developed by ACR Electronics Inc. of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, also notifies the device owner’s emergency contact, indicating a distress call was activated. All emergency beacons must meet the same requirements to ensure they work when needed. Every rugged, buoyant, handheld devices have a five- to 10-year battery life.
SARSAT began operations in 1982, becoming an international collaboration in 1985. The flight and ground technologies used globally were originally developed at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. Now there are 62 satellites in the program and 45 nations contributing services, from operating ground stations to providing rescue crews. More than 63,000 lives have been saved.
SARSAT by the Numbers
The Search and Rescue Satellite-Aided Tracking system developed over several decades by NASA and other government agencies saves lives on land or at sea.
- 1982 — the start of U.S. operations
- 1985 — the start of international operations
- 62 operational satellites
- 45 nations contributing services
- 63,000+ lives saved
One rescue in 2024 demonstrates how it all comes together.
- 40 miles off the Mississippi Gulf Coast
- 5-person team participating in a fishing competition
- 30 seconds for a boat to sink
- 200 pounds of bait dumped to make a cooler buoyant
- 3 close encounters with wildlife, likely sharks and eels
- 4 hours in the water
- 1 personal locator beacon
- 1 Coast Guard rescue boat
- 5 lives saved
“If it has anything to do with NASA, it's got to be awesome.”
EASTOn Barrett
ACR Customer
